Hi Mohammad,

1. The prerequisite is to know that C::GPU works in center-of-mass frames, 
like Chrono in general. The accompanying vector and matrix that you specify 
during *AddMesh *are intended to be used as some sort of pre-processing for 
your mesh file. To cut to the chase, if your mesh file is created such that 
the mesh is already in its center-of-mass frame, then for all purposes, you 
should always call *gpu_sys.AddMesh("../Screw_CM.obj", ChVector<float>(0,0,0), ChMatrix33<float>(1), 
screw_mass);*

If your mesh is not already in its center-of-mass frame, or you want to 
scale it before loading it, then you can supply those arguments. 
*ChMatrix33<float>(1)* would create an identity matrix, and this matrix 
will be applied to every point in your mesh (as a side note, the matrix is 
applied before the vector is also applied to every point in your mesh), as 
a part of the pre-processing. Obviously, the identity matrix does nothing 
to your mesh. If it was a diagonal matrix, it would "scale" your mesh; if 
it was a unitary matrix, it would rotate your mesh; if it was a general 
matrix the it would "rotate and scale" your mesh, hence its name.

Because of what I said, I do not recommend using this *ChVector *argument 
to set the initial CoM (I just want to be more specific; you can call it 
initial position, too) of the mesh in simulation, it is against its design 
purpose. I said not recommend, but it can functionally work as a initial 
position specifier: think about it and you'll figure out why. Also, while
symbol: Re: Spinning Wheel-GPU

text:
initial position, too) of the mesh in simulation, it is against its design 
purpose. I said not recommend, but it can functionally work as a initial 
position specifier: think about it and you'll figure out why. Also, while 
other things may work fine, you will get strange torque readings from the 
mesh if you do that: again you can figure out why.

In principal, use *ApplyMeshMotion *to control mesh position/velocity in 
simulation, including the initial position.

2. As you can see, this is managing a ChBody and has nothing to do with the 
mesh in your gpu_sys. *SetPos *just sets the position of that ChBody. 
Because it has nothing to do with *gpu_sys*, if you need it to be at a 
location, you need to set it separately. In this co-simulation example, the 
mesh you loaded is the proxy in DEM simulation for this ChBody. The *gpu_sys 
*will collect the contact force on the mesh, feed this info to the ChBody, 
and the ChBody will use this force info to update this body's location, and 
then the new location is used to update the mesh location in *gpu_sys*. 
ChBody can manage more complex rigid body motions such as those involving 
joints, so it is used to help manage external objects in the DEM simulation.

3. If you now understand the above, then you can see you are really just 
setting the mesh position (in *gpu_sys*) for the very first time here. *ApplyMeshMotion 
*is called at every time step, so every quantity here is not just some 
initial value, but the values throughout the simulation. Some of the values 
are changing every step (because *t *changes), such as *mesh_rot*; others
symbol: Re: Spinning Wheel-GPU

text:
*is called at every time step, so every quantity here is not just some 
initial value, but the values throughout the simulation. Some of the values 
are changing every step (because *t *changes), such as *mesh_rot*; others 
such as velocities happen to be constants in this simulation. *mesh_rot* is 
a quaternion which represents the rotation status of the mesh (or 
specifically, the mesh's local coordinate system). If that sounds 
unfamiliar then it is probably helpful to read a bit more about quaternions.

Hope it answers your questions!
Ruochun

Hi Mohammad,

I think that *demo_GPU_mixer.cpp* demo does exactly what you needed. While 
you are looking into this demo, I just want to mention one thing to avoid 
confusion: in terms of controlling the mesh motion in C::GPU, the *Transform 
*call before *AddMesh *should only be used to "align" the mesh with its CoM 
before the simulation starts, so that when the mesh is loaded it is 
expressed in its centroid and principal frame; it should not be used to set 
the initial location of the mesh. Instead, like in the demo, use *ApplyMeshMotion 
*to control the mesh motion throughout the simulation.

Hope it helps!
Ruochun

There is no “Project Chrono” program.  Chrono is a set of middleware libraries and as such the user must write a main program which makes calls into whatever Chrono library you need to use.  The various demos distributed with Chrono are short examples of such main programs.

Upon a successful configuration and build of Chrono, you should be able to run any of the generated demos by simply typing something like:
% ./demo_CH_buildsystem

How are you trying to run these demos?  Please provide more information about your setup (OS, etc).

When you determine the volume of  the settled particles, make sure that the 
top of the surface of the settled particles is flat. When I run the code, 
the particles appear to stick to the side of the wall, since 
GetMaxParticleZ() is used to determine the top of the particles, there 
would be extra space on top. See the figure attached. 

[image: Screenshot from 2022-05-25 10-17-16.png]

Since you've implemented your own cohesion/surface tension model, this 
might result in more particles sticking to the wall, and a larger void 
ratio.

Here are what you can do to get a better approximation of the void ratio:

   1. Rest a weighted plate on top (see a direct shear example here 
   <https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono-projects/blob/develop/projects/gpu_tests/test_GPU_directshear.cpp>, 
   this script has void ratio computation as well)
   2. Push a boundary plane (BCPlane) downward (see demo_GPU_movingBoundary)
   3. Remove the particles on top that's not even, you can use 
   *SetParticlePosition*(int sphereID, const ChVector<double> pos) to move 
   them somewhere.
   4. If you don't want to change the surface profile, you can find a cubic 
   domain (like 16*16*5 cm) of particles within the settled ones, and use 
   those for void ratio calculations. You can write a subroutine to count the 
   number of particles in that domain.

Subject: RE: [chrono] Real data integrated simulation
From: Dan Negrut
Date: Tue, 14 Dec 2021 02:55:21 +0000

Hi Chanoh – in my mind, one way to use that information is to do calibration on the model.
This is a tough inverse problem since the terrain can be very nonhomogeneous as you probe underground from place to place.
I’d use that information to try to come up with a decent choice of model parameters – stiffness, damping, rolling resistance, etc. In other words, I would tune these model parameters until the results between the simulation and your measurements are small (in some sense).
I must acknowledge that this is easier said than done.

At any rate, if you’re contemplate using Chrono, the SMC is what needs to be used, so that it propagates a shock wave. To see the difference between SMC and NSC, see here<https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.96.042905>.

BTW, here’re some older Chrono sims that looks at shockwave propagation in gran material:
https://uwmadison.box.com/s/rjzjafuajf2vvt46y3ak8im9i9wgj1ju

Subject: Re: [chrono] ChLoader for line load in local beam coordinates?
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Wed, 2 Feb 2022 14:16:25 +0100

Dear David

unfortunately ChLoaderBeamWrenchDistributed works in different ways 
depending on how the ComputeNF function is implemented in the beam 
elements. For instance in ChElementBeamIGA it assumes
- force is global
- torque is local
to be aligned with the assumption of Chrono where node dofs are 
{x_vel,w_vel} with x_vel in absolute frame and w_vel (rotation) is in 
local node frame, and same for conjugated quantities (forces -abs.-, 
torques -local-)

So, if you want to provide a distributed load that is expressed in local 
beam coords (i.e. "material" coords of the beam, as in some literature) 
then my suggestion is that you provide a custom class

ChMyBeamWrenchInMaterialCoords

inheriting it from ChLoaderU. Ex. take inspiration from how the 
ComputeF() function is implemented in ChLoaderUdistributed. In such 
function you must rotate the distributed force by some rotation matrix R 
that would be function of the /const double U/ parameter (well, you'll 
need to access the internal data of the beam element to know how R must 
be rotated depending on U, this is the tricky part). And remember that 
the F vector computed in this way should be compatible with the 
ComputeNF() function of the element you are loading.

Otherwise, if you are not interested in the automatic Gauss quadrature, 
inherit your class directly from ChLoadBase and do the quadrature by 
yourself.

Note also that you do not need to build OpenCRG as a shared library.  A static library will also work (but you do need -fPIC anyway).

For demo_FEA_basic, you do not need any additional packages and do not need to enable any optional Chrono modules.  Of course, you still need to specify the path to the Eigen headers.

But first things first.  What version of Chrono are you using? I recall you saying that you cloned the repository. Please make sure you are on the *develop* branch.

Ideally, you would use cmake-gui or ccmake which will guide you better through satisfying all requirements.  Do you not have access to one of those in your distribution?

The cmake command line you posted below has several issues:
- there are no Chrono cmake variables named "CMAKE_ENABLE_MODULE_***"
- we expect to set the variable EIGEN3_INCLUDE_DIR
- IRRLICHT_LIBRARY should be set to the Irrlicht library *file* (not a directory)

I suggest you try a minimal build, adjusting appropriately the following command which works fine on my machine:

cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DEIGEN3_INCLUDE_DIR=/home/radu/Packages/eigen-3.4.0 -DENABLE_MODULE_IRRLICHT=ON -DIRRLICHT_ROOT=/usr/include/irrlicht -DIRRLICHT_LIBRARY=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libIrrlicht.so ~/Repositories/chrono

(Several of the options you set explicitly default to those values anyway)

--Radu

Hello Stefan,

I guess you want to try to speed things up to ensure that you can run 
your simulation in real-time? As far as I know there is no way to 
dramatically speed up the simulation at the moment. You need a 
relatively small time step to keep it all stable and there is no easy 
way to run those calculations in parallel. The only thing you can do to 
speed things up is to decouple physics from graphics so they run on 
separate cores.

Greetings, Marcel

Date: Wed, 12 Jan 2022 11:17:52 +0000

Kenny,

The bodies in these Chrono::FSI demos (for example demo_FSI_CylinderDrop) are in fact rigid bodies.  These demos are fluid-rigid interaction problems that are solved using a co-simulation approach.   You can also use Chrono to solve problems where fluid interacts with deformable bodies (such as demo_FSI_Flexible_Elements) but those are also set as co-simulation problems with the flexible bodies being simulated with the Chrono’s FEA support.

--Radu

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Could a known steady response speed up the Irrlicht
 application?
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Wed, 17 Nov 2021 09:17:31 +0100

Hi Luis,

you do not need to create an Irrlicht visualization system to get the K 
R M matrices, just create bodies and FEA and get them after a 
mysystem.Update(), or better after a mysystem.DoStaticNonlinear(..) in 
case the neutral position is not the one you need - say K must include 
geometric stiffening for prestretched structures.

Note, in your case there is a difficulty related to the fact that 
'steady state' for rotating structures is not a thing that can be solved 
via DoStaticNonlinear(). For example, DoStaticNonlinear() would not 
consider the gyroscopic damping in R like in the Jeffcott rotor case, as 
it works in zero-speed assumption. Note that recently I was working on a 
new type of pseudo-static analysis exactly for this class of problems, 
that considers rheonomic constraints like motors, but it proved to be 
less 'automatic' than expected and the user still had to provide some 
helper input, so in the end I am still using the brute force approach: 
run N time steps until steady state, and get K R M at the end. To run 
the N time steps, you do not need the Irrlicht stuff. Just call 
mysystem.*DoStepDynamics*(mystep)

Alessandro

Subject: Re: Custom Cohesion Model in GPU Module
From: Luning Fang
Date: Thu, 20 Jan 2022 09:16:22 -0800 (PST)

Hello Darwin,

The workflow makes sense. The major difference between 
computeSphereContactForces_matBased() and computeSphereContactForce() is 
that the first one use material-based property in contact force model, 
namely, youngs modulus, poisson ratio and coefficient of restitution, the 
second one use user-defined parameters. Take a look at 
demo_GPU_balldrop.cpp, where UseMaterialBasedModel(true) is used and 
parameters are set, when you run the simulation, 
computeSphereContactForces_matBased() is called. The default setting is 
using user-defined parameters of kn, gn, kt, gt, associated with 
spring-damper model of contact forces, in which case, 
computeSphereContactForce() is called. There are other small differences 
between these two, more details are in this paper 
<https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9717/9/10/1813/htm__;!!IKRxdwAv5BmarQ!Ka1qJSD6q6OcNFcqnG1rWrS8yNSYzz5ifgImVXuo13ickDxwVP-V5oC9BJ1KEA$> equation 
(3), (4) (18) and (19).

I looked at your changes, when implementing your own force model in GPU, 
you need to convert the units into simulation units. Because in GPU, 
integers are used to describe particle positions for fast performance. To 
maintain the resolution, particles are scaled a lot larger so every integer 
can be used. Basic units conversion in length, mass and time are 
pre-calculated and stored, so you can use them freely in your own force 
model, like gran_params->LENGTH_UNIT.

Take a look at switchToSimUnits() in ChSystemGpu_impl.cpp, it shows how
symbol: Re: Custom Cohesion Model in GPU Module

text:
model, like gran_params->LENGTH_UNIT.

Take a look at switchToSimUnits() in ChSystemGpu_impl.cpp, it shows how 
LENGTH_SU2UU, MASS_SU2UU and TIME_SU2UU are computed, where SU2UU stands 
for "simulation unit to user unit", and the conversion goes: length_uu = 
length_su * length_su2uu. That part of the code also use basic units to get 
conversion of other quantities, like acceleration, torque, stiffness, etc. 
For example, youngs modulus, E_su2uu = mass_su2uu / (length_su2uu * 
time_su2uu^2). You will have to do this for your interfacial surface energy 
parameter.

The default output of positions and force handles conversion from SU to UU, 
but if you want to customize the cohesive force output, you will have to do 
your own conversion as well.

Thank you,
Luning

Derek,

Could you please elaborate on what exactly you are interested in achieving?

  1.  If you are interested in working with JSON files from the user Python code, why not use a native module (“import json”)?
  2.  The JSON reading utilities in Chrono::Vehicle (and similar others in other Chrono modules) are really internal to the code.  There should not be any need for a user of Chrono to invoke them directly.
We could expose some of them (e.g., ReadChassisJSON) but not others (such as ReadFileJSON).  For the functionality provided by the former, you should use a Python module (see #1).  The latter would require wrapping the RapidJSON library (which is not something we want to do for a library not maintained by us).
--Radu

Hi Yu,

All integrators in Chrono are single step, meaning you can set the state of the body at any step within your main simulation loop without any issues.  Simply use ChBody::SetRot(). Of course, you’ll want to make sure you do that only once, at the time you want, and not also at all subsequent steps.

--Radu

text:
Subject: RE: [chrono] SCM and contact friction
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 22 Jun 2022 12:00:51 +0000

Hi Klaus,

You are not doing anything wrong.
Indeed, the coefficient of friction specified on an object that interacts with SCM terrain is currently not taken into account.   This is because the friction is embedded in one of the SCM terrain parameters (Mohr_friction, passed in degrees to SCMDeformableTerrain::SetSoilParameters, and used in the Janosi-Hanamoto formula for tangential forces).

Try varying that value and see if you obtain the desired effect.

I thought about also taking into consideration the coefficient of friction specified on the impactor object (e.g., a rigid tire) and may do that in the future.  Note however that that would have to be used in conjunction with two different sets of SCM parameters (for soil-soil and tire-soil interactions) and with the ability in the Chrono SCM implementation of optionally specifying both (see https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/CHANGELOG.md#changed-scm-deformable-terrain-improvements)

--Radu

text:
Subject: RE: [chrono] Do all modules of Chrono Engine work on Parallel?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 5 Feb 2022 19:37:53 +0000

Deniz,

Several modules and algorithms in Chrono are implemented such that they can make use of multicore parallelism using OpenMP. Examples include FEA in the main Chrono module (which uses some parallel for loops over FEA nodes and elements), the SCM deformable terrain (which performs ray casting in parallel), collision detection (the default Bullet option has some parallel for loops, while the Chrono internal option uses OpenMP directly and through the Thrust library), the Pardiso and MUMPS linear solvers, and so on.   This is indicated in the documentation of ChSystem::SetNumThreads<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_system.html#adf3592c000a03bcb3da9d80099370ba8>.

However, you must be careful: the optimal number of threads is highly dependent on problem and hardware.  This is why I compromised on the default setting in SetNumThreads and why, in general, you should explicitly call this function and set proper values (as is done in some demos).

Lastly, the Chrono::Multicore module (you must be using a pretty old version of Chrono as we renamed this module quite a while ago) uses multicore parallelization, both directly through OpenMP and using Thrust with the OpenMP backend, to perform the entire solution in parallel.  For that it manages all data and internal states in completely different data structures from the rest of Chrono.  As such, only a subset of Chrono features (and hence modules) can be used with Chrono::Multicore.  For instance, FEA is not supported and neither is SCM deformable terrain.

text:
However, you must be careful: the optimal number of threads is highly dependent on problem and hardware.  This is why I compromised on the default setting in SetNumThreads and why, in general, you should explicitly call this function and set proper values (as is done in some demos).

Lastly, the Chrono::Multicore module (you must be using a pretty old version of Chrono as we renamed this module quite a while ago) uses multicore parallelization, both directly through OpenMP and using Thrust with the OpenMP backend, to perform the entire solution in parallel.  For that it manages all data and internal states in completely different data structures from the rest of Chrono.  As such, only a subset of Chrono features (and hence modules) can be used with Chrono::Multicore.  For instance, FEA is not supported and neither is SCM deformable terrain.

As with any OpenMP-based code, you must again be careful to make sure that you are gaining something in terms of efficiency.  That depends on the problem you are trying to solve, as the overhead of OpenMP threads may actually hurt your performance for "simpler" problems.  In the case of vehicle simulations, Chrono::Multicore is primarily used for simulations on granular terrain.

I hope this helps clarify things,
--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] Re: Project Chrono for games
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 9 Jan 2022 11:48:29 +0000

A quick clarification: The core Chrono library can use Thrust now that I exposed an alternative parallel collision detection system (if Thrust is not available, that functionality is not included in the build and only the default Bullet collision detection system can be used).

Having said that,

  *   you will likely not benefit (from a computational efficiency point of view) from the parallel collision detection anyway for the type of problems you describe.  That collision system is more appropriate for large granular dynamics problems.  (A second reason for implementing it is that, unlike Bullet, it can use more precise analytical narrow phase algorithms for certain pairs of collision shapes)
  *   the version of the Bullet collision system currently implemented in Chrono can also take advantage of OpenMP parallelization. Depending on problem size and set up, this may or may not help computational speed (some experimentation will be required). So, keep OpenMP support enabled and then experiment with providing more threads for collision detection; see ChSystem::SetNumThreads<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_system.html#adf3592c000a03bcb3da9d80099370ba8>.

Radu

Hi

I have experience in industrial automation. In the past I dealt with OPC
for an automation project. It is a very powerful communication layer -
however if I could choose, I would stick with plain Ethercat or CAN
fieldbus es, if hard-real time M2M communication is the only requirement.
The OPC complication pays back when SCADA and HMI enter in the game, imho.

Anyway: if you really need OPC, one solution is that you directly generate
OPC datagrams via a c++ API for OPC (if I remember, there are some open
source libraries to this end) and send/receive them to your PLC, straight
from a c++ simulator with Chrono. I do not see the need for passing through
Excel... it could add latencies etc.
By the way: if you do not use c++ and you prefer PyChrono, probably there
are also OPC APIs for Python.

A side note. Note that this would be soft real time, not hard real time
(even more true if the simulation runs in Python). If you aim for a 5ms
control frame with deterministic periodicity, it would be questionable -
ok, "statistically" it may work. (A true hard RT with HIL, after all, would
need that you run a true RT OS on your simulation side, ex. WxWorks, RTAI,
etc., or that Win patch that Beckhoff delivers in TwinCAT for his PLC
stuff. But this might be too far from your actual needs).

allowing your HIL, but it depends on the complexity of the model. To give
an idea: on a fast CPU I can run a robot model with a dozen of bodies and a

the communication of real-time 
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real-time_computing> plant data between 
control devices from different manufacturers"
Essentially in the case you can open an OPC connection between excel and 
the PLC for your target variable in the PLC.

[Excel] LaserA_PLCVariable = 1 -----> [PLC] LaserA = 1 ------------> Logic 
State Changes 

3) A PhotoCell as a common detector used for presence detection in 
industrial processes, typically it changes state if the light it emits is 
interrupted or reflected by an object.

typically used for closer detection, within a few inches.

There is no explicit support for this, also because this type of monitoring is quite application specific.  A couple of suggestions:
1.       If it is enough to monitor only a point on the object, you could implement your own “point in volume” check using the specific shape of your test volume. You may find some useful functions and algorithms in the chrono collision system (see ChCollisionUtilsPRIMS.cpp<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/chrono/collision/chrono/ChCollisionUtilsPRIMS.cpp>).
2.       If you want to use the actual collision shape of the object to trigger the detection, you can use the `NarrowphaseCallback` mechanism provided in Chrono.  See this example<https://github.com/rserban/chrono/blob/develop/src/projects/contact/sequential/test_CTC_sentinel.cpp> for an illustration.  The idea is to:
a.       Als create a collision shape for the “test volume” (you will need to create a body to carry that collision model – in your case likely the “ground” body).
b.       Implement and register a custom object of type `NarrowphaseCallback`.
c.       Intercept all reported collisions during the narrowphase (in the overridden OnNarrowphase() method of your narrowphase callback object).  At each time step, this method is called for all current collision pairs identified by the narrowphase algorithm.

a.       Als create a collision shape for the “test volume” (you will need to create a body to carry that collision model – in your case likely the “ground” body).
b.       Implement and register a custom object of type `NarrowphaseCallback`.
c.       Intercept all reported collisions during the narrowphase (in the overridden OnNarrowphase() method of your narrowphase callback object).  At each time step, this method is called for all current collision pairs identified by the narrowphase algorithm.
d.       Identify if a particular collision involves the “test volume” and the desired object:

                                                                           i.      If yes, process information as desired and return false (so that this particular collision is discarded and does not generate contact forces).

                                                                         ii.      If no, simply return true (so that contact forces are generated).

Of course, all the above are in C++, but it should be straightforward to recode in Python as needed.  I don’t recall off the top of my head if we provided a Python wrapper for the NarrowphaseCallback mechanism;  let us know if that is not in place and we can easily add it.

--Radu

Of course, all the above are in C++, but it should be straightforward to recode in Python as needed.  I don’t recall off the top of my head if we provided a Python wrapper for the NarrowphaseCallback mechanism;  let us know if that is not in place and we can easily add it.

--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] Adaptive Step in NSC contact model
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 24 Oct 2022 14:29:05 +0000

Hi Kirill,

For several reasons (which I will not elaborate on here), we currently only support fixed-step integration in Chrono.
The only integrator that has some time adaptivity is HHT (which can internally vary the step size below the value passed by the caller to DoStepDynamics.  Note that this is not always as robust as we’d like; I plan on working on that integrator anyway soon and will revisit that part as well.
In the future, we may add a fully adaptive integrator to Chrono (for use in problems where that makes sense and most likely not for an NSC system).

The variables and associated functions for setting min and max step sizes are not used and I will remove them right away.

--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] Soft real-time timer behavior...
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 30 Jun 2022 13:20:51 +0000

Hi Marcel,

Thank you for bringing this up.

I don’t think having soft real-time enforced by default is necessarily a bug, but I agree that it’d be best to have it default to false.   I pushed some changes related to this and changed all vehicle demos to use the real time timer embedded in ChVehicle (and not take care of this themselves).  The modification also makes it so that a correct RTF value is reported whether soft real time is enforced or not.

As for your last point, I would argue that this goes beyond the scope of what Chrono::Vehicle is designed for. Real time was not and is not a goal in itself for this code.  Adding this additional logic would complicate the code unnecessarily and could conflict with cases where the vehicle is embedded in a larger simulation (like is the case with many Chrono applications) in which case it is not the vehicle that dictates time stepping.

I believe such a feature is best left to user code, if their particular application could benefit from the ability to catch up to real time later in the simulation.  Note that, in typical applications for Chrono::Vehicle, that is unlikely to be possible (either the vehicle can be simulated in or below real time or it cannot).

Thanks,
Radu

text:
Subject: [chrono] Soft real-time timer behavior...

Hi all, I was just looking into the behavior of the timer that is used in most of the demos that ship with Chrono (ChRealtimeStepTimer) and there are a few things I would like to discuss:

The first is something I would consider a bug, and this is that by default, ChVehicle embeds and enables a ChRealtimeStepTimer that, every time its Advance() is invoked, will wait for at least a single "step size" in real-time to have passed. I would argue that by default this embedded timer should at least be disabled (if it needs to be present in ChVehicle at all, one could argue it has not place there at all). My proposal would be to initialize m_realtime_force to false in all constructors. The demos all use their own ChRealtimeStepTimer that, after invoking Synchronize() and Advance() on all modules, will wait for "step size" to have passed anyway.

The second is more of a design question. ChRealtimeStepTimer will currently, every time you invoke Spin(double step_size), wait for at least step_size seconds to pass. That means that if the simulation is running slower than step_size for any single step, it will fall behind and never recover. I think it would be better to at least have the simulation try to catch up. Of course, if the simulation is structurally way too slow to run in real-time, that won't help at all, but in cases where occasionally it is a bit slow, it can still catch up and will arguably run "better" in real-time than when it can't catch up at all. Of course it is possible to simply implement a different "MyRealtimeStepTimer" and I'm currently playing around with one. Is this of interest to anyone here?

Of course it is possible to simply implement a different "MyRealtimeStepTimer" and I'm currently playing around with one. Is this of interest to anyone here?

Greetings, Marcel

From: Marcel Offermans
Date: Tue, 28 Jun 2022 06:12:16 -0700 (PDT)

Hi all, I was just looking into the behavior of the timer that is used in 
most of the demos that ship with Chrono (ChRealtimeStepTimer) and there are 
a few things I would like to discuss:

The first is something I would consider a bug, and this is that by default, 
ChVehicle embeds and enables a ChRealtimeStepTimer that, every time its 
Advance() is invoked, will wait for at least a single "step size" in 
real-time to have passed. I would argue that by default this embedded timer 
should at least be disabled (if it needs to be present in ChVehicle at all, 
one could argue it has not place there at all). My proposal would be to 
initialize m_realtime_force to false in all constructors. The demos all use 
their own ChRealtimeStepTimer that, after invoking Synchronize() and 
Advance() on all modules, will wait for "step size" to have passed anyway.

The second is more of a design question. ChRealtimeStepTimer will 
currently, every time you invoke Spin(double step_size), wait for at least 
step_size seconds to pass. That means that if the simulation is running 
slower than step_size for any single step, it will fall behind and never 
recover. I think it would be better to at least have the simulation try to 
catch up. Of course, if the simulation is structurally way too slow to run 
in real-time, that won't help at all, but in cases where occasionally it is 
a bit slow, it can still catch up and will arguably run "better" in 
real-time than when it can't catch up at all. Of course it is possible to

If by "the same issue" you mean the mesh was not felt by the granular 
material at all and goes through it, then I was not able to reproduce it 
using your script: the mesh and granular material interact normally. 
However, your simulation does crash when the cone touches the granular 
material, and that is because the moments of inertia of this cone is set to 
be extremely small, compared to the mass of this cone (screw_inertia is 
something like 7e-4 while its mass is ~100). This is not physical and 
causes the cone to rotate at a huge angular velocity, leading to large 
mesh--particle penetration and destabilize the simulation.

numbers, for example, just using those cone_inertia_xyz in your code: 
*cone_body->SetInertiaXX(ChVector<>(cone_inertia_x,cone_inertia_y,cone_inertia_z));*
I hope this answers the question.

Ruochun

Benjamin,

(FYI, I am copying this to the user mailing list – I prefer to keep these answers public so that they are available to all interested users.  Please post follow ups to the mailing list as well.)

Happy to hear that the changes I made work as expected.

Regarding your proposal, I’m afraid that is not something we will include.  Indeed, the callback mechanism I added for visualizing collision shapes is generic and supposed to work with any concrete collision system which chooses to implement this functionality.  There are two such collision systems in Chrono: one based on Bullet, the other our own multicore collision system.  For the former, the collision shape visualization functionality is implemented by wrapping Bullet’s own mechanism (which was actually the inspiration for the generic one in Chrono).  For the multicore collision system, I provided functionality to render only a selected number of collision shapes.

Having said that, while I could code a request that a particular collision system provide the option that only certain shapes be rendered, implementing that for Bullet would require changing Bullet code which we do not want to do (some of the Bullet files embedded in Chrono are modified for our own use, but we try to keep these changes to a minimum so that upgrading to a new version of Bullet requires as little work as possible).

--Radu

Indeed, we do not give this kind of low-level access through the C# interface.  And even if we did, accessing a ChCollisionShape would not help you.  This is a base class (see here<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1collision_1_1_ch_collision_shape.html>) that only carries information on the contact material associated with that shape.  The actual geometric representation is left to derived classes from different collision systems.  In particular, the Bullet collision system stores that information in Bullet objects which we do not plan to ever expose in C#.

While you could simply draw the data from the “source” you used top generate the convex hull collision shapes, I understand that this is probably not that useful (in case you want to check that the collision system uses the correct convex hull shape).

So the best solution is to use the new generalized mechanism I added for rendering collision shapes.  See demo_IRR_visualize_collision<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/irrlicht/demo_IRR_visualize_collision.cpp> for an example which uses Irrlicht rendering.  You should be able to do the exact same thing by overriding the DrawLine() method of a user-supplied callback class derived from chrono::collision::ChCollisionSystem::VisualizationCallback to use Unity for rendering a line between the two specified points.

While I have not tested this myself with our own Chrono-Unity interface code, it should work (it works with the Python bindings).

To use this feature, you will need to pull the latest Chrono code from the ‘develop’ branch of the GitHub repository and rebuild. I just pushed a couple of necessary changes to expose this.  Let me know if you encounter any issues.

Date: Tue, 8 Feb 2022 13:03:33 +0000

Indeed, we do not give this kind of low-level access through the C# interface.  And even if we did, accessing a ChCollisionShape would not help you.  This is a base class (see here<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1collision_1_1_ch_collision_shape.html>) that only carries information on the contact material associated with that shape.  The actual geometric representation is left to derived classes from different collision systems.  In particular, the Bullet collision system stores that information in Bullet objects which we do not plan to ever expose in C#.

While you could simply draw the data from the “source” you used top generate the convex hull collision shapes, I understand that this is probably not that useful (in case you want to check that the collision system uses the correct convex hull shape).

So the best solution is to use the new generalized mechanism I added for rendering collision shapes.  See demo_IRR_visualize_collision<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/irrlicht/demo_IRR_visualize_collision.cpp> for an example which uses Irrlicht rendering.  You should be able to do the exact same thing by overriding the DrawLine() method of a user-supplied callback class derived from chrono::collision::ChCollisionSystem::VisualizationCallback to use Unity for rendering a line between the two specified points.

While I have not tested this myself with our own Chrono-Unity interface code, it should work (it works with the Python bindings).

Tobias,

There are many ways to represent orientation in 3D.  Assuming you cannot directly use a unit quaternion to represent body orientation (which is what GetRot() returns), what do you need?  I doubt it’s the vector returned by Q_to_Rotv() which encodes the Euler axis and angle (as in Euler’s rotation theorem).  Do you need the rotation matrix, some set of Euler angles, something else?  There are methods in ChQuaternion to give you any of these representations.

--Radu

Radu Serban schrieb am Freitag, 28. Januar 2022 um 11:56:41 UTC+1:
Hi Tobias,

The full HMMWV model (in which the suspension control arms are modeled with rigid bodies) is a pretty well tested and validated model.   The capabilities of that model (including steering capabilities) are whatever the HMMWV vehicle is supposed to be able to do.

The “reduced” model (in which the suspension control arms are modeled through distance constraints) is more of a demonstration of obtaining a reduced-order model in Chrono::Vehicle.  Any such model simplification requires approximations and “cutting some corners”.  In this case, the problem is with specifying where the suspension spring and damper are attached to the unsprung mass.   On the real vehicle and in the full model, these are attached to the lower control arm.  But that body doesn’t exist in the reduced model!   So, I just attached them to the upright body.  This of course affects the steering capabilities of the resulting model; but I didn’t see any point in spending too much time tweaking parameters for what is effectively just an illustration.

In this case, the problem is with specifying where the suspension spring and damper are attached to the unsprung mass. This of course affects the steering capabilities of the resulting model; but I didn’t see any point in spending too much time tweaking parameters for what is effectively just an illustration.

To make a long story short, a Chrono model (and any other model for that matter) is only as good as the data (parameters) you put into it.  You should not expect a simplified model to do as well as a more complex one.  And you cannot expect a model of a HMMWV to behave like a race car!   You will have to tweak parameters in that model (likely beyond what is physically meaningful) to get whatever vehicle behavior you want for your game - you can certainly make even the HMMWV model take turns at unreasonable speeds without roll-over.   Unless you strive for realism, in which case you should get the proper topology and parameters for the race car you’re trying to model.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Discrete/Continuous hybrid DAE system
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 10 Jun 2022 09:18:08 +0200

Hi Guan,

well, the architecture of Chrono allows the solution of custom DAEs, but 
it requires that you go through a very complex process of inheriting 
from ChPhysicsItem c++ classes and that you override lot of member 
functions (after some manipulation of your DAEs so that you can write 
them in semi explicit form), etc. etc. Shortly: I would not reccomend 
this. Maybe in future we'll implement some sort of "easy base-class for 
custom DAEs equations" where one just have to implement a lambda or a 
callback for the function evaluation and constraint evaluation, plus few 
minimal other things, but it is not planned in the short term.

As a workaround, I'd suggest you to do some cosimulation, as Dan suggested.

Alessandro

text:
Subject: RE: [chrono] Discrete/Continuous hybrid DAE system
From: Dan Negrut
Date: Thu, 9 Jun 2022 20:00:04 +0000

Guan – you cannot append a simple DAE system example (e.g. 3 equation with 3 unknowns) to Chrono and have it solved.
You should define a Chrono model that will lead to those DAE equations.

One way to go about it, is to run a cosimulation, say with Matlab or Python. You define your equations, you solve them, and during the solution process you can talk with Chrono. In this sense, Chrono is not like Modelica. I’m not a Modelica user, so perhaps Alessandro Tasora, if he reads this, might provide a better answer than mine…

Dan

Subject: New Blender plugin
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Sat, 29 Apr 2023 06:54:45 +0200

Dear Chrono users

at
https://api.projectchrono.org/development/introduction_chrono_blender.html
you can find an introduction to the new Blender plugin that will allow high
quality rendering of Chrono simulations.

This is the first release of the plugin, in beta version, so some features
might be incomplete or with bugs - please report if so.

This Blender postprocessing plugin is meant to replace the POVray
postprocessing system.
A first reason is about quality: Blender can use the Cycles rendering
engine, which is a modern path tracing algorithm with unbiased
physically-based rendering, whereas Povray is based on a older method (ray
tracing, biased, not physically-based).
A second reason is that Blender is also a modeler with a 3D interactive
GUI, so you can navigate the scene before rendering it in high quality, or
you can even add additional assets (landscapes, clouds, other objects) or
modify/edit/improve the meshes exported from the Chrono side.

Best regards

Alessandro Tasora

Hi,

To answer the questions:

1. They can be different. In that test, I didn't choose to set them 
differently though. Is there anything that makes you concerned about this 
choice?

2. Mesh material properties are specified by those S2M parameters. Compared 
to real-world materials, the properties we use tend to be much less stiff. 
This is to make the simulation easier to run, and it is a common practice.

3. and 4. are very related, I'd like to talk about them together. The short 
answer is that in your case you should use material-based properties, 
instead of specifying stiffness and damping numbers. An example of using 
material-based properties is demo_GPU_ballDrop. There, you specify Young's 
modulus and Poisson's ratio and friction coefficient and such, and the 
solver calculates the rest without you worrying about it. For aluminum or 
titanium, you should know those material properties. But I should notify 
you that using true Young's modulus could necessitate an extremely small 
time step size for your simulation to run, and it is questionable whether 
using true properties means much for increasing the fidelity of your 
simulations.

I admit that Eq.18 and Eq.19 make the text a bit less intuitive to 
understand. Eq.18 and Eq.19 basically say that when you set normalStiffS2S, 
normalDampS2S and such in the code, you are setting \hat{k} and 
\hat{\gamma}, rather than k and \gamma. We need to convert \hat{k} and 
\hat{\gamma} to k and \gamma to understand the physics, because Eq.3 and 4
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: the GPU module and the multicore module

text:
normalDampS2S and such in the code, you are setting \hat{k} and 
\hat{\gamma}, rather than k and \gamma. We need to convert \hat{k} and 
\hat{\gamma} to k and \gamma to understand the physics, because Eq.3 and 4 
use k and \gamma. But Chrono::GPU uses a nonlinear force model where the 
force is proportional to \delta^{1.5}, rather than \delta. That is to say 
the k and \gamma in Eq.3 and 4 are not independent of \delta. And indeed, k 
and \gamma contain a \delta^{0.5} in them, as indicated in Eq.18 and Eq.19. 
Also, k and \gamma are dependent on R and m, meaning that smaller particles 
are effectively stiffer given the same material, and this is a part of the 
force model. As for how to convert Young's modulus and such to k and 
\gamma, as indicated in the paper you are referred to *Fleischmann, J.; 
Serban, R.; Negrut, D.; Jayakumar, P. On the importance of displacement 
history in soft-body contact models. J. Comput. Nonlinear Dyn. 2016, 11, 
044502*. Using this paper you can probably figure out a stiffness param k' 
which is in front of \delta^{1.5}, then you know k' is independent of 
\delta (since we use a force model proportional to \delta^{1.5}), and then 
based on the particle size and mass, you can figure out \hat{k} which is 
completely independent, and the solver asks for \hat{k}.

After reading all these, you probably already decided to use the 
material-based model. I would like to comment that the way \hat{k} and 
\hat{\gamma} were implemented is more force model-oriented, without 
considering much about the implications on materials (mindset: as long as 
we can explain how they make into the force model, it is fine). This is
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: the GPU module and the multicore module

text:
\hat{\gamma} were implemented is more force model-oriented, without 
considering much about the implications on materials (mindset: as long as 
we can explain how they make into the force model, it is fine). This is 
related to the fact that the stiffness and damping choices in many 
situations are numerical viability-driven, rather than trying to capture a 
specific material. You probably don't believe this now, but faithfully 
setting the true stiffness and damping, in some DEM simulations, makes them 
much more difficult to run while offering little accuracy boost for the 
application you try to simulate.

One last thing: If you use DEM-Engine, the only default model is 
material-based, so know that if you switch to that tool you don't have to 
worry about all these. Also note that the friction coefficient between two 
materials, if you use the material-based model in Chrono::GPU, will always 
be the larger one between the two. Whereas in DEM-Engine, you can specify 
explicitly the friction coefficient between any pair of two materials 
involved in a contact.

Ruochun

Hi,

Simulations failing randomly is not a good sign... Perhaps the simulation 
parameters are just on the verge of being valid. Or, it's also possible 
that Chrono::GPU has some suspicious memory operations that cause troubles 
in some scenarios such as yours. But I cannot be sure. To answer your 
questions...

   1. Yes, this package is dimensionless. That means when it reads a file, 
   it reads numerics only, not unit systems. Honestly, I don't think your mesh 
   file has a unit system baked into it either. Once it is exported from your 
   CAD system, there is no way to know the unit system you used, nor does 
   Chrono care about it. So if you created mesh in your CAD using an *mm*-based 
   metric system and then in the simulation set the sphere radius to be 1, 
   thinking it means 1cm, then this is the inconsistency I talked about 
   earlier. The way you are doing it implicitly makes this "1" in sphere 
   radius mean 1mm. There is no such thing as a switch in Chrono::GPU that 
   changes the way it interprets unit systems, the only thing that can be 
   relied on is that you do the scaling and unification of unit systems 
   properly under the hood.
   2. Chrono::GPU cannot do that. But the new DEM-Engine can do that.
   3. In this case, you should use the material-based force model (by the 
   way, the default force model in DEM-Engine is also material-based). It's 
   best if you check out the *demo_GPU_ballDrop *example. There you can see

OK this mesh has an extremely sharp tip. That is a demanding physics in 
terms of numerical simulations, you agree? DEM is based on geometry 
penetration/overlap. Capture that microscopic particle--mesh overlap at 
that mesh tip is not easy, considering the geometry's own thickness. But 
other than that, the mesh seems valid.

I don't know what exact simulation you are running but say if you are using 
particles of diameter 0.5cm or something and a Young's modulus 1e9, then I 
suppose the time step size has to be 1e-6s or something like that. It's 
likely that 1e-5 won't cut it. As for not getting any force readings, I 
suspects it's because the simulation crashes right after the mesh tip hits 
the particles and all the readings you got were before the particles and 
mesh made contact, so they're all 0.

To quickly do a proof of concept you can make a similar mesh that does not 
have the tip, and repeat the simulation to see if it is easier. I even 
attached one, but it's just your mesh with the tip and most of the top 
structures removed. I imagine however, that tip is the key of the physics 
you are trying to simulate. If that is the case, eventually you have to add 
that part back, and go with small time step sizes since you have to.

Thank you,
Ruochun

Hi,

I think you did the right thing in terms of resolving the 
too-many-triangles problem. C::GPU assumes that the triangles in the mesh 
you use are about the same size or bigger than the particle size. It has 
difficulty processing triangles that are much smaller than particles. The 
idea is that the mesh features preserved only by triangles that small will 
not benefit the simulation accuracy, since at that point the bottleneck for 
geometry representation accuracy becomes the particles/spheres. 

But you have to make sure your resultant reduced mesh is valid. The problem 
of not seeing forces or too many triangles in an SD could be because of 
that. The mesh needs to have correct outward normals, and should not have 
things like duplicate points/facets and such. If it is a small mesh, you 
can send it here and I could quickly check if it is alright. Also, when you 
use *CollectMeshContactForces *you have to make sure you are querying the 
correct mesh, meaning the first argument, the integer, needs to match the 
returned numbering of the mesh when you load the mesh into the system.

The negative local pos or too-many-sphere-in-SD type of error is more 
common. Uninspiring as it sounds, it is most likely due to a 
diverged/destabilized simulation. What you should do is: Reduce the time 
step size further; add more damping; or reduce the stiffness. Just those 
things that make DEM easier to run. The unusual splash as shown in your 
picture is one common symptom of insufficient temporal resolution. But I

things that make DEM easier to run. The unusual splash as shown in your 
picture is one common symptom of insufficient temporal resolution. But I 
cannot say for sure, since there could be other causes, such as bad meshes.

Hi,

Chrono is dimensionless. So as you noted, there is an underlying consistent 
set of units. In Chrono GPU, the length is usually assumed to be in *cm *(no 
demo uses *mm *as its length unit), the mass is usually in *g*, the rest 
are in SI units. The force is therefore in *g·cm/s²*. Those are just one 
possible interpretation, and any interpretation that has consistency would 
go.

normal stiffness is *g/s²* (the same as *k* in Eq. 3), and the unit of 
normal damping is *1/s* (similar to /gamma in Eq. 3, but Chrono ::GPU's 
damping will be multiplied by particle mass to form /gamma).

Ruochun

Hi,

What you wanted is possible. There is no problem creating two systems in one script, the only problem is their interaction. You can do that via co-simulation. Like a said, demo_GPU_ballcosim may give you an idea on how to do that. The general idea is that your complex mechanical system involving ChBodies and joints and such, will still be managed by a Chrono SMC system. Those ChBodies can be instructed to receive external forces and torques via accumulators; those external forces and torques in this case should be queried from Chrono::GPU simulations. That is, you load obj meshes into a Chrono::GPU system, and in each time step, you let it compute the contact forces between meshes and particles, then feed that information to ChBodies to update the locations of those bodies, then feed the new locations of these obj meshes back to Chrono::GPU to complete one time step, and then repeat.

Hi,

The GPU module does benefit a lot from more recent hardware. If your test 
case does not feature a huge number of bodies, say some 10k, then multicore 
can be a good choice. It probably requires less learning from you too.

It should be noted that Chrono::GPU is not "Chrono on GPU". Most Chrono 
core classes and methods cannot be used in Chrono::GPU. For all 
purposes, Chrono::GPU can be seen as a standalone DEM solver for 
monodisperse spherical particles, implemented on GPU. It should be used to 
simulate granular materials, and it can interact with Chrono (core) so that 
it becomes possible to bring a small number of more complex objects (such 
as your spoon) into the simulation as well. So if you would like to use 
Chrono::GPU, you have to start from its demos, to learn how to use its own 
methods to instantiate and manage granular particles. Chrono::GPU's main 
advantage is being fast. If your simulation has to involve millions of 
granular particles, then multicore will not do and GPU is the choice.

More specifically, *CreateCylindricalContainerFromBoxes*  is not a 
Chrono::GPU thing at all. *cohesion_ratio* is about the cohesion between 
Chrono::GPU particles, and it has nothing to do with gravity, which is set 
by *SetGravitationalAcceleration* in Chrono::GPU.

a new direction. The support for complex granular particle shapes will be 
added and it will become a duo-GPU solver. It will be based on SBEL's new

On a different note, Chrono's DEM/granular support on GPU is moving towards 
a new direction. The support for complex granular particle shapes will be 
added and it will become a duo-GPU solver. It will be based on SBEL's new 
DEM Engine <https://github.com/uwsbel/DEM-Engine>. Apart from being more 
general and having higher efficiency, the usage of it is similar to 
Chrono::GPU, as a standalone helper to Chrono core which manages the 
granular part of the simulation, or work on its own as a dedicated DEM 
solver. If from the previous conversation you believe Chrono::GPU is for 
you, then likely this package will be of interest. More documentations and 
user guides are being added to it. But again, it does benefit from recent 
GPUs though.

Hi Fabio,

That's a bit surprising. As there's essentially no compute in this demo, 
the 10-minute time is probably all spent on CPU-side JIT compiling. Even on 
ancient systems, I'd say it's too much, and I expect something more like 20 
seconds.

It's somewhat impractical to test with this efficiency. If you wish to 
continue using it, I suggest locating where the biggest overhead is. You 
can time the Initialize() step to see if it really took 10 minutes; then 
the script already shows the time spent on actual computing (if they add up 
to something much less than 10 minutes, then you probably have big delays 
elsewhere). You can also test on WSL2 Ubuntu to see if it drastically 
reduces the total time.

Thank you,
Ruochun

Subject: RE: [chrono] SetSteeringOutput seems to cause problems
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 23 Mar 2021 17:46:53 +0000

Unless your vehicle has 3 or more steering mechanisms, you are accessing out-of-bounds memory.
The first argument of ChWheeledVehicle::SetSteeringOutput identifies the index (0-based) of the steering mechanism for which output is requested.  For a vehicle with a single steering mechanism (most common case), that first argument should be 0.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Difference between Multicore and GPU module
From: Ruochun Zhang
Date: Wed, 29 Sep 2021 16:35:43 -0500

Hi Julian,

Good questions. My answers are...

1. You can have a look at *demo_GPU_ballcosim.cpp* for a co-simulation
example. By co-simulation I *mainly* meant coupling the GPU module with
other Chrono modules. Chrono and all its modules serve as a middle library,
and here this idea translates to that, Chrono GPU cares about the meshed
shapes (input as ChTriangleMeshConnected or Wavefront OBJ files) and
positions/velocities of those external objects only; it does not care how
you obtain that information. You can feed that information based on the
simulation results from other Chrono modules (most prominent and easy
approach I suppose), or if you have your own oracles you can use them too.
Loading step-based mesh files is also possible, considering you write your
own simulation *for* loops, you can just read a *step_%05d.obj* at each
iteration. I hope by saying those I gave you an idea of why I called it a
middle library and the freedom and associated responsibility that you can
expect from using Chrono. A caveat I have to mention: the interplay between
GPU module and Chrono core module is well tested, it handles the
interaction between external rigid bodies and granular material
efficiently; however we lack demos for the interplay between GPU module and
other modules such as FEA; reading new meshes at each simulation step (only
needed when the object is deformable) can be very inefficient too. But the
caveat is by itself a different topic, we can always discuss those if we go
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: Difference between Multicore and GPU module

text:
other modules such as FEA; reading new meshes at each simulation step (only
needed when the object is deformable) can be very inefficient too. But the
caveat is by itself a different topic, we can always discuss those if we go
that far, and we can do further development if needed be.

2. From what I understand, the Distributed module is based on Multicore,
and aims to enable doing granular dynamics with MPI. Very loosely speaking,
it lets you distribute your granular dynamics problem across a couple of
desktops/workstations to accelerate it. GPU module at its current stage
aims to do granular dynamics with a graphic card. For a naturally
fine-grain parallel problem like granular dynamics, you can expect using
GPU gives you a much better per-dollar performance. But I do not use the
Distributed module so maybe someone else can do a better job explaining.

3. The short answer is yes and we are doing that. Actually, more than that.
We will allow not only polydisperse particles but also complex grain shapes
(sphere clumps). And as a first step we plan to allow at least 2 GPUs to be
used at the same time in this new generation code. Open source-ness and
efficiency will still be the focus---in fact, we feel it can be faster than
this current Chrono GPU, even with complex geometry supported. 6 months is
a good estimate for the wait time. That is the road map I can give.

4. From what I know, we are preparing documentation for a new release that
happens in 2 months. This is for all Chrono modules. I cannot say for
others but I'll do my best in preparing that, whatever my best is. The

Hi Yi,

Judging from the problem size you are aiming at, GPU module is your best 
bet. GPU module uses SMC, and you can use co-simulation in GPU to achieve 
modelling soft external structures too. GPU scales with millions of 
particles easily, whereas from what I heard from Multicore users, millions 
of particles lead to substantial simulation time for Multicore. Note GPU 
modules currently deals with monodisperse spherical particles only, but it 
has cohesion and rolling friction models which you can make use of, so that 
effects such as particle interlocking and soil elasticity are (to some 
extend) accounted for.

Thank you,
Ruochun

Dear Thomas

ChNodeXYZrot cannot be attached to a spring or similar loads for various reasons (ex. they are not inherited from one of the ChLoadable interfaces, whereas ChNoteXYZ is). The fact that ChNodeXYZrot is already inherited from ChNodeXYZ is not enough to overcome this issue.

I am already thinking of modifying ChNodeXYZrot so that it can be used for this purpose in the short term. (Btw. this fix would be more intricate than it seems, because of how the class hierarchy was originally designed in Chrono. Probably in future we will redesign some part of the class hierarchy to avoid get stuck with situations like this, but it will require some time.)

regards

Alessandro Tasora

From: Radu Serban

Having said that, the formula for Bxa on line 601 is actually incorrectly implemented in the code.  It should be:

double Bxa =  ( m_PacCoeff.rbx1 + m_PacCoeff.rbx3 * pow(sin(gamma), 2) ) * cos(atan(m_PacCoeff.rbx2 * kappa)) * m_PacScal.lxal;

Note the missing parentheses.  With this, it is clear that this is just an extension of the classical formula which includes an additional effect of the camber angle gamma (and reduces to the classical formula at 0 camber).

I’ll make sure to incorporate this fix as well.

Thank you Szabolcs and Rainer!

Hi Szabolcs,

thanks again for looking into details.
1. During the simulation X1 is the argument of the atan() function. It is just to prevent chrono from calculating atan(+-90°), which might happen in extreme manoeuvers. In 'normal' situations, there shouldn't be any difference indeed.
2. It is a formula I found in the Adams/Car documentation, it is not official. Some of our users know adams and have access to Pacejka tir files or are just familiar with it. It is a simple form of combining Fx+Fy. I didn't find any great effect yet. The official Pacejka method for combined forces is actually not implemented. We will do it, when we can get a validated data set, which includes the respective coefficients, or test data.

Subject: RE: [chrono] ChTriangleMeshShape doesn't respect ChVisualization::Pos
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 10 Aug 2021 11:56:39 +0000

You are correct.  This is an inconsistency in the Chrono::Irrlicht run-time visualization module where the ChVisualization::Pos and ChVisualization::Rot are ignored for some assets (such as trimeshes).  We are planning a redesign of the visual asset system in  Chrono anyway (for other reasons) and will try to take care of this as well at that time.  In the meantime, the solution for adding any translation or rotation when attaching a trimesh asset is the one you mentioned: transforming the underlying geometry.

--Radu

To: ProjectChrono<mailto:projectchrono@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [chrono] ChTriangleMeshShape doesn't respect ChVisualization::Pos

I am not sure if this has been caught by someone else already, but I just noticed that to change the position of  a chrono::ChTriangleMeshShape object for visualization, we can't simply get it done by setting the Pos attribute it inherited from ChVisualization. Instead, we need to apply the changes directly to the geometry::ChTriangleMeshConnected object we passed to it.

I haven't tested if it's also happening to ChVisualization::Rot or the collision model. Just want to give everyone a heads up.

Unfortunately, this is not going to be anywhere close to real time.
To use a fully resolved approach, with DEM, the simulation time step for 2 um particles would probably be in the range of 1E-7 seconds, if not smaller. It’ll take a very, very long time to simulate this.
To use a continuum approach and use a fluid for deposition is a very tough problem. We just started to do in our research something close to this (one paper will come out next week, another paper was submitted last week), and unfortunately the CFD code is not at a point where it could be used for production runs (is not in the main Chrono repo).
My two cents: try to reformulate your problem and try to model it in a smart way that gives you qualitative insights into the process. I would be really surprised if there is a solver that can solve this fast enough (real time) if you stick with a high fidelity model and try to capture 2 um particle motion.

Dan

From: Dan Negrut

Unfortunately, this is not going to be anywhere close to real time.
To use a fully resolved approach, with DEM, the simulation time step for 2 um particles would probably be in the range of 1E-7 seconds, if not smaller. It’ll take a very, very long time to simulate this.
To use a continuum approach and use a fluid for deposition is a very tough problem. We just started to do in our research something close to this (one paper will come out next week, another paper was submitted last week), and unfortunately the CFD code is not at a point where it could be used for production runs (is not in the main Chrono repo).
My two cents: try to reformulate your problem and try to model it in a smart way that gives you qualitative insights into the process. I would be really surprised if there is a solver that can solve this fast enough (real time) if you stick with a high fidelity model and try to capture 2 um particle motion.

Dan

  2.  AFAIK, there is no explicit support for electrostatic forces. However, being open source I imagine it is fairly straight forward to implement a solution by defining your own force element that captures this type of interaction. Again, share with us what you have in mind and we might be able to offer an alternate path for modeling this

Hi David,

Happy to hear you appreciate our work 😊

I assume you are talking about Chrono::Vehicle models, correct?
If that is the case, you can simply get a handle to the ChShaft attached to each wheel using ChVehicle::GetSuspension() and then ChSuspension::GetAxle(), for example:
    auto shaftFL = my_vehicle.GetSuspension(0)->GetAxle(VehicleSide::LEFT);
Then use ChShaft::SetAppliedTorque() to apply a torque to that shaft (which is rigidly attached to the wheel spindle body).

Having said that, you must take into account that, as long as a driveline and powertrain subsystems are attached those may/will interfere with any of your externally applied torques (which will propagate through the driveline and powertrain).

Maybe you can provide more details on what exactly you attempt to achieve.  Are you trying to model a vehicle with independent motors actuating each wheel (I plan on eventually implementing such support in Chrono::Vehicle)? Or is it something else?

--Radu

From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 9 Jan 2022 16:22:30 +0000

I see, you are using your own visualization system.  In that case, unless you have it fully interfaced to the Chrono asset system, you will not be able to use that to visualize the collision shapes (you cannot overlay Irrlicht or OpenGL on top of your rendering).

For now, I suggest you use the Bullet collision system (if you design your Chrono code appropriately, you can switch between the two collision systems with one flag) and use the btIDebugDraw mechanism as illustrated in that demo (replacing the underlying call to the Irrlicht line drawing function to one using your own visualization system).  In principle, it’s not all that difficult to provide a similar mechanism for rendering collision shapes when using the parallel Chrono collision; I’ll look into that at some point.

--Radu

Radu Serban schrieb am Sonntag, 9. Januar 2022 um 12:17:44 UTC+1:
Run-time visualization of Chrono modeling elements (mostly bodies, but also some connections such as linear and rotational springs) is done by attaching visual assets to these elements and then using a run-time visualization module such as Chrono::Irrlicht (which you must enable and configure during CMake configuration).

Once you configure and build Chrono with Irrlicht support enabled, look at any of the demos named “demo_IRR_***” for examples of attaching visual assets to your bodies and having those rendered during simulation.

Look also at demo_IRR_debugDrawer_collisionModels which may be exactly what you want.  That uses a class derived from btIDebugDraw and interfaces to Irrlicht calls for the actual rendering.

Radu Serban schrieb am Sonntag, 9. Januar 2022 um 12:17:44 UTC+1:
Run-time visualization of Chrono modeling elements (mostly bodies, but also some connections such as linear and rotational springs) is done by attaching visual assets to these elements and then using a run-time visualization module such as Chrono::Irrlicht (which you must enable and configure during CMake configuration).

Once you configure and build Chrono with Irrlicht support enabled, look at any of the demos named “demo_IRR_***” for examples of attaching visual assets to your bodies and having those rendered during simulation.

Look also at demo_IRR_debugDrawer_collisionModels which may be exactly what you want.  That uses a class derived from btIDebugDraw and interfaces to Irrlicht calls for the actual rendering.

--Radu

Hi Yi,

So is this similar to shrinking the radius of a cylinder to compress the
material? This is quite a special use case, I am pretty sure there is no
easy "one-liner" in Chrono::GPU that helps you do that. There are however,
several approaches that you can consider.

1. Use several planar BCs to mimic a cylindrical boundary. You can
gradually offset those planes towards the center axis. This is probably the
most straightforward...
2. Implement a cylinder radius offset functionality yourself. Look into
*ChSystemGpu_impl::setBCOffset* function to see how it is done for
quantities such as cylinder center location, and write something similar.
When you are done, you can use it to change your cylinder radius over time
steps. This is some coding but maybe not too hard. Sorry right now I can't
do that for you.
2. You can do that via supplying a deforming mesh to represent this
shrinking cylinder at each time step. If you are more comfortable working
with meshes, then let me know, because we may need to work together a bit
to make it happen. This is probably a bit more work than the other
approaches.

I hope it is helpful and let me know your questions, thank you,
Ruochun

Hi Yi,

If you mean whether it is possible to move a boundary not by a prescribed 
motion, but by simulating its dynamics, then it can be done. Depending on 
how complex its dynamics is, you may or may not need Chrono Engine in 
addition to Chrono::GPU. In any case, the ingredient you need from 
Chrono::GPU is *GetBCReactionForces* or *CollectMeshContactForces*, 
depending on whether you represent this boundary by a Chrono::GPU boundary 
or a mesh. Then, with the granular force information, if the dynamics is 
simple enough, like granular material pushing a piston along a fixed 
direction, then just inside your script you can write a small snippet to 
calculate the velocity, position etc. for your boundary, then offset or 
SetMotion your boundary accordingly. If the boundary is a part of a complex 
mechanism then it is a co-simulation, you probably need to do the dynamics 
of your parts with Chrono Engine, then feed it back to Chrono::GPU. To put 
it simply, it is not clear what a stress/force would do to an abstract 
boundary, to move it or to deform it, unless you put that boundary in a 
scenario. You are the one who knows that scenario, so only you can manage 
its dynamics.

If you mean whether it is possible to directly apply external forces to 
some particles at certain user-defined locations, such as near a boundary, 
then no, Chrono::GPU currently does not have an API specifically for that. 
But like I said you can inspect the force granular particles exert on a

Subject: RE: [chrono] Multicore Questions
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 26 Aug 2021 07:36:20 +0000

Justin,

Your problem seems a very good candidate for a co-simulation setup.  This would allow you to use the best numerical methods and parallelization for the different physics involved.  You could use a ChSystemSMC with the HHT integrator and a direct sparse linear solver for the FEA meshes (this does some work in parallel using OpenMP) and Chrono::Multicore (OpenMP-based parallelization) for the spheres.

The two additional objects could be included on either side (ideally on the Chrono::Multicore side as they are rigid objects, just like the spheres, but that may require some tweaks to the code to allow Cascade bodies in Chrono::Multicore).

As long as you are fine with spherical shapes and SMC, you could in principle also use Chrono::Gpu for the simulation of the spheres, but the complete support to co-simulate with flexible elements is not yet in Chrono::Gpu.

So I’d stick with Chrono::Multicore for now.  Note that this would also allow you to use either SMC or NSC for contact between spheres and between spheres and the FEA cables (more precisely whatever “proxies” you would create for the FEA cable elements on the Chrono::Multicore side).  The contact interactions between the FEA cables themselves would be resolved with SMC on the other side.

Setting up such an (explicit,  force-displacement) co-simulation framework is not absolutely trivial, but not all that difficult.  You need to decide how you want to handle communication (I suggest MPI which is what I’ve always used for such problems) and decide how to represent the proxies for the FEA elements on the Chrono::Multicore side.  Then you communicate FEA state information to the Multicore side, update the proxies there and resolve contacts among spheres and proxies, and communicate back contact forces on the FEA proxies (which are included as external loads on the FEA cables).

Setting up such an (explicit,  force-displacement) co-simulation framework is not absolutely trivial, but not all that difficult.  You need to decide how you want to handle communication (I suggest MPI which is what I’ve always used for such problems) and decide how to represent the proxies for the FEA elements on the Chrono::Multicore side.  Then you communicate FEA state information to the Multicore side, update the proxies there and resolve contacts among spheres and proxies, and communicate back contact forces on the FEA proxies (which are included as external loads on the FEA cables).

You can see a description of such an approach in the following two papers (where we were interested in FEA flexible tires interacting with deformable granular terrain):

  *   https://www.researchgate.net/publication/317196609_A_high-fidelity_approach_for_vehicle_mobility_simulation_Nonlinear_finite_element_tires_operating_on_granular_material

Subject: RE: [chrono] About the coulomb friction model
From: Dan Negrut
Date: Thu, 14 Oct 2021 13:19:53 +0000

Hi Liu – there are SMC (smooth contact) and NSC (non-smooth contact) approaches to handling friction and stiction in Chrono.
The former looks at the history of micro-displacements to figure out when to stick and when to slip. In other words, the solver keeps track of the history of the contact.
Details are here:

  *   On the Importance of Displacement History in Soft-Body Contact Models | J. Comput. Nonlinear Dynam. | ASME Digital Collection<https://asmedigitalcollection.asme.org/computationalnonlinear/article/11/4/044502/477537>
  *   https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9717/9/10/1813/pdf

For NSC, there is a complementarity approach that uses the friction cone to switch between friction and stiction. Details are here:

  *   Posing Multibody Dynamics With Friction and Contact as a Differential Complementarity Problem | J. Comput. Nonlinear Dynam. | ASME Digital Collection<https://asmedigitalcollection.asme.org/computationalnonlinear/article/13/1/014503/384577>

A comparison of SMC and NSC is presented here:

  *   Phys. Rev. E 96, 042905 (2017) - Compliant contact versus rigid contact: A comparison in the context of granular dynamics (aps.org)<https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.96.042905>

Regarding whether this is an improvement over Bullet – we have not compared them head-to-head so I can’t tell.

I hope this helps. Thank you for your interest in Chrono.

Dan

--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] Global coordinate system
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 6 Aug 2021 12:10:01 +0000

Roberto,

All reference frames in Chrono are right-handed.  What you see is simply an issue with the Irrlicht run-time visualization which uses left-handed coordinate systems.  So everything you render using Irrlicht is shown mirrored left/right.

Furthermore, Chrono does not impose any particular orientation of the global reference frame.  The default gravity acceleration is set along the negative Y axis, but you can change that to anything else.

--Radu

I took a look at this and found the cause of the problem.  It turns out that the ChLoad implementation had a bug for the case of  meshes with nodes that are set as “fixed” (like in this example).  We didn’t see this problem before because we only used pressure loads for FEA meshes used to model flexible tires in which no nodes were such constrained.

I pushed a fix and the code is now available in the ‘develop’ branch of the Chrono GitHub repository.

Hi Yi,

You can find rolling and friction modes defined in *ChGpuDefines.h*. Right
now, each of them has 3 possible selections thus mapped to 0, 1 or 2. As
for the checkpoint file, if you did not set those modes, then the default
values were written to the file. You can always load the checkpoint file as
is, then change the rolling friction setting later in your script. You can
set the rolling mode with something like this:
*gpu_sys.SetRollingMode(CHGPU_ROLLING_MODE::SCHWARTZ)*. Is there no GPU
demo showing this? Well, then there will be one in the next release.

I think *SCHWARTZ* is the only implemented rolling friction mode (despite
another was planned... but then we shifted focus towards developing the
new-gen Granular code). You can have a look at how it works in a device
function called *computeRollingAngAcc*.

Hi Szabolcs,

sorry for the late answer, there were some other things to be done. I 
modified the original demo_VEH_HMMWV_Accel so that it produces a chart 
similar to yours.
It look ok to me. During the acceleration by the engine the vehicle gets a 
roll angle caused by inertia effects. The engine/gearbox must generate a 
reaction torque to the 
car body. In low gear positions the effect is higher than in higher gear 
positions. During the shifts 1->2 and 2->3 you can see a peak. This peaks 
comes from the 'too' high 
revolute speed of the engine that has to be pulled down for the higher gear.

After the maximum speed is reached, the vehicle is braked to zero, the 
engine inertia effects are a bit lower, but the vehicle itself is not 
completely symmetric. That leads
to differences in the tire forces. Generally also the tire forces are not 
symmetric for -kappa:+kappa and -alpha:+alpha in the Pacejka tire models.

Rainer
