Subject: [chrono] [BUG] Copy constructor of ChSystem is unusable

Hello,
I ran into a crash when attempting to use the copy constructor of a ChSystem, and I found the reason why in ChSystem.cpp.

if using something like :
ChSystemNSC* copied_sys = new ChSystemNSC(original);

The copy constructor calls the function SetTimestepperType (line 108).
In this function we test if the timestepper type is the same as the one we want to set by comparing it with GetTimestepperType (line 461), which is simply calling copied_sys->timestepper->GetType(), without any kind of check.
This produces a crash, as the timestepper for this is empty at this point.

I'm sorry I'm not familiar enough with GitHub to open an issue there, but I still wanted to report this.

problem's solved. for those beginners who has a similar problem.
1. loading the newer version of GCC (I use GCC/9.2.0)
2. toggle advanced mode in cmake
3. copy/paste my current c++ path to CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER (it has to be

Hi Wen-Huai,

I believe the issue is that you use a too old version of GCC (4.4.7).  In the installation guide you linked to, we indicate that you need GCC 4.9 or newer.  Check with your sysadmin on how to get access to a more recent version of GCC (which is now at version 11!).

As to your questions about the CMake configuration:

  *   It is OK if you do not have Ccache (that helps with speeding up recompilation – likely something you do not care about).
  *   CUDA is not required, unless you enable the FSI or GPU modules of Chrono.
  *   The way you provide Eigen should be fine.
  *   You need to have a Linux build of Irrlicht if you want to use Chrono::Irrlicht.  You need to talk to your sysadmin about making that available (or else build the Irrlicht sources yourself).  There are prebuilt Irrlicht packages for various Linux distributions.
  *   You may want to build the Chrono libraries in “Release” (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE) for performance.

Hope that this helps,
--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] generic quaternion (ChLinkMotor)
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 20 May 2021 11:27:08 +0200

dear Laurent,

my suggestion, in general, is that you generate quaternions using the 
function

  Q_from_AngAxis(alpha, v)

that takes an angle alpha, in radians, and an axis of rotation v, of 
unit lenght. A frame is generated in this way: you assume an initial 
frame with absolute alignement, then it is rotated about v by an angle 
alpha (clockwise, looking in the direction of v). Look also a primer on 
coordinates and rotations in Chrono at this page:

 https://api.projectchrono.org/coordinate_transformations.html

By the way, once you define a ChFrame for a ChLinkMotor*Rotation* motor 
constraint, _the Z axis of such frame is used for the rotation axis of 
the motor_. So just generate a ChFrame that is rotated in space where 
you prefer, using for example Q_from_AngAxis(alpha, v), up to the 
alignment that has Z in the direction you like as a motor shaft./Note 
that the v in Q_from_AngAxis(alpha, v) is not the Z shaft, in fact./

Alternatively: you can build a 3x3 rotation matrix from 3 orthogonal 
axes , using the constructor

ChMatrix33 
<https://api.projectchrono.org/group__chrono__linalg.html#ga1731277b7b93ed8a6c8d5d4802bd7698> 
(const ChVector 
<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_vector.html><> &X, 
const ChVector 
<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_vector.html><> &Y, 
const ChVector 
<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_vector.html><> &Z)

for example ChMatrix33<> my_rotation(my_X, my_Y, my_Z) ; and then you
symbol: Re: [chrono] generic quaternion (ChLinkMotor)

text:
<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_vector.html><> &Z)

for example ChMatrix33<> my_rotation(my_X, my_Y, my_Z) ; and then you 
extract the quaternion as ChQuaternion<> my_quaternion = 
my_rotation.Get_A_quaternion(). In this approach, my_Z is exactly the Z 
axis of the frame, hence it is also the shaft of the motor you need. 
Maybe more intuitive.

For ChLinkMotor*Linear : *same stuff, except that this time _the X axis 
of the frame is used for the direction of the linear guide_.

regards

Alessandro

Hi Lindy, 
thanks for sharing the code, I found the error. You are defining "builder" 
three times, so what happens is that your node A1/B1/C1 and A2/B2,C2 are 
actually referring to the same nodes, aka the first/last node of the latest 
definition of builder. In other words, A1 is "the first element of the list 
"builder" " but since the instance to which builder refers to changes, so 
does A1. You can see this by moving the print statement AFTER you define 
the third builder.
To solve this, just use 3 different names for the 3 different builders (or 
build the build in an iterable...)
Please find attached the fixed version of the script.
Simone

Hi Geoffroy,

I hope that you've already worked this out, but I ran into the same problem 
and am posting here now in case someone else encounters the problem.

For me, what caused the issue was copying over the *Release *DLLs for 
ChronoEngine.dll etc. to my  C:/workspace/my_project_build/Debug folder 
instead of the *Debug *dlls/pdbs. These should be located in your  
C:/workspace/chrono_build/bin/Debug folder (assuming you compiled both 
Release and Debug versions of Chrono when you installed, which you should 
do). Replacing these files allowed me to compile and run in debug mode. 
This is written up in the tutorial page "Building a Project that uses 
Chrono" located here 
<https://api.projectchrono.org/tutorial_install_project.html>under the 
heading "Important Information for Windows Users", but I found it rather 
difficult to parse.

Anyway, hope this helps someone!
David

   with CMake and VS, it's not a big deal to enable the pychrono module and 
   build it yourself on your machine.
   - option 2: the python interpreter you are using does not correspond to 
   the one you installed pychrono for, in this case, Anaconda "base" env. 
   Speaking of which, installing packages in the base env is not recommended, 
   you usually create a new virtual env and work there, so that if enythning 
   goes wrong you can just delete the environment without messing up the whole 
   Anaconda installation.

Hi Michael, 
thanks for sharing the code, I found the error. You are defining "builder" 
three times, so what happens is that your node A1/B1/C1 and A2/B2,C2 are 
actually referring to the same nodes, aka the first/last node of the latest 
definition of builder. In other words, A1 is "the first element of the list 
"builder" " but since the instance to which builder refers to changes, so 
does A1. You can see this by moving the print statement AFTER you define 
the third builder.
To solve this, just use 3 different names for the 3 different builders (or 
build the build in an iterable...)
Please find attached the fixed version of the script.
Simone

Subject: RE: [chrono] Add a towed objet
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 9 Sep 2021 08:44:19 +0000

Hi David,

Yes, Chrono::Vehicle includes support for modeling trailers and their connection to a vehicle.  A trailer is a special type of a “rear chassis” and is connected to the main chassis with a hitch “chassis connector” (there are other types of rear chassis and connectors for different applications).  For wheeled vehicles, there is a class named ChWheeledTrailer<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/chrono_vehicle/wheeled_vehicle/ChWheeledTrailer.h> which combines these two components together with an arbitrary number of axles.

You can see an example of a concrete template instantiation of a trailer in the Kraz truck model (https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/chrono_models/vehicle/kraz/Kraz_trailer.h). See also one of the associated demos, for example demo_VEH_Kraz_ OpenLoop<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/vehicle/wheeled_models/demo_VEH_Kraz_OpenLoop.cpp>.

A trailer system can also be specified through JSON files (see class WheeledTrailer<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/chrono_vehicle/wheeled_vehicle/vehicle/WheeledTrailer.h>).  A sample set of JSON files, modeling a Ultra_Tow 40in x 48 in trailer, is provided in the Chrono data directory (under vehicle/ultra_tow/<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/tree/develop/data/vehicle/ultra_tow>).  See demo_VEH_WheeledJSON<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/vehicle/wheeled_models/demo_VEH_WheeledJSON.cpp> for an example of using that model with one of the JSON-specified Chrono vehicle models (you will need to enable the creation of a trailer by modifying line 201 in that demo)

Subject: Re: [chrono] Moving on rails
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 7 May 2021 11:45:22 +0200

Hi Konstantin

There are different options in train multibody dynamics, depending on 
the level of detail of the model, for example:

1- simplified kinematic models like point-over-spline, that simply guide 
the wheels on a precise direction, but lack of complex effects like the 
unilateral contact property (otherwise the wheel would never detach from 
the rail) and the fact that the wheel can slide few millimeters 
laterally *and vertically* climbing a bit over its ridge so the contact 
force bends to counteract the lateral force, but this vertical-lateral 
coupling would be lost.

2- advanced models based on 3D contact patch force estimations, as 
Kalker theory. Those are very precise, and capture the real 3D and 
unilateral nature of the rail-whell contact, but require lot of 
computational efforts.

3- models that approximate the effects of 3D contact patch models, ex. 
by precomputing Kalker values and putting into a lookup tabel to be used 
in multibody simulation, or similar ideas.

If you just want to simulate things like sloshing of tanks, or 
pantograph dynamics, or the estimation of overall centrifugal forces, or 
basic longitudinal dynamics for max-min acceleration etc., then the idea 
n.1 (ideal rail constraint) could be accepted, but once you enter the 
study of stability, train suspensions, comfort, safety, etc., then a 
simplified kinematic constraint is not enough and you should use 
approaches 2 or 3.

A short paper wish some bibliography on models:

https://re.public.polimi.it/retrieve/handle/11311/1136785/511879/IAVSD2019_contact%20in%20MBS_full%20paper_BINBIN%20LIU.pdf

There are many other similar papers dealing wiht the same problem of

Unfortunately, in Chrono there is not yet any custom constraint that

From: Radu Serban

Omar,

The function you used returns the terrain surface normal direction (always a unit vector).

What you want to use is the function ChTire::ReportForce which returns a struct which includes the terrain-tire force, momentum, and an application point.  Supposedly, you want the vertical component of the force.  In PyChrono, you would do something like:
   tf_FL = vehicle.GetTire(0, veh.LEFT).ReportTireForce(terrain)
   tire_force_z_FL = tf_FL.force.z
Here ‘0’ represents the front axle (axles are numbered starting with 0 at the front) and ‘veh.LEFT’ indicates the vehicle’s left side (use ‘veh.RIGHT’ for the right side).   As mentioned, tf_FL is a struct with fields ‘force’, ‘moment’, and ‘point’.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] GPU module error local pos in SD
From: Ruochun Zhang
Date: Wed, 20 Oct 2021 21:12:02 -0500

Hi Dallas,

Almost all such problems are caused by some sort of inefficient contact
event capture, so 2 particles tunnel through each other, leading to huge
contact force being calculated, particles launched at extreme velocities,
then crushing the simulation. Kinda like what happens every day in Source
engine games.

You can do the following:
1. The best way is to reduce the simulation time step. I tried, 1e-7 would
work for your test scenario. You can probably get away with something
larger like 5e-7, but note 1mm radius particles are already very fine and a
step size this small can be required.
2. Increasing the damping can help, albeit not as much as time step size.
And if your model mandates a selection of damping coefficients, then do not
change it.

A different note: the Chrono version you are using is sort of old. If you
decide to update to the newest, you can use my attached script, it
just reflects a few API changes. The new Chrono::GPU version also allows
checkpointing so you potentially don't have to use the same time step size
all along.

Thank you,
Ruochun

Subject: Re: [chrono] rigid contact accuracy
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 29 Jul 2021 11:36:29 +0200

Dear Farhad

the problem is that if you use obj files, the collision engine uses the 
mesh-mesh algorithm to detect the contact points. This is a slower and 
less reliable algorithm, that should be used as a last resort if you do 
not have other choices: maybe that the contact points aren't the same 
number (and quality) of the ones that you generate using the primitives 
(ex box vs box). This is especially true when the obj meshes are 
face-to-face in near singular situations, like the case of the wall of 
bricks, where many faces are aligned, many are matched, etc. Probably 
the result is more reliable if your obj meshes are a bit randomized in 
terms of initial positions, or if they have some bevel at the edges, etc.

Alessandro Tasora

Subject: Re: Simulation Crash
From: Ruochun Zhang
Date: Mon, 23 Jan 2023 14:59:52 -0800 (PST)

Hi Mohammad,

If it is still working fine, then that is good and I can explain this new 
fix. For an end user, it is however not a big concern. 

There is a step in the domain discretization that is materialized by doing 
two essentially identical kernels in serial, one for allocating the correct 
size of memory and one for actually filling out the memory. The code used 
to rely on those two kernels producing the same result, and in most cases 
they do. However, when triangles are involved, there is something like a 1 
in ten or one hundred billion chance that they do not agree, presumably 
because of the floating point arithmetic execution order. It can in the end 
leave one integer slot at a random state, and that one will then be used as 
an index, causing a segmentation fault. It is subtle, and I did learn 
something in the process of chasing it down.

Thank you,
Ruochun

text:
Subject: RE: [chrono] Purpose of TrackShoeStates and TerrainForces
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 13 Jul 2021 08:30:50 +0000

Chrono::Vehicle is designed to work in both monolithic mode (where all systems and subsystems are simulated within Chrono, as in most demos) and in co-simulation mode (where vehicle-terrain interaction is done outside Chrono).  These two different modes are supported for both wheeled and tracked vehicles.

In the latter case, the supported co-simulation mode is explicit, of force-displacement type.  In such a framework, the vehicle provides the (track shoe / wheel spindle) body states (the “displacement”) and the external terrain provides the forces acting on the (track shoe / wheel spindle) bodies (the “force”).

When the vehicle-terrain interaction is also done by Chrono (e.g., in the demo you mentioned) no data needs to be exchanged and so the BodyStates and TerrainForces are not needed/used (but they still need to be defined for some of the API calls).

--Radu

symbol: Re: DEM-engine parameter calibration

text:
Subject: Re: DEM-engine parameter calibration
From: Ruochun Zhang
Date: Wed, 28 Jun 2023 09:42:00 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Giovanni,

1. In general, we should still use the "true" material properties since 
they have physics meanings. In my opinion, in DEM simulations, Young's 
modulus, CoR, grain shape and such, should be obtained from the grains in 
use and their material, not the other way around. However, if using true 
properties is too numerically challenging or does not give some bulk 
properties we wanted, or some physics properties are just not available, we 
could relax/tune some of them. To start off, I suggest just hand-tune it: 
Try reproducing the experiments that show friction angles, viscosity etc. 
(one of the demos is the repose angle test, and maybe we should add a 
flowrate demo too...) with DEM-Engine, then run them with your educated 
estimation of material properties, then measure the bulk properties in 
question (for example, see line 224 in the ConePenetration demo to see how 
bulk density is measured). Change the grain properties then repeat the 
process to understand how the bulk properties change w.r.t. them, until you 
have satisfactory bulk properties. For the properties you are interested 
in, Young's modulus and CoR and nu are probably minor, and *mu, rolling 
resistance (Crr), grain mass and grain shape* are probably more impactful. 
Just a suggestion: Even if you are using DEM particles much larger than 
true powder grains, try to use clump particle shapes that sort of resemble 
the powder grain shape (or at least somewhat deviant from pure spheres),
symbol: Re: DEM-engine parameter calibration

text:
Just a suggestion: Even if you are using DEM particles much larger than 
true powder grains, try to use clump particle shapes that sort of resemble 
the powder grain shape (or at least somewhat deviant from pure spheres), 
because the particles shape is probably very impactful but less easy to 
alter between simulations.

Of course, if you have many material properties to tune and many bulk 
properties to match, it is possible to automate the process using data 
science technologies. That would be a longer discussion. Usually educated 
estimates and a few trial runs work well for relatively simple physics like 
you are simulating.

2. If you just want to total force and total torque, then you can use *tracker 
*objects to get that information. You may look into the Centrifuge demo 
line 167 to see how contact acceleration and angular acceleration are 
extracted from an object (note it is acceleration, so to get force you need 
to multiply that by masses, as in the demo). You *Track *an object, then 
obtain information about the tracked object using the *tracker *handle. 
Force information can only be obtained from the simulation, the 
visualization tool can do nothing about it. 

However, if you would like all the forces pairs (maybe for example, when 
you need to do structure deformation co-simulation), you have two choices. 
One is that you write contact pairs to files. See an example in the 
GRCPrep_Part1 demo line 167, *WriteContactFile *method. You will have the 
locations and forces of all the contacts. You should extract the "SM" type 
of contacts only, that is the sphere--mesh contacts. The second choice is
symbol: Re: DEM-engine parameter calibration

text:
GRCPrep_Part1 demo line 167, *WriteContactFile *method. You will have the 
locations and forces of all the contacts. You should extract the "SM" type 
of contacts only, that is the sphere--mesh contacts. The second choice is 
doing something like in the FlexibleMesh demo (it's a new demo and you may 
need to check out the newest version), line 253, use a tracker to get all 
force pairs concerning a tracked object. The benefit of that is you get the 
locations and forces as C++ vectors directly, so you may use it directly in 
your script for other purposes. It makes more sense to visualize pairwise 
forces too (for example using Paraview Glyph), should you need a force 
visualization like in one of DEME's frontpage GIFs. But based on your 
description you probably just need a total torque.

Let me know if there is anything else,
Ruochun

From: Ruochun Zhang
Date: Wed, 6 Oct 2021 21:49:18 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Darwin,

The current CohesionRatio is more in line with the Bond number: it is a 
ratio between the adhesive force (pull-off force) and the particle weight. 
It is a simple model where if 2 particles are in contact, there will be a 
constant cohesion force *F = C * ||mg|| * n* between them, where *C* is the 
CohesionRatio, *n* is the contact normal, *||mg|| *is the weight of one 
particle. It is only related to one variable in the code, which is called 
*cohesionAcc_s2s*. *cohesionAcc_s2s* gets its value in 
*ChSystemGpu_impl.cpp*, and participate in force calculation in 
*ChGpu_SMC.cuh*. It would not be too hard to modify this model to suit your 
purpose.

In the mean time, we happen to be investigating the effect of cohesion too, 
and more sophisticated cohesion models such as the one you mentioned, may 
be added to the code, soon.

Thank you,
Ruochun

Subject: Re: [chrono] ChBody Mass Matrix - Are nonuniform translational

From: Letournel Lucas
Date: Mon, 8 Mar 2021 09:26:37 +0100

Hello David,

We actually changed the mass variable of Chrono, to a 6x6 mass matrix 
including added mass, in FRyDoM (see links below), which is based on 
Chrono v4.0.

It's a bit tricky, and a colleague of mine implemented it, so I can only 
give you the basic concept : we derived ChVariables to 
FrVariablesAddedMass in which we can modify the mass matrix and added 
this new variable in FrBodyBase, which derived from ChBodyAuxRef. We had 
to override IntToDescriptor and IntFromDescriptor methods to take into 
account this new variable, and all methods related to the manipulation 
of the variable.

We then set this variable in FrMorisonModelBase::SetupInitial() (same 
method in FrRadiationModelBase, for the radiation with the potential 
linear theory). We can change the added mass, computed with the Morison 
theory at each time step, in FrMorisonModelBase::Update. We also had to 
override IntLoadResidual_Mv method, since our Morison model is based on 
a ChPhysicsItem class.

While this method give good results with multi bodies simulations, 
including kinematic links, from Chrono, we are aware that it does not 
work when we have FEA elements. It's a limitation related to the solving 
methods in the ChMesh, which cannot take into account the new variables 
injected in the bodies, that we still need to work on.

You can take a look in FRyDoM at

  * front page : https://frydom.org/ <https://frydom.org/> (links on the
    front page are broken, sorry...)

Thank you very much for your insight and comments. I really appreciate them.
About your comments:
“maybe just my impression, but I see that the flywheel starts with a non-uniform angular velocity, like it is subject to some residual torsional vibration that later disappears”

I believe that the behavior at the beginning is related with the homogenous rotor’response contribution. As far as the particular (forced) response “dominates “, that contribution vanishes. That the reason user has to wait 1 sec. before “acquiring” the measurements, as an attempt just to collect mainly the forced response. By now, that 1-sec period has been empirically set up (I have to work on it).

“I already implemented some Jeffcott rotor test ( in c++ in demo_FEA_beamsIGA.cpp), are you aware? “

 it would be nice if you implement also an automatic computation of the Campbell diagram of the rotor... this would require some modal analysis features that are not yet in the develop branch of Chrono, but will be in future.”

Thanks for that kind suggestion. By now, I am trying to focus on modelling only the measurements we expect to get from a typical experiment in a rotor kit experiment. I mean, it is up to user to figure out how to process the discrete time-domain measurements he (she) got from the virtual rotor kit’ experiments. Those “measurements” are delivered by the application as simple txt files. I like to think this approach encourage the user (e.g. student) to look for a strategy to process the measurements.

From: Radu Serban

Hi Alan,

This is an issue when running from *within* Visual Studio, whether you hit F5 (“Start debugging”) or Ctrl-F5 (“Start without debugging”), and has to do with the “Working Directory” property of the project (in this case the VS project of whichever demo you are trying to debug).

More recent versions of CMake provide a mechanism to properly set this at configuration time and so the latest Chrono code will automatically take care of this for you.   However, this was not available at the time we released Chrono 4.0.

The solution is simply to go in the Properties of the demo VS project, go to ‘Debugging’ and change ‘Working Directory’ from $(ProjectDir) which is likely what it is right now to $(OutDir).

Best,
--Radu

P.S.  I strongly encourage you to update to the latest version of Chrono!

Darwin,

What do you mean by “when I build the solution in Visual Studio, it is unable to build the gpu module”?

Look through the output from CMake for a message line ‘==== Chrono GPU module ====’.  What do you see right after that?
From what you describe, I suspect that even though you enable the GPU module, the CMake script ends up disabling it, either because of a CUDA or Eigen issue.  So, you are actually never building the GPU module nor any of the associated demos.

--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] Re: Revolute joint friction?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 19 Jan 2025 11:38:51 +0000

Hi Michele,

You didn’t specify if you are interested in non-smooth (NSC) or smooth (SMC) contact formulation.  As Alessandro pointed out, for the latter, there’s no need to mess with the friction constraints. For SMC, you could include the proper friction forces by using a ChRSDA (for revolute joints) or ChTSDA (for prismatic joints) with custom TorqueFunctor<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/75fb6835587d33fa1e2956f5ae40d50d5688b965/src/chrono/physics/ChLinkRSDA.h#L74> or ForceFunctor<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/75fb6835587d33fa1e2956f5ae40d50d5688b965/src/chrono/physics/ChLinkTSDA.h#L117>, respectively.  In the implementation of these custom callbacks, you have access to all quantities you would need to implement a friction model (such as Coulomb).

--Radu

It is not easy to do because (at least in a context of DVI nonsmooth dynamics) it requires some low level stuff in terms of ChVariable and ChConstraint class hierarchy - even if probably one could just reuse the ChConstraintTwoTuplesFrictionT class that was meant for 3d contact, and put it inside a ChLinkMate-inherited new constraint along with other ChConstrainTwoBodies. Hi Tianyuan,

This was not exactly a problem with the INP file, but rather an issue 
with the Chrono loader function which was not dealing properly with 
Windows line endings ('\r\n'). I pushed a fix (in the 'develop' branch 
of the Chrono repository). Please pull the latest code and let me know 
if this fixes the error.

Regarding your other questions:

  * Note that 'demo_FEA_cosimulate_load' (in the main Chrono
    distribution) and 'test_FEA_cosimulate_granular' (in the
    chrono-projects repository) do not solve similar problems. In the
    former, the tire interacts with a flat rigid surface (implicitly
    defined in the functino PerformEsternalCosimulation). The latter
    considers a granular terrain.
  * 'test_FEA_cosimulate_granular' uses two separate and independent
    systems (one for the tire, the other for the terrain). Run-time
    visualization can be done for one or the other system. The demo
    happens to do it for the tire side and as such you will not see the
    granular material.
    You could modify the code to render at run-time the simulation on
    the granular terrain side; that is the Chrono::Parallel system in
    that program. There, you could visualize at run-time the granular
    terrain particles as well as the proxy bodies corresponding to
    elements in the FEA tire mesh.
  * The animation you see in the video was generate in post-processing
    (as you can see in the code, during the simulation we save data that

Subject: RE: [chrono] Add DOF to vehicles imported using json files
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 21 Feb 2023 13:33:54 +0000

The connector used in the articulated vehicle demo is one of several provided in Chrono::Vehicle (namely ChChassisConnectorArticulated which allows actuation – in this case based on steering input).  We also provide ChChassisConnectorHitch which is modeled as a passive ball joint (used for example to connect a trailer) and ChChassisConnectorTorsion which is modeled as a revolute joint with a rotational spring-damper.  The latter is used in some of our vehicle models to model chassis torsional compliance (with the axis of that revolute joint aligned with the longitudinal (x) vehicle axis).  If this is what you are trying to model, look at the MTV vehicle models in Chrono (https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/tree/main/src/chrono_models/vehicle/mtv) and associated demos.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Saving simulation results in an output file
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 5 Aug 2020 10:07:53 +0200

Thomas,

Qiyuan is correct. The philosophy of Chrono is that this is left up to 
the user, since it is the user who controls the main simulation loop 
(this is true for both the C++ and Python APIs). Inside the main loop, 
after taking a step you can query whatever element you need and extract 
the desired information (states, forces, etc) and process that however 
is most convenient for you.

We provide a very simple utility class (CSV_Writer, see 
https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/chrono/utils/ChUtilsInputOutput.h) 
which can be used to output common Chrono types to ASCII files. Look at 
demo_VEH_HMMWV for example.

--Radu

On 8/3/2020 5:35 PM, 'Qiyuan Zhou' via ProjectChrono wrote:

text:
Subject: Re: Saving simulation results in an output file
From: Qiyuan Zhou
Date: Mon, 3 Aug 2020 08:35:30 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Thomas,

In your simulation somewhere, you should see a loop that looks something 
like this:

while(myapplication.GetDevice().run()):     
  myapplication.BeginScene()
  myapplication.DrawAll()
  myapplication.DoStep()
  myapplication.EndScene()

This is the loop which runs your simulation while either the irrlicht 
window is open, or while you are exporting frames to POV-Ray.

To save quantities of interest (let's say a body's position vs time), you 
simply need to make the following changes:

times=[]        # Array to store times
pos_x=[]        # Array to store x positions
pos_y=[]        # Array to store y positions
pos_z=[]        # Array to store z positions

while(myapplication.GetDevice().run()):  
  myapplication.BeginScene()
  myapplication.DrawAll()
  myapplication.DoStep()

  # Append quantities of interest to arrays
  times.append(my_system.GetChTime())
  pos_x.append(my_body.GetPos().x) 
  pos_y.append(my_body.GetPos().y)
  pos_z.append(my_body.GetPos().z) 

  # Print the current time in the console (optional)
  print ('simulation time: ', my_system.GetChTime())   
    
  myapplication.EndScene()

In fact, you can throw any time dependent quantity inside of this loop. An 
example of specifying a time dependent force is shown in this post 
<https://groups.google.com/forum/?oldui=1#!searchin/projectchrono/sin%7Csort:date/projectchrono/jRzOT6uG5IA/ZepTXFC-BwAJ>
.

Hope this helps

-Qiyuan

From: Radu Serban

Hi Emin,

By default, a TSDA is declared as "non-stiff" which disables Jacobian 
calculation. You must explicitly declare such an element as "stiff" 
which will trigger calculation of Jacobians and inclusion in the KR 
matrices. See ChLinkTSDA::IsStiff 
(http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_link_t_s_d_a.html#a6d66843eb00335c68cf22deb670a8af6)

Best,
--Radu

Subject: Re: Rigid body interacts with granular materials
From: Ruochun Zhang
Date: Tue, 8 Dec 2020 16:39:38 -0800 (PST)

Hi Yi,

For question 1, yes, if you need to load in a mesh for interaction with the 
granular material, overwrite with mesh API.

For question 2, I would suggest you always use meshes for cosimulations, 
and this is the general idea we had in developing it. There are several 
integrated boundary shapes in Chrono::Granular (spheres, planes...) which 
have potential usage in representing rigid bodies, but they work better 
with prescribed motion only. Besides, if the shape is simple then meshing 
it won't be hard, if the shape is complex you need a mesh anyway.

To define mesh MOI and volume centroid properly I tend to use CAD packages 
to pre-compute them, like I can use Rhino...

Then with some knowledge of Chrono core module you should be able to feed 
that into the cosimulation.

One thing to note... as of now, please load in a mesh whose volume centroid 
is at exactly (0,0,0), OR, use the mesh translation option during
* load_meshes* to make it so, if you wish to do a cosimulation (don't need 
to do this if no cosimulation, just prescribed mesh motion). You see, there 
are no API for you to feed in the mesh centroid now, so being at (0,0,0) is 
an implicit assumption. I'm doing stuff to allow users to specify mesh 
centroid in future updates, but if you keep this convention, nothing should 
ever break with current or future releases.

Thank you!
Ruochun

Milad,

For the ‘convex hull’ collision shape, the order of the points does not matter.
What ChConvexHullLibraryWrapper does is eliminate points inside the convex hull and also create a trimesh that is suitable for visualization.
In you case, working with convex hexahedrons, you already know all 8 points are in the convex hull and it may be simpler to manually create the visualization trimesh.
As far as demos go, you can look at demo_IRR_earthquake – that one uses (convex) shapes with 20 vertices but still relies on ChBodyEasyConvexHull.

--Radu

On Wednesday, August 5, 2020 at 1:26:22 AM UTC-7, Radu Serban wrote:
Milad,
If your hexahedrons are convex, I think the best option is to use a convex hull collision shape (explicitly, through ChCollisionModel::AddConvexHull or using the ChBodyEasyConvexHull function).  For concave hexahedrons (if you even allow for non-quadrilateral faces) you can easily decompose that into two convex pieces and use two convex hull collision shapes.
By the way, collision for FEA is done differently: the exterior surface is extracted and, for collision purposes, that is represented either as a node cloud or as a triangular mesh.  In other words, there is nothing special done for a particular FEA element (such as the 8-node brick).

--Radu

The solver settings you mention are relevant when using *NSC *contact. 
For an example of using spinning friction with that contact formulation, 
look at demo_PAR_friction 
(https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/parallel/demo_PAR_friction.cpp).

utest_SMCp.h 
(https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/tests/unit_tests/smc_contact/utest_SMCp.h) 
which is used for several SMC unit tests with Chrono::Parallel.

Note that in order to obtain accurate results with frictional contact in 
the SMC formulation, it is important to use the so-called "MultiStep" 
tangential displacement model (as set in utest_SMC.h; see the function 
SetSimParameters). Currently, this model is available in 
Chrono::Parallel, but *only *for sphere-sphere and sphere-box interactions.

I hope this helps,
--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] Issue with multi-core module
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 4 May 2021 13:51:48 +0000

Hi Ivan,

The custom collision detection library in Chrono::Multicore does not do well with mesh-mesh interactions.  In the core Chrono engine (which currently uses the collision detection from Bullet), this particular pair-wise interaction is treated separately (and comes at a performance cost).  This is because typical generic narrow-phase algorithms (MPR in Chrono::Multicore and GJK in Bullet) are really meant for (strictly) convex shapes and do poorly on triangle-triangle collision detection.

If/when possible, we actually recommend to use primitive shapes and, when that is not possible, decompose concave meshes (such as your “tank”) into convex parts and use ConvexHull collision shapes.  Collision detection with convex hulls is more robust and performant than with triangle meshes.


I hope that this helps,
--Radu

Le vendredi 3 octobre 2025 à 15:41:17 UTC+2, Radu Serban a écrit :
Antoine, happy to hear that solved the issue.

That value represents a “thickness” for the mesh (which mathematically has zero thickness) which can significantly - as you observed - improve the robustness of the collision detection between two meshes (for collision of a mesh with some other primitive, leaving that value at zero will work because the necessary “thickness” is provided by the other shape).

Collision between two triangles is broken down into collisions between features of the triangles. This thickness value effectively changes vertices to (small) spheres, edges to (thin) capsules, etc.  Consider the case of an edge-edge collision. With this value to zero it’s almost sure the collision will be missed.

Antoine, happy to hear that solved the issue.

That value represents a “thickness” for the mesh (which mathematically has zero thickness) which can significantly - as you observed - improve the robustness of the collision detection between two meshes (for collision of a mesh with some other primitive, leaving that value at zero will work because the necessary “thickness” is provided by the other shape).

Collision between two triangles is broken down into collisions between features of the triangles. This thickness value effectively changes vertices to (small) spheres, edges to (thin) capsules, etc.  Consider the case of an edge-edge collision. With this value to zero it’s almost sure the collision will be missed.

Although the default value is set to zero, it is crucial to set a small positive value, especially when interested in mesh-mesh collisions. Maybe I’ll just change the signature of that function so that it does not have default arguments.  Typing a few more characters is better than getting incorrect results.

--Radu

Derek,

The reason you do not see interaction between the "tires" of the simple 
car model and the CRG terrain is that those are simple rigid cylinders 
and as such rely on the collision system to support the vehicle. That 
means you need a collision shape for the terrain (a large rigid box, a 
trimesh, etc). On the other hand, the CRG terrain subsystem in 
Chrono::Vehicle is designed to work with tire models such as Pacejka, 
Fiala, TMeasy which perform their own geometric calculations and only 
expect a terrain subsystem to provide height, normal, and coefficient of 
friction at any given point.

There is an option in the Chrono::Vehicle CRG terrain to export a mesh 
generated from the CRG terrain specification. That mesh is primarily 
intended for visualizing the CRG terrain, and not to use it with a rigid 
tire (which is not an appropriate model for serious vehicle dynamics).

The simple car demo (which precedes Chrono::Vehicle) is kept there as an 
example of modeling a more complex multibody system with Chrono. It is 
not intended as an example of doing vehicle dynamics with Chrono. Note 
also that Chrono::Vehicle provides a simplified double wishbone 
suspension template which uses distance constraints to eliminate the 
upper control arms; of course, that's not as simplified as the 
"suspension" in the simple car demo (because the mass of the lower 
control arm is typically larger).

Long story short, a comparison of accuracy is not very meaningful with
symbol: Re: [chrono] CRG Terrain with demo_IRR_suspension

text:
control arm is typically larger).

Long story short, a comparison of accuracy is not very meaningful with 
that toy model.

--Radu

P.S. A vehicle in Chrono::Vehicle need not be specified through JSON 
files. It can also be specified through a set of C++ classes. See the 
models in the models library.

Vito,

Here are a couple of suggestions of things to try:

I would recommend using HHT with one of the direct linear solvers with ANCF 
meshes.  Below is part of a previous forum reply from Radu on this topic.  
Note that there are also some direct linear solvers in Eigen that are also 
exposed SparseLU & SparseQR in addition to Pardiso (from MKL) and MUMPS..

   - For models with FEA meshes, you should prefer using the HHT (or maybe 
   the implicit Euler) timestepper, not the implicit linearized Euler. The 
   latter will work, but the results will not be accurate. Furthermore, for 
   models that also include 3D bodies, you should use the “ACCELERATION” mode 
   of HHT (which is the standard HHT scheme and also the default for the 
   Chrono HHT integrator).  This is because the “POSITION” mode is technically 
   incorrect when quaternions are present (that mode may be a bit better for a 
   model with only FEA meshes.
   
   - In conjunction with an implicit integrator (such as HHT), I recommend 
   always using a direct sparse linear solver (either Pardiso through 
   Chrono::MKL like you were doing, or else the Mumps solver through 
   Chrono::Mumps).  Iterative linear solvers are prone  to stagnate on our 
   type of problems (saddle point) especially since we do not have a good 
   preconditioner (except for the simple diagonal preconditioner we provide as 
   an option).  Having said that, if you do want to experiment with a Krylov 
   solver, you’re better off using GMRES.  Since you are using the latest code
symbol: Re: FEA: High frequency oscillation in reaction forces

text:
preconditioner (except for the simple diagonal preconditioner we provide as 
   an option).  Having said that, if you do want to experiment with a Krylov 
   solver, you’re better off using GMRES.  Since you are using the latest code 
   in ‘develop’, you are aware that I have recently refactored the Chrono 
   solvers and now interface to the iterative linear solvers provided in 
   Eigen.  The MINRES solver from Eigen seems to be particularly fragile – 
   this is an issue I’ve been looking at lately.

You could also look at shrinking your step size as well.

Note: I believe that all of the ANCF elements use a damping model that is 
proportional to the strain rates (i.e. a linear Kelvin-Voigt model).  This 
is a different damping model than Rayleigh damping.

Best Regards,

Mike

Hi Declan,

Yes, this is possible, but not the way you attempted. Instead, you have 
to access the "active camera" in your main simulation loop and modify 
its location and/or target point as desired.
You can see how this is done in Chrono::Vehicle (look at the 
implementation of the function ChVehicleIrrApp::Advance).
Simpler yet, look at demo_VEH_DeformableSoil 
(https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/vehicle/demo_DeformableSoil/demo_VEH_DeformableSoil.cpp). 
There, the camera location is unchanged but its target point is 
continuously updated (so the camera tracks a body). To move the camera, 
also call its SetPosition() function with the desired 3D vector.

--Radu

to model it like this, it would be quite similar to the compressibility 
test we usually do in our paper. Then it should be very easy to model the 
problem in Chrono::FSI (we already have a demo therein). I would model like 
this: have a cylinder that has that particular shape for its bottom. Then 
simply drop water in it, and measure the pressure. Ideally, we need to 
model this system as a three-phase problem which includes granular 
material, fluid, and solid body. The current version of Chrono::FSI can 
support either fluid-solid interaction or granular-solid interaction 
problem. This three-phase problem is still under development. But I think 
the three-phase modeling might be quite similar to the pure two-phase 
fluid-solid interaction modeling in terms of the force on the wall.
Let me know if this makes sense to you.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Upgrade from Chrono 2.0 to 5.0?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 9 Nov 2020 15:45:53 +0100

Hi Geoffroy,

Version 2.0 is from way back in 2013. A code written for that version 
will definitely not work with the most recent Chrono code and the 
changes are likely too many to list.

The change related to shared pointers is due to the adoption of Eigen 
for basic linear algebra in Chrono (but please note that you do not 
replace shared pointers with chrono_types::make_shared, but rather you 
should replace std::make_shared with the new function). Anyway, this is 
one of several API changes that have occurred over the last 7 years.

There are likely more changes you'd have to do, including dealing with 
classes that have been obsoleted and new/better ways of modeling certain 
aspects.

Having said that, I strongly recommend you upgrade to version 5.0 (and 
better yet to the latest code in the 'develop' git branch which is 
already 7-8 months ahead of the last released 5.0 code). This may be a 
bit of work right now and, given the large gap you have to accommodate, 
I think the best way to do this is a top-down approach (i.e., starting 
from what your software needs from Chrono) rather than a bottom-up 
approach (i.e., just trying to fix Chrono API issues).

For the future, once you get this back up and running, it would be a lot 
easier if you did such Chrono upgrades more often.

Best,
--Radu

In fact the ChElement* sources make a large use of linear algebra, and 
this might put some pressure on the template expression machinery hidden 
in the Eigen matrix library (we recently switched to Eigen from our own 
matrix libraries, there are many benefits but one drawback is that Eigen 
requires long building times especially for the way it used templating 
to simplify matrix expressions at compile time)

Alessandro Tasora

Shipeng,

To follow up on Simone’s answer, Chrono includes a model of a legged robot and associated demos on various terrains.  This model is also exposed in PyChrono and, in fact, Simone and I discussed at some point doing some RL work with that particular robot.  As already mentioned, real-time on deformable soil can currently be achieved only with the semi-empirical SCM option.

See:
https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/robot/robosimian/sequential/demo_ROBOT_RoboSimian_SCM.cpp
https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/robot/robosimian/multicore/demo_ROBOT_RoboSimian_Granular.cpp
https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/python/robot/demo_ROBOT_RoboSimian_Rigid.py

--Radu

Hi Shipeng,
Chrono can certainly simulate legged robots. This being said:
1. There are multiple ways to achieve this, depending on your needs, could you please add more details?
2. The easiest way would be to use PyChrono with gym chrono. It features compatibility with openai gym environments and tools (such as sub proc vec env)
3. If you want real-time you want to use SCM terrain. Obviusly simulating millions of particles is not the way to go, but empirical models are probably what you are looking for.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Question about ChBeamSectionAdvanced::SetSectionRotation
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Sun, 9 Aug 2020 20:41:26 +0200

Dear David

pay attention: Sy Sz and Cy Cz are always defined in the original (not
rotated) system. The section rotation affects the direction along which you
compute the Iyy and Izz second moments of area - where the origin for
computing those Izz Iyy is the centroid Cy Cz.
Shortly: the reference for Izz Iyy is the coordinate system which is first
translated by Cy Cz, then rotated.

Note that in the latest push I added a new ChBeamSectionEulerGeneric, that
optionally does not need Izz Iyy, but rather uses two bending rigidity
values about Y and Z axes: the concept is the same anyway (those bending
rigidity values are assumed computed in translated then rotated reference)

Alessandro Tasora

Hi

I suspect that you need to use the MKL solver, because the plain 
iterative MINRES solver here is not using any special preconditioner, 
and most often iterative solvers need preconditioning when handling FEA 
problems with structural elements (beams, shells) as they lead to badly 
conditioned matrices.

Try the MKL solver and tell me.

Alessandro Tasora

From: Simone Benatti

Hi CK, 
my guess was right: just move the initialization of the torqueFunctor 
OUTSIDE the for loop, like
torque = MySpringTorque()
for z in range (4):

AND create it just ONCE, since 
- every time you call it within the loop, "torque" refers to a new object, 
thus the old "torque" is no longer referenced. for this reason the garbage 
collector deletes it and when it is called by the spring you get an error.
- the same goes for initializing once per loop
Since there's no good reason for having more than one TorqueFunctor, just 
create one instance before the loop and you are good to go. There are some 
cases on which you want different instances, and in these cases you should 
populate a list to keep a reference to the objects but again, this is not 
the case! :-)
Simone

From: dr.ratz...@gmail.com
Date: Mon, 13 Jan 2025 22:31:57 -0800 (PST)

Thanks for the example!

Irrlicht3d and VulkanSceneGraph are fundamentally different under the hood. 
3D objects in VSG must be given as indexed face sets with proper shading 
setup. Size, orientation and position must be set by a transformation 
matrix. For a couple of primitive objects (box, shere, cone,...) we have 
convenience functions. User defined objects can be loaded via 3d-graphic 
files. We recommend the wavefront file format (*.obj/*.mtl) because it is 
human readable and has an easy structure.

demo_VSG_assets shows 3D objects bound to bodies and scenery objects, which 
are meant for decoration (treas, houses, animals,...). The scenery objects 
can also be moved, oriented and sized. In the demo you have the 
(Utah)teapot, the (Stanford)bunny, the teleporting sphere and of course the 
forklift truck. You could try at first this basic approach.
It should give you a similar result you have in the Irrlicht based demo. 
The sizing of an object only by a transformation matrix is of course 
limited and does not consider shape changes of the object during 
expansion/compression it is just linear mathematical sizing. There is a 
more sophisticated solution with vertex/normal/color updates but this is 
tricky and should not be tried as a first approach.

Good luck!

Date: Sat, 18 Jan 2025 10:27:41 -0800 (PST)

Hello Roozbeh,

While my background is not solving thermal PDEs, I can provide some ideas. 
I also need some clarifications. 


   - Are the three scalar fields (temperature, humidity, and chemical 
   content) coupled or decoupled? Implementing a solver in Chrono with all 
   three fields coupled is a lot more complicated, and I suggest starting with 
   a small problem with 2 fields coupled. 
   - When you mention that you have "generalized the 1D routine for the 
   diffusion of 3 scalar fields", does it mean, 
      - you customized your own node class based on the ChNodeFEAxyzP.h to 
      handle 3 scalar fields? That's doable, but you have to properly initialize, 
      populate and assemble all the fields. 
      - Or you created three separate meshes, each for one field variable? 
      This should work for a decoupled case; make sure you adjust the thermal 
      conductivity and specific heat values to match the governing equations for 
      humidity and chemical content. You can still use the same API call, since 
      under the hood, the same type of equations is solved. 
   - Regarding the the error you saw from Eigen, this usually happens when 
   some matrix/vector access is out of bounds. Maybe the indices are 
   incorrect, or the fields are not initialized properly. I suggest that you 
   step through the code with a debugger, check the dimensions, and also 
   verify the matrix/vector size after initialization. 

Hope my suggestions help.

text:
Subject: RE: [chrono] Real-Time Capability of Rigid Body Vehicle Model on
 Rigid Terrain
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 6 Aug 2025 09:32:13 +0000

Hi Stefan,

Let me provide a little bit more background and details on this.

Decoupling the physics and rendering in two separate threads or processes is common practice, especially in the gaming industry. Since you already do that, I will not elaborate further.

Regarding simulation of (wheeled) vehicle-terrain with Chrono, please keep in mind that Marcel is only using the so-called “handling tire models” available in Chrono::Vehicle (Pacejka, TMEasy, TMSimple, Fiala).  What all these models have in common is that the only information they need from a terrain system is the terrain height and normal at a point on the terrain below a query point (Chrono::Vehicle provides several options, using 1, 4, or more query points in order to establish the tire-terrain geometric relationship).  Identification of the point on the terrain corresponding to a query point is done by casting rays from the query point(s) into the (collision) terrain surface.

In Chrono::Vehicle we did not special-case a mesh that is used to represent a rigid terrain. Instead, we use a “generic” Chrono collision mesh which can also be used for the typical Chrono collision and contact interactions. What we suggested to Marcel and what he did in his simulator was to specialize meshes that represent a terrain, taking advantage of the characteristics of these meshes (e.g., the fact that they are mostly “flat” and as such, one can implement an efficient broad phase (e.g., using binning in the “horizontal plane”) for ray casting that quickly discards most mesh triangles as intersection candidates.

What all these models have in common is that the only information they need from a terrain system is the terrain height and normal at a point on the terrain below a query point (Chrono::Vehicle provides several options, using 1, 4, or more query points in order to establish the tire-terrain geometric relationship).  Identification of the point on the terrain corresponding to a query point is done by casting rays from the query point(s) into the (collision) terrain surface.

In Chrono::Vehicle we did not special-case a mesh that is used to represent a rigid terrain. Instead, we use a “generic” Chrono collision mesh which can also be used for the typical Chrono collision and contact interactions. What we suggested to Marcel and what he did in his simulator was to specialize meshes that represent a terrain, taking advantage of the characteristics of these meshes (e.g., the fact that they are mostly “flat” and as such, one can implement an efficient broad phase (e.g., using binning in the “horizontal plane”) for ray casting that quickly discards most mesh triangles as intersection candidates.

I contemplated implementing this type of optimization in Chrono::Vehicle. The problem for us is that we also have other tire models available (e.g., rigid tires and FEA-based tires) which rely on the underlying Chrono contact formulation to generate the tire-terrain forces.  That means that a specialization of terrain meshes would need to deal not only with ray casting, but also collision detection against arbitrary collision models present in the Chrono system.  That is doable but is not a very high priority.

Thank you both for your responses.

Dan – I truly appreciate the pointer to The Last Garage. It’s an impressive piece of work, and I fully understand that such results are the outcome of sustained effort—not something to be achieved in a short afternoon. I certainly don’t underestimate the complexity involved in building robust real-time simulations.

Marcel – your practical insights are very helpful, especially the emphasis on decoupling rendering from the physics loop. That’s indeed the architecture we follow as well.

In our case, the 1 kHz target is not due to fast motion dynamics, but rather stems from the requirements of the motion cueing system and real-time hardware integration. While we employ classical motion cueing algorithms (e.g., washout filters and tilt coordination), which operate in the lower frequency range (typically below 10 Hz), the simulation loop needs to run at high frequency to ensure low-latency signal delivery and stable control of the motion platform. Our setup involves full dynamic simulators with a human operator onboard, so the control interface must respond smoothly and predictably to external disturbances.

By way of background: I’ve been developing simulation software myself for many years and have been involved in scientific research in multibody dynamics and real-time applications. We’ve developed our own simulation kernel that achieves real-time performance for rigid MBS, but it currently lacks in tire modeling and terrain interaction. This is where Chrono appears promising—especially due to its open architecture and extensibility.

Your replies have given me the confidence that a prototype based on Chrono is a worthwhile path forward. I’m particularly interested in exploring how customizable the tire-terrain interaction can be for our application.

marcel.o...@gmail.com<mailto:marcel.o...@gmail.com> schrieb am Donnerstag, 31. Juli 2025 um 19:00:20 UTC+2:

Hello Stefan, Dan,

Let me chime in here as that's "my" project. It indeed uses Chrono to run real-time vehicle physics (with a lot of work on top as well as Dan mentions, I've been working on this full-time for over three years now).

Let me answer your questions though:

As to how to achieve "stable" simulation at 1000 Hz (to be honest, you don't always need 1000, 500 might be fine too, but that's another discussion), what I've done is completely removed the graphics rendering from the core simulation loop as a first step: you certainly don't need to render every 1 ms, most GPUs won't be able to keep up with that, no monitors can. So decouple that and make a physics loop that does just that: calculate the physics. Well, there is one other thing you want to do there and that's read controller inputs (and possibly provide force feedback effects to wheel and pedals). Then you simply need that thread to keep up with real-time and pace it as well as you can. Most modern computers will be fast enough. Most operating systems you run this on won't be (hard) real-time OS'es and that means you have to settle for a "best effort" synchronization with time. In practice that is very do-able though in my experience.

Let me chime in here as that's "my" project. It indeed uses Chrono to 
run real-time vehicle physics (with a lot of work on top as well as Dan 
mentions, I've been working on this full-time for over three years now).

Let me answer your questions though:

As to how to achieve "stable" simulation at 1000 Hz (to be honest, you 
don't always need 1000, 500 might be fine too, but that's another 
discussion), what I've done is completely removed the graphics rendering 
from the core simulation loop as a first step: you certainly don't need 
to render every 1 ms, most GPUs won't be able to keep up with that, no 
monitors can. So decouple that and make a physics loop that does just 
that: calculate the physics. Well, there is one other thing you want to 
do there and that's read controller inputs (and possibly provide force 
feedback effects to wheel and pedals). Then you simply need that thread 
to keep up with real-time and pace it as well as you can. Most modern 
computers will be fast enough. Most operating systems you run this on 
won't be (hard) real-time OS'es and that means you have to settle for a 
"best effort" synchronization with time. In practice that is very 
do-able though in my experience.

As for the solver, I agree with Dan's feedback, start with the defaults. 
I found them pretty good.

As for performance bottlenecks on a non-deformable, triangulated mesh, I 
would say you might run into some bottlenecks there if you end up with a

Dear Chrono Team,

I am currently implementing a simplified tractor model in Chrono for use in a real-time simulation environment. The model consists of a rigid chassis, a fixed rear axle with steered and driven wheels, and a front axle modeled as a rigid beam suspended via a central pivot (as commonly used in tractor front axles) with additional steering. The goal is to capture the essential dynamic behavior of the vehicle—particularly in heave, pitch, and roll—sufficiently well for deployment on a motion platform.

The vehicle operates on a rigid, non-deformable terrain, represented by a tessellated triangular mesh. The primary excitation arises from terrain-induced vertical disturbances with dominant frequency components up to approximately 10 Hz.

My core question is:
What is the expected feasibility of running such a model in real time using Chrono? In particular:

  *   Are there benchmarks or best practices for achieving stable simulation at control loop frequencies ~1 kHz?
  *   Which solver/integrator is recommended for this type of setup?
  *   Are there known performance bottlenecks when using non-deformable terrains modeled as triangular meshes?

Any insights—especially from prior experience with real-time vehicle simulation or motion cueing applications—would be highly appreciated.

Best regards,
Stefan Oberpeilsteiner

You should be able to model the rover wheel (“tire”) with solid FEA elements, even using an Abaqus INP file. See demo_FEA_abaqus_wheel<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/main/src/demos/fea/demo_FEA_abaqus_wheel.cpp>.
However, as I said before, these element types are currently not supported in Chrono::FSI, so you will not be able to use it on the SPHTerrain.

On the other hand, I am working on the vehicle co-simulation module (which uses a slightly different way of interfacing between an FEA mesh and an SPH system) and, while it is not my first priority to support tires modeled with such elements, I will look into that if I have time. Those would be Chrono::Vehicle tires of type FEATire<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/main/src/chrono_vehicle/wheeled_vehicle/tire/FEATire.cpp> which also loads an Abaqus mesh.

To make a long story short, you cannot do what you want right now, but hopefully sometime not too far in the future.

--Radu

Alex,

First, a couple of questions:
- do you model the FEA tire yourself (if yes, what kind of elements?) or do you use a Chrono::vehicle deformable tire?
- what does "complex" mean? Profile of the tire or tread pattern?

Currently, Chrono::FSI can only deal with a small number of element types. I intend to come back to this eventually and extend it to support all FEM we have in Chrono (but this will not happen in the very near future).  In other words, using directly the FSI module you can right now only use a tire (or any other flexible object) that is modeled with ANCF shells.

However, we support Chrono::Vehicle FEA tires interacting with any of the Chrono deformable terrains (including FSI-based) in the vehicle co-simulation module.  This assumes you would be using one of the FEA tires defined in Chrono::vehicle and not some arbitrary FEA mesh you define yourself (even if in the "shape" of a tire).

If you are working with a Chrono::vehicle FEA tire (supposedly a ChFEATire since you said an ANCF shell tire is not good enough for you) using the co-simulation framework should allow you to do these simulations.

But flexible tires were not yet tested extensively in the co-simulation framework.  Having said that, I am currently revisiting that module and, as soon as I return from travel next week, I intend to work precisely on co-simulation of FEA tires. I will be focusing on ChANCFTire and ChReissnerTire, but will also test ChFEATire.  Stay tuned.

From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 5 Aug 2020 07:09:13 +0000

Hi Declan,

The functions you listed below are internal Chrono functions and should not be invoked directly by the user (moreover, these particular functions will likely be obsoleted at some point).

The question is: what do you want to happen when the spring length reaches that threshold value?  If all you want is for it to not generate a force anymore, you can use the callback mechanism provided in ChLinkTSDA and implement the desired logic in the user-supplied override of ForceFunctor::operator().  If however, you want the two bodies to be constrained not to approach any further, you will have to enforce that through your kinematics (i.e. include appropriate joints / constraints for whatever kinematics you want) or maybe through contact.

--Radu

Hi Lucas,

Just a couple of additions to Luning's comprehensive reply.

  * The envelope is an outward distance from each collision shape. As
    Luning mentioned, this is needed in the NSC formulation in order to
    include potential collisions before they occur (too small an
    envelope results in instabilities; too large of an envelope is
    inefficient). In the SMC formulation we only care about
    interactions with non-zero penetration; as such, the envelope should
    be 0 for SMC (and is automatically set to that).
  * The margin is an inward distance from each collision shape. It is
    used internally by the Bullet collision system in order to switch
    between two different algorithms in the narrow phase for performance
    and reliability (the GJK algorithm works efficiently for disjoint
    shapes).
  * The setting for "stiff contact" is meant to trigger calculation of
    the Jacobian of contact forces to be used by the integrator (if
    supported). Note that this is not fully functional yet.
  * The additional options currently available for SMC in
    Chrono::Parallel will be implemented in Chrono in the near future.
    The contact history tracking (for the MultiStep tangential
    displacement mode) is a bit trickier to get with the current code
    and will likely take longer; note that even in Chrono::Parallel that
    is limited to only sphere-sphere and sphere-box collisions (so
    effectively for simulations using spherical particles in a container

Hello Lucas,


There are two ways to model contact in Chrono. One is smooth contact, SMC 
model, where small penetration is allowed when bodies come into contact; 
the other is non-smooth contact, called NSC, where bodies are assumed to be 
rigid. The parameters and models you are asking about is more related to 
SMC.


   - Contact Force Model: calculates normal contact force, assumes a 
   general form of Fn = kn*delta_n - gn * vn, where kn is stiffness, gn is 
   damping coefficient, delta_n is contact penetration, vn is relative 
   velocity in normal direction. There are three ones implemented:
      - Hooke - kn is constant, linear model
      - Hertz   - kn is dependent on delta_n, the normal penetration, 
      nonlinear model
      - Plain Coulomb - both kn and gn dependent on delta_n
   - AdhesionForceModel: adhesive force between two bodies
      - Constant: a constant value is subtracted from normal force
      - DMT: DMT_coefficient * sqrt(radius) subtracted from normal force
   - TangentialDisplacementModel: calculates friction force as Ft = 
   kt*delta_t - gt * vt, where kt is tangential stiffness, delta_t is 
   tangential displacement, gt is damping, vt is relative velocity in 
   tangential direction
      - None: no friction force
      - OneStep: tangential displacement delta_t = vt * time_step_size
      - MultiStep: will be implemented in Chrono, track the contact 
      history, more accurate than one step, available in Chrono::Parallel
      - NOTES: 1. Coulomb condition is assured so that |Ft| <= mu * |Fn|;
symbol: Re: Contact parameters

text:
- MultiStep: will be implemented in Chrono, track the contact 
      history, more accurate than one step, available in Chrono::Parallel
      - NOTES: 1. Coulomb condition is assured so that |Ft| <= mu * |Fn|;  
      2. If using Plain Coulomb model for “Contact Force Model”, the friction 
      force is treated as mu * tanh(v_t) * Fn, can not be paired with OneStep 
      Model.
   - user-specified stiffness and damping coefficient: there are two ways 
   to specify the stiffness and damping coefficient in normal and tangential 
   force, namely, kn, kt, gn, gt. Users can: 1) specify these values;  2) or 
   provide material properties: young’s modulus, poisson ratio and coefficient 
   of restitution, the solver calculates kn, kt, gn, gt depending on the 
   normal force model, therefore, the contact force is more physics-based. 
   Note that kn sometimes has to be tuned by two or three orders of magnitude, 
   because a stiff kn means smaller step size and it affects the performance. 
   - restitution and adhesion parameters:  Coefficient of restitution 
   affect damping coefficient in normal direction, gn, in the contact force 
   model; Adhesion parameters can be set either constant or as a DMT model
   - envelope and margin size on the collision shapes: This is related to 
   contact detection; to the best of my knowledge, it only comes into play for 
   NSC, and it has to do with making sure that you start tracking bodies 
   before they collide (since the moment when the envelops overlap, as opposed 
   when the actual bodies overlap; helps with solver stability).

Subject: RE: [chrono] Coordinate system handiness
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 12 Jan 2022 11:28:12 +0000

You are correct, most (if not all) physics engines will use right-handed frames, Chrono included.  For historical reasons, many visualization systems use left-handed frames (with a few notable exceptions, like the more modern VulkanSceneGraph).

You cannot simply flip a switch and start using left-handed frames in Chrono.  Having said that, Chrono does not explicitly enforce this and so you could model some Chrono mechanisms in left-handed frames (but you will need to be careful with the meaning of inputs – applied forces/torques, etc. - and outputs – reaction forces/torques, joint frames, etc.).  Other Chrono systems (most notable Chrono::Vehicle and vehicle systems) assume right-handed frames and will give incorrect results otherwise.

I suggest you do the conversion between right- and left-handed frames in the interface between Chrono and whatever visualization system you use (by the way, what do you use?).  That’s a very simple reflection transformation.  That will save you possible headaches down the road.

--Radu

From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 7 Sep 2020 12:53:28 +0200

Hi Michael,

In general, using a lock-lock joint is a valid solution to this problem.

However, in your case I would consider simply "updating" the existing 
body. You can add new visualization and collision shapes (as you've 
already done). In order to properly update the inertia properties, look 
at the utility class CompositeInertia 
(http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1utils_1_1_composite_inertia.html). 
That will allow you to calculate the new mass, inertia, and COM location 
which you can then assign to the body. For this approach, I would 
recommend using a ChBodyAuxFrame so that you can easily modify the COM 
location without affecting existing visualization/collision shapes (the 
base ChBody assumes a centroidal body reference frame).

--Radu

Vanessa,

This doesn’t seem to be a problem related to that particular Chrono demo. In fact, likely not a Chrono issue at all.

You are probably not looking in the right folder.  Chrono demos will be created in a subdirectory bin/ of your build tree (which you specified during CMake configuration). If nothing else, look at that *.exe.recipe file (it’s a text file) and the full path to the actual executable will be listed there.

Hi RS,

Have you looked in the chrono-projects repository 
(https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono-projects 
<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono-projects>)? All programs in 
that repository are set up the same way as you've probably set up your 
own project (i.e. linking to external Chrono libraries). For example, 
check whether or not test_FEA_shellsANCF works (that uses the PardisoMKL 
solver).

Otherwise, the problem may well be with your model. In particular, if 
you have a model with constraints, ensure that there are no redundant 
constraints. That would lead to a singular system matrix and PardisoMKL 
has issues with such a problem. In that case, consider using the MUMPS 
solver, or else the SparseQR solver from Eigen (also exposed in Chrono).

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] save and restart @WheeledVehicle
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 25 Feb 2021 19:24:00 +0100

Dear Nomoto,

the easiest way may be this:

1) save just the state (pos vector, vel.vector) of your system using

ChSystem::StateGather 
<http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_system.html#aad89e99d7f0d4f6cf90e88134af7748d> 
(ChState <http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_state.html> 
&x, ChStateDelta 
<http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_state_delta.html> &v, 
double &T)

followed by a streaming of the x and v vectors on the disk,

2) and then retrieve it via disk loading and:

ChSystem::StateScatter 
<http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_system.html#a502b6ec64956992c6d5f639b1cf61c80> 
(const ChState 
<http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_state.html> &x, const 
ChStateDelta 
<http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_state_delta.html> &v, 
const double T, bool full_update)

Note that when you "scatter" the x v state, the system must be already 
populated with the same bodies and constraints that were in place when 
you did the "gather", but this might not be an issue given the type of 
problem that you are describing.

Regards,

Alessandro Tasora

A possible solution for a simple case can be storing the current state of 
simulation and using it as an initial condition for the next simulation.
In another word, you can save and store all of the positions, velocities, 
accelerations, forces, and so on at the end of your simulation and start 
the new simulation using these values as initial conditions.

This might be complicated if you have too many parts. There is way to get 
an output in vehicle class here 
<http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1vehicle_1_1_ch_vehicle_output.html#abbb5ef6af21903d85c2daa8c12d227c4a2e52867f99bf00051fc01116f779e8ad>
.
I haven't used this method, but you might be able to export a json file at 
the end of your simulation and use that as an initial condition for your 
next simulation. 

Saman

Hi Emin,
incorporating constraint Jacobian into the analysis is something that is 
little documented.
Our first source of information was this A Direct Eigenanalysis of 
Multibody System in Equilibrium 
<https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220535605_A_Direct_Eigenanalysis_of_Multibody_System_in_Equilibrium>
but most of the work has been done from scratch.

You may also be able to find some consideration on constrained systems in 
some papers of Simoncini, but the approach is more "mathematical/general" 
since it starts directly from matrices on, so you don't find any mention to 
"multibody systems" or anything about the problem from which the matrix 
could be retrieved.

We are probably going to release some (white?)paper on the topic so to have 
a reference point.

Dario

Hi Konstantin,

I think you should be able to use the functionality in ChLinkTSDA which allows it to carry some additional dynamics (assumed to be modeled using an ODE) and have the force generated by this element depend on these additional states.
You would then use this additional ODE (specified through a user-supplied callback class) to model simplified 1-dof dynamics of the “connector body”.  You would also provide a custom functor class to calculate the TSDA force (which can query and use the current values of the additional states).

Of course, you will still end up with a stiff problem, but you would not have to model the full dynamics of the (relatively) small connector body.

You can see these capabilities of ChLinkTSDA used in the implementation of the shock in the FEDA Chrono::Vehicle model (https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/chrono_models/vehicle/feda/FEDA_DoubleWishbone.cpp)

Hope this helps,
--Radu

Let's see how the timing stats are. And you decide the physics. If 
inserting one by one is what you need, then... even if it's a 1000s 
simulation, you probably have to brute force through.

You know, in your case I think the best approach is a hybrid one: You 
UpdateClumps() each time with a small batch, say 1000 spheres. All those 
1000 spheres start with a dormant family. Then they are activated one by 
one. Once they are all done, you add another batch of 1000. This should 
scale better (theoretically scales with the number of currently alive 
clumps), and since the batch is bigger, you don't have that many 
UpdateClumps(), so it's not too expensive there, either. But of course, if 
the load balance is indeed very bad, this probably does not resolve 
everything.

Thank you,

Hi Yves,

In terms of further simplifying the computation, my understanding is that 
if the scale of your simulation is around 50,000 or 100,000 particles, then 
saving time by partially "relaxing" the simulation domain is probably not 
necessary. This is because the number of bodies is low anyway, and further 
reducing the "effective" number of active simulation bodies might further 
blur the performance edge of a GPU-based tool. However, letting the 
simulation cover a longer simulation time using fewer time steps should 
always help.

I feel the best approach is to dynamically select the time step size. If 
you know during certain periods of the simulation, everything is relatively 
"dormant", then you can use large time step sizes during it, using the 
method *UpdateStepSize*. You can change it back using the same method if 
you believe a collision that requires fine time steps to resolve is about 
to happen.

If you still wish to "relax" a subset of the clumps in the simulation, then 
perhaps family-based magics are the way to go. If you believe some clumps 
are effectively fixed in place during a period, then you can again, freeze 
them using the approach I discussed above. This indeed saves time because 
those clumps will simply not have contacts among themselves. You could also 
massage the material associated with a subset of the clumps using the 
method *SetFamilyClumpMaterial*. However, I have to mention that different 
material properties hardly make any impact on computational efficiency.
symbol: Re: DEME-Engine single sphere drop performance

text:
massage the material associated with a subset of the clumps using the 
method *SetFamilyClumpMaterial*. However, I have to mention that different 
material properties hardly make any impact on computational efficiency. 
Soft materials with more damping could allow for a more lenient time step 
size selection, but the step size is still determined by the "harshest" 
contact that you have to resolve.

The ultimate tool is of course the custom force model. If you can design a 
model that is fast to solve and accurate enough for you, and potentially 
resolves different parts of the simulation domain differently like you 
wished, that's probably the best. For a starter, if you do not need 
friction, then try calling *UseFrictionlessHertzianModel()* before system 
initialization to use the frictionless Hertzian contact model. And you can 
develop even cheaper and more specific models after that.

Thank you,
Ruochun
