Hi Yves,

I only had a brief look at the script. So what you needed is to add more 
spherical particles into the simulation, one by one, and I assume you need 
to do this thousands of times.

The problem is that adding clumps, or say *UpdateClumps()*, is not designed 
to be called too frequently, and it's really for adding a big batch of 
clumps. When you call it, you need to sync the threads (perhaps the cost of 
one round of contact detection), then the system goes through a process 
that is similar to initialization (no just-in-time compilation, but still a 
lot of memory accesses). Although I would expect it to be better than what 
you measured (6.2s), maybe you also included the time needed to advance a 
frame in between---I didn't look into that much detail.

In any case, it's much better to get rid of adding clumps. If you know how 
many you will have to add eventually, then initialize the system with them 
in, but frozen (in a family that is fixed and has contacts disabled with 
all other families). Track these clumps using a tracker (or more trackers, 
if you want). Then each time you need to add a clump, use this tracker to 
change a clump in this family (using offset, starting from offset 0, then 
moving on to 1, 2... each time) to be in a different family so it becomes 
an "active" simulation object. Potentially, you can SetPos this clump 
before activating it. This should be much more efficient, as a known-sized 
simulation should be. As for material properties, I don't think they have

Hi Sara,

The nppi library was split into several smaller libraries, which cmake 
packages into the CUDA_npp_LIBRARY variable which Chrono::Sensor uses. The 
issue may be that older versions of cmake try to append the 
CUDA_nppi_LIBRARY to CUDA_npp_LIBRARY for all CUDA versions greater than 5. 
As of cmake 3.10.0, CUDA_nppi_LIBRARY is excluded for CUDA versions 9.0 and 
above.

Ultimately, an older version of cmake may not be fully compatible with a 
more recent version of CUDA. We will make sure to add a check in 
Chrono::Sensor or enforce a higher version of cmake to prevent this issue 
in the future. If you do have a compatible version of cmake (looks like 
3.10.0 or greater), you could check that the CUDA_VERSION variable is 
correctly populated as this determines if cmake looks for 
CUDA_nppi_LIBRARY. Hopefully this helps.

Best,
Asher

text:
Subject: RE: [chrono] Error reading .obj files with subprocess.run()
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 21 Jul 2023 08:20:10 +0000

Hi Vanessa,

All Chrono demos, as they are distributed, assume a certain location of the data/ directory, relative to where the demo is located and run from.  Running the demo through the Python script does not respect this anymore and as such, the underlying (unmodified) Chrono demo cannot find files in the data/ directory.  Whatever demos you say you were able to run from your Python script do not attempt to use any files from the Chrono data/ directory (as is the case with demo_IRR_raycast_test).

The solution is to modify the C++ code to make an explicit call to chrono::SetChronoDataPath() and provide the location of the data/ directory you wish to use.

In general, I strongly suggest not to modify demos inside the Chrono distribution. Those are set up the way they are so that they can run from the location where they are built (and only from there), regardless of the particular user setup.
What you should do is copy the Chrono demo you are interested in somewhere else and then set it up as an external project.  Look at the sample we provide in template_project<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/tree/main/template_project> and the additional instructions at https://api.projectchrono.org/tutorial_install_project.html.

When you do this, make sure to modify the copied demo so that it makes a call to SetChronoDataPath() before any other calls to Chrono library functions, just as is done in my_example.cpp<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/2c254b61fb8cf3111f2430565e2836a32e5e21cd/template_project/my_example.cpp#L30> at line 30 and point it to, say, the data/ directory in the Chjrono source tree.  If you set that to an absolute path, you should then be able to invoke the resulting executable from your Python script, regardless of the relative locations of the Chrono executable and the Python script.

No, you cannot (easily) do that. A tire is not a body (except for the 
special case of rigid tires), but rather a "force element". 
Theoretically, you could model only the spindle bodies and after export 
(i.e. in Chrono) create tire elements. However, that is not 
straightforward, as the tire models are designed to work with 
Chrono::Vehicle.

You could maybe look at how I implemented the ChTireTestRig (which also 
uses a tire model "outside" a proper vehicle model).
But I think you'd be better off working with Chrono::Vehicle from the 
beginning and extend it as needed for the particular vehicle topology 
you're interested in.

--Radu

You have the following 3 options for a SolidWorks plugin (see 
http://projectchrono.org/download/)

 1. Chrono::SolidWorks add-in for SolidWorks 2018 and higher. Compatible
    with the develop branch of chrono.
 2. Chrono::SolidWorks 5.0 add-in for SolidWorks 2018 and higher.
    Compatible with Chrono 5.0.
 3. Chrono::SolidWorks 4.0 add-in for SolidWorks 2014 and higher.
    Compatible with Chrono 4.0.

If you want to continue using the Chrono version from the *master 
*branch (that's version 5.0), you should use *option 2* above.

But unless you have a strong reason not to, I suggest you switch to the 
*develop *branch of Chrono (which, as indicated, is compatible with 
*option 1* above).

Hi Joe,

The load (force) must be added to a "load container" which itself must

load_container = chrono.ChLoadContainer()
mysystem.Add(load_container)

force = chrono.ChLoadBodyForce(mbody2, chrono.ChVectorD(100,100,100), 
False, chrono.ChVectorD(0.1,0.1,0.1), True)
load_container.Add(force)

Date: Tue, 24 Nov 2020 16:42:31 -0800 (PST)

Hi Lennart,  

Sorry for the *late* reply but we did look into it. It turns out to be a 
lot to explain.

For your first question I think it's always reasonable to modify 
AVERAGE_SPHERES_PER_SD_X/Y/Z_DIR to suit your need, however the TOO MANY 
SPHERES! issue is not caused by this limit. It is caused by that the old 
version performs no collision detection on Windows (I would be surprised if 
you weren't using Windows) due to a different compilation environment. So 
in the end the *simulation* drives the spheres to pack so densely together 
at the bottom, that the SD sphere limit is breached.

Right now we fixed this issue along with many others... better late than 
never I'd say. If you are still considering using Chrono::Granular, *please 
pull the newest version from the develop branch, compile and re-run your 
test script*. Note that, the *.csv* file you attached in this post is not a 
runnable profile, because the spheres overlap heavily and it's not 
physical; I suppose you got this as an output from a previous (buggy) run. 
What you can do is to start the simulation anew, from your initial profile, 
and I'm sure you'll get a reasonable result.

Thank you!
Ruochun

After some simulation time without problem, I often got the "TOO MANY SPHERES! SD xxxx has yyy spheres" error. As I understand it, it warns of too many sphere contacts in one sub domain, which is limited to 256 contacts / SD (for memory allocation reasons). The standard size of a sub domain in one dimension is 3.5 spheres, or 7 sphere radii. This is in my opinion a bit too large for a closely packed setting. For spheres with a radius of 1, the sub domain would have a volume of 7^3 = 343 and, with a sphere filling factor of lets say 60%, would house an average of 343 / (4/3 * pi) =~ 49 spheres. This leaves space for around 5 contacts per sphere, which in my simulation seems to be too few for some sub domains. I suppose in a perfect simple cubic lattice structure, every sphere would have 6 contacts to neighbouring spheres and some sub domains come close to that.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Switching to version 5
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 7 May 2020 11:32:39 +0200

There were several significant changes, including public API changes.
I think the best way to figure out the required modifications to user 
code is to compare side-by-side Chrono demos from version 4 and version 
5 (or from the current develop branch, if you want to start using that).

Starting with version 5, Chrono uses the Eigen library for both dense 
and sparse linear algebra. The most important consequence on user code 
has to do with creation of shared pointers to Chrono objects. As you 
can see in the current version of the demos, you should replace any use 
of std::make_shared with chrono_types::make_shared. For more details on 
this, see the Change Log at 
https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/CHANGELOG.md
With the switch to Eigen, the Chrono solver hierarchy was also changed, 
some obsolete solvers were removed, a few new ones were added, and the 
API for setting solver parameters slightly modified (e.g. better, more 
consistent "Set" function names).

To make a long story short, switching from version 4 to version 5 will 
require some modifications to your code, but these are relatively 
confined and shouldn't take too long.

If you consider switching to the current development version, there is 
one other important change that I made which unfortunately impacts more 
user code. This change, which will be part of the next release, has to 
do with the association between collision shapes and contact materials. 
See 
https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/CHANGELOG.md#changed-collision-shapes-and-contact-materials

Hi,

Just because the complex nature of a ROS setup, we will need to know more 
about your environment and enable extra logging to help you with this.

Are you using Docker(if so please share Dockerfile)? What base OS version 
are you using(officially ROS2 Humble only support Ubuntu22.04, other 
version can cause unpredictable issues). 

To collect extra log, please help me with the following:

Use ROS2 Logging, execute line by line in the same folder you build 
custom_handler:

export RCUTILS_CONSOLE_OUTPUT_FORMAT="[{severity}] [{time}] [{name}]: 
{message}"
export RCUTILS_LOGGING_BUFFERED_STREAM=1 
export RCUTILS_LOGGING_USE_STDOUT=1 
export RCUTILS_CONSOLE_STDOUT_LINE_BUFFERED=1 
RCUTILS_LOG_MIN_SEVERITY=DEBUG ./custom_handler

Use strace:
strace -f ./custom_handler 2>&1 | tail -50

Use ldd: ldd ./custom_handler | grep "not found" 


Hopefully one of these will yield some insights, please upload the info 
generated by each debugging step, if not we will go the core dump analysis 
route.
libconsole_bridge.so is mainly used for ROS2 logging purposes, though it 
should not happen, it shouldn't be catastrophic and cause a segfault 
either. We will see if ldd points to this.


Best,
Patrick Chen
Simulation Based Engineering Lab

Dear chrono users

In my master's thesis, I conducted coupling simulation between vehicle-aerodynamics and vehicle motion using Chrono.
The purpose of the research is to compare the driving stability with and without aero parts.
I think that users who are interested will also say, so I will share the outline.
For vehicle aerodynamic analysis, I used CUBE, which is under development at RIKEN  R-CCS.
By coupling CUBE and Chrono, we were able to execute a simulation  on a supercomputer that takes into account all of vehicle motion(wheel rotation, Steering angle,  6DoF of chassis etc...), vehicle aerodynamics, and driver reaction.

Subject: Re: [chrono] What is the purpose of FEA ChNodeXYZ::SetMass ?
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Wed, 15 Jul 2020 10:52:49 +0200

Dear Tobias

I understand what you mean here, in fact the SetMass() function in
ChNodeFEAxyz is not 100% working.

In theory, it could be used to "attach" point-like (atomic) masses to
meshes, if the mass of finite elements is not enough. Currently almost all
finite elements generate some mass from a density, and that mass is
automatically lumped to the nodes, but you might want to override this, or
add additional point masses.

The atomic node mass should affect
1- inertial forces
2- gravitational loads

The problem is that the implementation is currently incomplete, and only
the first effect is generated (that is, added mass is NOT generating
gravitational loads). Because of this bug, you get the result of your test:
the motion  is slower (because of more inertia) but weight is the same.

Instead, for comparison, if you look at ChBody::UpdateForces, you see how
gravity is correctly working in ChBody - and howewer there is no equivalent
in ChNodeFEAxyz. Will be fixed.

Completing the feature was in my to do list, but later I forgot about this
because none was using it. Now I am out of office for a week, I will see
how to fix this ASAP. I  the meantime please do not use that SetMass
function unless you are simulating problems in zero gravity.

Alessandro Tasora

Hi David,

First of all, I am not exactly sure what you mean by "net force" here.
Considering m*a = Fr + Fa, where Fr are reaction/constraint forces 
(e.g. from joints) and Fa is the resultant of all external applied 
forces, I assume you mean Fa. Indeed, you Fr can be obtained for each 
connected joint separately and converting to the body reference frame.

ChBody::Get_accumulated_force and ChBody::Get_Xforce only provide a part 
of the applied forces and may miss some contributions from other sources.
Because that was confusing, I pushed recently the following changes:

  * Two new functions ChBody::GetAppliedForce and
    ChBody::GetAppliedTorque report the total resultant applied force
    and torque, respectively.
  * Note that the quantities returned from these functions *do not*
    include constraint forces and torques (i.e., nothing from the term
    Fr above)! In particular, they do not include contact forces if
    using the NSC (nonsmooth contact) formulation; but they do include
    the contact forces if using the SMC (smooth contact) formulation.
  * Removed ChBody::Get_Xforce and ChBody::Get_Xtorque.
  * Note that ChBody::Get_accumulated_force is still there to deal
    specifically with forces applied through the force accumulators.

See also the notes about this change in the Change Log at 
https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/CHANGELOG.md.

These changes are available in the latest Chrono code on the 'develop' 
branch in the GitHub repository. It seems to me that you are using

Subject: RE: [chrono] Re: Disable Visualization for Faster Simulation (Pychrono)
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 9 Sep 2021 08:18:46 +0000

Luis,

There’s no built-in capability to use Irrlicht for post-processing.  Having said that, we routinely save enough information from our simulations for off-line rendering and movie generation.  We don’t use Irrlicht, but rather tools such as POV Ray, Mitsuba, VTK, Blender, etc.  Currently, there’s no Chrono support for a formal pipeline for such use, but we are working on one (based on Blender) which will also support PyChrono and will be available hopefully in the not too distant future.

--Radu

Dear Rohit

- the MINRES solver (actually, a projected variant of the MINRES 
solver) was experimental and probably will be removed in future, btw on 
can replace it by the GMRES solver, ex. for finite elements problems but 
without any contact.

- the PSOR is known to be critical when stiff bushings and/or ill-posed 
constraints are used, it is a typical limitation of all stationary 
methods (SOR, Gauss Jacobi, SSOR, etc), nothing strange then.

My hint its that you use the BARZILAIBORWEIN method if using both NSC 
contacts and complex constraints. Yet, BARZILAIBORWEIN cannot handle 
stiffness matrices such as in the case of the bushing you are using, and 
in case of FEA in general. So far there is no solver yet that can handle 
both stiffness matrices and NSC, except some experimental stuff (an 
interior point method and the projected minres). A new solver for this 
scenario will be available in next months hopefully. For the moment, if 
you have FEA and/or stiff bushings, just do not use NSC and simply use 
SMC smooth contacts together with a short timestep.

regards

Alessandro

Well, the eigenvalues should be the same, indeed except for tolerances 
implied by the eigenvector solution procedure (most are of iterative 
nature, I do not know what you are using).

Just remember that:

- in the case of constraints, you cannot do eigenvalue analysis on the M 
and K matrices alone, you must work on 'bordered' matrices M' and K' 
where you add the constraint jacobians to the side of the K matrix, as in

M' = | M Cq|
  | Cq 0 |

K' = | K 0 |
  | 0 0 |

- therefore, if you have constraints, like the chrono.ChLinkMateGeneric 
locking the 6 DOFs, your eigenvalue vector has 6 additional values that 
you must discard (small or negative values). Also rigid body modes can 
be discarded in the same way (small / zero values). The remaining ones 
should be quite the same as the ones you get with the SetFixed(True).

I attach here part of an eigenvalue analysis I did with Pychrono + 
numpy/scipy so you get an idea:

mysystem.DumpSystemMatrices(True,True,True,True,"")

  mrow.append(int(splitline[0])-1)
  mcol.append(int(splitline[1])-1)
  mdata.append(float(splitline[2]))
  return 
sparse.csr_matrix((np.array(mdata),(np.array(mrow),np.array(mcol))))

Subject: Re: [Ext] [chrono] Sensitivity study in Chrono
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 26 May 2020 11:02:33 +0200

Hi Rohit,

Unfortunately this is not a trivial task. Ignoring for the moment the 
issue of efficiently solving the combined system of original EOM and 
sensitivity EOM, deriving the sensitivity equations requires information 
that we do not completely have available in Chrono. We could generate 
the necessary terms in the sensitivity equations through finite 
differencing (note that this is not the same as using FD on the outputs) 
but that is also not a simple and quick thing to do for a code like Chrono.

Extending Chrono with SA capabilities (forward and ideally even adjoint) 
has always been on my "wish list". But that is a major undertaking and 
I don't see it happening anytime soon.

I am afraid the only practical solution for generating local sensitivity 
information with the current Chrono code is through finite differences 
(FD) on your outputs of interest. You may be able to use tools such as 
Dakota (https://dakota.sandia.gov/) even for helping with FD-based local 
SA, even though they are more focused on global SA (along the lines of 
DOEs).

--Radu

Hi Rohit,

There is currently no support in Chrono for (local) sensitivity 
analysis. If you need sensitivities at the nominal design, your only 
solution is using a finite-difference approximation through successive 
simulations at properly perturbed problem parameters. As you may know, 
this has some issues both in terms of accuracy (requiring special care 
in selecting parameter perturbations) and certainly efficiency (although 
all of the required simulations are independent and so could be done in 
parallel).

On the other hand, if you are interested in exploring the whole 
parameter space you should indeed look into DOE, as suggested by dmulroy.

--Radu

it depends... for example if you set a constant torque to some shaft you 
may end with a rotating structure with linearly increasing rotational 
speed (constant angular acceleration), unless you have some nonlinear 
resisting torque that avoids such increasing unlimited drift.

In general it is unlikely that you will provide a torque to some 
actuator in a pure "feedforward" mode, ie. without implementing also 
some type of feedback to correct errors, ex. a PID. Well, this if you 
want to follow some desired position (or speed) setpoint.

Alessandro

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Strange Motor Collision Behavior
From: Alessandro TASORA
Date: Tue, 16 Aug 2022 12:43:53 +0000

Yes, the reason is the one that you quoted.
Both ChLinkMotorSpeed and ChLinkMotorAngle are Rheonomic (or "Rheonomous" in some literature), that is: the position is strictly enforced by some function of time, in a "geometric sense". Hence they don't allow compliance if they conflict with other constraints, and results can be impredictable.

Only by using force- or torque-based motors like ChLinkMotorTorque (and adding PID controllers for keeping approximately the position via feedback loops, for instance) you can simulate that hard-stop scenario you need. But at the cost of more complication, and some compliance and latency and reduced bandwidth - just like realistic servo motors, by the way.

Best regards
Alessandro Tasora

Hi.

I’m trying to simulate a cantilever beam with a bending moment applied at the free end. Here are the datas:

Rectangular section b=30 cm, h=40 cm

Elastic Modulus E=30000 MPa

Length=5 m

M=100 kNm

Density=0

 
The analytical solution gives a constant internal bending moment of 100 kNm, no axial and no shear internal forces.

The displacement at the free end is:

J=1/12*b*h^3=160000 cm4

w=M*L^2/(2EJ)=100*10^6*5000^2/(2*30000*160000*10^4)=26.04 mm

 
I’m using PyChrono for this. Here is the script:

 
import pychrono as chrono

import pychrono.fea as fea

import pychrono.mkl as mkl


print ("Cantilever with end moment");

   
# Create a Chrono::Engine physical system

my_system = chrono.ChSystemNSC()


my_mesh = fea.ChMesh();


msection = fea.ChBeamSectionAdvanced()


#Beam props

beam_wy = 0.3

beam_wz = 0.4

msection.SetAsRectangularSection(beam_wy, beam_wz)

msection.SetYoungModulus(30e9)

msection.SetGshearModulus(10e9)

msection.SetBeamRaleyghDamping(0.01)

msection.SetDensity(0)


# Add an EULER-BERNOULLI BEAMS:

beam_L = 5

startVector = chrono.ChVectorD(0, 0, 0)

endVector = chrono.ChVectorD(beam_L, 0, 0)

hnode1 = fea.ChNodeFEAxyzrot(chrono.ChFrameD(startVector))

hnode2 = fea.ChNodeFEAxyzrot(chrono.ChFrameD(endVector))


my_mesh.AddNode(hnode1)

my_mesh.AddNode(hnode2)


belement1 = fea.ChElementBeamEuler()

belement1.SetNodes(hnode1, hnode2)

belement1.SetSection(msection)

 
my_mesh.AddElement(belement1)


#Ensure mass=0

print('total mass = ',belement1.GetMass())

Subject: Re: [chrono] ChLinkMotorLinearForce change force directions
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 21 May 2020 07:58:30 +0200

Hi Yi,

The "master frame" here represents the joint reference frame on the 
"master" body, which is the 2nd body connected by the linear motor, as 
specified in the Initialize() function. You specify (either explicitly 
or implicitly, depending on which form of the Initialize() function you 
use) what that frame is, so you can indeed orient the direction of the 
motor's axis however you need by rotating that frame to have its X axis 
is along the desired direction.

In demo_IRR_motors.cpp 
(https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/irrlicht/demo_IRR_motors.cpp), 
all linear motor links are constructed with joint frames that happen to 
have an identity rotation, something like
  motor->Initialize(body1, body2, ChFrame<>(location));
but you can change any of them to have a different rotation. For 
example, to rotate the motor's axis by 30 degrees about the Y axis, use 
something like
  motor->Initialize(body1, body2, ChFrame<>(location, 
Q_from_AngY(CH_C_PI / 6));

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] FEA Module, Using Nodal Displacement as Boundary
 Condition
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 24 Apr 2020 10:38:47 +0200

Dear Qian,

in fact, there is no way to impose directly the displacement to a body 
dusing the simulation using a function like SetBodyDisplacement().

Note that you might be tempted to create a body, set it fixed via 
SetBodyFixed(true), then update the position in the while() simulation 
loop using truss->SetPos(...), but this is WRONG. Some users did this, 
and it works only in limited and lucky cases.

What you must do is:

- create two bodies: a _truss _and a _body A_. Only the first has 
SetBodyfixed(true).

- look at *demo_IRR_motors.cpp * to learn how to impose the _motion of a 
body A respect to the truss_. (This is ok if your motion is linear or 
rotational. Alternatively, look at demo_IRR_imposed_motion.cpp that 
tells how to impose generic rototranslational motions).

- use the ChLinkPointFrame constraints to _join your FEA nodes to body 
A_, as you already know.

best,

Alessandro

Correct, you can get the reaction force and torque for a joint using 
Get_react_force and Get_react_torque, respectively. Note that the 
return vectors will be expressed in the link's coordinate frame. You 
can re-express this in whatever frame you need, for which you will 
likely need to query GetLinkRelativeCoords or GetLinkAbsoluteCoords.

You can access the links using Get_linklist assuming you know the index 
of the links you are interested in. Otherwise, you can search for the 
link by its name (SearchLink) or simply use the handle from when you 
created the link (assuming that is in scope).

Get_linklist in Python?

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] bullet collision detection - multi thread
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 23 Apr 2020 13:09:09 +0200

Ok, now I understand what's happening.

There is an optimization for RigidTerrain with multiple patches that I 
have to do but didn't get to yet (and which was only made possible by 
some recent refactoring I did in Chrono related to collision shapes and 
contact materials).
Until I get a chance to put that in, you have 2 options:

 1. use a single patch (if that is easy and straightforward for your
    particular setup)

 2. use multiple patches, but ensure that collision detection is
    disabled between all patch collision shapes. You can do this by
    adding the following two lines after you set up each patch:
    patch->GetGroundBody()->GetCollisionModel()->SetFamily(7);
    patch->GetGroundBody()->GetCollisionModel()->SetFamilyMaskNoCollisionWithFamily(7);
    Here I picked family 7 arbitrarily. But beware that some collision
    family values are already "reserved" for Chrono::Vehicle
    simulation. Any value above 5 is fine. Just make sure you use the
    same one for all terrain patches.

    In other words, your RigidTerrain setup code should be something like:

      RigidTerrain terrain(my_sys);
      int terrain_coll_family = 7;

      auto patch1 = terrain.AddPatch(patch1_mat, ...);
      ...
    patch1->GetGroundBody()->GetCollisionModel()->SetFamily(terrain_coll_family);
    patch1->GetGroundBody()->GetCollisionModel()->SetFamilyMaskNoCollisionWithFamily(terrain_coll_family);

      auto patch2 = terrain.AddPatch(patch2_mat, ...);
      ...

From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 20 Apr 2020 09:11:55 +0200

Hi Nachshon,

Indeed, that issue will hopefully be addressed if/when we embed a newer 
version of the Bullet collision detection (or roll out our own collision 
detection system).

For the tracked vehicle, there's not much that can be done -- the 
vehicle-terrain interaction is always based on rigid body contact (in 
addition to the other contacts internal to the track assembly).
For wheeled vehicle, I am guessing you use rigid tires, correct? One 
thing to try is a different tire model (TMeasy, Fiala, Pac89, or 
Pac02). These not only will give you more appropriate tire behavior, 
but they also do not use the Bullet collision detection. Instead, these 
tire models use a custom collision detection that only queries the 
terrain for height and normal information below a given point. This 
falls back on ray casting in the terrain collision model (also done with 
Bullet). For best performance, also make sure to set the tire collision 
detection mode to "SINGLE_POINT" (which is in fact the default).

--Radu

Hi,

I did not use the spider, but I copied this code for my own purposes. 

One different between ChLinkEngine and ChLinkMotor is that you initialize 
the later with three arguments, instead of just two. For ChLinkMotor, you 
also need the absolute frame that the second body will rotate about. Check 
out Initialize here: 
http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_link_motor.html

You will have to open the spider in SolidWorks or look at the .py file to 
see which marker you need for each of the motors. Then you can do something 
like frame1_1B = chrono.ChFrameD(m1_1B) and pass this frame1_1B as the 
third argument in Initialize. (This is just an example, the m1_1B is the 
name given to one of the markers on Line 32)

Another difference is you do not use the Set_eng_mode or Set_rot_funct. I 
think the spider works by specifying motor angles, in which case you can 
use ChMotorRotationAngle 
http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_link_motor_rotation_angle.html and 
then use SetAngleFunction.

This code uses ChMotorRotationSpeed for my_motor, but the syntax is almost 
exactly the same as ChMotorRotationAngle: 
http://api.projectchrono.org/tutorial_pychrono_demo_crank_plot.html

Hope this helps,

Hannah

Subject: Re: Pychrono optimization opportunities
From: Simone Benatti
Date: Thu, 23 Apr 2020 03:00:19 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Dave,
SetMaxSolverIterations sets the maximum number of times the for loop within 
an iterative solver can run. If is set 1, the iterative solver will run 
once and then stop, regardless of the residuals. In other words, you will 
get a result faster, but there's no guarantee about its accuracy, so that's 
probably not what you want.
Regarding the amount of resources:
- more clock are always welcome
- more RAM wouldn't improve performance, simulations are not memory hungry
- The number of core is a more complicated point: Python processes can use 
multiple cores if they are wrapped around a code that does (regardless of 
the GIL), and chrono linear algebra, based on Eigen, can leverage multiple 
cores. This  being said, the size of the system you described is probably 
too small to effectively. If you could profile how the simulation time 
scales with the number of bodies and cores and report the results that 
would be much appreciated.
Thanks,
Simone

Subject: Re: The problem of the tractor-trailer model
From: Rainer Gericke
Date: Thu, 2 Apr 2020 01:21:00 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Qianwen,

your Adams model uses 'toebar steering' (like in out UAZ bus model) and you 
use 'pitman arm steering' (like in out HMMWV models you said) in your 
model. 

The pitman arm steering fits to our rigid axle suspension model, no problem 
as such.

In your truck model the pitman steering system is located before the axle 
center and in the HMMWV model it is located behind the axle center. That 
means the steering direction is flipped (left curving turns to right 
curving and vice versa).

What you can do:

flip the steering arms to the rear side of the axle and shift the pitman 
arm system behind the axle until it fits again with the steering arms of 
the knuckles.

Or easier, look at this area in the json file of the steering system:

"Revolute Joint":
{
"Location": [0, 0.249, 0],
"Direction": [0, 0, 1], // change this to [0, 0, -1]
"Maximum Angle": 50
},


Best

Rainer

Qianwen,

A few questions/suggestions:

  * Please try to disable the path follower lateral controller and
    instead explicitly set the driver inputs to be
    throttle = 0.5, braking = 0, steering = 0
    Does the vehicle follow a more or less straight path? Of course, it
    may deviate a bit due to possible left/right imbalances (and that's
    why we typically use a path follower even for a straight path).
    However, this will help figure out if the problem is in the vehicle
    model or with the setup of the path follower controller.

  * If the above works, the issue is likely with the setup of the path
    follower controller.
    Have you tried visualizing this with Irrlicht? If you follow the
    example in demo_VEH_SteeringController, you will see I also rendered
    two sentinel points. The red one is rigidly attached to the vehicle
    (at the lookahead distance from the origin of the specified body,
    "vehicle_body" in your case); the green one is the closest point to
    the red point on the path.
    Do these behave as expected? Two things to check:
     1. Is the green dot following the path you expect?
     2. Is the look ahead distance correct? Is the red dot somewhere in
        front of the steerable axle? Not knowing where the reference
        frame for your "vehicle_body" is, it's difficult to say if a
        lookahead distance of 5 is appropriate (that is tuned for the
        HMMWV vehicle used in demo_VEH_SteeringController).

frame for your "vehicle_body" is, it's difficult to say if a
        lookahead distance of 5 is appropriate (that is tuned for the
        HMMWV vehicle used in demo_VEH_SteeringController).

  * I am not sure at what location you start the vehicle. Keep in mind
    that the path in the Chrono data file "paths/straight.txt" is a path
    of length 250, at y=-125 and between points x=-125 and x=+125.
    You may want to use a path tailored to your setup. The easiest way
    to do that is to create a Bezier path programatically. I included

    that these are appropriate for your truck.

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] HMMVW pychrono
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 30 Apr 2020 10:26:28 +0200

Use the SetInitPosition method to change the initial location and/or 
orientation by specifying a coordinate frame. For example:

init_yaw = 30 * (math.pi / 180)
init_loc = chrono.ChVectorD(10, 10, 1)
init_rot = chrono.Q_from_AngZ(init_yaw)
my_hmmwv.SetInitialPosition(chrono.ChCoordsysD(init_loc, init_rot))

As for the vehicle falling through the floor, how do you define your 
"floor"? Do you use a terrain object? That is required when using a 
tire model other than "rigid tires".

So you have two options:

 1. if you use a tire model such as veh.TireModelType_TMEASY (or Fiala,
    Pac89, Pac02), you *must* include a terrain in your system. Look at
    any of the demos provided with the Chrono distribution on how that
    is done.

 2. if you want to define the "floor" as being some body with one or
    more collision shapes, then you are limited to using rigid tires on
    your vehicle (as the only tire types that interact with the
    environment through Chrono's underlying collision system):
    my_hmmwv.SetTireType(veh.TireModelType_RIGID)

I recommend option 1 as it allows you to try out different tire models. 
Note that you can use a RigidTerrain; besides a patch defined as one 
large collision box, as used in the Chrono python vehicle demos, you can 
also add RigidTerrain patches that are specified using a triangular mesh 
(from an OBJ file) or using a height field defined with a gray-scale BMP 
image.

--Radu

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Timesteps, control system integration
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 26 Feb 2020 10:19:43 +0100

Hi Dave,

Iterations relate to an underlying (linear, possibly with constrain 
projection) iterative solver that is used at every time step to solve 
for state corrections. This is for the default settings for an NSC 
system (EulerImplicitLinearized timestepper (integrator) and the PSOR 
solver (iterative). You can have other combinations, but to answer 
your first question: no such calls to physics items are made during the 
solve phase.

You should indeed put your control code in the simulation loop. But you 
must be careful with using myapplication.DoStep, especially if you set 
it to enforce soft real-time (which is done in the example you linked 
to, see the call to myapplication.SetTryRealtime(True) before the 
loop). Indeed, the way this is implemented, it may dynamically change 
the step size to a value below what you specify with 
myapplication.SetTimestep. Having said that, with or without soft 
real-time enabled, myapplication.DoStep will only advance the system 
state once per execution of the simulation while loop.

But when coupling a control system, you may want to just disable soft 
real-time and maybe even just replace the call to myapplication.DoStep 
with a call my_system.DoStepDynamics(step_size). In that case, you can 
still enforce soft real-time, but with an alternate mechanism (which 
does not change the step size); see my answer to Lucas's question here: 
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/projectchrono/6x2R4-H_NHA. Note 
that you can still have the Irrlicht visualization, even if you don't

does not change the step size); see my answer to Lucas's question here: 
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/projectchrono/6x2R4-H_NHA. Note 
that you can still have the Irrlicht visualization, even if you don't 
let the Irrlicht app manage your time stepping; in other words, you can 
simply do:

while(myapplication.GetDevice().run()):
myapplication.BeginScene()
myapplication.DrawAll()
for substep in range(0,5):
my_system.DoStepDynamics(0.001)
myapplication.EndScene()

From: milad rakhsha
Date: Wed, 15 Jan 2020 09:13:34 -0800 (PST)

Yes the TDR is what I suspected is the culprit,
Regarding the memory problem you encountered, this is because of the size 
of global memory on your GPU and the fact that larger systems require more 
space for storing the intermediate state variables for calculation. 
Currently, unified memory is not employed in chrono::FSI, so you will run 
out of memory as soon as your simulation hits your GPU memory capacity. 
This is even more critical for the IISPH method, as it stores a few 
coefficient matrices for your system. As an alternative, you may want to 
look into the ExplicitSPH method which has a smaller memory footprint.

Milad

From: Radu Serban

Rob,

Your issues are due to incompatibilities between your installed version 
of Chrono and the demo that you are working with/modifying. The Chrono 
code changes all the time (including API changes) and demos are kept 
up-to-date. As such, a demo corresponding to the latest Chrono version 
(in the GitHub 'develop' branch) may not work with Chrono v5.0 and will 
certainly not work with Chrono v4.0.

You should *always* look at demos that are compatible with your version 
of Chrono. In your case, these should be in your install directory.

As for your other issues:

  * We will look at the issues you reported about the Windows installer
    for version 5.0. By the way, Chrono must be built in 64-bit so if
    the latest Windows prebuilt binaries install under "Program Files
    (x86)" that also needs to be fixed.
  * You should definitely use a version more recent than 4.0. There were
    significant changes between 4.0 and 5.0 (including the switch to
    using Eigen, which is by the way the reason for these
    incompatibilities in your case). Unless you have a compelling
    reason to use v. 5.0 or to only use the Windows installer, I
    strongly encourage you to build Chrono from the latest sources in
    the 'develop' branch of the GitHub repository.
  * I am not sure I understand exactly what the problem is building from
    sources. During CMake configuration, you must set the variable
symbol:

text:
the 'develop' branch of the GitHub repository.
  * I am not sure I understand exactly what the problem is building from
    sources. During CMake configuration, you must set the variable
    EIGEN3_INCLUDE_DIR to point to the root of your Eigen installation
    (i.e. the path to the directory that contains a subdirectory Eigen/).
    Are you using a proper version of Eigen (see
    http://api.projectchrono.org/development/tutorial_install_chrono.html)

Finally, Chrono is a set of middleware libraries. As such, some 
experience with C++ is necessary. Note that we also provide a Python 
interface to Chrono (http://projectchrono.org/pychrono/) if you're more 
comfortable with that. But keep in mind that not all of the C++ Chrono 
API is exposed in Python (although a pretty large part is).

Hope that this helps.

--Radu

Yi,

Chrono::Granular uses the so-called SMC contact formulation which is a 
penalty-based approach. As such, depending on the values for contact 
material stiffness and damping it will lead to stiff differential 
equations which require smaller step sizes for stability reasons. The 
unstable integration in the granular system likely results in large 
(non-physical) forces that lead to an unstable integration of the 
mechanical system (and hence the constraint violations you see).

Besides experimenting with the step size, you can also try to "soften" 
the contact materials. Does that allow stable integration with the 
larger step size?

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Compliance
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Mon, 17 Feb 2020 18:19:55 +0100

Hi Thomas,


In fact, this model is independent on shape. That is, it bypasses all 
the computations that the software might do with Mindlin-Cattaneo-Hertz 
theory of deformable surfaces, and just assumes that you provide a 
precomputed value of compliance (1/stiffness), on a per-point basis. How 
you get such value, is not chrono's business. For instance: you can 
assume shapes have always the same curvature and yung modulus, compute 
Mindlin-Cattaneo-Hertz formulas on a piece of paper, then input the 
result in Chrono. Or: use a non-physical compliance just in sake of 
regularization (ie. avoid degenerate cases such as a table on 4 legs, etc.).


No way to get it from a material database, unless you do your 
computation using assumed curvature, young, poisson, etc.

Maybe in future we'll align the NSC model to the SMC model so that the 
compliance can be inferred from young / Poisson / curvature, however we 
postponed this until we'll have a new collision detection engine that 
will be more robust in terms of returning the curvature of contacted 
surfaces (currently we're using Bullet and we have some limitations).

NOTE: the fact that you can use 'compliance' in a non-smooth context 
might be surprising, but it is not. In fact, even in case of compliance 
the contact law can be set valued (ex. friction sticking!) and/or with 
sharp changes that advocate the use of the non-smooth formulation.

best,

Alessandro Tasora

Subject: Re: [chrono] how to properly build the template project?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 16 Jul 2020 10:02:18 +0200

It seems that you are setting Chrono_DIR incorrectly. That should 
point to the cmake/ directory in a *build* tree, not in the *source* 
tree (by the way, I assume you use out-of-source build, as recommended 
in our installation guides).

The Chrono source tree has a *template *for a configuration script in 
its subdirectory cmake/ (that template is named 
ChronoConfig.cmake*.in*). When you configure Chrono with CMake, an 
*actual *CMake project configuration script (ChronoConfig.cmake) is 
automatically generated in the build tree, under a subdirectory also 
named cmake/. It is this latter one that you must use to set the CMake 
variable Chrono_DIR when configuring some project that requires Chrono 
(such as the sample template project we provide).

--Radu

Hi Qiyuan,

First of all, thank you for sharing with everyone these detailed instructions.  I am sure many will find them very useful.

I have a few comments/recommendations:

  *   As mentioned on the Chrono documentation site (http://api.projectchrono.org/development/module_parallel_installation.html), if using a recent version of Blaze (3.2 or newer) you do not actually need Boost at all (Boost is a dependency of older versions of Blaze, not of Chrono::Parallel itself).  As you can see from the CMake snapshots you included, you were never asked for the location of the Boost libraries.
  *   I would also recommend getting a pre-packaged version of Blaze (version 3.6 will work just fine), instead of cloning their repository. In other words, treat Blaze the same way you treat all other dependencies in Step 1.  You can get a tarball from https://bitbucket.org/blaze-lib/blaze/downloads/
  *   Currently, Chrono::Granular does not build properly on Windows (and you mention the related errors you get in Step 3).  As such, I suggest simply *not* enabling this module for now; in other words, do not select ENABLE_GRANULAR during CMake configuration in Step 2.
  *   Also, you do not necessarily need to enable USE_PARALLEL_CUDA.  That is a Chrono::Parallel option which would enable some CUDA code in Chrono::Parallel (support for MPM).  Note that this CMake option has nothing to do with the FSI or Granular modules (which do require CUDA)

Best,
Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: ChProbe usage?
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 13 Feb 2020 10:19:13 +0100

Dear Dave,

the ChProbe is a quite old part of Chrono and maybe it will be made 
obsolete in new releases.

If you need to record some data from a simulation into some array-like 
data structure there are many other options, for example I'd suggest you 
to use directly the ChFunction_recorder - just use the AddPoint() 
function at each time step like in


ChFunction_Recorder ref_X;
...

where in your while() simulation loop do something like:

  double my_value = my_body.GetPos().x(); // for example
  ref_X.AddPoint(my_time, my_value);


For example later you can use the POSTPROCESS module to plot the 
ChFunction_Recorder via GNU plot like in:

ChGnuPlot mplot(gplfilename.c_str());
mplot.Plot(ref_X, "-U ref.", "pt 4 ps 1.4");
...

Alessandro

Subject: Eigen sparse matrices and updates to direct sparse linear solvers
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 16 Nov 2019 13:52:13 +0000

Dear Chrono users,

A few days ago, I pushed to the ‘develop’ branch the second set of changes related to our migration to Eigen.
Now, we also use Eigen for all our sparse matrix needs (which are relatively limited and have little, if any, direct consequence on the public API).
A ChSparseMatrix is just a type alias to an Eigen SparseMatrix with double scalar type, row-major storage order, and int storage index type.

The main effects on public API relate to concomitant updates we made to the sparse direct linear solvers (the Chrono::MKL interface to the Intel MKL Pardiso solver and the Chrono::Mumps interface to the MUMPS solver).  While we now rely on Eigen’s own interface to Pardiso, Chrono::Mumps still implements a custom interface to MUMPS (ChMumpsEngine).

For examples of usage, see demo_FEA_cablesMKL and demo_FEA_cablesMUMPS.

Both sparse direct solvers (and any others that may be provided in the future) share the same functionality in terms of controlling the identification and update of the matrix sparsity pattern.  The main features implemented in the base class ChSolverDirect are:

  *   sparsity pattern lock
The sparsity pattern lock skips sparsity identification or reserving memory for non-zeros on all but the first call to the solver setup. This feature is intended for problems where the system matrix sparsity pattern does not change (or changes very little) from call to call.  See ChSolverDirect::LockSparsityPattern.
  *   sparsity pattern learning
symbol: Eigen sparse matrices and updates to direct sparse linear solvers

text:
*   sparsity pattern lock
The sparsity pattern lock skips sparsity identification or reserving memory for non-zeros on all but the first call to the solver setup. This feature is intended for problems where the system matrix sparsity pattern does not change (or changes very little) from call to call.  See ChSolverDirect::LockSparsityPattern.
  *   sparsity pattern learning
The sparsity pattern learning feature acquires the sparsity pattern in advance, in order to speed up matrix assembly.  Enabled by default, the sparsity matrix learner identifies the exact matrix sparsity pattern (without actually setting any non-zeros). See ChSolverDirect::UseSparsityPatternLearner.
  *   In situations where the problem structure changes but relatively infrequently, it is still desirable to lock the sparsity pattern.  However, if using the sparsity pattern learner, an update must be explicitly triggered by the user after a problem modification (by calling ChSparseDirect:: ForceSparsityPatternUpdate).  For an example, see demo_FEA_beams_extrude.
  *   Finally, there is an option to provide an estimate for the matrix sparsity (a value in [0,1], with 0 corresponding to a fully dense matrix). When the sparsity pattern learner is disabled, this value is used if/when required to reserve space for matrix indices and non-zeros. See ChSolverDirect::SetSparsityEstimate.

If appropriate and warranted by the problem setup, it is highly recommended to enable the sparsity pattern lock. This can significantly improve performance for more complex problems (larger size and/or problems which include constraints).

Subject: Re: [chrono] Threads management

Hi Fabio,

Try disabling automatic "thread tuning" (which defaults for true on any CPU with more than one core) by adding to the demo code the following line:
msystem.GetSettings()->perform_thread_tuning = false;

The logic for this feature in Chrono::Parallel needs a bit of work.  As it is currently implemented, if thread tuning is on, it is free to use up to the maximum number of threads (i.e. up to the value returned by omp_get_num_procs).

--Radu

Hi Alan,
I think the best solution to this problem is one that does not involve touching the underlying tire code in Chrono::Vehicle.  Instead, all required coordinate transformations could be confined to an appropriately modified ChWheel object and a slightly modified ChWheeledVehicle.

A while ago, I wrote a piece of code to test using Chrono::Vehicle tires when attached to a multibody system modeled *outside* Chrono::Vehicle and in a Y-up reference frame.  It required a little bit of additional work to bring it in sync with the latest changes to Chrono & Chrono::Vehicle.   The code is attached to this message. 

This code should have all the required transformations (of wheel states going into the tire model and tire forces to be applied to the spindle body) but the mechanism I used only checks that the vertical and longitudinal forces are evaluated and applied correctly.  But I expect the lateral force also comes out right.   The test builds two systems, one mimicking the ISO frame used by Chrono::Vehicle, the other (MechanismYUP) using an equivalent setup modeled in a Y-up frame and checks that the two simulations are consistent (same wheel states and same tire forces, but represented in their corresponding frames).   All required coordinate transformations are implemented in 3 stand alone functions (YUP->ISO for a wheel state, ISO->YUP for moments of inertia, and ISO->YUP for tire forces).

Subject: Re: [chrono] Object collision: Object falls through another?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 27 Mar 2020 23:01:46 +0100

Jon,

A possible reason for the different results at different runs is due to 
the line:
  application.SetTryRealtime(true);
right before your simulation loop.

If you are using a version of Chrono before 16 March, the way this was 
implemented was by adjusting the underlying step size (reducing it if 
possible) so that simulation time is close to wall-clock time. In your 
case, if the simulation for a step is measured to be less than 5 ms, the 
step size for the next step would be reduced accordingly. Depending on 
current load of your machine, the sequence of step sizes will vary from 
run to run, which could explain the differences you report.

A while ago I implemented an alternative mechanism for enforcing soft 
real-time which does not rely on modifying the step size (and thus 
results in deterministic and reproducible results over different runs). 
However, the ChIrrApp class still used the old mechanism. With the 
commit from 16 March I eliminated the old mechanism altogether and so 
ChIrrApp now uses the new method (based on spinning in place until real 
time catches up with simulation time).

Please try one of the following two things:

 1. the quickest test is to simply comment out the line above in your
    code in which case your code will always run with a step size of 5
    ms (but possibly complete the step in less than 5 ms, thus running
    faster than real time).
 2. if you still want to be able to enforce soft real-time, update the
symbol: Re: [chrono] Object collision: Object falls through another?

text:

    faster than real time).
 2. if you still want to be able to enforce soft real-time, update the
    code to the latest version in the develop branch of the GitHub
    repository. In that case, you can keep the setting for attempting
    soft real-time, but the simulation will always be advanced with your
    specified step size of 5 ms.

and let us know if that resolves the issue.

--Radu

Hi Jonathan

please do not change the rotation / position of a body during a 
simulation, the result can be unexpected. Even if the body is set as 
'fixed'.

If you need to move something like in your example, you need the 
ChLinkMotion... classes. Look ad demo_IRR_imposed_motion.cpp for examples.

Basically, you need to create a dummy 'ground' object that is fixed, 
than you create the 'deck' (not fixed!), then you control the rotation 
of the deck respect to ground via one of the ChLinkMotion objects.

Alternative, for simplier motions like tilting on an axis: just use the 
examples in demo_IRR_motors.cpp

best regards

Alessandro Tasora

Hi CK,

I'm not sure I understand why you would consider dynamic variable 
names. That is definitely something to be discouraged. But it's 
perfectly fine to reuse local variables in a loop. As soon as you add a 
body or joint to the Chrono system, that local variable in the loop is 
not needed anymore and can be reused for the next segment.

Now, in your loop you should create both new bodies and the joints to 
connect them to the last body added in the previous iteration. Maybe 
this is the source of your confusion.
Say you want to build a chain with the following topology
[B1]-(j1)-[B2]-(j2)-[B1]-(j1)-[B2]-(j2)-[B1]-(j1)-[B2]-(j2)-[B1]-(j1)-[B2]-(j2)......[B1]
with two different types of bodies [B1] and [B2] and two different types 
of joints (j1) and (j2).
Then your "building block" would be
  (j1)-[B2]-(j2)-[B1]
and you could organize your construction along these lines:

b1 = create, add body to system
for i = 1:n_blocks
  b2 = create, add body to system
  j1 = create, connect b1 & b2, add joint to system
  b1 = create, add body to system
  j2 = create, connect b2 & b1, add joint to system
end

An alternative to this is to simply create lists of bodies and joints of 
appropriate size before the loop and then create your bodies and joints 
at increasing indices in those lists while you iterate in the loop (note 
that a list + an index in that list serves precisely as your "dynamic 
variable name").

You should also create your "millipede" in a straight initial

You should also create your "millipede" in a straight initial 
configuration, that will make setting up the proper body and joint

Maybe because you just copied the configuration from the demo I pointed 
you to?

Hope that this helps and puts you on the right track.

CK,

In addition to that, you should make sure the universal joints are 
properly oriented. I assume you want the 2 rotational DOFs to be about 
axes that are perpendicular to the axis of your millipede. Keep in mind 
that for a universal joint these 2 rotational DOFs are about the x and y 
axes of the *joint* frame. If you build the millipede along the global x 
axis as you seem to do, for the particular form of the Initialize 
function you use for your joints that will probably require including a 
rotation about the z axis in the ChFrameD passed to Initialize.

A couple of suggestions:

  * look at demo_IRR_ujoint
    (https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/python/irrlicht/demo_IRR_ujoint.py)
    for an example of how to properly connect two bodies with a
    universal joint. Note that the two connected bodies there are
    aligned with the global z axis, unlike your case where I believe you
    intend them aligned along the global x axis; that dictates the
    proper orientation of the U-joint.
  * start by defining only one "segment" of your millipede (i.e., one
    box, one rod, and the U-joint between them) and make sure that is
    working as expected before extending it to its final configuration.

Subject: RE: [chrono] Loading in a new vehicle with pychrono
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 22 Jun 2025 15:04:29 +0000

Dan - this is not an issue of missing features in PyChrono. All of Chrono::Vehicle is exposed to Python users.

Edward - the problems are with your code.  Did you look at demo_VEH_WheeledJSON.py? I think that is exactly what you try to do (simulating a HMMWV vehicle constructed from a set of JSON specification files).  Start from that and modify as needed.

Note that WheeledVehicle does *not* have a "SetContactMethod" function.  A concrete vehicle model may provide that, but one built from JSON files does not.  I suspect that you saw that used in places such as demo_VEH_HMMWV.py; but that demo uses a concrete class implementing the HMMWV model (which is *not* the same as constructing a HMMWV vehicle from a set of JSON specification files).  It is that concrete HMMWV class that happens to provide a "SetContactMethod" function.

Please also make sure you always look at demos that are *consistent* with the conda package you installed; see the note at https://api.projectchrono.org/tutorial_table_of_content_pychrono.html.

Finally, you do not say what version of the conda package you use or what OS.  I inferred the latter to be Windows from your code, but this is the type of information that you should always provide when posting.

Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] settiing a limit for ChLinkSpringCB compression
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 16 Jan 2020 07:24:48 +0000

A few comments and clarifications:

  *   Please switch to using ChLinkTSDA.  This new element does everything ChLinkSpringCB does and also has the capability of carrying additional internal dynamics (if, for example, you want to implement an active suspension).  ChLinkSpringCB is deprecated and will be removed in a future version.
  *   You can implement the effect of "bump stops" in your shock absorber by increasing the stiffness after a certain deformation (compression or extension).  This approach is used for all vehicle suspensions in Chrono::Vehicle.  In fact, you can find (in the file src/chrono_vehicle/ChSubsysDef.h) a bunch of different ready-to-use functor objects for a ChLinkTSDA.  Look for LinearSpringBistopForce and MapSpringBistopForce. Start from one of these and modify as needed for your particular application.
  *   The spring rest length (or spring free length) is an input value which represents the undeformed spring length (i.e., the length at which the spring does not generate force).  It is typically used when modeling a linear spring (the default for both ChLinkTSDA and ChLinkSpringCB), as in:   F = -k * (L - L0) where k is the spring constant, L the current spring length, and L0 the rest length.

--Radu

I'll just talk about what I know, i.e. hydrodynamic modeling : if you 
reduce all your floating forces, including radiation ones, on a single 
force-torque, you may got instabilities. These might indeed come from 
the added mass terms multiplied by the accelerations, which are part of 
the radiation. That's why we chose in FRyDoM to ensure first that the 
hydrodynamic modeling is correct, before incorporating flexible bodies.

I can think however of two ways to solve your problem.

  * iterate multiple times during one time step to get rid of the
    instabilities, with the approach you mention,
  * or, within FRyDoM, to fix a ChMesh onto the FrBody, with all the
    hydrodynamic modeling. You might want to distribute the weight on
    the body and the ChMesh, I'm not so sure of this... You will however
    need to modify FRyDoM to add ChMesh, since it's not possible yet.

I can't answer your first question though : which method to add external 
force on a ChMesh.

Lucas

Subject: Re: [chrono] How to get mass and stiffness matrices using PyChrono?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 21 Nov 2019 15:53:08 +0000

Luis,

I assume you want to get the current mass matrix for debugging?
For simulation purposes only, the user need not worry about any sparse matrices (if needed, they are assembled and used internally).  This is why ChSparseMatrix (which in the C++ code is now a type alias to an Eigen sparse matrix) is not even exposed in PyChrono.
This means that you cannot use GetMassMatrix in PyChrono.
However, if you want to inspect the system mass matrix, you can invoke the DumpSystemMatrices method of ChSystem, for example with
    my_system.DumpSystemMatrices(True, False, False, False, False, './debug')
which will write a file debug_M.dat with the sparse mass matrix in Matlab format (i.e., one line per non-zero element, each line having row index, column index, value, with indices starting from 1)

--Radu

Hi Alan,

I am not sure how exactly you coupled Chrono and Unity3d, but keep in mind that in Chrono::Vehicle the wheel (and, as a matter of fact, tire) objects do not have an associated separate body.  Instead, they "share" the same body as that of the associated spindle (and only contribute additional mass and inertia to it).  This is done for efficiency reasons, as otherwise a wheel body and the associated spindle body would have to be connected through a "weld" (0 degree-of-freedom) joint.  In the MBD formulation used in Chrono, that would result in an unnecessary increase in problem size (additional states + additional constraints).

--Radu

From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 22 Oct 2019 17:21:11 +0000

Hi Alan,

I am not sure how exactly you coupled Chrono and Unity3d, but keep in mind that in Chrono::Vehicle the wheel (and, as a matter of fact, tire) objects do not have an associated separate body.  Instead, they "share" the same body as that of the associated spindle (and only contribute additional mass and inertia to it).  This is done for efficiency reasons, as otherwise a wheel body and the associated spindle body would have to be connected through a "weld" (0 degree-of-freedom) joint.  In the MBD formulation used in Chrono, that would result in an unnecessary increase in problem size (additional states + additional constraints).

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] New Vehicle Class on SCM Deformable Terrain
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 20 Jun 2020 10:36:11 +0200

Hi Samuel,

The steering mechanism is more tightly coupled to the wheeled vehicle 
templates in Chrono::Vehicle than the powertrain is (although I suspect 
you mean the driveline, or also the driveline).
Having said that, it is not all that difficult to add new templates for 
any of the vehicle subsystems defined in Chrono::Vehicle to match the 
topology of your rover. Of course, you would also need a new vehicle 
template to combine those.
While the current templates in Chrono::Vehicle are focused on the more 
"traditional" wheeled and tracked vehicle topologies, we have 
implemented less conventional topologies, but did not formalize any of 
those yet.

In any case, I recommend you explore option 1 below. Option 2 is not 
really feasible, since the SCM deformable terrain is quite tied in with 
the rest of Chrono (in particular collision shapes and the collision 
system). You can of course implement your own (after all, our SCM 
terrain is a modification/extension of the original model from DLR)

--Radu

I am an academic research at CMU trying to simulate a planetary rover on 
lunar regolith using the Chrono's Vehicle terrain class. It seems that 
everything in the vehicle class is coupled and I would have to use the 
powertrain and steering class to simulate the planetary rovers. However, 
rovers do not use such systems and it would not be a good representation in 
the simulator.

Thus, I was thinking to approach the development in 2 ways mentioned below. 
However, I am not sure which is better and whether any of the methods are 
feasible. If anybody could give me some guidance that would be perfect.

   1. Developing a separate vehicle class that does not require the use of 
   powertrain / steering, which is more generic towards simpler robotic 
   vehicles.
   2. Integrate Chrono's physics engine (specifically the deformable 
   terrain) in other simulators.

Lastly, I was wondering if anybody has completed any similar development in 
the above mentioned areas and would be able to give me some advise? 
I am open to other suggestions as well!

Thanks in advance!

Regards,
Samuel

Subject: Re: [chrono] Vehicle Snapshot
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 13 Oct 2019 05:42:54 +0000

Hi Jacob,

I'm afraid something like this cannot be provided by the Chrono::Vehicle library itself.
Indeed, if you are thinking about writing out JSON files with the specification of subsystems in a current vehicle, that wouldn't be possible in general (e.g., because a vehicle specified through concrete subsystem classes, such as those in the vehicle models library, may not be fully representable in JSON).  On the other hand, even for a vehicle that is completely specified through JSON files, Chrono::Vehicle does not keep track of the input JSON files, so we couldn't copy these somewhere else; furthermore, it is possible (legal) to modify parameters extracted from a JSON file, so the current vehicle may not be perfectly equivalent to the original JSON files.

Having said that, you can certainly do this (i.e. copy the input JSON files next to your output files, or otherwise maintain some relationship between input and output files) in your user code, in whatever way is meaningful and correct given the setup of your main (driver) program.

--Radu

From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 10 Dec 2019 11:38:34 +0000

Hi Qiyuan,

This was an intriguing behavior, so I took some time to look at your model more carefully.  I attached a version of the code that has the expected behavior (I also wanted to have this as a test case for the future).

Some comments about what was going on:


  *   First issue was that the node gradient vectors were not normalized.  I believe this was the main reason for the “lateral motion” you were observing.
You could simply normalize the direction vector you were already computing through cross-products or else explicitly compute unit vectors from the torus parameterization.
By the way, you can look at the ANCFToroidalTire in Chrono::Vehicle for an example of meshing a (half torus) – it’s effectively what you were already doing.

  *   Second issue was that you were indeed “double counting” gravitational forces.  In combination with the issue above, this was the reason for the “higher rate of fall of the FEA mesh”.
As it turns out, the automatic gravity loader” that Alessandro mentioned in his reply is enabled by default.  But each ANCF shell element was also adding its own gravitational forces.
For ANCF elements, it is actually better (more accurate and more efficient) to let the elements compute their gravitational loads and therefore explicitly disable the generic automatic gravity load.  In the code I attached, I included a flag to use one or the other (but not both simultaneously).

  *   I removed the addition of point masses to each individual node, because I think you likely don’t need this in your model. But also because I suspect there might be an issue with such nodal masses not being properly accounted for in the EOM for the ANCF shell element in Chrono (I’ll look into this issue when I’ll have a chance).  So I explicitly set this to 0 (node->SetMass(0);)
symbol: RE: [chrono] Effects of gravity on ANCF bodies

text:
For ANCF elements, it is actually better (more accurate and more efficient) to let the elements compute their gravitational loads and therefore explicitly disable the generic automatic gravity load.  In the code I attached, I included a flag to use one or the other (but not both simultaneously).

  *   I removed the addition of point masses to each individual node, because I think you likely don’t need this in your model. But also because I suspect there might be an issue with such nodal masses not being properly accounted for in the EOM for the ANCF shell element in Chrono (I’ll look into this issue when I’ll have a chance).  So I explicitly set this to 0 (node->SetMass(0);)

  *   For models with FEA meshes, you should prefer using the HHT (or maybe the implicit Euler) timestepper, not the implicit linearized Euler. The latter will work, but the results will not be accurate. Furthermore, for models that also include 3D bodies, you should use the “ACCELERATION” mode of HHT (which is the standard HHT scheme and also the default for the Chrono HHT integrator).  This is because the “POSITION” mode is technically incorrect when quaternions are present (that mode may be a bit better for a model with only FEA meshes.

  *   In conjunction with an implicit integrator (such as HHT), I recommend always using a direct sparse linear solver (either Pardiso through Chrono::MKL like you were doing, or else the Mumps solver through Chrono::Mumps).  Iterative linear solvers are prone  to stagnate on our type of problems (saddle point) especially since we do not have a good preconditioner (except for the simple diagonal preconditioner we provide as an option).  Having said that, if you do want to experiment with a Krylov solver, you’re better off using GMRES.  Since you are using the latest code in ‘develop’, you are aware that I have recently refactored the Chrono solvers and now interface to the iterative linear solvers provided in Eigen.  The MINRES solver from Eigen seems to be particularly fragile – this is an issue I’ve been looking at lately.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Changing Stepsize during calculation
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 10 Oct 2019 14:08:58 +0000

Hi Nomoto,

ChVehicle::SetStepsize is an advanced feature that was needed in some specific case and I consider eliminating it in the future (precisely because its function is somewhat confusing).

What this function does is provide an upper limit on the step size for the Chrono system containing the vehicle system.  Look at the implementation of ChVehicle::Advance to see how that stepsize is used.  What happens is that (depending on the relative values of the step size you specify in the main simulation loop and the step size specified for the vehicle), ChVehicle::Advance may take multiple smaller steps to advance the state of the Chrono system by the 'step' duration you specify in the main loop.

If you monitor the system time (with ChSystem::GetChTime) in the main loop, you will see it incremented by this (larger) 'step' value. But the Chrono system is (potentially) advanced in smaller steps.

Until I obsolete this function,  I suggest you pass to ChVehicle::SetStepsize the same value as you use in the main loop (i.e. the same value of 'step' that you pass to, say, ChVehicle::Advance). In other words do something like this for your main simulation loop:

while (...) {

new_step_size = ...

WheeledVehicle.SetStepsize(new_step_size);
WheeledVehicle.Advance(new_step_size);

}

Please let me know if this provides the functionality you are seeking.

--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] Can I modify the length of the suspension in json?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 5 Aug 2024 12:22:49 +0000

Jay,

That distance is not specified explicitly, but rather it follows from the definitions you have for the various hardpoints in the JSON suspension specification file.

All suspension templates in Chrono::Vehicle have a hardpoint that specifies the location of the spindle relative to the suspension reference frame (recall that you only specify hardpoints on the left side of the suspension assembly, with the points on the right obtained through mirroring). The suspension wheel track is the distance between the two spindle hardpoints (left and right), so it end up being twice the y component of the 3D point you have in the JSON file for the spindle hardpoint (in the JSON files, that point is found as “Spindle”->”COM”.

Finally, keep in mind that you will likely need to adjust other hardpoints in the suspension template, else you may end up with a non-functional suspension assembly.

--Radu

Subject: Re: How to Calculate Stress and Strains in Elements?
From: Mike Taylor
Date: Wed, 18 Dec 2019 19:21:53 -0800 (PST)

Esteban,

Sorry its taken so long to get reply to you.

As far as I can find, there is currently not a good way to query an element 
to get the stress tensor.  There is a function "ChVector<> 
ChElementShellANCF::EvaluateSectionStrains()" that reports some strains.  
However it is just returns the 3 axial terms (i.e. it does not return any 
of the shear strain terms) and it is hard coded to only report them at the 
midpoint.  I think (but I'm definitely not sure) these strains are in the 
element coordinate system rather than the fiber coordinate system (for 
orthotropic materials) so it likely is not a straight forward process to 
calculate stress terms from these strains.

So unfortunately in the current state, it looks like it is up to you to 
generate these calculations.

We are working on improvements to several of the ANCF elements and this is 
a logical capability that should exist.  We'll add a feature to query stresses 
and strains in future when we make these updates, but I don't have a time 
estimate for that yet.   

Best regards,

Mike Taylor

Hi Alan,
The operation
m_tireforce.force = m_data.frame.TransformDirectionLocalToParent(m_tireforce.force)
transforms the tire force from the "tire frame" (with Z along the terrain normal at contact and Y along the tire's plane normal) to the "global frame" (with Z up in the vertical direction and some X and Y). 
This is because Chrono::Vehicle expects the tire forces and moments expressed in the global frame (when it applies them as "external forces" on the wheel spindle bodies).
You can see the reason for this transformation with a simple experiment: use a Chrono::Vehicle demo which initializes the vehicle aligned with the global frame (say demo_HMMWV), set it to use TMeasy tires, and then comment outlines like the one above which re-express the tire forces and moments in the global frame.  As long as you move the vehicle in a straight line things will work fine (because the rotation in m_data.frame will be close to identity), but not when you start steering.

On 11/1/2019 7:52 PM, Rainer Gericke wrote:

Hi Alan,

TMeasy can be parametrized by a full set of parameters or with the help of an estimation routine in ChTMeasyTire, which method did you try?

The collision detection is very easy for the handling tires, the principle is identical between Fiala, Pacejka and TMeasy. After calculation of the possible contact point the intersection of the tire contour (just a circle) and the road surface is determined. The difference between the undeformed tire radius and the height of the wheel center above the ground gives the tire deflection. To calculate Fz we have to multiply the deflection by cz (= vertical stiffness) and add the damping term. I guess this not new to you, I only mention it for finding possible error sources. Typical errors I made myself:
* the undeformed tire radius was not set -> Fz is alway zero and no interaction is recognized.
* cz is not a constant value but a function cz = cz(Fz). It is always updated in ChTMeasyTire::synchronize(). cz is in general nonlinear. cz(Fz=0) must be greater zero!

After calculation of the possible contact point the intersection of the tire contour (just a circle) and the road surface is determined. The difference between the undeformed tire radius and the height of the wheel center above the ground gives the tire deflection. To calculate Fz we have to multiply the deflection by cz (= vertical stiffness) and add the damping term. I guess this not new to you, I only mention it for finding possible error sources. Typical errors I made myself:
* the undeformed tire radius was not set -> Fz is alway zero and no interaction is recognized.
* cz is not a constant value but a function cz = cz(Fz). It is always updated in ChTMeasyTire::synchronize(). cz is in general nonlinear. cz(Fz=0) must be greater zero!
* if there is a smoothing term for the calculation of Fz remove it. 
Best

Rainer

Hi Alan,

The operation
m_tireforce.force = m_data.frame.TransformDirectionLocalToParent(m_tireforce.force)
transforms the tire force from the "tire frame" (with Z along the terrain normal at contact and Y along the tire's plane normal) to the "global frame" (with Z up in the vertical direction and some X and Y).
This is because Chrono::Vehicle expects the tire forces and moments expressed in the global frame (when it applies them as "external forces" on the wheel spindle bodies).

You can see the reason for this transformation with a simple experiment: use a Chrono::Vehicle demo which initializes the vehicle aligned with the global frame (say demo_HMMWV), set it to use TMeasy tires, and then comment outlines like the one above which re-express the tire forces and moments in the global frame.  As long as you move the vehicle in a straight line things will work fine (because the rotation in m_data.frame will be close to identity), but not when you start steering.

The transformation m_data.frame is computed in these ChTire::DiscTerrainCollision*** functions I mentioned before.  In Chrono::Vehicle, this calculation also makes the implicit assumption that all frames are ISO (in particular Z is up).
It sounds to me that this is again due to an inconsistency between Chrono::Vehicle and Unity frames.  Do you use directly the ChTire::DiscTerrainCollision*** functions form Chrono::Vehicle or did you implement your own? In either case, you must ensure m_data.frame contains a consistent rotation.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Constant velocity with other DOF fixed setting
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 26 Feb 2020 11:21:36 +0100

Hi Daye,

Sorry for the late reply.

You should indeed be able to model this by using a 
ChLinkMotorLinearSpeed between ground and your "small body" and set its 
speed function to a constant function (ChFunction_Constant) with desired 
speed value.

By default, this link acts like a prismatic joint. If you want to 
impose another set of constraints ("fix some DOF" as you put it), you 
can either:

  * set the motor's guide constraint to 'FREE', by calling
    my_motor.SetGuideConstraint(ChLinkMotorLinear::GuideConstraint::FREE);
    and also add whatever other kinematic joints you need while making
    sure you do not affect the linear motor's actuation direction, or
  * directly set the motor's other DOFs to be free or constrained, using
    the other signature of ChLinkMotorLinear::SetGuideConstraints, for
    example
       my_motor.SetGuideConstraints(true, true, false, false, false);
    to only constrain the y and z translations (orthogonal to the
    actuation).

What kind of guide constraints are you interested in?

--Radu

Declan,

The plane-plane joint is indeed what you need.  The plane orientation is specified by the Z axis of the reference coordinate system provided in the joint initialization.  In your case, to enforce movement in the x-z  plane, pass a coordsys whose orientation is Q_from_AngX(-CH_C_PI_2), that is a coordsys whose Z axis is aligned with the global Y.

See demo_IRR_plane_plane for an example.

--Radu
