Subject: Re: [chrono] PyChrono: Several instances of a system and loads in FEA
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 5 Feb 2020 09:14:26 +0100

Hi Sebastian,

What you are trying to do is dynamically-constrained optimization. From 
what you describe, your problem could also be considered an optimal 
control problem. To solve such a problem involving a chrono mechanism, 
I suggest an approach along the following lines:

  * decide what your optimization parameters are (the various inputs in
    the actuators?)
  * define your objective function, a measure of "goodness" of your
    system, which you would like minimized for a simulation over some
    fixed time interval (some measure of the stresses?)
  * set up your chrono system so that it is "parameterized" by the
    parameters you decided on above, meaning that it should be written
    in such a way that it can take any set of parameters, use them as
    appropriate, and produce a corresponding simulation (thus
    calculating the value of the cost function corresponding to that set
    of parameters)
  * encapsulate the simulation of your mechanism over the given time
    interval into a function that maps the parameters into a cost
    function value
  * pass this function to some optimization package (that will impose
    the actual form of the mapping function above) and let it find the
    set of parameters which minimize the specified cost function
  * the optimization tool will make multiple calls to this function with
    various combinations of the parameters (thus, each function
    evaluation will entail performing one chrono simulation of your
symbol: Re: [chrono] PyChrono: Several instances of a system and loads in FEA

text:
* the optimization tool will make multiple calls to this function with
    various combinations of the parameters (thus, each function
    evaluation will entail performing one chrono simulation of your
    mechanism using the given combination of parameters appropriately
    applied to the mechanism)

Of course, this is just the high-level description of the approach and 
there will be other details you need to work out (e.g., if using a 
gradient-based optimizer you may need/want to estimate the cost function 
gradient which you could do with a finite difference approach, by 
perturbing one parameter at a time).

For #3, the first option I suggested is the one I would prefer. I am not 
sure why you get a crash (maybe something you do after breaking out of 
the while loop?). I just tested this with demo_irrlicht.py and it works 
as expected.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Applying prestress (or pre-stretch) to beams, cables, or
 springs
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 12 Jun 2020 11:09:33 +0200

Hi Georgia,

there are different options to this end. Examples:

A)

use ChElementSpring (ex. see 
http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1fea_1_1_ch_element_spring.html) 
to connect two ChNodeFEAxyz. This is a non-preoload spring at initial 
state, but just after you create it, you can change the X0 reference 
position of the connected nodes, moving them apart via mynodeA->SetX0() 
etc., so this will create preload, because the rest length of the 
spring is computed as the difference beteween the two X0 positions of 
the two nodes.

B)

use ChElementBar (ex see 
http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1fea_1_1_ch_element_bar.html 
), and use the same trick of moving the X0 reference position of the 
nodes a bit far apart respect to the actual position of the nodes. 
Knowing the Young modulus, area, you can precompute how far apart, for a 
given preload.

regards

A. Tasora

Subject: FEA slower when using links
From: Vito Zago
Date: Tue, 20 Aug 2019 18:17:49 -0700 (PDT)

Dear developers,

We are working on the coupling of Project Chrono with GPUSPH (www.gpusph.org) 
to run fluid solid interactions, using Project Chrono to solve Finite 
Elements Analysis. The aim is the simulation of offshore structures 
interacting with sea waves.

A working version of the coupling, using Project Chrono 4.0.0, is already 
implemented but we are experiencing some issues with the FEM analysis.

Considering a four-legged platform, as shown in the picture below (numbers 
refer to the attached cpp code), we discretize it using ANCF elements, a 
grid of shells for the deck and cables for the legs. We use a series of two 
cables for each leg, so we can apply a force in the middle node.


Because of the way we setup the coupled SPH-FEM model in GPUSPH, we would 
like to attach the legs to the deck without necessarily having a direct 
correspondence of nodes. To this end we use ChLinkPointTriface constraints, 
connecting three points of a shell in the deck with the node of the cable.

We noticed that with a mesh built in this way, solution times are around 
25-30 seconds per iteration, varying according to the force we apply. The 
same elements directly connected sharing the same nodes lead to solution 
times at least one order of magnitude smaller (that we would like to 
further reduce anyway).

We run on a Intel® Xeon(R) Silver 4110 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 16 cores, and 48 GB 
of memory.

Same considerations can be done considering ChLinkPointPoint: attaching the 
legs using overlapped nodes and constraints, leads to solution times around

Same considerations can be done considering ChLinkPointPoint: attaching the 
legs using overlapped nodes and constraints, leads to solution times around 
one order of magnitude higher than those required by the single mesh.

Provided that we are using links correctly, is this extra time taken by 
Links normal?

Moreover, using joints brings very easily to stall in the solution, where 
Chrono shows messages referring to a normHE nan.


I attached a code of the platform mesh built as in the three cases 
described above.

Thank you,
Vito

Hi,

I have finally made some progress with the Unity3D integration of Chrono Physics, so far it's only partial, enough to set a chrono demo vehicle up.

What I have done is allow Chrono development to work as drag and drop assets within Unity, so all the suspension sub systems, powertrains, steering systems, brakes etc.  are pre-built visual 3D objects with the chrono scripts attached to them, all that has to be done is they are dragged into the scene, placed, and attach together, like shafts components to wheels, suspension revolute to chassis, or suspension to steering rack etc.  I have ported the RigidTire, Pac89 and TMeasy tire models directly into Unity.

Alan.

Subject: RE: [chrono] Re: Support of Project Chrono for parallelism on GPU
From: Dan Negrut
Date: Wed, 8 May 2019 16:43:58 +0000

Hi,
The short answer: The likelihood of Project Chrono, in its entirety, to “be compiled and run on GPU devices” , now or in the future, is perhaps nil.

Some context: GPU computing is good at some things, and not suitable for other things. To the extent possible, given the amount of person-power we have, we try to parallelize for execution on the GPU what fits the underlying hardware model exposed by GPU computing. In our experience, these are Chrono applications tied to large contact problems and CFD. Perhaps in the future, also parts of the FEA implementation. There are parts of Chrono though that more suitable for CPU rather than GPU execution.

I hope I answered the question you had in mind.
Dan

Subject: Re: [chrono] How to import the stl file of the truck
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 27 Nov 2019 10:13:30 +0000

A couple of things:

  *   currently, we only support meshes provided in Wavefront OBJ format, so you'll have to convert your meshes (CAD programs should be able to export to OBJ, or you can use MeshLab or an online converter)
  *   you will first need to split your full truck mesh into separate meshes that you can each associate with one rigid body
  *   for wheeled vehicles, Chrono::Vehicle supports mesh visualization for certain parts: the chassis, wheels, and tires.  See some of the models and demos for how that is done (e.g. the HMMWV model and demo_VEH_HMMWV)
  *   I assume you have modeled the trailer yourself (maybe following the example in demo_VEH_TractorTrailer?).  For that part, you will need to implement support for mesh visualization yourself (look at how that's done for the vehicle chassis for example)

--Radu

From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 7 Dec 2019 09:47:00 +0000

Hi James,

Mesh-mesh collision is supported. See for example demo_IRR_collision_trimesh or demo_FEA_contacts.

My suspicion is that you have left sphereswept_thickness, the last argument of ChCollisionModel::AddTriangleMesh, to its default value of 0.
A positive value "inflates" the collision mesh and significantly improves robustness, especially for mesh-mesh collision.  Without it, it is very likely to completely miss collisions, just like you experienced.

You will have to experiment some trying to settle on a good value for this quantity, to strike the proper balance between robustness of the collision detection and realism of the collisions.

--Radu

From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 14 Jan 2020 11:17:04 +0000

For what you need, you should use Get_react_force and Get_react_torque.  These will return the joint reaction force and torque, respectively, both expressed in the joint's reference frame.  To express them in the reference frame of the "master" body (the 2nd body specified in the joint's initialization call), use GetLinkRelativeCoords.  Look at the various tests "utest_JOINT_***" for example usage.

The force objects returned by functions such as GetForce_X, GetForce_Rx, etc. allow you to specify forces acting in the direction of the DOFs for a particular joint.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: How can I make ChLinkMateGeneric more resistant to separation?
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Mon, 6 May 2019 09:56:58 +0200

The default SOR solver is not fit for cases where very light objects are
mixed in the scene. At least you must increase the max number of iterations
of the solver.

Better, switch to the BARZILAIBORWEIN solver. Also in this case,  if you
simulate complex chains of bodies with odd mass ratios, you may need to
increase the max  number of solver iterations.

By the way: check that the inertia tensor of your tiny bodies makes sense.
Sometimes people adjust only the mass and forget to adjust also rotational
inertia.

Alessandro

Hi Daye and Rohit,

You are correct that there are issues with enabling double precision for 
the Bullet collision detection. This is an issue in the (quite old) 
version of Bullet that is embedded in and modified for Chrono use. We 
have looked at adopting a newer version of Bullet (which is supposed to 
have also fixed support for double precision), but ran into some 
performance issues. We put this on the back-burner, but will have to 
revisit it again soon. For longer term, we consider completely 
eliminating our reliance on Bullet for collision detection and either 
adopt a different collision detection library or else roll out our own 
(because of the special needs, we may have to bite the bullet and write 
our own collision detection system; obviously, this is not a trivial 
task and will not happen very soon).

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Inconsistent behavior between ChMarker and ChBodyAuxRef
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Wed, 9 Oct 2019 18:54:06 +0200

Dear Lucas,

sorry for the late reply.

In fact, your comments are correct: the ChMarker objects in the 
ChBodyAuxRef case do not behave intuitively. The fact is that marker 
'internal data' for coordinates is always relative to the COG. Once you 
move the COG, as you noticed, also the markers will follow.

The changes that you made in the patch below seem fine to me, but we are 
not fixing the issue with that patch right now, because we are planning 
to create a cleaner API for the marker functions (with more readable 
names) for the next major relase, where all these 'respect to 
COG/REF/absolute' cases will be more readable. In the planned new 
implementation, the internal marker data will still refer to the COG as 
nowadays, but easier functions will be given for all the subcases in a 
transparent way.

Last note: in your patch, tell me if I am correct!, you switched the 
internal coordinate data of ChMarker from expressing a COG-relative info 
to expressing a REF-relative info, that may be working fine everywhere 
except (if I recall correctly) when the ChMarker objects are used in the 
ChLink classes, i.e. when computing jacobians, because in that place the 
'to parent' coordinates are assumed respect to the COG anyway. So this 
may break the ChLink functionality.

(btw. thank you for giving feedback on Chrono)

Alessandro Tasora

Hello,

within FRyDoM framework, we rely quite heavily on ChBodyAuxRef and 
ChMarker and I came to notice a strange behavior when using these two 
classes concurrently (on Chrono V4.0.0), especially when moving COG ref.

In Chrono doc, marker positions are supposed to be specified with

auto frameREF_to_Abs = my_body->GetFrame_REF_to_abs(); csys.pos = ChTransform<>::TransformParentToLocal(m_coord.pos, frameREF_to_Abs.GetCoord().pos, frameREF_to_Abs.GetA());

instead of

GetBody()->TransformLocalToParent(*this, abs_frame);

// Restore marker/forces positions, keeping unchanged respect to aux 
ref. ChFrameMoving<> cog_oldnew = old_cog_to_abs >> new_cog_to_abs.GetInverse(); for (auto& marker :marklist) {

text:
Subject: Refactoring of (dense) linear algebra
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 11 Aug 2019 10:59:56 +0000

Dear Chrono users,

I recently pushed to the Chrono 'develop' branch a significant change, related to using Eigen for all dense matrix operations.
Please read the notes below for how this affects the API and user code, as well as various other considerations.  This was a major refactoring of Chrono and it affected a significant portion of the code base. While we tested the code as much as possible, it is possible there are still issues that need to be fixed.  Please let us know (on this mailing list) if you encounter any problems.

With this change, Chrono requires Eigen3 version 3.3.0 or newer.  Unless not possible for other reasons, I suggest you use their latest version, 3.3.7.

  *   Eigen is available for download at http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/
  *   Eigen is a headers-only library, so no install is required in order to use it in Chrono.
  *   If the location of the Eigen headers is not automatically detected by CMake, manually specify it by setting the CMake variable EIGEN3_INCLUDE_DIR.
  *   Note: CUDA 9.1 has removed a file (math_functions.hpp) which is referenced by Eigen prior to version 3.3.6.  As such, if you build any of the GPU-based Chrono modules (FSI or Granular) and use CUDA 9.1, make sure to use Eigen 3.3.7.

The switch to Eigen does come with a few strings attached

  *   On the flip side, this makes the code a lot cleaner, easier to understand and maintain, and facilitates several further developments on our road-map.
  *   Furthermore, performance did not degrade and in fact improved meaningfully on practically all our benchmark tests (measured with GCC and clang on Linux and MacOS).
symbol: Refactoring of (dense) linear algebra

*   On the flip side, this makes the code a lot cleaner, easier to understand and maintain, and facilitates several further developments on our road-map.
  *   Furthermore, performance did not degrade and in fact improved meaningfully on practically all our benchmark tests (measured with GCC and clang on Linux and MacOS).
  *   On the other hand, libraries that use expression templates metaprogramming techniques (as Eigen does) lead to longer compile times. Moreover, while release (optimized) code is faster, code built in debug mode will likely be (significantly) slower.
  *   Finally, because several Chrono classes now need to use an (Eigen-provided) overloaded operator new to ensure memory alignment and because of some limitations of the C++ language, this change has an important consequence on user code: std::make_shared cannot always be used safely. The solution I adopted is to provide chrono_types::make_shared replacement functions which should be used throughout (see below).

The new matrix and vector classes

  *   The "old" Chrono matrix types (ChMatrixNM, ChMatrixDynamic, ChVectorDynamic) are now nothing but type aliases of appropriate Eigen types (see ChMatrix.h).
In other words, use them as you would Eigen types (see https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TutorialMatrixArithmetic.html).
  *   For completeness, I introduced additional types (such as ChVectorN,  ChRowVectorN, ChRowVectorDynamic), all defined in ChMatrix.h.
  *   I only implemented a handful of extensions needed for Chrono (such as a method for computing the WRMS vector norm) using the "back-door" extension mechanism provided by Eigen (see ChMatrixEigenExtensions.h)

  *   For completeness, I introduced additional types (such as ChVectorN,  ChRowVectorN, ChRowVectorDynamic), all defined in ChMatrix.h.
  *   I only implemented a handful of extensions needed for Chrono (such as a method for computing the WRMS vector norm) using the "back-door" extension mechanism provided by Eigen (see ChMatrixEigenExtensions.h)
  *   The "old" base class ChMatrix was eliminated.  For the instances where a Chrono function needs to accept either a dynamic (ChMatrixDynamic) or a static (ChMatrixNM) argument, we rely on the Eigen::Ref mechanism. For this I defined various type aliases, such as ChMatrixRef and ChMatrixConstRef (see ChMatrix.h).  Currently, these assume a 'double' scalar type as this is all that's needed in Chrono (they could be templated by the scalar type, but this will be done only if absolutely needed).
  *   For 3x3 matrices, the ChMatrix33 class (as before, templated by the scalar type) is derived from a 3x3 fixed-size vectorizable Eigen matrix.  Using inheritance here was needed in order to implement various custom constructors and methods.
  *   For clarity and to properly separate responsibilities, I added a small set of 3x4 and 4x4 matrices specific to multibody dynamics.  These derived classes have strict and limited functionality and are unlikely to show up in user code (see ChMatrixMBD.h).
  *   Note: for now, the ChVector and ChQuaternion classes were left unchanged.
  *   See demo_CH_linalg.cpp for simple examples of matrix operations with the new Chrono classes and types.

  *   See demo_CH_linalg.cpp for simple examples of matrix operations with the new Chrono classes and types.

Obsolete/eliminated Chrono classes

  *   With the switch to Eigen, I eliminated ChLinearAlgebra.  More robust and varied matrix factorization and linear system solvers can be used directly from Eigen (see http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__DenseLinearSolvers__chapter.html).
  *   I also eliminated the custom sparse matrix classes ChLinkedListMatrix and ChMapMatrix.  For now, for the limited use of sparse matrices outside the MKL and MUMPS modules, we use ChCSMatrix.  Note that we plan to also convert Chrono to use Eigen sparse matrices, at which time more of these classes will be eliminated (possibly even the entire Chrono::MKL module, as Eigen3 provides its own interface to the MKL Pardiso solver).  Eventually, Eigen sparse matrices will also replace the use of Blaze sparse matrices in Chrono::Parallel.

Some considerations for developers

  *   Consult the Eigen documentation (http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/) and FAQs to understand what Eigen provides and how it should be used (e.g., when it's meaningful/appropriate to use fixed-size Eigen objects)
  *   Look at block operations with Eigen matrices and vectors (https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TutorialBlockOperations.html)

  *   Look at block operations with Eigen matrices and vectors (https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TutorialBlockOperations.html)
These make code much more clear (contrast this with the use of the old "paste" functions which was obfuscated and prone to mistakes).   However, always measure performance impacts;  in some cases (especially with smaller matrices), explicit loops may be more efficient than Eigen block operations.
  *   Beware of aliasing issues (https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TopicAliasing.html).
  *   Beware of memory alignment issues (https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TopicUnalignedArrayAssert.html)
In particular, if you create a class that has a fixed-size vectorizable Eigen type (a ChMatrixNM, a ChVectorN, or most common a ChMatrix33) make sure to overload its operator new.  For that, use the Eigen-provided macro EIGEN_MAKE_ALIGNED_OPERATOR_NEW (see https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TopicStructHavingEigenMembers.html)
  *   When creating shared pointers, make sure to use chrono_types::make_shared (see below)

API and user code

  *   Except for the limited situations where user code explicitly used the old-style matrix operations (which should now use the cleaner Eigen API; see e.g. https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TutorialMatrixArithmetic.html), the main impact on users has to do with the shared pointers in the Chrono public API.

API and user code

  *   Except for the limited situations where user code explicitly used the old-style matrix operations (which should now use the cleaner Eigen API; see e.g. https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TutorialMatrixArithmetic.html), the main impact on users has to do with the shared pointers in the Chrono public API.
  *   The issue has to do with the fact that std::make_shared uses 'placement new' to create a shared pointer with a single memory allocation.  This means that std::make_shared will not use an overloaded 'operator new' for classes that provide it (for memory alignment considerations).
  *   To maintain encapsulation (as much as possible) and not require users to know/care about the guts of Chrono (namely know which classes overload, or have a parent that overloads, their operator new), the solution I adopted is to provide custom make_shared functions (in the namespace chrono_types) and a mechanism to pick at compile-time which one should be used (conditional on the object's class having or not an overloaded operator new).   For classes that require aligned memory (i.e. classes that have an overloaded operator new), chrono_types::make_shared explicitly creates the shared_ptr.   Otherwise, it falls back on using std::make_shared (see ChTypes.h).
  *   As such, user code should always create a shared_ptr using something like:
auto foo = chrono_types::make_shared<T>(bar);
  *   See the various Chrono demos and tests for examples.

Best,
Radu

From: Alessandro Tasora

Dear Daye,

internally, Chrono uses Bullet for collision detection (except for the 
parallel version of Chrono, btw). The problem is that -after you added 
collision shapes to ChBody objects- you cannot access the 
btCollisionShape objects easily, as the API of the collision classes are 
designed to keep the user away from the internal implementation.

Anyway you cast the my_body->GetCollisionModel() object to a 
ChModelBullet , then you can call GetBulletModel() , that returns a 
btCollisionObject*, that you can peek into in order to find the 
btCollisionShape etc. just like in the regular Bullet.

Alessandro

Subject: Re: [chrono] Using Particle Factory in a Parallel System
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 28 Aug 2019 05:20:43 +0000

The Poisson disk sampler is supposed to do exactly that: generate uniformly distributed points with the guarantee that the distance between any two points is no smaller than a specified threshold.  I implemented this option to ensure that a collection of spheres of equal radius can be initialized without interpenetrations, just like you describe. Using your notation, I typically use something like R = 2 * (1.001 * r).

Could you maybe send a small, self-contained example that has issues?

--Radu

From: Radu Serban

The particle factory classes were not designed to be used with Chrono::Parallel.  Having said that, there is no fundamental reason why they could not be made to also work with parallel systems.  I will look into this when I get a chance.

In the meantime, depe3nding on what your particular needs are, you may be able to use the alternate mechanism for creating and initializing granular material that is offered by the classes in ChUtilsSamplers and ChUtilsGenerators.  I initially designed these precisely for large-scale granular simulations with Chrono::Parallel (but they can also be used with the usual Chrono systems).  Take a look at http://www.projectchrono.org/assets/slides_3_0_0/6_OtherModules/1_ChronoParallel.pdf (starting at slide 10) for the functionality provided by these classes.  We often use these classes to generate granular terrain for off-road vehicle simulations.  You can see them used in the implementation of GranularTerrain in Chrono::Vehicle or directly in demos such as demo_VEH_M113_Parallel.

--Radu

Subject: Re: Pychrono development environment options
From: Qiyuan Zhou
Date: Fri, 14 Feb 2020 10:20:07 -0800 (PST)

Most of the work done on the Python side of my group's research on windows 
(including project chrono) is done using the Anaconda distribution and 
Spyder IDE. This is our go to option for Python even when using Linux 
natively because of how easy it is to manage packages and the ability to 
view all variables inside Spyder. I highly recommend this approach and 
encourage you to give it a try: https://www.anaconda.com/distribution/

Do note that the latest release of Spyder (4.0.1) does not work well with 
visualizations done in project chrono. It is recommended that you downgrade 
spyder to 3.3.6 if you decide to go this route for PyChrono.

text:
I am trying to use the cohesion setting in chrono::granular to achieve a similar effect as the utah teapot demo<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HUTBTMdRb7A>, but have been running into some difficulties. I hope that somebody here would be able to help me out.

When setting the cohesion ratio to anything higher than ~100 in the .json file, errors are produced which cause the program to crash prematurely. The errors are usually of the nature:

  *   Sphere xxxxx is touching 12 spheres already and we just found another!!!
  *   No available contact pair slots for body xxxxx and body xxxxx
Looking in the source code for chrono::granular, it seems that both these errors are caused by a violation of the 12 contact theorem.

On the one occasion where the program did not crash while running with a cohesion setting higher than 100, the results (attached video) do not reflect the expected behavior one would associate with high cohesion.

It seems strange to me that there seems to exist a critical value of cohesion which causes models to behave in unexpected ways. I am wondering if anybody here has had success with using high values for cohesion in chrono::granular. If so, is it possible to give some advice on best practices when working with high cohesion ratios?

Thank you,
Qiyuan

You must pass the system to the ChTimeStepperHHT constructor:

my_timestepper = chrono.ChTimestepperHHT(my_system)

and then attach the timestepper to the system:

my_system.SetTimestepper(my_timestepper)

my_timestepper.SetAlpha(-0.2)

Look at demo_FEA_ANCF_Shell which I just updated to use HHT with custom parameters.

Hi Dmitry,

So here's my 2 cents on C::Granular damping...

The damping coefficient is related to *k*, *m* *and* the time step size. 
I'll use the tangential friction and damping as an example: in file 
*ChGranularHelpers.cuh* it can be seen *tangent_force = 
force_model_multiplier * (-k_t * delta_t - gamma_t * m_eff * vrel_t);*

That *delta_t* is basically *vrel * time_step_size*. So the intensity of 
damping is actually affected by the selection of step sizes; with a fixed 
step size, a certain amount of damping is needed but applying too much will 
incur numerical instability. Here's my experiment with one particle rolling 
on a mesh, and I plotted the force felt by the mesh (don't know how to 
include a video):

1) Damping set to 0, step size 1e-5: the force on *x* direction 
(essentially the direction along which the particle rolls; friction 
direction) oscillates:

[image: overall.png][image: forces.png] <about:invalid#zClosurez>


2) Damping set to 60, step size 1e-5: looks like hit a sweet spot, the 
force on *x* direction is stable:

[image: overall.png][image: forces.png] <about:invalid#zClosurez>


3) Damping set to 600, step size 1e-5: looks like over-damped, large 
oscillation in tangential direction:

[image: overall.png][image: forces.png] <about:invalid#zClosurez>


4) Damping set to 600, step size 1e-6: the damping coefficient seems to be 
doing its thing again, no oscillation:

[image: overall.png][image: forces.png] <about:invalid#zClosurez>

[image: overall.png][image: forces.png] <about:invalid#zClosurez>

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Cloth Simulation with Self Contact
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 3 Oct 2019 10:27:09 +0200

hi,

 at the moment, self collision is not possible if using the second 
method: ChContactSurfaceNodeCloud.

This means, for example, that self collision in a beam (as well as the 
simplier case of beam-to-beam contact) cannot work, because beam 
elements are converted in arrays of invisible spherical nodes (then fed 
to ChContactSurfaceNodeCloud) for collision detection purposes, and in 
ChContactSurfaceNodeCloud all mutual node contacts are not handled at all.

As self collisions was not a priority when we developed FEA collisions, 
this functionality was postponed. In future relases we will provide 
inter-beam collisions.

(Btw last month we were able to run beam self contacts for a benchmark, 
but using an ad-hoc solution that required us to do temporary changes 
the c++ source, and that is not general and user-friendly, so we are not 
going to release such patch.)

regards

Alessandro Tasora

I have attached one of my examples in PyChrono. If you run it until the FEA 
elements fall off the table, you will see that it does all sorts of self 
intersection.

The example attached sets up contact for both ChContactSurfaceNodeCloud and 
ChContactSurfaceMesh, but after looking through I realize that I did not 
add the ChContactSurfaceMesh to the system, which would explain its 
tendency to self intersect. Only nodes are being considered for contact 
since the contact mesh was not added to the system.

Adding the following before line 283 will add the contact mesh to the 
system, and should fix the self intersecting issue, though I was not able 
to visualize this in Irrlicht to confirm.
my_mesh.AddMeshSurface(mcontactmesh)

You will likely need to post process since running the mesh contacts will 
be too compute intense to visualize in real time with Irrlicht.

Hopefully this helps. Please let me know if you have success with this.

Qiyuan

Re: [chrono] POV-ray positioning of geometry

text:
Hello

I'm building different soil bins for simulation DEM-PM based particles within the chrono::parallel module.

When constructing the bin, I like using the ChBody, and then adding the serveral box geometries to the given ChBody, just like it is done within the chrono::parallel demos. (see picture for reference)

When building the bodies and running the simulation, the positioning and orientation of all bodies is as desired in OpenGL. However, when rendering the same simulation in POV-ray, all box geometries is placed in (0,0,0).

Is seems like the individual position of each box geometry set within utils::AddBoxGeometry(...) is not properly read by the POV-ray-exporter, and that the SetPos(...) of the ChBody is then used to define the position of each individual box geometry.

I know, that a work-a-round to this could be to create one ChBody per box geometry and then set the position via the SetPos(...) instead of within the utils::AddBoxGeometry(...). However i like the possibility of creating one ChBody consisting of several box geometries as this would save me a lot of unnecessary constrains between the geometries of the box, that could pontentially drift when the whole soil bin is moved.

Does anybody found a solution to this problem?

Best regards
Mads

Subject: RE: [chrono] Need for LSD ‘shafts’ for rallycross simulation with chronoUnity
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 6 Aug 2025 09:36:19 +0000

You are correct, we currently do not expose through the SWIG interfaces (which are used to automatically create the Python and C# bindings) any of the classes used to build new vehicle system templates. This is because we do not see Python and C# as development platforms for Chrono, but rather only user interfaces.  In other words, if you want to modify an existing driveline template or create a new one, you would need to do this in C++ and, expose that through the SWIG interface file, and recreate the Chrono C# libraries.

--Radu

From: projectchrono@googlegroups.com <projectchrono@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of A. Gachette
Sent: Tuesday, August 5, 2025 8:45 PM
To: ProjectChrono <projectchrono@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [chrono] Need for LSD ‘shafts’ for rallycross simulation with chronoUnity

Hello, I'm working on a rallycross simulation with chronoUnity (C# binding). I would like to use a Driveline4WD shafts for more realism but I also need a limited slip differential. Subject: Re: [chrono] Dynamic Domain for Granular Simulations
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 27 Aug 2019 00:28:21 +0000

Thomas,

The mechanism you describe could be implemented in principle, but it's not as straightforward as it may seem.  We do not have this exact feature available in Chrono.
Having said that, I did implement a similar feature in the GranularTerrain class of Chrono::Vehicle.  This is a so-called "moving patch" approach where a fixed number of particles are re-used so that the patch of granular material moves with the vehicle (and is therefore always under the vehicle).  This feature currently has some limitations (e.g., it can only be used with a vehicle moving in a straight line), but maybe it fits your needs.  Take a look at demo_VEH_MovingPatch for an illustration of the principle and at demo_VEH_HMMWV_Parallel for an illustration of its use within a vehicle simulation.

Regarding your other question: Chrono::Parallel provides support for multi-core (OpenMP-based) simulation.  On the other hand, Chrono::Distributed provides support for distributed (MPI_based) simulation.  In fact, Chrono::Distributed uses a domain decomposition approach wherein multiple instances of Chrono::Parallel (one per MPI rank) collaborate to solve larger problems.  Note that, currently, Chrono::Distributed is relatively limited in scope: it was designed specifically for granular terrain simulations (in the sense that it assumes little particle migration from one subdomain to another, due to the fact that no special care is taken for load balancing) and it currently only supports the penalty-based contact formulation (SMC).

How I understand it: dynamic domain is where only a given subset of bodies are simulated (i.e. motion integrated, contacts detected, ect.) at any given timestep, and the rest are frozen. That subset comprises of any particles that are within the volume of a dynamic domain box.

Example:
Say you have a wheel traversing over a bed of thousands of particles. Around that wheel you construct a box with dimensions slightly larger than those of the wheel and have the box follow it. As particles enter the box, you enable physics on those particles. As particles leave the box, you disable physics on those particles. So long as particles entering and leaving the box are nearly stationary, accuracy will not be affected and you will save on overall simulation time.

Has this been implemented in Chrono? Is there any reason it cannot be implemented?

Thanks,
~Thomas

Hi Pendi,

I'm a Mechatronic/Software engineer at Ultimaker. As you might know 
Ultimaker is located in the Netherlands and develops 3D printers and has 
the open source slicer Cura in its portfolio ( 
https://github.com/Ultimaker/Cura ). Last year I did an extensive design 
study for the development of a new liquefier and extrusion die, in other 
words "the hot-end". What Dan says is absolutely correct, and don't get me 
wrong, I love project chrono, but chrono isn't the tool for this problem. 
The molten filament acts as a temperature depended thixotropic fluid and 
that is exactly what chrono can't handle.
I made my own custom solver for this, where I split it up in a simpel 
thermodynamic linear problem (convection and conduction) and a micro fluid 
pipe problem.

Maybe it is to late and you are all ready finished with your project, if 
not feel free to mail me at j.spijker@ultimaker.com.

Fun fact I also did my bachelor thesis with help of project chrono. 
Simulating and controlling an autonomous operating underwater dredging bot 
which was propelled by two Archimedes screws 
( https://github.com/jellespijker/HAN-thesis/blob/master/report.pdf )

An other fun fact. I stumbled upon your message today because I was just 
starting up a personal hobby project of mine: a FDM gcode interpreter where 
the motion of the gantry can be simulated. You guessed it, with the help of 
Project Chrono and QT 3D. Which has apparently never  been done before

Subject: Re: [chrono] How to get accurate contact force
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 13 May 2019 11:27:49 +0000

Hi Jiaxi,

I believe that it is indeed a matter of misinterpreting the output from ChBody::GetContactForce.  This function returns the *resultant of all contact forces* acting on the body at any given time.  As such, for your example with two stacked boxes, this function will return (*for each body*) a resultant force that balances the weight of that body.   In particular, the lower box experiences two contact forces, one from contact with the upper box (equal in magnitude to the weight of the upper box) and one from contact with the ground (equal in magnitude to the sum of weights);  their resultant is equal to the weight of the lower box.

To get a resultant contact force that is equal to the sum of the weights of the two bodies, you would need to invoke GetContactForce on the *ground* body (see for example utest_CH_compute_contact).

If you are interested in the contact force for individual contacts, you need to use the ReportAllContacts approach, just like you did.

--Radu

Subject: Re: Does PyChrono really overcome Python's GIL?
From: Simone Benatti
Date: Thu, 13 Jun 2019 08:49:19 -0700 (PDT)

If you inspect the train_parallel.py code you can notice that we *don't* 
use multithreading,  but *multiprocessing *instead. This approach makes 
data sharing harder but doing so you can work around this limit, since 
every process has its own GIL.
In addition, as far as I know, parallelization can also be exploited at the 
lowest level, if the *underlying wrapped code* is able to do it. This is 
basically what Tensorflow (C++ and CUDA) and NumPy (Fortran) do.
Simone

From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 24 May 2019 19:29:38 +0000

Felix,

I didn't try to run your code, but just looking at what you posted I see an issue:  you create a ChBodyEasyBox to represent a slender bar of dimensions 0.05x1x0.05 and specify a density of 1.  This will result in a mass of 0.0025 and an inertia tensor with correspondingly small entries.  However, you immediately change the body mass to 23.5 (so 4 orders of magnitude larger), but you did not correspondingly scale the inertia tensor.  This type of modeling mistakes is a common source of instabilities like the ones you reported (look through previous postings to the user mailing list for similar issues).

--Radu

Subject: PyChrono: changes to Collison Callback
From: Simone Benatti
Date: Wed, 21 Aug 2019 07:01:53 -0700 (PDT)

Dear PyChrono users,

the old "ChReportContactCallbackP" class has been obsoleted. 
It was a Python-only class substituting the C++ nested class 
ChContactContainer::ReportContactCallback.
Since nested classes are now wrapped (and flattened,see 
http://api.projectchrono.org/development/pychrono_reference.html), 
in Python you can now call directly ReportContactCallback.
Moreover, you can now trace the name of the contactable object.
For additional details please check the new version of demo_python_2.py. ; 
of which I report a snippet below:

class MyReportContactCallback(chrono.ReportContactCallback):
    def __init__(self):
         chrono.ReportContactCallback.__init__(self)
    def OnReportContact(self,vA,vB,cA,dist,rad,force,torque,modA,modB):
         bodyUpA = chrono.CastContactableToChBody(modA)
         nameA = bodyUpA.GetName()
         bodyUpB = chrono.CastContactableToChBody(modB)
         nameB = bodyUpB.GetName()
         print ('  contact: point A=' , vA,  '  dist=',dist, 'Body A:', 
nameA, 'Body B:', nameB)


Please note that:
- In order to access to ChBody methods, you have to upcast the 
ChContactable objects (modA and modB)
- There are several derived classes of ChContactable. If the upcast is 
wrong, a runtime error is thrown.
- If the contactable is a ContactNode you can trace the mesh name (snippet 
below)

try: 
    bodyUpA = chrono.CastContactableToChBody(modA)
    nameA = bodyUpA.GetName()
except:
    try:
        UpA = fea.CastContactableToChContactNodeXYZ(modA)

At the present time, Chrono does not have a solver appropriate for FEA with NSC contact.  There is work done in that direction and we will hopefully be able to support that combination as well in the future.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Simulation unstable when the size of the bodies are
 small
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Tue, 23 Apr 2019 16:14:57 +0200

Dear Jiaxi

there may be different reasons for the instability at small scale:

  * have you resized masses and inertia tensors accordingly? See the Pi
    theorem about scaling etc.
  * have you scaled applied forces accordingly? Note that time constants
    (ex oscillation frequencies) change otherwise - or you might want to
    work with higher frequencies but then smaller dt is required, and
    all phenomena last less time.
  * are you scaling values way too much? I mean, when working with too
    small or too large numbers, the processor floating point algebra
    might suffer loss of precision - but I suspect this is not the case
  * if all is properly scaled (i.e. for the same dt, and for an expected
    equal duration of phenomena) but thisngs are still unstable, there
    might be these other issues:
      o the embedded collision engine (Bullet) seems to be affected by
        loss of precision when working with small shapes, for many
        reasons it is better to have shapes with sizes about -1...+1 in
        size. A reason for upscaling small objects, indeed,rather than
        downscaling big objects.
      o again, about collision detection: remember to change the
        'collision margin' and 'collision envelope' accordingly to your
        scale. Also 'contact breaking' threshold might be adjusted. This
        said, there are some other tolerances that are used in Bulled
        that are not changeable as easily - hence my suggestion to avoid
symbol:
Re: [chrono] Simulation unstable when the size of the bodies are
 small

text:
scale. Also 'contact breaking' threshold might be adjusted. This
        said, there are some other tolerances that are used in Bulled
        that are not changeable as easily - hence my suggestion to avoid
        too small shapes anyway, when using collisions.
      o other reasons that do not come to my mind now.

By the way: nice work with UE4!

Regards

Alessandro Tasora

Looks like you have a (very?) stiff problem, likely due to the parameters in your shock absorbers.  This may indeed require smaller time steps for stability reasons.
Another thing to try is using the HHT integrator, ideally in conjunction with a direct linear solver (such as Pardiso or MUMS, available through the optional modules Chrono::MKL and Chrono::MUMPS, respectively).  Please let us know how that works for you if you decide to give it a try.

--Radu

From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 9 May 2019 18:42:24 +0000

While you should be able to simulate a system with these components using Chrono::Parallel, I doubt you will see any performance gains.  This type of model is not really amenable to parallel computing.
Having said that, an iteration limit of 1800 (I assume this is what you meant, right?) would certainly explain the long simulation times.  This number seems excessive. You should check the model for problems that might lead to this poor convergence. For example, a common theme that comes up in many discussions on this forum: are you sure you have correct inertia matrices for all bodies in the system, consistent with their masses?

--Radu

Thomas,

A couple of additional comments:

I uploaded a fixed version of the paper on the project website a while ago (I thought I had replied to your initial message to indicate that, but it looks like I didn't)

Second, note that there's no actual difference between "adhesion" and "cohesion" in Chrono and Chrono::Parallel.  It's just an unfortunate use of different names for the same thing (which we will have to fix to remove the confusion).  We use the two terms interchangeably, but the computation of the additional normal force is done the exact same way, regardless on whether the two interacting shapes have the same (cohesion) or different (adhesion) contact material properties.

The two (simple) models currently available in both Chrono and Chrono::Parallel for SMC are (1) constant force and (2) a DMT-like (Derjaguin/Muller/Toporov) model in which the force is proportional to the square root of the effective contact radius.

--Radu

Thomas,
I believe your best bet right now is to use cohesion. The beam idea is probably not going to take you anywhere since (i) it would be really expensive, and (ii) that would not be a beam anymore (since the length in one direction would not be way larger than in the other two directions, which is the assumption for a beam – I’m saying this based on what I understood from your message).

The cohesion idea is probably not that bad. If you don’t like what’s in there right now, you can beef up the cohesion implementation to suit your needs. After all, you have access to the code. Also, perhaps it’d make more sense to do this in Chrono::Parallel and use as a starting point the SMC solution therein.

I hope this helps.
Dan

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] New system VS Repositioning
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 10 Aug 2019 08:35:05 +0000

Hi Francesco,

Because of the data structures used in Chrono::Parallel, it is non-trivial to move bodies from one parallel system to another.  There is an implicit assumption that bodies (and hence their associated collision shapes) are added to a parallel system only once, before starting simulation.  While not impossible, to go around this requires messing with the internal indices used for various levels of indirection in the Chrono::Parallel data arrays.  You can see some of this (for a limited number of collision shapes) done in Chrono::Distributed (which is meant for distributed parallel simulation of granular systems, using a domain decomposition approach and using a Chrono::Parallel system on each rank).

Of course, switching from a serial to a parallel system is further complicated by the fact that the two use different collision models.

--Radu

thanks a lot for the reply.

I added a few debug statements in my code in order to try isolating the issue. In this example explosion, I have a Chrono system of just 2 repositioned particles (so no extra bodies on the backburner, sleeping or fixed), both spherical, whose coordinates/velocities at the initial timestep (i.e., right after repositioning) are:

r1 = [-344.216, -409.212, -460.977]
v1 = [27.5252, 48.6912, 66.1802]

r2 = [-344.6, -408.39, -461.348]
v2 = [7.34839, 42.6939, 73.7849]

These are two particles that, in the previous outer timestep, where located in another Chrono system, and which came in contact and stuck together via gravity.

The diameter of the particles is 1, and the distance between the particles' centres is 0.980194. Thus they have a slight overlap. The next timestep, the two velocities become:

v1 = [-792.437, 617.491, 97.8683]
v2 = [827.323, -526.069, 42.1235]

So the x/y velocities increase 10-100 fold with respect to the previous timestep and they are much larger than the other velocities I am seeing in the rest of the simulation at this point.

Do you reckon that an overlap of 2% of the diameter is too much of an interpenetration? I have monitored my particles elsewhere in the simulation and I am seeing similar and higher interpenetrations without the exploding behaviour.

I have tried your suggestion of replacing SetSleep() with SetBodyFixed(true)/SetCollide(false), but alas it did not change the behaviour.

Hi Francesco,

Currently, the body state is comprised of the 4 quantities you listed.  For SMC systems, this will need to change in the future, when we add a missing feature in Chrono, namely keeping track of contact history needed in properly computing tangential contact forces (Chrono::Parallel already has this option for the case of simple spherical collision shapes).

So in principle, using a pool of available systems and reusing them the way you indicated should work.  "Explosions" like the ones you mention are likely due to collision shapes finding themselves in configurations with (relatively) very large penetrations.  The fact that you do not see this when recreating the various ChSystems from scratch leads me to suspect the bodies that you "put on the back-burner".  Instead of setting them as "sleeping", you may want to set them as "fixed to ground" (SetBodyFixed(true), which will completely eliminate their states from the system-wide state) *and* remove them from collision detection (SetCollide(false)).  Of course, these settings will have to be reverted if/when you later re-activate these bodies.

Currently, the body state is comprised of the 4 quantities you listed.  For SMC systems, this will need to change in the future, when we add a missing feature in Chrono, namely keeping track of contact history needed in properly computing tangential contact forces (Chrono::Parallel already has this option for the case of simple spherical collision shapes).

Instead of setting them as "sleeping", you may want to set them as "fixed to ground" (SetBodyFixed(true), which will completely eliminate their states from the system-wide state) *and* remove them from collision detection (SetCollide(false)).  Of course, these settings will have to be reverted if/when you later re-activate these bodies.

To confirm my suspicions, could you check that these "explosions" occur when one of the systems has some of these "extra" bodies?  Also, you can use a callback mechanism (ChCollisionSystem::NarrowphaseCallback) to inspect the collision pairs and look for large penetrations (you may only need to do this at the beginning of one of your "outer steps").

Finally, I am aware of some memory leaks in Chrono, but likely not all of them.  I'd appreciate if you could let us know of any you discover.

Subject: Re: [chrono] ChLinkSpringCB functor called several times within one
 simulation step?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 29 Apr 2019 07:44:57 +0000

Hello,

Indeed, that user-supplied function will be called more than once per time step (in fact, this is true of the entire system "Update" which is what ends up calling your function).  In many instances, likely including yours, this is unnecessary and it's on our todo list to address this issue (I plan on working on it in the near future).  Having said that, the changes I will be making will minimize the number of calls, but that may still be more than once per step!

In other words, you cannot expect/assume that such a function will always be called exactly once per step, as this depends on many factors (e.g. the type of integration method, solver, etc).  Like always in such cases (and this is true not only for Chrono), it is your responsibility to implement the proper logic in the user-supplied code to bypass or reuse any redundant calculations.

If in your particular case you have (presumable more costly) calculations that can be performed only once per step, one way to deal with that is by adding a function to your custom class derived from ChLinkSpringCB::ForceFunctor.  You can then call that function exactly once from within your simulation loop and have it perform and cache any calculations that only depend on current time.  Then, in your override of operator() simply use those cached values to calculate and return the output force magnitude.

--Radu

You are probably looking at some of the ChBodyEasy*** classes. Those are 
convenience classes which create bodies with a single shape.

Instead, you should create a ChBody and then attach an arbitrary number 
of visualization assets to the body and an arbitrary number of collision 
shapes to the body's collision model. See for example 
https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/irrlicht/demo_IRR_ballSMC.cpp.

you can attach additional ones. We also only create a "sphere" 
collision shape, but you can add additional ones to the body's collision 
model.

If I recall correctly, you use PyChrono. The demos I linked to are all 
C++, but it's pretty straightforward to translate them to Python.

Having said that, the tire models provided in Chrono::Vehicle (Fiala, TMeasy, Pacejka) are not very expensive (likely not much more than the rigid contact calculation for rigid tires).

If a toy model like the one in demo_IRR_suspension fits your needs, that's great.  But that's not really a proper vehicle model (including suspension kinematics and dynamics and, arguably more importantly, tire dynamics).

From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 17 Mar 2019 16:57:42 +0000

Hi Valentin,

Due to stability considerations, you cannot arbitrarily increase the step size.  For vehicle simulations, we typically use a step size of around 1-5 ms (and even lower when we use components that increase numerical stiffness, such as FEA tires).  With this, a single vehicle simulation on rigid terrain (flat or a coarse mesh) can run close to or below real time, but not a whole lot faster than that.   Note also that this is soft real-time.

I am working on several low-level changes in Chrono aimed at improving performance, but it is unlikely these will lead to speedups of 10x or so (which is what you allude to).

--Radu

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Static Analysis
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 12 Apr 2019 18:27:54 +0200

Dear Lucas,

some notes:

- the current code for static nonlinear analysis is still experimental: 
we are aware of its limitations, especially the following:

- the relaxation currently works in this simple way: it performs Newton 
iterations by slowly increasing the right hand side, ie.increasing /all/ 
applied loads from zero to max values (and then iterating few more times 
with the max values). The problem is that in a more robust setting, one 
should make a distinction between "internal loads" which should never be 
scaled, and "external" load(s) that deserves the incremental scaling. 
Example: internal loads might be spring forces in a catenary of springs, 
external load might be gravity. At the 1st iteration (10% of loads, say) 
the spring forces grow as much as needed for an equivalent linear 
analysis for the small 10% value of gravity, then at the 2nd iteration 
(20%) we need to start from that state to achieve a good convergence, 
with the already existing effect for the 10%-stretched springs, but if 
we scale /the entire/ right hand side by x0.2 as currently happens, at 
the 2nd iteration the springs are not acting 10% but 10%*0.2. I am not 
saying that the "internal"/"external" distinction is mandatory: actually 
the Newton loop could still converge, but in many cases it could require 
too many iterations, especially if the "external" load has a much 
different stiffness than the "internal" ones.

There is no way currently to modify Chrono in order to make a static
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: Static Analysis

text:
different stiffness than the "internal" ones.

There is no way currently to modify Chrono in order to make a static 
nonlinear analyisis by incrementing just an "external" set of loads, 
because of the way the API is written. Maybe in future.

So, for the moment the workaround could be that you simply repeat a 
static analysis (with ChSystem::DoStaticAnalysis() ) in your own 
for(...) loop, by incrementing just one (or few) selected load by 
yourself, i.e. the "external" load.

Alessandro Tasora

Hello,

after some code investigations, I understood the basic principles behind 
the different methods for the static analysis : linear, non linear and with 
relaxation. I just have one question left, related to our use of Chrono.

We introduced model forces, which derived from ChForce. For example, we 
added quasi-static catenary lines, which connect two bodies. The 
quasi-static solving is not done within Chrono engine, so we just impose 
forces on the bodies, via ChForces.

Without these forces, with Chrono only elements, the static equilibrium can 
be reached using the different methods (with some inherent limitations for 
the linear static method). However when I add our model forces, both linear 
and non linear static method fail to find the equilibrium. I can understand 
why the linear is not suitable but I would have thought the non linear 
method suitable. Is it because our forces are not linear models? Do you 
know of criteria on ChForces for the non linear method to be effective?

Anyway, we chose to rely on the relaxation method, that we modified a bit 
to be able to change the number of steps between two relaxations (hard 
coded in a strange way in the current version).

I saw that the static analysis implementations have not been changed in the 
last years, and is clearly not the main focus in last developments. Hence 
the sparcity of the documentation on this topic !

Lucas

From: Jeremy Mange
Date: Tue, 12 Mar 2019 13:30:53 -0700 (PDT)

I was able to replicate that error; I suspect the issue is that the static 
library name (libIrrlicht.a) was still cached by Chrono's CMake, so it did 
not know to look for the shared library (libIrrlicht.so) instead.  If you 
remove the CMakeCache.txt file from your Chrono build directory, re-run 
CMake, and point to the correct Irrlicht directory, I think it should all 
work.

One further quirk I noticed -- when I built the Irrlicht shared library, it 
created the library file "libIrrlicht.so.1.8.4" which is not found by 
Chrono's CMake, so I created a symbolic link without the version extension (ln 
-s libIrrlicht.so.1.8.4 libIrrlicht.so), which is then detected.  
Alternatively, you can "sudo make install" in the Irrlicht source 
directory, which installs the library and headers.

David - Another approach that might be helpful with the sampling issue is working off the number of steps (which is an unsigned int) as opposed to looking at the current time (which will be plagued by inherent round off error, unless you work with a step size that has an exact machine representation (of which powers of two are a subclass)).
In other words, although you have a time step of 0.01, 0.07 would have no round-off error since it would be the seventh step and so on.

On Thursday, February 13, 2020 at 11:21:35 PM UTC-5, Qiyuan Zhou wrote:
Hi Dave,

This is a limitation with floating point arithmetic rather than with SetStep(). Computers are binary machines, which means that all floating point numbers are represented as a sum of binary fractions. If a number cannot be perfectly represented using a sum of binary fractions, then there will be some round off errors. See: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html

If it is absolutely necessary that all error (including floating point errors) be eliminated from the input to your digital filters, then you should express the time step as a power of 2 such as ( A / (2^P) ) as described in this post from stack overflow<https://stackoverflow.com/questions/19473770/how-to-avoid-floating-point-errors>.

This is not surprising with the default iterative solvers which likely reach the maximum number of iterations at each step before being able to satisfy the constraints.
A first solution is to increase the allowed maximum number of iterations (of course, there will be a cost penalty associated with that, so you may want to change it after constraints are being satisfied).  You can, of course, also reduce the time step at the beginning of the simulation -- but that will still not satisfy constraints in "a couple of steps".
Alternatively, you can try the HHT integrator which, like the assembly algorithm, uses a Newton method.  Just like for the assembly problem, you may not be able to converge if starting from too far from an assembled configuration.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Constraints violation
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 11 Apr 2019 12:23:31 +0000

Hi Refaat,

This is not surprising with the default iterative solvers which likely reach the maximum number of iterations at each step before being able to satisfy the constraints.
A first solution is to increase the allowed maximum number of iterations (of course, there will be a cost penalty associated with that, so you may want to change it after constraints are being satisfied).  You can, of course, also reduce the time step at the beginning of the simulation -- but that will still not satisfy constraints in "a couple of steps".
Alternatively, you can try the HHT integrator which, like the assembly algorithm, uses a Newton method.  Just like for the assembly problem, you may not be able to converge if starting from too far from an assembled configuration.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Conservation of angular momentum
From: Alessandro Tasora

Francesco

This numerical dissipation issue is a typical drawback of most implicit
integration schemes,  where you can think at the nonsmooth timestepper (our
EULERO_IMPLICIT_LINEARIZED) as a special case.

Indeed,  there are just a few implicit timesteppers that has no
dissipation, one is the trapezoidal scheme. But it is known that
trapezoidal can become unstable when constraints are added, which makes it
rarely used.
In Chrono there is an experimental "trapezoidal linearized" scheme that
should also support nonsmooth contacts (that would make it the only other
option for nonsmooth contacts after the default Euler implicit linearized)
but it is still in testing phase and I'd not suggest using it.

Another non dissipative implicit scheme,  which we have also in Chrono,  is
HHT aka generalized alpha, under a proper choice of the alpha parameter,
but the HHT timestepper does not support nonsmooth contacts anyway. ( In
literature there is just a work by Acary et al. about how to use HHT
together with nonsmooth contacts, but I suspect that it would be quite cpu
intensive if we implement it.)

Side note: even after your particles get well packed in a cluster in zero
gravity, the cluster may "deform" and wobble cyclically for a while, with
microscopic frictional displacements between particles. This effect might
be overestimated when using the nonsmooth integrator if the cluster is
spinning quickly because that integrator, being of first order, cannot
match perfectly circular trajectories, expecially for long time steps.

Francesco,

The issues you're experiencing are indeed due to numerical dissipation.  As Simone mentioned, there's not a whole lot of choice for the DVI formulation in the case of non-smooth contact.
For problems without contacts we could maybe use a simplectic integrator (as simple as a Verlet-type).  Contacts with the SMC formulation (penalty-based) will already have damping which is probably not what you want for your particular simulations.
By the way, there is no choice of integrator in Chrono::Parallel.  Reducing step size is the only thing you can do, but that will only alleviate the problem, not eliminate it and it will obviously affect cost.  Maybe a careful scaling of your problem could help to some extent.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] system "explodes" after loading from a checkpoint
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 30 Nov 2018 08:55:32 +0000

Will,

It's difficult to say exactly what happens without knowing more details on how you do the checkpointing.

But I have a pretty strong suspicion that the problem is that you do not save/restore the *complete* system state.  The state of a 3D body is position (location and orientation) + velocity (linear and angular).   It seems to me that you do not save and restore any velocity information.  Note that, for spherical bodies you may get away without checkpointing the orientation (if the contact sphere is centered at the COM);  even then, you might still need orientation depending on how you set and define your links.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] What is easiest way to realize damping on a
 ChLinkLockRevolute
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 2 Apr 2019 14:05:09 +0000

Two options:

  1.  Use the ChLinkForce mechanism.
See demo_IRR_prismatic_force in the current 'develop' branch for an example; the demo uses the "Z" force on a prismatic joint, but  you can do a similar thing with the "Rz" torque on a revolute joint.

  2.  Use a rotational spring-damper element connecting the bodies joined by the revolute joint.  A ChLinkRotSpringCB element allows you to define an arbitrary torque expression (through a functor object).
See demo_IRR_rot_spring.

--Radu

Never mind, I found the solution to my issue.

The correct heading angle can be calculated by taking the arctan2 (quadrant 
aware arctan) of x and z components of a unit vector in the y direction 
rotated by the rotation quaternion from the robot:
q = bot1.GetRot()
d2 = q.Rotate(chrono.ChVectorD(0,1,0))
heading = np.arctan2(d2.z,d2.x)

Dear Manish:

A- I cannot tell you a precise estimate on the performance of Chrono at 
simulating a 3D car model with a motor model plus tire models, but as a 
ballpark figure I can tell you that I was able to run a vehicle with 
full suspensions in real-time with full suspensions on a single core. It 
was a 13 bodies + 20 constraint model, plus some LUT-based engine.
Note. We still do not have a 'simplified' 14-dof object as in videogames 
to make super-fast simulations, ex. with just K&C curves instead of full 
3d suspension, but maybe we'll have in future.
Maybe Dr. Radu Serban (here in CC) can comment on this, because he's the 
main developer of the vehicle module.

B- about Chrono+Unreal interaction: currently we haven't a solution for 
this, but as I worked a lot with Unreal for other projects, I can tell 
you that in principle it can be done.
B.1 - In fact, one or two years ago someone already made a simulator 
where Chrono sent simulation outputs to a TCP/IP socket, and a custom 
Unreal visualizer continuously updated 3D shapes on the screen depending 
on the TCP socket input. This maybe the simpliest way to go, but also 
the less powerful.
B.2 - A more tight interaction could be that you link directly the 
ChronoEngine.dll in the Unreal C++ build system, and you use it from 
within Unreal (in this case, remember that you could also exploit 
inheritance from Unreal's Actor classes and Chrono ChBody clesses, for 
example, but for all Chrono data you would loose the nice feature to

within Unreal (in this case, remember that you could also exploit 
inheritance from Unreal's Actor classes and Chrono ChBody clesses, for 
example, but for all Chrono data you would loose the nice feature to 
access class members via Unreal's introspection mechanism, that is based 
on the UPROPERTY macros. That is, Chrono classes would stay in Unreal 
except that you won't be able to use them via Blueprint scripting)

Subject: Re: Tire friction force in zero slip cases
From: Rainer Gericke
Date: Tue, 19 Feb 2019 09:18:54 -0800 (PST)

Hi Refaat,

you know, there can be two important case where tire slip can be zero:


   1. the vehicle stands still, no wheel rotation = no horizontal forces
   2. the vehicle is running with wheels rolling without relative sliding 
   to the road surface, here the horizontal force resulting from the tire 
   rolling resistance is still active

I think you are interested in the first case and wonder what happens when 
the vehicle is standing breaked on a slope, well it will begin to slide 
until there is slip again, which is indeed not handled. The same is 
actually true for Pacejka and Fiala. The rigid tire and the FEA based tire 
model should work correctly yet.

It is also worth to mention that the slip dependent tire forces in TMeasy 
are always zero at zero slip, this is a difference to the magic formulae 
which can have horizontal and vertical offsets. That reflects the measured 
tire forces of course but is not helpful to handle the stand still case. We 
are actually planing to find a better solution for the stand still problem 
that could be include in TMeasy, Pacejka and Fiala.

Best

Subject: Re: [chrono] Coupling Chrono with Hydrodynamic Software
From: Letournel Lucas
Date: Mon, 16 Sep 2019 09:08:57 +0200

Hi,

We actually did it in FRyDoM framework. Hydrodynamic forces are based on 
potential flow theory, with hydrodynamic database (added mass, radiation 
damping, excitation force, etc.) coming from various solvers (Nemoh and 
WAMIT). The last release takes into account multi-body hydrodynamic 
interactions. We also added a 3D quasi static line solver, for moored 
applications.

FRyDoM is in C++, open-source, co-developped with LHEEA lab (Ecole 
Centrale de Nantes) and available at

  * frydom.org/ <http://frydom.org/>
  * theory.frydom.org/ <http://theory.frydom.org/>
  * register.frydom.org <http://register.frydom.org/>
  * api.frydom.org <http://api.frydom.org/>(for registered users only)

You can also find some videos of possible applications on our youtube 
channel <https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCQfqgvAc7sTk8q-YuW1kVzA/videos>.

We are open to collaboration if you need features not already 
implemented, and discussion if you have more questions !

Lucas Letournel

From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 28 Aug 2019 15:06:21 +0000

Chrono is a set of middleware libraries.  As such, it does not provide an executable; instead, you have to write your own main function (C++ or Python) to set up a model and control its simulation.
Look at the various demos included in the distribution and browse the online documentation at http://api.projectchrono.org/

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Problem with generating template project
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 8 Mar 2019 15:50:10 +0000

Yes, the problem is that you end up linking your project build in debug against release Chrono DLLs.

This is a general Windows issue: when using dynamic libraries (DLLs), those need to be in a place where Windows can find them (either in your PATH or else copied next to the executable).  To make it somewhat easier for users, through some CMake macros, we are able to copy the release DLLs next to your executable.  However, we cannot know what configuration (debug or release) you are using at any time.

When you build your project in debug, you will have to manually copy the Chrono debug DLLs (from the Chrono build tree) next to your executable.

Note that there is a message highlighting this aspect that is printed when you configure with CMake your project.

--Radu

P.S. In the future, as much as possible, could you please post error message and such in plain text, instead of images?  That's preferable for many reasons, including the fact that the messages can be searched.

m_sound_engine->play2D(GetChronoDataFile("vehicle/sounds/carsound_old.ogg").c_str(), true, false, true);

Subject: Re: Variable length flexible cable for airborne wind energy system
 simulation
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Mon, 25 Feb 2019 04:07:40 -0800 (PST)

Dear Xander

- yes you could make cables using particles, ex small ChBody spheres (ex 
create them via ChBodyEasySphere) connected with constraints of 
ChLinkDistance type, however:

- my suggestion is that you avoid using particles for making cables, 
because the overhead for using FEA is low if compared to the idea above. 
You could use the ChBeamSectionCable FEA element, it's an ANCF torsion-less 
element, as demonstrated in* demo_FEA_cables.cpp*

- note that you can create and add elements (and corresponding nodes) to 
the mesh on the fly during the animation, but in this case just remember to 
call the my_new_element->SetupInitial() just after you add it to the mesh, 
because the SetupInitial happens for all elements at the beginning of the 
simulation, but in this case your new elements would explicitly need it as 
they are created after the beginning.

- depending on the n. of elements, a 20Hz tick can be obtained. With more 
than 100 elements it might be difficult. Btw for sake of performance in FEA 
I'd suggest you to build and use the optional MKL module. 

- keep in mind: unfortunately Chrono FEA stuff cannot work together with 
our efficient nonsmooth dynamics (i.e. if you need contacts anyway, you 
cannot use ChSystemNSC: you rather need ChSystemSMC, that uses smooth 
contacts with penalty formulation, hence requiring small time steps. This 
will behave as an implicit integrator -and it can be efficient too, thanks
symbol:

text:
cannot use ChSystemNSC: you rather need ChSystemSMC, that uses smooth 
contacts with penalty formulation, hence requiring small time steps. This 
will behave as an implicit integrator -and it can be efficient too, thanks 
to the MKL solver if you enable it- but small time steps are needed anyway 
because of the high nonlinearity in contacts). This limitation might be 
removed in future releases.

- there is a demo_FEA_beams_extrude that demonstrates an experimental class 
that automatically creates elements and nodes, as in 'unwinding' a wire. 
This is using the ChElementBeamIGA FEA element, that is a more powerful 
element than the ANCF cable. But this element can be overkill for your 
needs. Also, the demo is slow as it uses plasticity too. 

Last note: there is a tutorial in projectchrono GitHub repo, if I remember, 
that I wrote as an exercise to create a cable that falls on the ground with 
collision.

best regards

Indeed, Chrono::parallel has no support for FEA.  Given that there is no clear way on how to expose all of the FEA functionality in the parallel solver, there is currently no plan for this.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Chrono tire physics for performance vehicles
From: Rainer Gericke
Date: Fri, 19 Jul 2019 01:22:22 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Alan,

you can imagine its is not easy for me to give hints about a code I don't 
know. I can at least say something:

   - don't use the rigid tire model, it doesn't represent a vehicle tire 
   very well. It will not work at high speed (> 5 km/h!!)
   - Pac89 is ok, but make a plot of the forces and torques it can deliver, 
   so you can be sure to get meaningful results. The Pac89 parameters of our 
   HMMWV should do at least something for the first tests
   - for your model you don't need driveline shafts, you can apply a drive 
   torque directly to the rotating wheel body. Take care of the correct 
   direction of the torque vector!
   - you need the velocities vx and vy of the wheel center expressed in the 
   local tire coordinate system
   - calculate the slip values kappa [in percent], and the slip angle alpha 
   and the camber angle gamma [in degrees]
   - calculate Fz using the tire deflection and the vertical stiffness 
   value that you have in your Pac89 data set
   - calculate Fx, Fy, Mz... in the contact point of tire/road. Fz must be 
   in [kN], the results of Pac89 formulae are in [N] rsp. [Nm]
   - now that you have all the result values, you have to project them to 
   the wheel canter and make a transformation to the global coordinate system
   - a first test could be to accelerate the vehicle straight ahead by a 
   const drive torque and look carefully to all result values

Good Luck

Rainer

Subject: Re: [chrono] Imposing motion on bodies connected by joints
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 22 Dec 2018 09:43:40 +0000

Milad,

Keep in mind that setting a motion function on a marker, moves that marker *relative* to the body it is associated with.
The confusion probably stems from the fact that you think of the markers as always being rigidly attached to the associated body and think that motion functions on a marker would move the marker in global space (thus "dragging" the body after them). This is not the case with these motion functions: again, what they allow you to do is move the marker relative to the associated body. Think of a free body in a system with no gravity.  Applying a motion function to a marker on this body will not move the body.

A revolute joint has two underlying markers (think of them as two frames) that are constrained to always have the same origin and have their Z axes aligned (resulting in the 5 constraints that define a revolute joint).  So applying a rotation motion along that common axis to either one of these markers will not change the kinematics of your system.

For a spherical joint, the constraints on the two underlying markers are simply that their origins must coincide.  This means that rotating either one of these underlying markers (again, this rotation is relative to the associated body of that marker) will have no effect on the body relative motion.  What is meaningful to do for a spherical joint is specify translation motion functions; this would have the effect of sliding the location of the spherical joint (in other words, place the spherical joint at a different location on one body or the other).

text:
A revolute joint has two underlying markers (think of them as two frames) that are constrained to always have the same origin and have their Z axes aligned (resulting in the 5 constraints that define a revolute joint).  So applying a rotation motion along that common axis to either one of these markers will not change the kinematics of your system.

For a spherical joint, the constraints on the two underlying markers are simply that their origins must coincide.  This means that rotating either one of these underlying markers (again, this rotation is relative to the associated body of that marker) will have no effect on the body relative motion.  What is meaningful to do for a spherical joint is specify translation motion functions; this would have the effect of sliding the location of the spherical joint (in other words, place the spherical joint at a different location on one body or the other).

One other way of looking at this: specifying a motion function on a joint marker will affect the relative motion of the connected bodies *only if* that function will result in changing the constraints induced by the joint on the states of the connected bodies.

I modified a test program I used in the past to illustrate what is happening (attached) with different settings. This test uses a revolute joint (ChLinkLockRevolute), but you can easily modify it to experiment with a ChLinkLockSpherical.

--Radu

Milad,

The ChLinkLock::SetMotion*** functions do not do what you want (i.e., actuating the degree(s) of freedom of the joint).  Instead, they control the motion of the markers that define that joint; in other words, for a revolute joint they do not affect the body relative rotation about the joint's rotation axis; instead, they control the motion of that axis.

Note that this is old code which, as far as I know, is not used in any of our demos.  It's not well documented and (obviously) confusing.  I'm not sure we need this functionality, so maybe a good candidate to be obsoleted.
