Milad,

Well, I answered the question you originally asked.  Using the ChLinkLock::SetMotion*** functions you cannot actuate the degrees of freedom for a particular type of joint.  What you can do is "override" the constraints that the particular type of joint imposes.  This is why you were able to implement the functionality you wanted on a ChLinkLockLock (all translations and all rotations constrained).  This also means you will not be able to actuate the rotation on a ChLinkLockSpherical using this approach (you could however control the location of the spherical joint).

So, to get the functionality you want you should start with a ChLinkLockLock and impose motions on the DOFs you want.  With this you will be able to replicate the kinematics of a revolute joint, a spherical joint, etc (not exactly all possible kinematic joints, but a large number of them can be framed in this "link lock" formulation).

If you want to understand the implementation, look in ChLinkLock.cpp at functions such as UpdateTime() and UpdateState().

Finally, one clarification: the SetMotion*** functions are certainly useful for a ChLinkLockLock joint (like above).  When I talked about obsoleting this, I meant possibly leaving this functionality only for the ChLinkLockLock derived class and not for all ChLinkLock joints (also for efficiency considerations).

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: How to build my project
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 12 Apr 2019 08:12:40 +0000

Hi Yotaro,

The problem is indeed related to the path to the Chrono and Chrono::Vehicle data files.  The input files for Chrono::Vehicle (such as JSON specification files for vehicle subsystems) are assumed to be given *relative* to the location of the "vehicle data directory".  The default value for this location is "../data/vehicle/".  And similarly for other data files used in Chrono (which are assumed to be provided relative to a location with default value "../data/".

So when you move one of the existing Chrono demos into a separate project (or when you write your own Chrono-based project), you must invoke the functions chrono::SetChronoDataPath and chrono::vehicle::SetDataPath (typically right at the beginning of your main function) to point your code to the correct location of the data files.

If you are structuring your example based on the template_project, you can do this with only a couple of small changes:

  1.  In the CMakeLists.txt (line 129 in template_project/CMakeLists.txt), replace

  set_target_properties(myexe PROPERTIES
        COMPILE_FLAGS "${CHRONO_CXX_FLAGS} ${EXTRA_COMPILE_FLAGS}"
        COMPILE_DEFINITIONS "CHRONO_DATA_DIR=\"${CHRONO_DATA_DIR}\""
        LINK_FLAGS "${CHRONO_LINKER_FLAGS}")
with
  set_target_properties(myexe PROPERTIES
        COMPILE_FLAGS "${CHRONO_CXX_FLAGS} ${EXTRA_COMPILE_FLAGS}"
        COMPILE_DEFINITIONS "CHRONO_DATA_DIR=\"${CHRONO_DATA_DIR}\";CHRONO_VEHICLE_DATA_DIR=\"${CHRONO_VEHICLE_DATA_DIR}\""
        LINK_FLAGS "${CHRONO_LINKER_FLAGS}")
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: How to build my project

text:
COMPILE_FLAGS "${CHRONO_CXX_FLAGS} ${EXTRA_COMPILE_FLAGS}"
        COMPILE_DEFINITIONS "CHRONO_DATA_DIR=\"${CHRONO_DATA_DIR}\";CHRONO_VEHICLE_DATA_DIR=\"${CHRONO_VEHICLE_DATA_DIR}\""
        LINK_FLAGS "${CHRONO_LINKER_FLAGS}")

This will define an additional macro CHRONO_VEHICLE_DATA_DIR in addition to the already existing CHRONO_DATA_DIR (both of these are based on the CMake variables with equivalent names which are set by the Chrono project configuration script).

  2.  At the top of the main() function, add the following two lines:
  chrono::SetChronoDataPath(CHRONO_DATA_DIR);
  chrono::vehicle::SetDataPath(CHRONO_VEHICLE_DATA_DIR);

Please let me know if this solves the problem.

--Radu

On 11/7/2018 10:43 AM, lucas.letournel@dice-engineering.com<mailto:lucas.letournel@dice-engineering.com> wrote:
Hello,

I just ran into something that seemed bugged to me, in the ChQuaternion::operator*=. I am still using Chrono with the commit

934064d2ccf8e9690373a0fd03c93e91c7f4b2c8

The operator*= is based on the Cross method, applied to this :

this->Cross(*this, other);

But in Cross, this.data is modified on one line, and used also for calculating the following ones.

For a quick check, you can try this :


chrono::ChQuaternion<double> First (1.,0.,0.,0.);
chrono::ChQuaternion<double> Second (0.7,0.7,0.,0.);

chrono::ChQuaternion<double> Result;
Result = First*Second;
std::cout<<"Result : e0 = "<<Result.e0()<<", e1 = "<<Result.e1()<<", e2 = "<<Result.e2()<<", e3 = "<<Result.e3()<<std::endl;

First *= Second;
std::cout<<"First  : e0 = "<<First.e0()<<", e1 = "<<First.e1()<<", e2 = "<<First.e2()<<", e3 = "<<First.e3()<<std::endl;


Result and First should be equals to Second, since First is the unit quaternion. While the operator* gives the right result, the operator*= gives a wrong one.

I think this bug was not spotted earlier since the compositions of rotations are done usually using rotation matrices in ChFrame.

Best regards,

Lucas Letournel

Subject: Re: [chrono] orientation convection in Irrlicht
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Tue, 8 Jan 2019 14:56:13 +0100

Hi Mingwu,

the issue is that Irrlicht was designed for the left-handed frame 
representation, and there is no easy way to switch to right handed.

Once I tried to change the camera perspective matrix for the Irrlicht 
camera, ok, this can mirror the scene on horizontal direction and get a 
proper right handed view, but the problem is that most meshes will 
disappear because they are back-culled for performance reason, and 
back-culling depends on the camera projection matrix. Yes, one could fix 
this by enabling two-sided rendering for all meshes, but it would be a 
dirty hack. So we posponed the right-handed frame fix for the future, 
when we'll migrate to a more recent renderer.

regards

Alessandro

Subject: Re: [chrono] orientation convection in Irrlicht
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 8 Jan 2019 07:27:51 +0000

Mingwu,

You are correct: Chrono always uses right-handed frames but Irrlicht uses left-handed frames.
While in principle it would be possible to mirror everything for rendering purposes, we currently do not do this.  We do not plan on fixing this issue with Irrlicht rendering, but are considering switching to a different run-time rendering engine (which will be using right-handed frames).

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Rolling/sliding contact / Knee Implants
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Wed, 13 Feb 2019 16:44:55 +0100

Dear Joseph:

Yes, in PyChrono you can use mesh-vs-mesh contact. I just added a new 
demo_mesh.py last week. Preview the code at this address:

http://api.projectchrono.org/development/tutorial_pychrono_demo_mesh.html

Some hints:

- if using the default nonsmooth contact, ie. ChSystemNSC, the sliding 
contact between condyles would be a bit 'noisy' as it would happen if 
they were made of faceted steel,of course. The more the facets, i.e.the 
denser the mesh, the less noticeable this artifact is, but at the same 
time it would demand more cpu time. This is perhaps the faster and more 
robust simulation method, however.

- if using ChSystemSMC, you can have penalty based contacts that would 
give less 'sharp' effects. Maybe you prefer it. But if doing so, I'd 
suggest you to increase the "'inflating radius for triangles for 
increased robustness" - look in the py source code where I wrote a 
comment on this, at 
body_B.GetCollisionModel().AddTriangleMesh(....).This inflating effect 
would be beneficial also for ChSystemNSC, to increase robustness of the 
collision detection algorithm, but for ChSystemSMC is even more 
necessary because one would espect some interpenetration, and 
interpenetration is one of the major causes of loss of robustnessin 
concave-vs-concave collision detection. Note also that one can prepare a 
surface with negative offset X from a 3D CAD then use X asinflating 
radius in the AddTriangleMesh(), to keep things in order.

- using sphere decompositions for the contact is efficient and robust,

- using sphere decompositions for the contact is efficient and robust, 
but it may be tricky to set up. How do you create the spherical 
decomposition, by hand? or do you have some automatic method? Also, yes, 
convex smooth surfaces decompose well into clusters of 
spheres/ellipsoids, but concave ones do not decompose well.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Is it possible to creat a video from a simulation?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 5 Apr 2019 06:14:16 +0000

You should explicitly call the Irrlicht function writeImageToFile in your simulation loop (which would also allow you to control the FPS instead of saving every single frame), in which case you can specify the name of the image file for each frame (which can also include a path).  You can also use the  filesystem utilities to programatically create output directories as needed.

Take a look at demo_VEH_M113 (lines 36-364).  There, the function WriteImageToFile is a simple wrapper around the Irrlicht writeImageToFile (see ChVehicleIrrApp.cpp, lines 405-411).  You can simply inline that in your main loop.

--Radu

Hi Jessica,

As it happens, implementing a parser for URDF is on my todo list, but I 
couldn't tell you when I will get to it.
In the past, I built robot models in Chrono from a URDF specification, 
but didn't get to implement a generic parser. There is no particular 
reason why such a parser is not yet included, except for the fact that 
we are all stretched pretty thin, so have to prioritize what we work on 
and needs for funded projects take precedence.

The main challenge with such a parser is not in dealing with the STLs, 
but rather in generating a Chrono model (bodies, joints, etc) from the 
recursive description encoded in a URDF file to the so-called Cartesian 
formulation used in Chrono. Having said that, we did something similar 
in the past for parsing OpenSim input files (which also define a 
multibody system in a recursive fashion). See 
http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1utils_1_1_ch_parser_open_sim.html 
and demo_IRR_OpenSim_parser.

--Radu

Hi Jakob,

If I understand it correctly, you want to drive your motor to a given angle (with a given speed) and then have it stay at that angle?
If that is the case, you can use a ChLinkMotorRotationAngle with an angle function that is a combination of a ramp (with slope equal to your desired speed) up to the final angle value and then a constant. You can achieve this either using a custom function (derive from ChFunction and implement the virtual method Get_y) or else with a ChFunction_Sequence (combine a ChFunction_Ramp and a ChFunction_Constant).  You can see example of both in demo_CH_functions.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Object penetration issues with small shafts/bearings
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Mon, 12 Apr 2021 12:01:47 +0200

Dear Adrian,

welcome to the community.
I already worked on the simulaiton of watch movement simulations in the 
past, so I can give you some hints:

Very interesting, especilly because you are also using OpenCascade. Are 
you doing this using the c++ module and just load the STEP models from 
disk, or doing all in run-time using Chrono::Cascade side to side with 
the Cascade API (or PyChrono plus the PyOCC python module)?

This is quite challenging, I think, given the extremely tight 
tolerances. If this is your goal, you need to scale up all the 
geometries up to the point where the clearance is (at least) 2x the 
collision tolerances (collision envelope, collision margin).

By thge way: note that keeping the original sizing (of pivots and jewels 
and other parts) and scaling down the tolerances in theory would be the 
same, but in practice there numerical and practical issues: for example 
the collision detection is based on Bullet, that is tuned to work well 
with not-so-small numbers. To make a long story short, I strongly 
encourage to scale up the sizing of the parts and use moderate values of 
collision tolerances...

The best scenario is where colliding parts have an overall size of about 
1 units in Chrono. So for example in your case you can scale the model 
1000x, from millimeters to meters, or even more.

ok, so a 18'000 A/h escapement.

Questions:

1)
are you modeling the bearing as a 3D mesh?

2)
are you modeling the pivots as meshes?
symbol: Re: [chrono] Object penetration issues with small shafts/bearings

text:
2)
are you modeling the pivots as meshes?

I assume so, because you mentioned that you use OpenCascade, so I 
suppose that you conver the CAD shape of the bearing into a triangle 
mesh in some way, and this will call in the Chrono 3d mesh- 3d mesh 
collision algorithm.
Note that the 3Dmesh-3Dmesh collision algorithm is the least robust of 
the cases, in the sense that there are circumstances (too tiny 
triangles, odd concavities, large motion respect to size of triangles, 
too thin parts) that can make the collision to interpenetrate.

The best scenario is instead when you have chrono collision primitives 
(spheres, boxes, cones) colliding between them. This is much more robust.

An intermediate scenario is when a 3D mesh collide with collision 
primitives - still not as robust as primitive-primitive.

But: how to avoid mesh-mesh in case of pivots vs bearings?

I know that there is no wasy way to represent the_jewel bearing _as a 
primitive (there is no "hollow cylinder" collision primitive in Chrono, 
yet) so there are two possibilities: a) you continue to use the 3D mesh 
for it, or b) you approximate it as a circular array of boxes (this is 
still a faceted approximation, but may be more robust than the triangle 
mesh.. worth trying). This must be done "by hand" at the c++ level, or 
using some smart preprocessing tool - for example in the SolidWorks 
plugin I added the possibility of introducing sphere/box geometries on 
top of the CAD model just for collision purposes.

However, at least _pivots_ can be easily simplified. In OpenCascade the 
pivots are most likely modeled as (various) cylinders/toruses or other
symbol: Re: [chrono] Object penetration issues with small shafts/bearings

text:
However, at least _pivots_ can be easily simplified. In OpenCascade the 
pivots are most likely modeled as (various) cylinders/toruses or other 
canonical geometries, but when translated into Chrono, this info is lost 
and all becomes a big triangle 3D mesh. But here it is easy to create 
them by hand in c++ as cylinders, ie cylindrical collision primitives. 
This, unless you need some strange geometries and collisions like for 
anti-shock bearings etc.


As a rule of thumb, the envelope should be about the max distance that a 
part can travel within a single time step.

Once the collision is set up in a proper way (large sizing of parts, 
good collision geometries, proper margin/envelope), I suggest you to use 
a timestep that is /not lower than/ 1/200 of the period of the 
oscillation. Having scaled up all your system size, your period might 
not be 1/2.5 of a second, or may be yes in cased you scaled the forces 
(spring stiffness) accordingly - this does not matter, what is important 
is how many time steps per period of oscillation. If you want to capture 
complcate phenomena like the anchor engage/disengagement, etc., you need 
much smaller timestep. Even worse, if you have extremely small 
clearances and you want to simulate the backlash, as you are aiming at...
Btw. how much radial clearance do you have in your pivots, if this is 
not a confidential info?

I'm sorry but the simulation of escapements is one of the most critical 
scenarios to simulate because if you introduce too much approximations 
you loose the reason for simulating a clock, that is all about precision
symbol: Re: [chrono] Object penetration issues with small shafts/bearings

text:
I'm sorry but the simulation of escapements is one of the most critical 
scenarios to simulate because if you introduce too much approximations 
you loose the reason for simulating a clock, that is all about precision 
after all... If this was a toy or another mechanical device, you could 
live with long timesteps and the NSC dynamics would make enough sense, 
but for clock movements I suggest you to use small steps. At least you 
do not need millions of timesteps per oscillations like when one uses 
smooth dynamics + penalty for the contacts - one of my collaborators 
simulated an escapement using smooth dynamics and it took days just for 
two or three alternances.

best regards,

Alessandro Tasora

From: Zachary Ferguson
Date: Sat, 29 Dec 2018 09:13:03 -0800 (PST)

Thanks for the quick reply Alessandro. I tested some of your suggestions 
and found that:

- The BARZILAIBORWEIN solver did not reduce the constraint drift.
- The mass and inertia tensor are computed properly using the density 
parameter of the ChBodyEasyCylinder and are expressed in the correct units.
- The recovery speed was never set in the example I posted so it was the 
default value of 0.02 cm / s which, as you pointed out, is too small. I 
scaled it to the correct units, but it induces a lot of energy into the 
system.

One way of removing the constraint drift I discovered is to use the Euler 
implicit projected time-stepper instead of the Euler implicit linearized 
time-stepper. Using Euler implicit projected completely removes the 
constraint drift, even for larger time-steps. It was pointed out to me, 
however, that projection methods generally apply a post-stabilization 
correction at the end of each time step that generally comes close to 
guaranteeing constraint satisfaction at the cost of physical accuracy.

The same source suggested that generally, the best way to guarantee joint 
constraints being satisfied while maintaining physical accuracy at largish 
time step is to use a reduced coordinate formulation, i.e., in joint space, 
for the arm. (And full coordinates for the mesh-to-arm collisions and 
dynamics.) Does Chrono implement reduced coordinates for joints?

- Zach

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] ChLinkLockRevolute not preventing translation
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Sat, 29 Dec 2018 14:47:25 +0100

Hi Zachary

this looks strange because the constraint drifting you experienced is 
something that we encountered in the following cases:

- using SOR or SSOR or similar solvers with too few iterations (not your 
case, using APGD).

- using systems where the mass ratios of parts and/or their size aspect 
ratios are very odd, ex. a hinge with a long rod whose center of mass is 
too much offset. Seems not your case.

- using systems with too complicate mechanism compared to the number of 
iterations. Again, it does not seem your case.

Some suggestions:
- Have you tried the BARZILAIBORWEIN solver?
- Have you cheched that mass AND inertia tensor are properly computed, 
considering your scale (centimeters)? Odd-scaled inertia tensor may 
impact the solver convergence more than expected...
- The recovery speed value: it is 0.02 in your test, right? If in cm, 
this could be way too low, almost as if there is zero constraint 
stabilization (the drifting I see in your movie seems like the case of 
large timesteps WITHOUT the stabilization). When the stabilization is 
working properly, even large timesteps should not be a cause of drifting 
issues like yours.

Let me know.

Alessandro Tasora

From: Radu Serban

Hi Justin,

You are correct, I forgot to mention this issue. Unfortunately the Bullet collision detection library currently used in Chrono does not allow us to properly set the effective radius of curvature for the penalty approach.  And therefore we have to use this default, global value.  In your situation, where you look at a single interaction between two spheres, you can set this value to the correct value (just like you did).

For simulations with different shapes and different sizes, a workaround is to use the callback mechanism provided through ChCollisionSystem::NarrowphaseCallback and overwrite the effective radius of curvature for each pair interaction.  Obviously that becomes quickly expensive for larger problems (and, for certain shapes, you may not have all the geometric information needed).

We are planning on replacing Bullet for collision detection and/or implement our own narrow phase.  But this is not likely to happen in the very near future.

Regarding your follow up question, indeed you cannot mix SMC and NSC in the same simulation.  The contact formulation (and type of contact material) for a body must agree with the system type (ChSystemNSC or ChSystemSMC).  Even if we allowed mixing the two types of materials in the same simulation, we wouldn't be able to resolve contacts between shapes of different "models" (since for contact we must be able to characterize the pair, not only individual shapes).

If you want to stay with the SMC formulation, you should be able to specify a large modulus of elasticity for the wall.  The effective modulus of elasticity is calculated as
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: Max normal force between to spheres.

text:
Regarding your follow up question, indeed you cannot mix SMC and NSC in the same simulation.  The contact formulation (and type of contact material) for a body must agree with the system type (ChSystemNSC or ChSystemSMC).  Even if we allowed mixing the two types of materials in the same simulation, we wouldn't be able to resolve contacts between shapes of different "models" (since for contact we must be able to characterize the pair, not only individual shapes).

If you want to stay with the SMC formulation, you should be able to specify a large modulus of elasticity for the wall.  The effective modulus of elasticity is calculated as
inv_E = (1 - mu1^2 ) / E1 +  (1 - mu2^2) / E2
E_eff = 1 / inv_E

--Radu

On Wednesday, April 3, 2019 at 2:07:58 PM UTC-4, Radu Serban wrote:

Justin,

The value of kn you print out is *not* the value used for the contact force calculation.

The contact force computed with a formulation such as Hertz depends on properties of a composite material (obtained as a combination of the properties of the materials of the two colliding objects).

The value you print out is actually not even used with the way you set up your test.  Indeed, we provide two different ways of specifying the properties of a contact material for an object:

  1.  (default) specify E and nu
  2.  specify kn, gn, kt, gt

(you can switch to option 2 by calling ChSystem::UseMaterialProperties with an argument 'false')

In either case, the contact forces are computed using some different values, let's call them Kn, Gn, Kt, Gt which are combinations of the parameters from 2 materials (which may also be identical, like in your case).  In other words,
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: Max normal force between to spheres.

text:
(you can switch to option 2 by calling ChSystem::UseMaterialProperties with an argument 'false')

In either case, the contact forces are computed using some different values, let's call them Kn, Gn, Kt, Gt which are combinations of the parameters from 2 materials (which may also be identical, like in your case).  In other words,

  1.  Kn = Kn(E_1, nu_1, E_2, nu_2)
  2.  Kn = Kn(kn_1, kn_2)

and similarly for Gn, Kt, Gt.    (In fact, these quantities also depend on other things, such as the radius of curvature of the two shapes at the contact point and the penetration depth.)

Since you are using the default option (1 above), kn_1, gn_1, kt_1, gt_1 and kn_2, gn_2, kt_2, gt_2 don't come into play at all.   Even when using option 2, Kn != kn_1 and Kn != kn_2.

In either case, what you end up printing in your code is kn_1 (or kn_2) and you just pick up the default value of 2e5.   The quantity you seem interested in (which would be Kn in the notation above) is not accessible to the user.  For efficiency reasons we do not store these values and hence cannot provide access to them.  But for your simple test case, you should be able to hack the code and extract this information if you need it (it's a bit deep in the guts of Chrono, but look at ChContactSMC.h starting at line 188)

--Radu

Hi Prabhat,

To answer your question: You probably see a warning in your output file,
""""
WARNING! At least one clump is initialized with a position out of the box 
domain you specified.
It is found at 0.378, 0, 0.076383 (this message only shows one such 
example).
This simulation is unlikely to go as planned.
"""
This is the problem. It appears that the points you sampled live in x∈[0, 
0.4], but the x range of your simulation world is defined as something like 
[-0.25, 0.25]. This will make the particles to be initialized in unexpected 
locations, cause large initial penetrations, and then destabilize the 
simulation. I fixed the world size definition, and it seems to fix the 
problem. The extremely fine step size you are using is not necessary: The 
physics in this simulation is simple.

By the way, in the upcoming paper about DEME 
<https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04648>, we will include a Goldenberg test 
example, and provide the associated demo script. If you want, we can let 
you know when it is officially published.

Thank you,
Ruochun

From: Dario Mangoni

Hi Lewis,
yes, you just need the piece of code of the "How to use it" section that 
you found here 
<http://api.projectchrono.org/module_mkl_installation.html>. Preferably 
the one with Sparsity Pattern enabled (most of the time has positive 
effects).

I just add a little thing (that I should probably add to the reference 
manual).
Adding *permanently *the MKL-binaries folder to PATH is *not *actually 
the "good way" to do things.
One might do this:
- open the command prompt
- call the /mklvars.bat /script (contained in /C:\Program Files 
(x86)\IntelSWTools\compilers_and_libraries\windows\mkl\bin/) with 
appropriate arguments (e.g. for me it would be mklvars.bat intel64 lp64 
vs2017); this would /temporarly /add the MKL binary folder to your PATH 
envvar
- from that same command prompt launch your executable that uses Intel MKL

This is what /should /be done, but it's sometimes overwhelming for the 
average user. So, I preferred to suggest the hard-coded/ugly way to 
provide the binaries folder directly into PATH once and for all.
However, please mind that you may want to add *either *the MKL-binaries 
folder for /intel64 /*or */ia32/, preferably not both.

Dario

Subject: Re: [chrono] Reducing instability in a system involving large mass
 ratios
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 18 Mar 2019 13:56:08 +0000

Hi Lewis,

A mass ratio of 200:8 is not so large as to result in insurmountable convergence issues. We have simulations with similar, even larger mass ratios.  Having said that, the step size might be too large. You may want to try reducing that; would a step size of 1e-3 work?

Another option is to try the SMC contact formulation (unless there is a reason not to), in which case you could try to use the HHT integrator with one of the direct sparse linear solvers (Pardiso through Chrono::MKL or MUMPS through Chrono::MUMPS). We mostly use this combination for systems with FEA and have no tested it much with rigid multibody systems (but is something I plan on looking at in the near future).

Finally, another thing to try is to model this system without weld joints (if possible) and instead use single rigid bodies with appropriate mass and inertia representing the composite body. To calculate the mass, inertia, and CG for such a composite body you could use the Chrono utility functions Calc***Gyration and the utility class CompositeInertia (all of these in the chrono::utils namespace).

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] HMMWV9 in parallel still slow
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 22 Feb 2019 14:07:41 +0000

Sandro,

Chrono::Parallel will not be useful for the simulation of a single vehicle system.  Its main purpose is to accelerate large simulations of granular dynamics (e.g. a vehicle running over granular terrain).

Second, Chrono is not a real-time simulation engine, although we are mindful of performance as much as possible.  Having said that, the HMMWV-9 demo distributed with Chrono does run in about (soft) real-time on a commodity laptop (Intel i7-6600).

--Radu

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Can I adapt forces each timestep?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 7 Mar 2019 13:12:47 +0000

Cor,

Yes, you can.  The ChFunction objects that Simone mentioned implement functions of a single variable and they allow you to "modulate" the force generated by a ChLinSpring element something like:
    F = A * f1(t) - B*d*f2(d)*f3(v) - C*v*f4(d)*f5(v)
where A, B, C are constants that you would provide, f1..f5 are functions of a single variable that you can define through the ChFunction mechanism, t is the current time, d is the deformation, and v is the speed of deformation.

An alternative that gives you complete freedom is provided by the ChLinSpringCB elements.  In fact, I implemented this one precisely to be used in modeling vehicle suspensions.  The way this one works is that it expects a user-defined functor object which implements a callback.  In that callback you can use whatever code you want to return a force based on the current (t,d,v).  You can see how this is used in the Chrono::Vehicle module (for example, look at the base class ChDoubleWishbone.cpp/h and a concrete derived class such as HMMWV_DoubleWishbone.cpp/h)

--Radu

Hi Luis,

the GetRot method returns a quaternion (ChQuaternion). Quaternion elements 
are called e0, e1, e2, e3.
This being said, you probably prefer Euler angles (roll, pitch, yaw).
To do so, use the method called Q_to_Euler123 (but beware of singularities)
An example:

  
Rolls.append(n.GetRot().Q_to_Euler123().x)

A couple of suggestions: 

   - If you want to know what a function returns, ctrl click on it and the 
   IDE should open its definition in core.py (or fea.py) where you can find 
   the type of the input and of the return (left and right of the arrow in the 
   comment)
   - to inspect methods and attributes of a class look at the documentation 
   ( since I mentioned Quaternions go here 
   <http://api.chrono.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_quaternion.html>

Simone

Subject: PyChrono Update
From: Simone Benatti
Date: Thu, 9 May 2019 08:13:47 -0700 (PDT)

Dear PyChrono users,

We are releasing a new *main* version labelled "4.0", to install it with 
Anaconda type:

conda install -c projectchrono pychrono 

Whats'new since the last main version:
- All timesteppers are now available from Python. Code snippet:

ts = chrono.ChTimestepperEulerImplicit(mysystem)
mysystem.SetTimestepper(ts)

- Compatible with both SWIG 3.0 and 4.0
- Solved the bugs with chronoirr.ChIrrTools.drawSegment 
and GetContactContainer()
- Added templates to get tuples of nodes and elements from meshes
- Explicit downcast functions are now properly running.

Code snippet to highlight the last 2 points:

nodelist = my_mesh.GetNodes()
for n in nodelist: 
       m = fea.CastToChNodeFEAxyzrot(n)
       print(m.GetX0())


GetNodes() returns a tuple of ChNodeFEABase. The method GetX0() cannot be 
directly called from nodelist elements, we have to manually downcast them 
to their actual type, the (grand)child class CastToChNodeFEAxyzrot.

One last point: the last *develop* version already featured the downcast, 
but its syntax was slightly different. All functions ended with "shared" 
but since the Python user doesn't have to care about the std::shared_ptr 
management in the underlying code, we decided to omit it.

Old syntax example:
fea.CastToChNodeFEAxyzrotShared(n)

New syntax example:
fea.CastToChNodeFEAxyzrot(n)

Enjoy!
Simone

The level of difficulty depends on what you need. As you know, a 
complete interface (that is not mandatory) means that one should be able 
both to

A - import FMUs containing 3rd party models into a Chrono-based 
application, using Chrono as a server

B - import FMUs containing Chrono-based model into a 3rd party 
application, so Chrono is a client

On top of this, there are two sub-cases:
1 - support FMU "export for cosimulation" (each FMU has a timestepper 
embedded in its dll)
2 - support FMU "export for model exchange"

This leads to 4 total "cases" for a complete FMI support. Tell us what 
you are interested on. For example, case A.1 could be easier than B.1 or 
B.2, etc.

We can talk in private if you are interested in consulting services 
about this development,

best

Subject: Re: [chrono] How to install on linux
From: Radu Serban

Hi Yuki,

It seems to me that you conflate two different things:

 1. configuring, building, (and maybe installing) the Chrono libraries
 2. configuring and building your own project that depends on Chrono

For the former, you must continue beyond step 6 in that first tutorial 
and actually build the Chrono libraries. Unfortunately, the procedure in 
step 7 in the tutorial only mentions the case of using Visual Studio 
(for Windows users). In your case, once you completed step 6, CMake 
will have generated a hierarchy of Makefiles (the native build system on 
Linux). So you must run '*make*' from within the build tree (which you 
specified in step 6 during CMake configuration) and, optionally, '*make 
install*'. Once *make* completes, you should find a set of (shared) 
libraries in the sub-directory lib64/ and several executables (demos and 
unit tests, depending on what you selected during CMake configuration) 
in the bin/ sub-directory.

Once you have Chrono build, you can link your own project to the Chrono 
libraries, following the guidelines in that second tutorial. For that, 
in step 5 of this procedure, you will need to specify where the Chrono 
CMake project configuration file is located (i.e. set the CMake variable 
Chrono_DIR). You can point to either the Chrono build tree from above 
or else to the Chrono install tree (if you did perform the optional step 
of installing Chrono above). The tutorial uses a Chrono build tree.

I hope this helps. Let me know if you manage to build everything you need.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Triangle Mesh for Static Objects
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 24 Jul 2018 08:01:24 +0200

Kishor,

Indeed, you will have to generate your own ChTriangleMeshConnected 
object. To do that, you construct such an object and then set its 
vectors of vertices and normals (triplets of doubles, as many as there 
are vertices in your mesh) and its vectors of vertex and normal indices 
(triplets of ints, as many as there are faces in your mesh).

To see an example where this is done in Chrono, look at the 
RigidTerrain::AddPatch(...) function in Chrono::Vehicle (starting at 
line 267 in src/chrono_vehicle/terrain/RigidTerrain.cpp). That function 
also shows one way of calculating the normals at each vertex, as the 
average of the normals of the faces adjacent to the vertex.

For a contact mesh, you do not really need to define the normals and 
normal indices. But you may want to do so, in case you'll also use the 
mesh for visualization.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] OpenGL visual asset bug
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 5 Nov 2018 10:54:54 +0000

Hi Maxim,

In Chrono::OpenGL, visualization meshes are maintained in a map keyed by the mesh name.  The problem was that ChBodyEasyMesh did not set a name for the ChTriangleMeshShape it creates.  I pushed a fix which should resolve your issue.

On a different note, keep in mind that ChBodyEasyMesh derives from ChBodyAuxRef and not from ChBody.  As such, you may want to consider setting the initial position and orientation of the auxiliary frame through ChBodyAuxRef::SetFrame_REF_to_abs instead of ChBody::SetPos and ChBody::SetRot (which will set the position and orientation of the body's centroidal frame).

--Radu

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Tire tilt at lane change
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 17 Apr 2019 12:49:16 +0000

Hi Nomoto,

The issues you see are most likely due to some incorrect (inconsistent) parameters in the JSON files.  We typically use the vehicle models specified through concrete classes in the ChronoModels_vehicle library and not so much those specified through JSON files.    We will have to revisit the parameters in the various JSON files in the Chrono distribution and ensure they match those in the library models (maybe you can help with this?).  Looking at the animations you uploaded, my suspicion is that the culprit is the suspension stiffness.  It is very much possible that the data for the suspension spring and shock in the HMMWV_DoubleWishbone***.json files is not quite right.  We will revisit this and try to match it as well as possible with what's implemented in HMMWV_DoubleWishbone.cpp, but I cannot promise when we will find time to do this.  If you are willing to work on this and share it with us (through a pull request), that would be greatly appreciated.

The behavior you notice at the end of the path is partially due to the suspension parameter issue above, but also to the fact that the lateral controller implemented in ChPathFollowerDriver is not all that sophisticated.  When the end of the path is reached, the controller ends up attempting to make a u-turn and follow the path in the opposite direction.  However, during that maneuver the controller generates steering input signals that instantaneously go from -1 to +1 and vice-versa resulting in non-physical accelerations.  You can try to use the  ChPathFollowerDriverXT driver instead (which attempts to correct some of these limitations).  Otherwise, simply stop the simulation before the vehicle reaches the end of the provided path (that special case is really not in the range of applicability for the given controller), or else generate your own path data that defines a smooth curve (e.g., by closing the path back to the start).

Subject: Re: Collision of bodies with large mass is ineffective
From: Lewis Bowes
Date: Thu, 28 Feb 2019 01:52:50 -0800 (PST)

*PROBLEM SOLUTION*: The inertia tensor of the cylinder was not being 
calculated correctly, and as a result force generation between the cylinder 
and floor was not correct. 

For anyone else with a similar problem in the future, the result of 
*chrono::utils::CalcCylinderGyration(...)* must be multiplied by mass as 
gyration tensors do not scale the tensor by mass.

On Wednesday, 27 February 2019 13:57:13 UTC, Lewis Bowes wrote:
symbol: Re: Collision of bodies with large mass is ineffective

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Collision of bodies with large mass is ineffective
From: Lewis Bowes
Date: Thu, 28 Feb 2019 01:48:46 -0800 (PST)

Hi Alessandro,

Thank-you very much, this lead me to the problem! I was using 
utils::CalcCylinderGyration(...) to get what I thought was the inertia 
tensor of the cylinder. After your post I realised that this function knows 
nothing about the object's mass, and on further research, sure enough the 
gyration tensor does not scale the tensor by mass. Multiplying my result by 
8000 solved the problem and everything is working perfectly now! I should 
have noticed it would have been called 'CalcCylinderInertia' if it did 
calculate inertia...

Thanks again!

On Thursday, 28 February 2019 07:06:39 UTC, Alessandro Tasora wrote:
symbol: Re: [chrono] Collision of bodies with large mass is ineffective

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Collision of bodies with large mass is ineffective
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 28 Feb 2019 08:06:37 +0100

Hi

Maybe you can check this: is your body inertia tensor (Ixx etc) as huge as
it's mass?

If you created the body with ChBodyEasyBox or similar stuff,  the inertia
tensor (and mass) is automatically computed from the object shape and
density,  so all is fine. But if you used SetMass(8000) and you forgot to
adjust also inertia tensor,  the latter will remain the default diagonal 1,
1, 1. And this unbalanced case will give issues to the solver as contact
force computation would converge badly.

Alessandro

Subject: Re: [chrono] Collision of bodies with large mass is ineffective
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 28 Feb 2019 06:51:20 +0000

Lewis,

Now that you mention that you are using NSC, I'm a bit puzzled by what exactly "as if moving through quicksand" really means. I had assumed the simulation is properly converged, but maybe that's not the case. If your example is self-contained and not too large, could you please share the code?

Does your model include other bodies (of vastly different masses/inertias)? You may want to try reducing the step size, increasing the number of solver iterations, and/or trying a different solver (e.g., Barzilai-Borwein or APGD).

I also suspect that the default value for the collision envelope (0.03) may not be large enough, especially given the large approach speed of the two bodies, but that is also connected to the step size you use.  Not sure this is a problem though (since you say the issue goes away with a cylinder mass of 1).

--Radu

symbol: Re: [chrono] Collision of bodies with large mass is ineffective

text:
If that is correct, one thing to try is the non-smooth (complementarity) formulation, as that will disallow any penetration (provided the collision are "seen" and there is no "pass through").

For the SMC, the behavior you describe suggest that not enough force is generated and you have a so-called "punch through" effect.  There are various reasons that could lead to this:

  *   first, the contact material may not be stiff enough.  Note that the default material is pretty soft:  E = 2e5 (if you use the option of finding the contact stiffness from material properties, the default setting) and kn = 2e5 (if you indicated to use directly stiffness and damping coefficients).  Unless you already did that, you should try making the materials stiffer.  You can change the contact material properties for each collision model (you can access the material from the body).   Keep in mind that increasing E (or kn) will make the problem numerically stiffer, so you may need to decrease the integration step size for stability considerations.
  *   another (less likely) possible explanation is geometrical:  indeed, the SCM contact force model requires the radii of curvature at the collision points for two colliding shapes.  The Bullet collision detection used in the sequential Chrono systems does not provide this information (a different collision system, such as the one used in Chrono::Parallel, might -- at least for certain pairs of colliding geometries).  As such, we use a default radius of curvature.  This value is set at 0.1 (maybe too small for your large collision shapes).  You can change this value through the (static) function ChCollisoinInfo::SetDefaultEffectiveCurvatureRadius.

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Intel C++ Compiler
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 15 Jan 2019 11:14:51 +0000

Jack,

In my test, I had the following Chrono modules enabled: Cosimulation, Irrlicht, MKL, OpenGL, Parallel, Postprocess, Vehicle.
I also enabled building the benchmark tests (BUILD_BENCHMARKING) which is set by default to OFF.

I did however (and you should too) disable building the CUDA stuff in Chrono::Parallel (you likely don't use that anyway).  In other words, set USE_PARALLEL_CUDA to OFF.
The errors you are getting have to do with your CUDA installation which refers to the GNU compilers.

I also suggest you enable verbose makefiles in CMake (CMAKE_VERBOSE_MAKEFILE).  This will help identifying issues if they still occur.

Finally, ignore for now the warnings about the option '-xsse'.  This has to do with the issue I mentioned before (SSE and AVX support with Intel compilers) which I will fix when I get a chance.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Mesh loading / querying
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 23 Jun 2018 12:48:32 +0200

Hi Jeremy,

I can only address some of you questions.

I looked at the code and found two issues related to the terrain height 
query.  As you are aware, I recently changed the underlying 
implementation of the RigidTerrain class in Chrono::Vehicle to permit 
multiple patches defined either as a flat box, a triangle mesh provided 
through a Wavefront obj, or a mesh constructed implicitly from a height 
field provided through a gray-scale bmp image.  To unify treatment over 
all these cases, the calculations of terrain height and normal at a 
given (x,y) location rely now on ray-casting into the collision model. 
In Chrono, the default collision system uses the Bullet library (this is 
different in Chrono::Parallel).

The first issue was that the Chrono wrapper function around the Bullet 
ray casting did not properly account for the collision envelope (this is 
a quantity that is relevant for non-smooth contact and is typically 
non-zero for a ChSystemNSC; when using a ChSystemSMC, the collision 
envelope is automatically set to 0). I pushed a fix to this bug.

The second issue is that, while the default in Chrono is to use double 
precision, Bullet uses single precision by default. I pushed a change 
to the CMake configuration files to add an option to use double 
precision within Bullet. However, Bullet's support for double precision 
is "partial" -- indeed, there are several places where they hard-code 
use of 'float' instead of their custom type 'btScalar'. For this reason
symbol: Re: [chrono] Mesh loading / querying

text:
precision within Bullet. However, Bullet's support for double precision 
is "partial" -- indeed, there are several places where they hard-code 
use of 'float' instead of their custom type 'btScalar'. For this reason 
(and to make sure other users do not see anomalous results in existing 
code), I decided to default the new CMake option (USE_BULLET_DOUBLE) to 
OFF. If you want to force double precision in Bullet, re-configure 
Chrono and enable USE_BULLET_DOUBLE to ON.

Long story short, the above fixes (primarily the first one) address the 
issue of the reported height in your test example not being exactly 1. 
Note that, due to roundoff error, you will still not get exactly 1 (but 
should be now much closer to 1 than before).

Unfortunately, I cannot address the issue with the SGI-based platform as 
I do not have access to such hardware. We can take this offline and see 
how you could track down what might be happening there.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: How to create a force between two bodies
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 13 May 2019 22:22:02 +0000

You are correct, I did a pretty extensive refactoring of ChLinkLock.  In particular, I changed the ChLinkLock internal memory management for link forces and link limits, which led to API changes.  The link forces (of type ChLinkForce) and link limits (of type ChLinkLimit) are now managed internally by ChLinkLock (using unique pointers) and the user can get a writable reference to the corresponding wrapped object.   I also changed the names of some ChLinkForce and ChLinkLimit member functions.

Assuming you have created and initialized a
  shared_ptr<ChLinkLockRevolute> my_revolute;
to activate the link force acting on the Z rotational degree of freedom and set its constant force value to Fval, all you have to do is:
  my_revolute->GetForce_Rz().SetActive(true);
  my_revolute->GetForce_Rz().SetF(Fval);
In other words, you do no longer need to create the ChLinkForce object yourself and then attach it to the joint (ChLinkLock::SetForce_Rz and similar functions were completely eliminated).

Similarly, you can get access to link forces acting on other degrees of freedom using GetForce_X, GetForce_Y, etc.

As I mentioned, there were also several function name changes for ChLinkForce:
  Get_active / Set_active               are now   IsActive / SetActive
  Get_iforce / Set_iforce               are now   GetF / SetF
  Get_K / Set_K                         are now   GetK / SetK
  Get_R / Set_R                         are now   GetR / SetR
  Get_modul_iforce / Set_module_iforce  are now   GetModulationF / SetModulationF
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: How to create a force between two bodies

text:
Get_K / Set_K                         are now   GetK / SetK
  Get_R / Set_R                         are now   GetR / SetR
  Get_modul_iforce / Set_module_iforce  are now   GetModulationF / SetModulationF
  etc...
as well as similar function name changes for ChLinkLimit.
You can look at the changes to ChLinkForce.h and ChLinkLimit.h in commit 51485ff80 (21 March 2019) and/or look at the list of member function for these two classes in the current API documentation at
http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_link_force.html
http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_link_limit.html

I also added a new demo_IRR_prismatic_force that illustrates the use of link forces on a prismatic joint.

--Radu

On Wednesday, 17 April 2019 16:16:37 UTC+2, Radu Serban wrote:

You could use the approach you suggested, but arguably a better alternative is to use a ChLinkSpring element which can model an inter-body force of the form:
symbol: Re: [chrono] How to create a force between two bodies

text:
On Wednesday, 17 April 2019 16:16:37 UTC+2, Radu Serban wrote:

You could use the approach you suggested, but arguably a better alternative is to use a ChLinkSpring element which can model an inter-body force of the form:
  force = f * F(t) - [ k * K1(d-d0) * K2(d') ] * (d-d0) - [ c * C1(d) * C2(d') ] * d'
where f, k, c are user-specified scalar values, F, K1, K2, C1, C2 are ChFunction objects, t is the time, d is the distance between the two points, d' is the rate of change of that distance (and d0 is the rest length).

If you cannot fit your particular force to the above expression, you can then use ChLinkSpringCB which allows you to define an arbitrary force between two points on two bodies
  force(t, d, d')
through a user-provided functor object.

--Radu

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] How to create a force between two bodies
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 17 Apr 2019 14:16:13 +0000

You could use the approach you suggested, but arguably a better alternative is to use a ChLinkSpring element which can model an inter-body force of the form:
  force = f * F(t) - [ k * K1(d-d0) * K2(d') ] * (d-d0) - [ c * C1(d) * C2(d') ] * d'
where f, k, c are user-specified scalar values, F, K1, K2, C1, C2 are ChFunction objects, t is the time, d is the distance between the two points, d' is the rate of change of that distance (and d0 is the rest length).

If you cannot fit your particular force to the above expression, you can then use ChLinkSpringCB which allows you to define an arbitrary force between two points on two bodies
  force(t, d, d')
through a user-provided functor object.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Link gets disconnected during simulation
From: Alessandro Tasora

hi,

most likely you neet to increase the precision of the solver by

- increasing the number of iterations (press 'i' in the irrlicht view, 
go to settings tab and move the iteration slider up, or better set this 
in the C++ code - see demos)

- set the BARZILAIBORWEIN solver, that is more precise than default SOR, 
for the same n of iterations (again, search "BARZILAIBORWEIN" in the 
demos cpp source and you see how to swhich the solver to this)

Note: structures like yours often have large mass ratios and/or size 
ratios, that tend to slow down the convergence of all iterative solvers. 
In chrono we have also an optional MKL solver, that is a direct solver 
and that is not affected by mass ratios. However MKL cannot work if : a) 
you have redundant constraints and/or b) you have nonsmooth contacts.

Alessandro

I believe (although I didn’t check) that NSC will make both bodies move together after impact (since NSC always treats the impact as plastic; our NSC works for contact well, but not for impact).

SMC: when you have small grain and extremely large stiffness (like you do) it’s very likely that the “double” precision is not enough to capture what happens. Some numbers will be obtained, but the question is how much you can rely on them. Also, the integration step size should be made super super small… Davide, this is a tough problem, if you make progress please let us know how things work out.

My two cents.
Dan

Matt,

I believe it was you who also posed this question as a GitHub issue. I 
answered you there. For the benefit of everyone else, I copy below my 
answer on GitHub as this may be relevant for other situations as well:

We recommend using the CMake-based procedure of configuring and building 
your own project depending on Chrono that is described at 
http://api.projectchrono.org/tutorial_install_project.html. This relies 
on using a project configuration script that was automatically generated 
when you configured Chrono. Of course, you would have to modify the 
sample CMakeLists.txt provided in template_project/ to suit your own 
project (e.g., requesting that Chrono had been configured with the 
Chrono::Cascade module enabled).

You can also look at the public GitHub repository chrono-projects 
(https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono-projects) which contains 
several projects configured as above. I just pushed there an example on 
how to configure demo_CAS_robot as an external project. Once you clone 
chrono-projects, look at configuration_tests\cascade\CMakeLists.txt. A 
couple of things:

  * On Windows, make sure to define WNT (see line 74 of CMakeLists.txt).
    This is required for projects using Chrono::Cascade.
  * The source of the demo itself is unchanged from what is in the
    Chrono repository, except for the very first call in main() to
    SetChronoDataPath (see CMakeLists.txt on how the macro
    CHRONO_DATA_DIR is specified in this particular case; you can use a

Chrono repository, except for the very first call in main() to
    SetChronoDataPath (see CMakeLists.txt on how the macro
    CHRONO_DATA_DIR is specified in this particular case; you can use a
    different mechanism).

The configuration examples in the chrono-projects repository can be used 
as starting points for other user projects depending on various 
combinations of Chrono modules.

Matt, the answer to your latest question is in the 2nd bullet above: 
you must call the SetChronoDataPath function to specify the location of 
the Chrono data directory, so that subsequent calls to functions such as 
GetChronoDataFile can find the assets.

Hope that this helps,
Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] FEM mathematics
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 21 Jun 2018 13:04:19 +0200

dear user,

if you look at demo_FEA_cosimulate_load.cpp, you see that the basic idea 
for this simple cosimulation scenario is:

    mmeshload->OutputSimpleMesh(vert_pos, vert_vel, triangles);

    PerformEsternalCosimulation(vert_pos, vert_vel, triangles,
    vert_forces, vert_indexes);

    mmeshload->InputSimpleForces(vert_forces, vert_indexes);

where *OutputSimpleMesh *is used to retrieve the actual position of all 
vertexes of the mesh, then *PerformEsternalCosimulation *is whatever 
user-defined procedure that takes the positions of the 
vertexes/triangles and computes some forces that must be applied to the 
vertexes, and finally *InputSimpleForces *is used to apply those forces 
to the vertexes of the mesh.

In detail: the InputSimpleForces function just does some bookkeeping to 
scatter the vector of forces "vert_forces" to the appropriate nodes of 
the FEA model, i.e getting multiple 3D vectors  F_i  that must be 
applied to the i-th node of the FEA mesh. These forces F_i are "node 
loads" that are automatically inserted in the right-hand side of the 
linear system of the FEA problem thanks to Chrono bookkeeping.

Some notes:

- the F_i forces are assumed constant until the next time 
InputSimpleForces is called (usually, at each time step, so they can 
represent time-varying forces)

- the F_i forces do not produce jacobians (i.e. if using some stiff 
integrator, as most of Chrono timesteppers, in an optimal scenario all 
the stiff forces would introduce some jacobian in the linear system,
symbol: Re: [chrono] FEM mathematics

text:
- the F_i forces do not produce jacobians (i.e. if using some stiff 
integrator, as most of Chrono timesteppers, in an optimal scenario all 
the stiff forces would introduce some jacobian in the linear system, 
which would help the timestepper to stay in the stable regime even with 
large timesteps; however for these F_i forces, they are assumed to vary 
slowly in time, so no jacobian is computed - we made this assumption 
mostly for performance reasons)

regards

Alessandro Tasora

Qihan,

Support for RoundedBox is currently not implemented in the Bullet-based 
collision library for Chrono (sequential). It is supported in 
Chrono::Parallel (which uses its own custom collision detection 
library), but you may want to check that it's working properly (this 
shape has not seen much use as far as I know).

By the way, to see if collision support for a particular shape is 
implemented for Chrono, look in the file ChCModelBullet.h. If the 
corresponding virtual method override (e.g., AddRoundedBox) simply 
returns 'false', then support for that shape is not currently available.

   /opt/chrono/build

   - Disable everything expect ENABLE_MODULE_PYTHON

   - PYTHON_INCLUDE_DIR: /home/my_username/anaconda3/include
   - PYTHON_LIBRARY: /home/my_username/anaconda3/lib/libpython3.6m.so
   - PYTHON_LIBRARY_DEBUG: empty
   - PYTHON_LIBRARY_RELEASE: empty

   - SWIG_EXECUTABLE: /usr/local/bin/swig
   - SWIG_VERSION: 3.0.12
   - Click Configure
   - Click Configure again

   To have access to the Chrono::Python wrapper modules, after building and 
   (optionally) installing, append one of the following to the PYTHONPATH

   For the modules in the BUILD tree: ...

symbol: Re: [chrono] Rotational Inertia of Euler Beams

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Rotational Inertia of Euler Beams
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Tue, 31 Jul 2018 19:01:53 +0200

Hi David,

two ideas:

- connect a ChBody as you already suggest, or..

- just set the inertia to the desired ChNodeFEAxyzrot node of the 
ChElementBeamEuler (by default the inertias of FEA nodes is null, but 
you can set nonzero values to have atomic inertias in the node positions).

Btw currently the Euler and IGA beams use lumped inertias in FEA, for 
Euler beams the lumped rotational inertias are inferred by the section 
xx yy zz areas moments of inertia, whereas for IGA beams it is inferred 
by the section drawing thickness, as in section->GetDrawThicknessY() etc.)

Alessandro

Hi Victor,

I'll try to answer all the questions together as they should be all related 
to the mesh.

First, I was surprised that the "smaller" wheel mesh is around 10000 times 
smaller than the other one... I don't know why it's designed this way, but 
it leads to problems: If you directly use it, then it's too small to 
represent anything physically meaningful; Most of the 6 or 7 digits that 
you have presenting the XYZ of each node are wasted since they are used to 
store the mesh's offset from the origin (0,0,0), rather than the relative 
difference in spatial locations among mesh nodes. This mesh is probably 
yanked from something else bigger, but that doesn't mean you don't have to 
pre-process it to make it reasonable.

Speaking of scaling a mesh that is not centered at the origin: It will also 
enlarge the distance between the origin and the mesh. This is because the 
scaling function will just multiply the XYZ of each node---it's a very 
lightweight utility anyway. For example, since your mesh originally sits at 
Y coordinate being around 5, so if you want the mesh to appear in the 
simulation at Y being near 0, then the initial Y coordinate of the mesh 
must be -5; and if the mesh is enlarged 10 times by *Scale*, then you have 
to set the initial to be -50. You could correct the CoM (drag it back to 
0,0,0) of the mesh by using *Move *before setting the initial location of 
the mesh, but I guess at this point, the easiest thing you can do is
symbol:
Re: Question regarding the wheel file format in the DEME demo
 WheelSlopeSlip

text:
to set the initial to be -50. You could correct the CoM (drag it back to 
0,0,0) of the mesh by using *Move *before setting the initial location of 
the mesh, but I guess at this point, the easiest thing you can do is 
instead just re-create the mesh, so its CoM lies directly on the (0,0,0) 
point of your mesh. 

Also you should *InstructBoxDomainDimension *to make sure your domain is 
big enough to hold everything you have in the simulation.

I suspect the many anomalies you observed are caused by the wheel being at 
unexpected locations and having unexpected sizes or shapes when the 
simulation starts. But all these you should be able to spot by outputting 
and rendering the system after initialization. Did you try that and can you 
show us if the initial status of the simulation looks all right?

Thank you,
Ruochun

Hi Victor,

First, I'd suggest that you ensure enough RAM is on the system, so we 
exclude that as a cause for performance or stalling issues. Then...

1) Using a smaller wheel in this case should have a minimal impact on the 
performance. If you say it's slower than using a clump wheel, then that is 
possible. But if you say that's several times slower than before, that's 
not normal. I suggest you visualize the simulation to see if the particles 
are behaving normally (if the simulation is near-divergence, it may run 
slowly), and gauge how much slower it has become. A comparison between the 
metric output (timing stats, collab stats) is also important, and that's 
why I always have them in the demos. 

2) Yes. The *Scale *function changes the size of that object in each 
direction by the amount specified as arguments, not scaling the object to 
that size specified by the arguments. It won't work as intended if you just 
use wheel radius and width as arguments. Instead, you have to figure out 
the ratio between the target size and the original size of the mesh.

3) Looks like the initialization didn't even finish. It's hard to say 
anything without seeing the mesh (if that's the only thing that got 
changed). Note that the mesh size is not important but the mesh quality is 
usually super important. You have to use a valid mesh: use a surface mesh 
that you would safely do FEA with. That aside, it's still hard to break the

usually super important. You have to use a valid mesh: use a surface mesh 
that you would safely do FEA with. That aside, it's still hard to break the 
initialization though. Is the mesh so refined that it uses all the memory?

Hi Victor,

Sounds to me like the simulation diverged. I note that in this demo, when 
you change the two variables, you don't automatically change the size of 
the wheel, because there is no scaling or anything applied to the mesh you 
loaded so it's still the same as before (you may want to add a *Scale *call 
to it). So by changing the radius and width, you just modified the mass and 
the moment of inertia of the wheel. And it appears that you didn't change 
the overall load (used to emulate the chassis the wheel carries), so it 
probably just makes the wheel hit the soil with a higher initial velocity, 
leading to divergence. There could be other reasons.

To resolve that, you could try reducing the step size, or making the total 
load lower so that the simulation setup is more consistent with what you 
wanted (a.k.a. the suggestion given by the solver: relaxing the physics). 
Perhaps you just need to use a smaller step size for the starting one 
second or so, and remember you can change the step size on-fly via 
*UpdateStepSize*. I want to note that this current step size, 2e-6s, is 
already quite demanding, since there are super small particles involved in 
this GRC representation. For mobility tests or for project prototyping 
purposes, you can consider using much larger particles for the terrain to 
speed the simulation up without sacrificing too much accuracy, like in

Subject: Re: Full Vehicle Simulation - Electrical, mechanical, hydraulic
From: Jason Nicholson
Date: Tue, 16 Oct 2018 06:00:11 -0700 (PDT)

Let me talk a bit about what I have seen that does not work:


   - A mechanical engineer who doesn't know how to code tries to implement 
   a C code S-function for Simulink because he things C is fast. This person 
   wrote bad C code that was compiler dependent. This person had no idea how 
   to efficiently use C code. Therefore, they did not take advantage of 
   vectorization or other features related to the language. Everything was 
   done on the stack with a for loop. The lesson is bad C code is not faster 
   than just building the model in Simulink.
   - Masked subsystems in Simulink loose there initialization code when you 
   transpile to C or C++ with Simulink Coder. This causes lots of problems 
   that require custom solutions that Mathworks Tech Support can't immediate 
   point to what you do about it.
   - A poor understanding of ODE solvers will cause major slow downs. As my 
   audience probably knows, all ODE solvers are Taylor Series based. Thus, if 
   you break the continuity of the ODE system with discontinuous functions 
   such as sign(), abs(), etc., then you will break the Taylor series and 
   therefore slow down the ODE solver. This is common misunderstanding with my 
   mechanical and electrical engineering colleagues; often their models run 
   slow because of all the discontinuity in the model that acts like 
   artificial stiffness. Programming in C/C++ or Simulink cannot fix this 
   problem. Bad expression of the ODE/DAE system cannot be fixed with the

Subject: RE: [chrono] Changing color of body during simulation
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 17 Nov 2021 14:47:46 +0000

Roberto,

Here’s how I would do something like this (using demo_IRR_collision_trimesh.py as an example):


  *   After creating the body, attach a color asset to it and cache the asset:
color_A = chrono.ChColorAsset()
color_A.SetColor(chrono.ChColor(0.8, 0.4, 0.4))
body_A.AddAsset(color_A)

  *   In the simulation loop, when desired, modify the color of the color asset and let the Irrlicht app know about the update:

color_updated = False

while(myapplication.GetDevice().run()):

    if not color_updated and mysystem.GetChTime() > 5:

        color_A.SetColor(chrono.ChColor(0.4, 0.4, 0.8))

        myapplication.AssetUpdate(body_A)

        color_updated = True


    myapplication.BeginScene()

    myapplication.DrawAll()

    myapplication.DoStep()

    myapplication.EndScene()

--Radu

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] How to apply different height to each wheels of the
 vehicle, so as to test the suspension response
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 29 Apr 2019 07:22:15 +0000

Hi Ni Tao,

The approaches you tried will indeed not work as the vehicle must be kept in an assembled and consistent state throughout the simulation.

If I understand it correctly, you have GPS/IMU sensor data that is generated elsewhere (presumable from sensors on an actual vehicle?) and you want to force the simulation to follow the resulting trajectory, correct?

Assuming this is the case, I can think of some options.  The first one - more complicated, but arguably the best - is to implement a driver controller that generates vehicle driver inputs (steering, throttle, and braking) that force the vehicle to follow the desired time trajectory implicitly defined by your sensor readings.  Implementing such controllers is not trivial, but you can start by looking at the ones we provide for path following (a very similar problem to yours).  Look at demo_VEH_SteeringController and at the ChPathFollowerDriver used therein.  You will likely need to do something a bit more sophisticated (at least for the longitudinal controller which outputs throttle and braking signals).

If you have a situation where the vehicle actually moves in a straight line over variable-height terrain (i.e. steering input can be fixed to 0), you could construct an auxiliary rig around the vehicle to force it to move at the desired speed (as defined implicitly by GPS readings).  However, in order to properly capture the suspension dynamics, you cannot simply rig at the suspension level, but rather at the vehicle (chassis) level.  What you would need to do in this case is add an intermediate body and then (1) connect that body to ground with a linear motor (ChLinkMotorLinear***) in the forward X direction; and (2) connect that intermediate body to the vehicle chassis body with a translational (prismatic) joint in the vertical Z direction.  You can then drive the linear motor to specify the (forward) vehicle speed or location to match GPS data, while the vertical prismatic joint will allow the vehicle suspension to properly "follow" the terrain at the current wheel locations.

text:
If you have a situation where the vehicle actually moves in a straight line over variable-height terrain (i.e. steering input can be fixed to 0), you could construct an auxiliary rig around the vehicle to force it to move at the desired speed (as defined implicitly by GPS readings).  However, in order to properly capture the suspension dynamics, you cannot simply rig at the suspension level, but rather at the vehicle (chassis) level.  What you would need to do in this case is add an intermediate body and then (1) connect that body to ground with a linear motor (ChLinkMotorLinear***) in the forward X direction; and (2) connect that intermediate body to the vehicle chassis body with a translational (prismatic) joint in the vertical Z direction.  You can then drive the linear motor to specify the (forward) vehicle speed or location to match GPS data, while the vertical prismatic joint will allow the vehicle suspension to properly "follow" the terrain at the current wheel locations.

Of course, this second option cannot deal with steering input and none of the wheels would be driven.  In fact, short of the first option listed above, I cannot think of any other approach that would properly take into account the steering capabilities of the vehicle you are modeling.

Finally, another possibility along the same lines s the 2nd option above is to use the suspension test rig implemented in ChSuspensionTestRig (see demo_VEH_SuspensionTestRig for an example).  With that test rig you would look at only one of the vehicle axles at a time.  What you would need to do in this case is control the heights of the two posts of the rig to reflect the time history of the terrain height as it is implicitly defined by your GPS data.   The ability of specifying the time history of rig post displacements is currently not implemented in ChSuspensionTestRig, but it is on my todo list and I will add it sometime soon.

text:
Of course, this second option cannot deal with steering input and none of the wheels would be driven.  In fact, short of the first option listed above, I cannot think of any other approach that would properly take into account the steering capabilities of the vehicle you are modeling.

Finally, another possibility along the same lines s the 2nd option above is to use the suspension test rig implemented in ChSuspensionTestRig (see demo_VEH_SuspensionTestRig for an example).  With that test rig you would look at only one of the vehicle axles at a time.  What you would need to do in this case is control the heights of the two posts of the rig to reflect the time history of the terrain height as it is implicitly defined by your GPS data.   The ability of specifying the time history of rig post displacements is currently not implemented in ChSuspensionTestRig, but it is on my todo list and I will add it sometime soon.

Anyway, I hope one of these options will work for what you are trying to do, or at least give you an idea on how to get there.

--Radu

text:
Subject: API changes (triangular meshes for collision and visualization)
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 14 Oct 2018 13:29:48 +0000

Chrono Users:

I pushed several changes to the Chrono 'develop' branch to address an issue related to use of triangular meshes as collision shapes.  The previous implementation was such that it required the ChTriangularMesh object passed to ChCollisionModel::AddTriangleMesh to be kept alive for the duration of the simulation.  Note that this was the case only when using the Bullet-based collision detection in Chrono (so not an issue when using Chrono::Parallel for example).  See the discussion in the following thread: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/projectchrono/nIBHQg0jpYU/Gd9mdrnNAgAJ.  This was a source of confusion and bugs and led to awkward user code for larger projects.

The modification involves passing a shared_ptr to a ChTriangularMesh object.  For uniformity, I changed the signature of several other ChCollisionModel functions.  The modified functions are:

  *   for ChCollisionModel (and derived classes)
AddTriangleMesh
AddConvexHull
Add2Dpath

  *   for ChModelBullet
AddTriangleMeshConcave
AddTriangleMeshConcaveDecomposed

  *   Additional API changes for function signatures in ChUtilsCreators
AddConvexCollisionModel

Furthermore, I changed the implementation of the visualization asset ChTriangleMeshShape to maintain a shared_ptr to a ChTriangleMeshConnected object (instead of a copy).  This is a more efficient implementation for situations where the same triangle mesh is used for both visualization and collision.  This means that functions such as ChTriangleMeshShape::SetMesh and ChTriangleMeshShape::GetMesh take and return, respectively, a shared_ptr (instead of a reference) to a ChTriangleMeshConnected.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Cohesion setting
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 29 Mar 2018 11:37:28 +0200

Hi Davide,

cohesion is a "per point" value, so it is expresed in [newton].

It is not a pressure, that would be easier to manage. In fact, being a 
per-point value, the overall effect changes depending on how many points 
the collision detection stage is creating, ex. with two flat surfaces 
one might have from 3 to N arbitrary contact points. However, when 
dealing with spheres, this is not an issues because you have always 1 
point per sphere pair. If possible, then, try using spheres or cluster 
of spheres as collision shapes if you can.

Note that cohesion acts until the separating distance between the 
colliding points is not beyond the contact breaking , a global tolerance 
setting. Example, just after you create the ChSystem, type something 
like this:

collision::ChCollisionSystemBullet::SetContactBreakingThreshold(0.0001);

Also, at the time of writing, the cohesion is reversible (ie. if you 
return close enough to re-create the contact, i.e. under the "collision 
envelope", the cohesion effect is restored again).

About materials: in real life cohesion can be linked to 'bulk' physical 
properties of materials only in limited cases, otherwise in most cases 
you must start from experimental data.

Alessandro Tasora

In fact this is possible with PyChrono,  namely adding and removing
constraints, etc. (except I do not remember if the ray casting has been
wrapped).

Your concerns about the speed of Python are partially true - but remember
that when using PyChrono most of the cpu burden like linear algebra and
tight loops happen in the wrapped c++ side, wereas  you'll use python just
for instancing objects,  setting parameters etc.,  so in the main while ()
loop there will be few high-level statements like DoStep etc. and if there
are no tight loops then the speed will be 99% as the c++ equivalent.

Alessandro

Some of the features I added/modified are:

  1.  Three choices for the base platform. flat, single angle tilt, dual angle tilt.

  4.  Fixed views relative to each axle for 'quick' measurements along with a movable cursor to extract visual data.
  5.  New ChDoubleWishboneLR which enables different left and right suspension arms, camber, etc. for left-hand circle track racing. BTW, Wisconsin the heart of SLM racing in the US :).

Subject: Re: [chrono] Imposing a motion on a body
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 20 Sep 2018 12:28:54 +0200

Dear Ricardo,

if you want to impose the motion to a body, the ChLinkTrajectory is not 
enough because it imposes the translation to a point, and it does not 
constrain rotation etc (unless you use a 
ChLinkMateGeneric(false,false,false,true,true,true) to lock the Ry Ry 
Rz, for example).

So a more general way is to create a ChLinkLockLock constraint between 
your body and a fixed ground body. At this point, you can access the 
various ChLinkLockLock::SetMotion.... functions that provide a way to 
specify x y z translations and also rotations if you need. Or, keep 
these motions to zero, and change the ChMarker motions respect to owning 
body, where the marker is one of the two in the link.

have a nice day

In detail, there is a new function ChIrrTools::drawCollisionShapes() 
that calls the Bullet wireframe debug stuff.

Even easier: now the GUI of ChIrrAppInterface has a new checkmark to 
enable the draw of collision shapes, just open the panel by pressing "i" 
and check the "Draw coll.shapes" box, ex see the blue wireframe boxes in 
this figure:

Notes:

- shapes are drawn 'inflated' by the amount given by the "collision 
envelope" tolerance

- this is based on the drawing functions available in Bullet, so if 
using the ChronoParallel version you won't see the shapes

- the original Bullet implementation also draws xyz lines for the local 
coordinate system of each shape. I removed this because it was 
cluttering the view.

- some shapes are drawn simplified (ex spheres, which are drawn as two 
pyramids, or convex hulls, which are drawn as a zigzag polyline 
connecting the vertexes, not passing through all edges)

- I added the support for drawing the wireframe of concave triangle 
meshes, which were not available in the original Bullet library, but are 
available in Chrono (ex when using a ChBodyEasyMesh)

Kishor: let me know if it is ok to remove your demo, because now this 
functionality is available everywhere in all demos, just by checking the 
box in the GUI.

Alessandro Tasora

Hi Juan,

first some general remarks. You only need sudo, if you want to install 
chrono to a place where you don't have access normally - like /usr/local. 
If you keep everything in your user owned directories it is better to avoid 
sudo because you loose your rights and need sudo again to remove or change 
it. Chrono is a living work in progress and will be often be rebuild due to 
enhancements of different kinds. It is ok to keep the chrono directories in 
the user file space. The install process is optional - you can make the 
tests also in the build directory.

You saw some errors from the Irrlicht library after program start, this is 
harmless and can be ignored.

No we come to the real problems: the resource files can not be found. The 
strange thing about this is that they are present and in the right place. 
You can test it, go to the bin directory and type in the terminal window:

ls ../data

you should see not an error but the listing of the data content. I found 
out that Irlicht programs on the Mac need a special treatment, the have to 
be converted from a simple executable file to a Mac application bundle. For 
my personal use I wrote a converter script called 'irrAppS', you get it as 
attachment. It is a shell script and you have to edit it - the irrlicht 
directory might be on a different path on your machine. After editing copy 
it to a diectory, where it is found automatically, the type in the terminal 
window

chmod +x irrAppS
