Hi Juan,

you cannot use windows libraries on MacOS. We have made an update to the 
chrono docs, but it has not been updated on the web site. But it is no 
problem, I can give you some hints at this place also.

I highly recommend not to use irrlicht-1.8.2 but irrlicht-1.8.4 instead. 
The 1.8.4 is only slightly too old for your Xcode configuration. But you 
can test the following it on 1.8.2 too, if you want. First you need to 
expand irrlicht-1.8.4.zip to a place of your choice, let's take your home 
directory $HOME. Start a terminal session, type in

*cd irrlicht-1.8.4/source/Irrlicht/MacOSX*

You have to make an important change in the file CIrrDeviceMacOSX.mm with a 
text editor (CotEdit, BBEdit...). Search for the string 
NSFileManagerDelegate and replace it by the string NSApplicationDelegate. 
Save your changes!! The type in the terminal window:

*xcodebuild*

After a short time you should see the message: *** BUILD SUCCEEDED ***

You fill find a new directory called build now. in build/Release there is 
the library file libIrrlicht.a. The best practice is to copy this file into 
irrlicht-1.8.4/lib/MacOSX to make in consistent with the windows and linux 
versions of irrlicht. To be completely correct, type into the terminal 
window after copying:

*cd $HOME/irrlicht-1.8.4/lib/MacOSX*
*ranlib*

When you run cmake as command line utility, you can write:

*cmake 
-DCH_IRRLICHTLIB:FILEPATH=$HOME/irrlicht-1.8.4/lib/MacOSX/libIrrlicht.a *(+

Subject: Re: [chrono] Impact simulation
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 24 Mar 2018 22:00:11 +0100

Davide,

I took a quick look at your code and found at least two issues.

First, you have:
  ChVector<> inertia = (1/6)*mass*2*dim*2*dim*ChVector<>(1,1,1);
This will evaluate to a zero vector (because of the integer division 
1/6; you probably want something like 1.0/6).
This is the main reason for the issue you see (bodies with zero 
inertia). Note that states of bodies that are set as "fixed to ground" 
are not included in the equations of motion at all (so their inertia 
properties are irrelevant, hence why they render where you expect them).

Second, note that the functions that define a collision box, whether 
ChCollisionModel::AddBox() or the wrapper utils::AddBoxGeometry(), take 
as argument the box half-dimensions. So make sure you set that 
properly, else you will have deeply interpenetrated collision shapes.

I hope these two hints will put you on the right track.

--Radu

Davide,

Michael is correct and this is likely an issue with too large a step 
size for that configuration. Indeed, depending on the size of your 
collision objects and their relative velocities, it is possible to get 
this tunneling effect where collisions are missed.

Skimming the code you provided, it seems to me that while you have a 
variable 'time_step' you do not use it anywhere to actually make Chrono 
use that as its integration step size. Look at the various Chrono 
demos for how to set the integration step size.

Finally, on a different note, Michael is incorrect when he says that 
"Chrono::Parallel does not use Irrlicht as visualization". Indeed, the 
solver and visualization system are two disjunct things and you can 
actually visualize a Chrono::Parallel simulation using Chrono::Irrlicht 
if you so desire. For your information and in case someone else might 
be interested in this, I attached a test program that shows how that can 
done.

--Radu

Dear Liu,

currently there is no plasticity in the Chrono FEA module (except from 
an experimental Drucker-Prager plasticity model for the IGA brick), but 
look: I am working on introducing plasticity right now. I do not expect 
it to be ready in few days, anyway. Maybe months.

Currently I just implemented 1D plasticity for beams, also with with 
optional hardening (isotropic or kinematic or mixed), linear or 
nonlinear. Later, when this will be tested and validated, I will extend 
the same computational architecture to materials for 3D continuum (ie 
for tetrahedrons, bricks etc.)  and finally to shells too. But it will 
take time, sorry. The difficulty is providing an API that is as general 
as possible, so that the user can design and plug custom material models 
if needed.

best regards,

Alessandro Tasora

Hi Qihan,

 From what you describe, I think you should go the NarrowphaseCallback 
route. We do not have a demo showing how that can be used, but it 
should be pretty straightforward. A couple of suggestions:

  * if you're not doing this already, when possible (and that seems to
    be the case here) prefer a convex hull to a triangular mesh.
    In other words, one you have a ChTriangleMeshConnected (e.g. read
    from a Wavefront obj file), use ChCollisionModel::AddConvexHull
    instead of ChCollisionModel::AddTriangleMesh.
  * If you have multiple collision shapes associated with the same body
    (are your "wings" and the "round edge of the wings" on the same
    body?), for the purpose of using the narrowphase callback, it may be
    easier to use two different bodies connected with a weld joint (i.e.
    a 0-dof joint).
    This is because it will be easier to figure out which shape is which
    within the OnNarrowphase() method -- indeed, the ChCollisionInfo
    argument contains pointers to collision models not to collision
    shapes (in other words, it's simpler if you use collision models
    that contain a single collision shape each).

An alternative to letting Chrono perform the collision detection and 
using the NarrowphaseCallback mechanism to override the effective radius 
value is to do your own collision detection for the "wings" and "wing 
edges" against the plane. You can do this by first making sure that

(by using SetCollide(false) on the body(ies) that have those collision

Hi Qihan,

This is a very good question and the solution in Chrono is currently not 
complete. The problem stems from the fact that the radii of curvature 
at a contact point (R_1 & R_2) are geometric quantities that should be 
computed by the collision system (during its narrow phase).

For "sequential" Chrono simulations, we use an embedded version of 
Bullet which, unfortunately, does not compute this quantity (but see for 
workarounds further down).

However, if your problem is such that you can use Chrono::Parallel and 
depending on the collision shapes you are interested in, these radii of 
curvature will be calculated. This is because Chrono::Parallel uses a 
custom collision system based on analytical formulas for collisions 
between simple primitive shapes; for pairs of shapes that we can treat 
analytically (e.g. sphere-sphere or sphere-box), we also calculate the 
curvatures at the contact point. Note that there also we fall back on a 
generic collision algorithm (Minkovski Portal Refinement) if we do not 
have an analytical implementation for a certain collision pair. MPR does 
not calculate curvature either.

So the problem is: what effective radius of curvature should be used for 
a contact for which the collision system did not provide the curvatures 
on the two surfaces at the contact point? Until recently, this was 
hardcoded to a global constant value (the 1.0 for sequential Chrono that 
you mention) and the user couldn't even modify this value (unless
symbol:
Re: [chrono] Effective Radius in Contact Model -- Maybe a bug in the
 Chrono Engine

text:
on the two surfaces at the contact point? Until recently, this was 
hardcoded to a global constant value (the 1.0 for sequential Chrono that 
you mention) and the user couldn't even modify this value (unless 
changing the code and rebuilding Chrono). About 6 weeks ago (commit 
#3d8d9b2 on 29 February) I pushed changes to the 'develop' branch on 
GitHub to relax this constraint: the default value was changed to 0.1 
and I provided a mechanism for the user to change it, by calling the 
(global) function 
collision::ChCollisionInfo::SetDefaultEffectiveCurvatureRadius(). This 
will set a constant, global R_eff to be used for all collisions at all 
times.

If your system is such that it contains collision shapes for which a 
single value of the effective radius of curvature is appropriate (e.g. 
equal spheres), you can pre-calculate the correct value and set it.

Otherwise, there is a "back door" that you can use and set the correct 
(or a better estimate) of the effective radius of curvature on a 
per-collision case. Indeed, using 
collision::ChCollisionSystem::RegisterNarrowphaseCallback() you can 
register a user-supplied callback object that will be invoked each time 
a new collision is found during the narrowphase.  This object must be 
derived from collision::ChCollisionSystem::NarrowphaseCallback and must 
implement the virtual method OnNarrowphase() which takes as argument a 
reference to a ChCollisionInfo. In there you can calculate the correct 
effective radius of curvature for *that* collision and overwrite the 
member in the ChCollisionInfo argument.

Eventually, we will replace/enhance the various implementations of
symbol:
Re: [chrono] Effective Radius in Contact Model -- Maybe a bug in the
 Chrono Engine

text:
member in the ChCollisionInfo argument.

Eventually, we will replace/enhance the various implementations of 
collision systems in Chrono. The requirement that this additional 
geometric quantity is calculated and reported will be among the criteria 
we will use in selecting the new collision system(s) provided with 
Chrono. In the meantime, I hope the above comments will help.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Develop or master branch?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 24 Jul 2018 08:17:11 +0200

The 'master' branch contains the code for the 3.0 release (August 
2017). The 'develop' branch has the latest code which includes 
additions, enhancements, and some bug fixes. Of course, the code on 
'master' is more stable as it was not touched since it was released. 
However, we strive to keep the code on 'develop' as stable as possible 
at each push.

If you are working with your own Chrono build (and not, say, a 
system-wide installation), I suggest you use the 'develop' code as new 
features are added all the time. Note however that, every now and then, 
we make changes that affect the API; in these cases, you would have to 
update your own projects as needed.

--Radu

Justin,

I'm not sure what exactly worked and didn't work.   So let me assume that:
(1) you are able to configure and build Chrono, with the desired modules enabled (in your case Chrono::Cascade).
(2) the Chrono demos compile and build fine and you are able to run them.
(3) you want to write your own, external project that uses Chrono::Cascade functionality.
(4) you use CMake to configure your project

So for this discussion, I will use the sample codes in the chrono-projects repository (in particular the demo_CAS_robot.cpp).

  1.  The CMakeLists.txt script to configure this demo as an external project is the one at:   https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono-projects/blob/develop/configuration_tests/cascade/CMakeLists.txt
This relies on the Chrono project configuration script to find a valid build/install of Chrono with the necessary modules enabled; see lines 22-25:
find_package(Chrono
            COMPONENTS Cascade Irrlicht
            CONFIG
)
As you already know, you may have to point CMake to the proper location of the ChronoConfig.cmake script (e.g. in the 'cmake' subfolder of your Chrono build tree).

If Chrono and the required dependencies are found, the ChronoConfig script makes available several variables which you then use to configure your project (CHRONO_INLUDE_DIRS, CHRONO_CXX_FLAGS, CHRONO_LINKER_FLAGS, CHRONO_LIBRARIES); see the remainder of the above CMakeLists.txt script in chrono-projects.

On Windows, if your project links against Chrono::Cascade, your CMakeLists.txt script must also add the WNT definition (needed for OpenCASCADE); see lines 73-75.

On Windows, if your project links against Chrono::Cascade, your CMakeLists.txt script must also add the WNT definition (needed for OpenCASCADE); see lines 73-75.

  2.  Before moving on, there's an additional thing that you must take care of.  If your project uses any data from the Chrono distribution, you must somehow specify (in your code) where this data directory is.  This is done by calling the function SetChronoDataPath(path_to_chrono_data_dir).    The ChronoConfig script also sets a CHRONO_DATA_DIR CMake variable that contains this path.

There are various ways to use this CMake variable to make this path available in your code.

One option is to define a preprocessor macro. If you look at line 40 of https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono-projects/blob/develop/configuration_tests/cascade/demo_CAS_robot.cpp, you will see that the call to SetChronoDataPath uses the macro CHRONO_DATA_DIR.    This macro is set in CMakeLists.txt (see line 93) based on the CHRONO_DATA_DIR CMake variable mentioned before (here I just opted to name for the macro identifier the same as the CMake variable, but that does not have to be so).

Another option is to have CMake generate a header file to provide this information.

  3.  If everything goes well with the above, you should be able to properly configure and build your project depending on Chrono::Cascade.  The remaining issue (the errors you currently get) is to make the required shared libraries available.  This is a problem on Windows (with DLLs).  The various Chrono DLLs are generated in the Chrono build tree (e.g., in <chrono_build>\bin\Release).

Another option is to have CMake generate a header file to provide this information.

  3.  If everything goes well with the above, you should be able to properly configure and build your project depending on Chrono::Cascade.  The remaining issue (the errors you currently get) is to make the required shared libraries available.  This is a problem on Windows (with DLLs).  The various Chrono DLLs are generated in the Chrono build tree (e.g., in <chrono_build>\bin\Release).

One option is to add this folder to the Windows environment variable 'Path'.   But this is probably not a great idea unless you use an installed version of Chrono.

The alternative is to copy the necessary Chrono DLLs (from the Chrono build tree) next to the executable for your project (e.g., to <my_project>\bin\Release or whatever that location is in your case).    To help with this copying, I provided in the ChronoConfig.cmake script a utility function add_DLL_copy_command that adds a custom VS command to the VS solution for the external project.   In the case of the demos in the chrono-projects repository, this CMake function is called in a parent CMakeLists.txt script (https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono-projects/blob/develop/CMakeLists.txt).   You can figure out how to adapt this to your particular project CMakeLists.txt.

Having said that, the add_DLL_copy_command only works for the Release Chrono DLLs.   If you want to compile your project in Debug mode, then you will have to manually copy the debug Chrono DLLs next to your executable (e.g., copy all Chrono DLLs from <chrono_build>\bin\Debug to <my_project>\bin\Debug).   Of course, this implies that you would have built Chrono in Debug mode first.

Having said that, the add_DLL_copy_command only works for the Release Chrono DLLs. Of course, this implies that you would have built Chrono in Debug mode first.

Note also that the mechanism provided through this add_DLL_copy_command CMake function is not very robust and sometimes it fails to copy even the Release DLLs.  In that case, the safest thing is to simply copy the DLLs manually (like you have to do always do for Debug DLLs).

  4.  Finally, one of your errors is about a missing MSVCP100.dll.   This is a Microsoft VS DLL that is required by the particular installation of OpenCASCADE 6.9.0 that we both use (which was apparently built against VS 2010).   To get this DLL, you probably have to install the Microsoft Visual C++ 2010 Redistributable.   This should install that DLL in C:\Windows\System32 which is in the DLL search path (so one you have it there, that error will go away).

Subject: Re: [chrono] MPI Support
From: Kishor Bhalerao

Hi Radu,
Thanks for the detailed response.

On Wednesday, March 21, 2018 at 2:01:28 AM UTC-7, Radu Serban wrote:
symbol: Re: [chrono] MPI Support

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] MPI Support
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 21 Mar 2018 10:01:11 +0100

Hi Kishor,

Note that Chrono::Distributed is very much work in progress. It's still 
being developed and was not yet merged in the main development branch.

We are currently focused on supporting only smooth contact (SMC, or 
penalty-based, or soft-body). We plan on extending it to non-smooth 
contact (NSC, or complementarity-based, or rigid-body) and there is no 
fundamental show-stopper (as long as we rely on an iterative solver, we 
only need to extend that to work on distributed arrays).

Regarding the available integrators, for now that is the only one 
supported. The reason for this is that we designed Chrono::Distributed 
to leverage our multi-core solver (Chrono::Parallel) to give us a hybrid 
MPI-OpenMP solution. Because Chrono::Parallel was coded to support both 
the SMC and NSC formulations, it only implements an integrator that 
works for both.

Right now (and likely for the near future), Chrono::Distributed is 
limited to granular dynamics and does not support articulated 
mechanisms, i.e. no bilateral constraints (since we're only doing SCM 
for now, also no unilateral constraints). The way we plan on using 
this with multibody systems (our first target application is to use 
Chrono::Distributed for granular terrain in vehicle simulations) is 
through co-simulation. This work is ongoing, simultaneously with 
completing the distributed granular dynamics code.

I hope this answers your questions.
Best,
Radu

to model it using Chrono::Distributed?

Kishor.

Date: Wed, 31 Oct 2018 19:23:42 +0000

Jeremy,

That is controlled through the parameters (of type irr::SIrrlichtCreationParameters) used when creating the Irrlicht device.
Since this was a quick change, I pushed code to allow specifying the logging level as an (optional) argument to the constructors for ChIrrAppInterface and derived classes.   The default value is the same as before (i.e. irr::ELL_INFORMATION), but you can now override that by passing irr::ELL_NONE to disable all Irrlicht logging.  See demo_VEH_HMMWV9 which now does this.

--Radu

On 10/31/2018 6:10 PM, Jeremy Mange wrote:
I was curious if anyone knew of a way to suppress the Irrlicht message that is printed on stdout when the device is first created (particularly when using ChVehicleIrrApp).

Based on this Irrlicht forum post<http://irrlicht.sourceforge.net/forum/viewtopic.php?f=4&t=1633>, it sounds like the only way to do this might be to create a custom event receiver for the log event, since setting the Irrlicht log level can only happen after the device is created and that first message is displayed.  But since the actual event handlers exist behind the scenes in the ChVehicleIrrApp, there may be no way to do this without creating the Irrlicht app directly?  Am I understanding that correctly?

This is not a pressing issue, but I'd appreciate any insight or ideas if anyone has them!

Francesco,

For now a couple more pointers to help with your current simulations.

I agree with your assessment of what was happening when using a small number of bins.  Indeed, the binning works by first finding a global AABB (which encompasses all AABBs of collision shapes in the system) and then dividing that large box in equal-size bins.  The small number of bins and the clusters in your simulation effectively led to a large number of sequential tests within the crowded bins.

As you can probably see, this is still an issue if you have bodies which get farther and farther from your domain of interest.   There is one trick in Chrono::Parallel that you can use to address this issue, but you will need to ensure that does not affect the physics of the problem you're trying to solve.  Indeed, you can specify a large AABB that will define a boundary that your bodies cannot cross.  If you enable this option, as soon as a body reaches the boundary of this AABB, the body will be deactivated (it will not be removed from the system, but it will become a zombie).   This feature ensures that the computational domain stays bounded and a single body being "ejected" does not negatively affect performance of the collision detection.

You can enable this feature with code like this:
      my_system.GetSettings()->collision.use_aabb_active = true;
      my_system.GetSettings()->collision.aabb_min = bmin;
      my_system.GetSettings()->collision.aabb_max = bmax;

text:
my_system.data_manager->host_data.aabb_min
   my_system.data_manager->host_data.aabb_max
However, these arrays are indexed by a shape id.   So you can loop over all shapes in the system, access its current AABB, find the id of the body associated with that shape, and so on.  But not the other way around (at least not efficiently).   You can get a better picture of this if you look at the implementation of a function such as ChCAABBGenerator::GenerateAABB in ChAABBGenerator.cpp (line 110).

One more thing: the AABBs stored in the above two arrays are shifted such that they all lie in the 1st octant (i.e. they all have only positive values).  You can find the current value of the offset in
   my_system.data_manager->measures.collision.global_origin
and undo the offset if needed (i.e. apply the inverse of the shift implemented in ChBroadphase::OffsetAABB).

Having said that, I think it'd be possible to provide an implementation for ChCollisionModelParallel::GetAABB (currently absent).  I'll look into this.

--Radu

From: Radu Serban

Hi Francesco,

One of the settings that you should *not* leave at default value is the number of bins used for the broad-phase collision detection.  If I recall correctly, the default is something like 20x20x20 or 10x10x10.  You will likely need quite a bit more than that, but will need to experiment to find the sweet spot.   As a rule of thumb, I suggest you try some values that lead to roughly 2-4 objects per bin per direction (in other words, bins with 8-64 objects each).

Indeed, Chrono::Parallel does not use the collision detection from Bullet.  Instead it uses a custom grid-based algorithm for broad-phase and a combination of Minkovski Portal Refinement + analytical for narrow-phase.   The broad-phase algorithm used in Chrono::Parallel (based on bins on a uniform grid which is assumed to be aligned with the global reference frame) is nowhere near as sophisticated as it should be and works best for objects of roughly the same size and for simulations where there is little "flow" of the collision shapes: situations like those encountered in terramechanics when modeling soil as granular material.  Which means that, for the type of simulations you are doing, a bin setting that works well at the beginning of the simulation may not be all that great when bodies coalesce.

You can in principle adjust the bin setting as the simulation progresses.  However, the current implementation assumes a uniform grid (i.e. bins of equal size in a given direction), so this will anyway be sub-optimal for your problems.   One solution is to allow for a non-uniform grid (and allow the user to control this, in a problem-dependent manner, as the simulation progresses) -- a modification along these lines is on my todo list, but I do not know when I'll get to it.

A while ago (must be 2-3 years now) we did some extensive testing trying to find the best scheduling for the various parallel for loops in Chrono::Parallel.  What is implemented right now is the best compromise we converged on at that time, using certain benchmark problems that unfortunately may not be representative of what you are doing.

You are also correct that Chrono::Parallel supports only a subset of what can be done with the serial Chrono solver (most notably, here is no support for FEA).
Indeed, removing bodies from a Chrono::Parallel system is not implemented (this has to do with the underlying data structures used in the parallel code); there is some experimental code to allow that, but it had to be commented out due to some bugs.
Also, not all queries you can make for a serial Chrono system can be made for a Chrono::Parallel system, or at least not with the same API.  For your specific question, I think there should be a way to access the current AABBs.  If that is critical for you, I can look into this and give you a definite answer.

Hi Francesco
Let me comment some points here,  even if the "parallel" version of Chrono
is not my contribution (I am mostly involved in the development of the
"serial" version).

1
The fast SOR_MULTITHREAD solver,  which is available in the default
"serial" Chrono, was experimental and it is non-deterministic in the sense
that different processors can give different results (same issue for
different runs),  therefore it should not be used for scientific work.
Prefer using SSOR or SOR for tests, and BARZILAIBORWEIN for better
precision at the cost of slower performance. Note that BARZILAIBORWEIN
already uses some OpenMP multithreading,  although I admit that it could be
optimized.

2
The serial chrono,  except for those few OpenMP optimizations,  uses mostly
one core. This said, I am surprised that the parallel version is loading
just one core in your tests...

3
The ChSystem::SetParallelThreadNumber() setting is a bit obsolete. It was
used only by that SOR_MULTITHREADING code I mentioned before. Otherwise,
the N of threads should be automatically set by OpenMP in the rest of the
code.

4
Yes, at the moment not all features of Chrono serial are available in
Chrono parallel. Sorry for this issue. In future we'll port more
functionalities in the parallel part. Do you need some specific missing
feature apart from that AABB stuff that you already mentioned?

By the way: nice work in your video...

Best regards

Alessandro Tasora

Subject: Re: [chrono] Hardware recommendation for Chrono
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 21 Jul 2018 11:49:44 +0200

Chrono::Parallel supports almost everything in Chrono::Vehicle.

For wheeled vehicles, the limitations are related to tire models. 
FEA-based tire models are not supported (because Chrono::FEA is not 
supported in conjunction with Chrono::Parallel). The (semi-)empirical 
tire models (Pacejka, Fiala, TMeasy) should in principle work but are 
not used in practice with Chrono::Parallel simulations; this is because 
you would use Chrono::Parallel for a vehicle simulation when using 
granular terrain (and until we implement a simple deformable tire model 
that can work on granular terrain, the only option is the rigid tire).

For tracked vehicles, you cannot use the continuous-band track models 
(which rely on Chrono::FEA).

See the two demos provided with Chrono: demo_VEH_HMMWV_Parallel & 
demo_VEH_M113_Parallel.

--Radu

Subject: Re: Slurry flow through a channel. Ideas?
From: milad rakhsha
Date: Tue, 1 Oct 2019 15:37:56 -0700 (PDT)

Regarding the fluid domain, there is no support for inlet/outlet condition 
in the sense that Eulerian solvers implement it. There is, however, support 
for periodic inlet/outlet, which in many cases could be a replacement for 
the boundary conditions you need. You can look into 
the demo_FSI_Poiseuille_flow for an example.
If the interaction of the fluid domain with solid particles is of 
interested to you, you will need to populate your solid bodies with the so 
called "BCE" fluid markers that enforce fluid-structure coupling. Look 
into demo_FSI_CylinderDrop to see how this is done for interaction of a 
cylindrical object with fluid.  

I can give you my suggestions on how to inject particles from one side but 
others may have better solutions in this case. I would try to add the 
particles inside the loop where you do DoStepDynamics with some initial 
velocity in the direction you like to inject those particles. If you it 
this way, you need to make sure that you follow the same procedure that you 
performed before doing the time-stepping, e.g. adding the particles to the 
system, finalizing the system construction and so on. Another alternative 
method that might be easier and safer to do is to generate every particle 
at the beginning of the simulation and only activate them gradually during 
the time-stepping loop.

Milad

Subject: Re: [chrono] Simulation multiple vehicles
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 18 Jul 2018 13:26:30 +0200

Hi Francisco,

I believe you probably got the rough simulation setup right, but it 
would be useful if you could describe at a bit of a higher level what it 
is that you try to achieve.

As I understand it, you are interested in having a main vehicle (your 
Roadcar) evolve in traffic, with the latter represented by these 
"traffic agents" (other vehicles). Depending on what you want to do 
(will the main vehicle be driven interactively? are you looking into an 
autonomous vehicle?) as well as the scenarios you are interested in (for 
example, do you want to look at physical interaction between your main 
vehicle and other traffic agents?), you can take various approaches. 
You can indeed use other full Chrono::Vehicle models for the traffic 
agents and have their behavior prescribed using the mechanism provided 
by the ChDataDriver. Or else you can have simple "stand ins" for these 
traffic agents (going as far as representing them as single bodies that 
are moved kinematically (overriding their state in the simulation loop).

Efficiency is an issue. Depending on model complexity and simulation 
settings (integration step size, number of iterations, etc.), you should 
be able to simulate a single vehicle in (soft) real time. As you add 
more complexity to your overall system, performance will obviously 
drop. I don't think there's much code optimization you can do on your 
side to help with this, beyond tuning simulation settings. We plan on 
doing some work in the near future on improving performance in Chrono

Subject: Re: [chrono] Simulation multiple vehicles
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 6 Jul 2018 08:13:59 +0200

Francisco,

You can construct multiple vehicles within the same Chrono system. The 
cleanest way to do this is to explicitly create the system and then use 
the appropriate Chrono::Vehicle constructors (which create the vehicle 
components within a specified Chrono system). Then, in your simulation 
loop, you must advance the state of that single system (by calling 
DoStepDynamics).

The purpose of the ChIrrApp::AssetBindAll function is different: it is 
used to associate the generic Chrono visualization assets with Irrlicht 
objects. You still need to do that, but only for visualization purposes.

I created a simple demo (demo_VEH_TwoCars) and pushed it to the 
'develop' branch of the Chrono repository. For simplicity, I used the 
HMMWV_Reduced model (which encapsulates the vehicle, powertrain, and 
tire subsystems), but this should give you an idea on how to set up your 
own simulation.

--Radu

From: Alessandro Tasora

hi Giovanni

yes, I know, but this is intentional in the code. The reason is that the 
actuator should not have discontinuous length functions,and the case you 
comment here is a similar concept. If the solver finds that there is 
such 'jump', it uses a/stabilization /term that gradually closes the gap.
How fast is this gradual stabilization, it depends on the ChSystem 
parameter of "max.recovery speed"; you may increase such parameter using
   mysystem->ChSystem::SetMaxPenetrationRecoverySpeed(100)
for example, but if you use unilateral contacts it will affect also the 
stable stacking of colliding objects, that's why the default value is 
quite low, i.e. 0.6 m/s if I remember.

No, it is only a side effect if using discontinuous 'jumps' in the 
actuator length. For the rest, the motion profile should be followed 
exactly (of course, assuming you used a solver with high enough number 
of iterations).

No, it assumes infinite stiffness, perfectly rigid behaviour. If you 
need some damping/stifness, there isnot at the moment, but you can fake 
it by putting an intermediate body and a ChLinkSpring . Again, the 
'damped' behaviour you see is just a numerical artifact because you 
start with the 'jump'.

Have a nice day

Alessandro

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Friction / NSC Solver
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 16 Jul 2018 10:10:38 +0200

Hi Kishor,

Indeed, the contact material properties for a pair of colliding shapes 
are obtained from those of the materials associated with the two bodies 
using a particular composition strategy. The default strategy is 
implemented in the base class ChMaterialCompositionStrategy (in 
ChMaterialSurface.h). In particular, the coefficient of friction of the 
composite material is set to be the minimum of the two values.

If you want to implement your own composition strategy, you must write 
your own derived class, overriding one or more of the composition laws 
(virtual methods), and register your class by calling 
ChSystem::SetMaterialCompositionStrategy.

Note that whatever composition strategy you use, it will be global -- in 
that it will be used for all contact interactions in the system. If you 
need finer control, I thought I'd mention another related Chrono 
feature: you can use a callback mechanism to modify the composite 
material, on a collision-by-collison basis. For this, write your own 
callback object, derived from ChContactContainer::AddContactCallback and 
implement the virtual method OnAddContact(). Once you register your 
class using ChContactContainer::RegisterAddContactCallback, the 
OnAddContact method will be called every time a new contact pair is 
created, giving you the opportunity to modify the composite contact 
material for that pair only (on entry, the composite material would have 
been created using the current composition strategy). You can see an

material for that pair only (on entry, the composite material would have 
been created using the current composition strategy). You can see an 
example of using such a callback object in demo_IRR_callbackNSC.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Tire forces SCM-deform terrain
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 28 Oct 2017 20:20:44 +0200

James,

The tire forces cannot be easily recovered from the wheel body (since 
you couldn't separate it from other applied forces, such as 
gravitational forces).

I pushed some changes to the 'develop' branch of the Chrono repository 
to provide the missing functionality. Note that this required a bit of 
redesign of the Chrono::Vehicle API related to obtaining tire forces. 
There are now 2 different (virtual) functions:

  * GetTireForce() returns the generalized tire force (point of
    application, force, moment) to be passed to the vehicle system and
    applied to the wheel body. For tire models that use underlying
    Chrono functionality (e..g, contact for ChRigidTire or constraints
    for ChDeformableTire), this function *must* return zero force and
    moment (else tire forces are double counted). Note that this
    function does not have an argument anymore.
  * ReportTireForce() returns the generalized tire force, for reporting
    purposes or for obtaining the tire force in a co-simulation
    framework. It is passed a pointer to the terrain system (for tire
    models where that is irrelevant, pass 'nullptr').

Use the 2nd function for what you need. For a rigid tire on SCM 
terrain, you must pass a pointer to the terrain system.

Please let me know if this works for you.

--Radu

P.S. Note also that there were a few other recent changes to 
Chrono::Vehicle that you may want to take into account when using the 
latest code on the 'develop' branch. In particular, we now expect mass

P.S. Note also that there were a few other recent changes to 
Chrono::Vehicle that you may want to take into account when using the 
latest code on the 'develop' branch. In particular, we now expect mass 
and inertia properties to be provided separately for the wheel body and 
a tire attached to it. We also added a utility function 
(ChTire::EstimateInertia) that you can use to get an approximation of 
the tire moments of inertia.

   true, irr::video::EDT_OPENGL);*

Subject: RE: [chrono] Change mass of FED Alpha vehicle
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 8 Aug 2024 09:35:08 +0000

While the various vehicle system templates are parameterized, the concrete vehicle models included in the Chrono distribution have parameters that are fixed to values corresponding to that model. In general, changing a parameter means effectively modeling another vehicle. Having said that, I agree that the mass and inertia properties of the vehicle chassis represent a special case, because these could change due to different payload conditions (I assume this is the difference between your test vehicle and the one we used to set up the Chrono::Vehicle FEDA model). I will look into adding a mechanism in Chrono::Vehicle to control this (different payload levels).

In the meantime, to match the vehicle mass of your test vehicle, you will need to modify locally the FEDA model (in particular, adjust the chassis mass in FEDA_Chassis.cpp<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/22acf38c21563497fdeda6b4b1794f28d96ea6eb/src/chrono_models/vehicle/feda/FEDA_Chassis.cpp#L40>).  Note that for some of the vehicle models in Chrono we also provide a specification through JSON files, in which case such adjustments are easier to do (as they would not require recompilation). That was not possible for the FEDA model because of the more complex model of the FEDA suspension which required custom code (for the air springs and shocks; see FEDA_DoubleWishbone.cpp<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/main/src/chrono_models/vehicle/feda/FEDA_DoubleWishbone.cpp>) and could not be reproduced with the limitations imposed by a JSON specification.

Subject: RE: [chrono] How to configure the articulated vehicle JSON file ?
 Including coordinates, units and other issues.
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 30 Dec 2022 08:46:17 +0000

I am not sure I understood your question exactly, but I assume you want to modify the sample articulated chassis vehicle model to represent your own vehicle.
Assuming you understand how vehicle modeling works in Chrono::Vehicle and what a subsystem template is (a parameterized generic model of a particular topology), you will need to adjust the various hard-point locations to match the geometry of your vehicle.
See https://api.projectchrono.org/manual_vehicle.html

In particular, you will need to properly set the locations of the suspension subsystems relative to the chassis reference frames (properly set “Suspension Location” in ACV_Vehicle.json). Similarly, you will need to properly adjust “Rear Connector Location” in ACV_FrontChassis and “Front Connector Location” in ACV_RearChassis. Together, these parameters should match the actual wheelbase of your vehicle.  Then, you need to properly position the spindle in ACV_RigidSuspension.json to obtain the actual wheel track (track width) of your vehicle.

In general, you must go through all JSON specification files and change *all* parameters to match the geometry, mass properties, and other settings to correspond to the measurements of the vehicle you are trying to model.

--Radu

Hi Guandong,

there is no need to use "delete" when using shared pointers. Actually, it
is forbidden.
Say you created some body my_body,  you added it to a system,  and maybe
later you want to delete it. The only thing you have to do is to call

   my_system.Remove(my_body)

This done,  if no one else is using the body,  the shared pointer mechanism
will take care of deleting the body automatically (ex. when exiting the
function scope {...} where my_body is used). This automatic mechanism is
based on a hidden reference count.

Alessandro Tasora

Liu,

Chrono::Parallel does not use the GPU for granular dynamics. The GPU 
usage you see while running demo_PAR_ballsNSC is likely due to rendering 
(using the Chrono::OpenGL module). You should be able to check this by 
disabling rendering (simply undef CHRONO_OPENGL at the top). As for why 
you don't see any GPU usage while running your code that's either 
because you do not do any rendering or because the simulation is so slow 
that the GPU doesn't have much work to do in rendering.

 CUDA?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 11 Dec 2017 11:21:51 +0100

Hi Wen,

As I was saying in a related thread a few days ago, there is no CUDA 
support for rigid body frictional contact in Chrono::Parallel. The 
USE_PARALLEL_CUDA option is there for a separate functionality in 
Chrono::Parallel (MPM) which is not relevant to your problem.

Currently, Chrono::Parallel targets only multi-core architectures (via 
OpenMP). To see benefits, you need to run it on a processor with enough 
cores.

Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Spring and Shock Curves
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 14 Feb 2018 11:10:46 +0100

Hi Jacob,

There is indeed a bit of inconsistency in how spring data is assumed to 
be specified in Chrono::Vehicle (including when doing this through a 
suspension JSON file). The tabular data assumes to receive pairs 
{displacement, force} where a negative displacement indicates 
compression (jounce). This is because we define:
  displacement = current_length - rest_length
Unfortunately, we used the assumption that the data would specify a 
negative force for jounce (and a positive one for rebound).

Having said that, internally the code negates the force value it obtains 
through (linear) interpolation from the provided data at a given 
configuration (current_length) so that the force applied to the two 
bodies (e.g. chassis and lower control arm for a double wishbone 
suspension) is in fact positive for jounce and negative for rebound.

You can convince of this yourself by monitoring the current spring 
displacement and force in the suspension. Note that the accessors to 
obtain these quantities are defined on various derived suspension 
classes (not all suspensions are assumed to have a spring, so these 
accessors are not defined on the base class). For example, assuming 
your model uses a DoubleWishbone suspension on the front, insert the 
following lines in your main loop to monitor the spring displacement and 
force in the front-left spring:
  auto suspF = 
std::static_pointer_cast<DoubleWishbone>(vehicle.GetSuspension(0)); // 
pick front suspension
  double displ = suspF->GetSpringDeformation(LEFT); //
symbol: Re: [chrono] Spring and Shock Curves

text:
std::static_pointer_cast<DoubleWishbone>(vehicle.GetSuspension(0)); // 
pick front suspension
  double displ = suspF->GetSpringDeformation(LEFT); // 
deformation of left spring
  double frc = suspF->GetSpringForce(LEFT); // force in left spring
You will see that a negative displacement (compression) is associated 
with a positive force.

In summary: when specifying spring data (in the JSON file), use a 
negative force for a negative spring displacement and a positive force 
for a positive displacement. The code will flip the sign during 
simulation.

I will consider fixing this inconsistency in a future release of the 
code, but that will unfortunately invalidate some Chrono::Vehicle models 
out there.

Hope that this answers your question.
--Radu

Hi Jacob,

Sorry for the late reply.

You are correct, the suspension test-rig class does not currently 
include an (optional) ARB subsystem.    I strongly encourage you to try 
to extend it in this direction yourself and maybe contribute this back 
to our main repository through a pull request.   I will try to help as 
much as I can if you get stuck.

To get you started, note that I implemented the suspension test rig 
(ChSuspensionTestRig.{h,cpp}) as a class, derived from the ChVehicle 
base class, that "mirrors" a wheeled vehicle (ChWheeledVehicle).  Like a 
full-blown vehicle, a ChSuspensionTestRig is a composite class that 
contains all necessary vehicle subsystems and is in charge of (i) 
initializing the vehicle subsystems and (ii) intermediating the 
communication between its constitutive subsystems and external systems 
(the "driver" system and the "tire" systems).  These two phases are done 
in the overrides of the Initialize() and Synchronize() virtual 
functions, respectively.

Unlike a full-blown wheeled vehicle, a ChSuspensionTestRig has exactly 
one suspension subsystem (i.e., one axle), at most one steering 
subsystem, and exactly two wheel and two tires.  In addition, it also 
contains the parts (bodies and joints) needed for the test-rig mechanism 
itself.

Note also that (at least currently), a test-rig can only be constructed 
from a test-rig JSON specification file or from a (wheeled) vehicle JSON 
specification file (by selecting and using one of the vehicle's
symbol: Re: [chrono] Suspension Test Rig

text:
Note also that (at least currently), a test-rig can only be constructed 
from a test-rig JSON specification file or from a (wheeled) vehicle JSON 
specification file (by selecting and using one of the vehicle's 
axles).   To deal with that part of the code, you'll need to familiarize 
yourself a bit with RapidJSON which is the third-party library we use 
for reading/writing JSON files (RapidJSON is already included with the 
Chrono code).

Finally, note that there's another set of related classes (a base class 
ChDriverSTR and derived classes ChDataDriverSTR and ChIrrGuiDriverSTR) 
which implement the "driver" system to be used in conjunction with a 
test-rig (these provide the inputs: steering and post up/right).  But to 
add an ARB to the test-rig, you should not have to worry about this part 
of the code.

To test your code while you develop this new feature, I suggest you use 
demo_VEH_SuspensionTestRig and use as "vehicle_file" the model in 
generic/vehicle/Vehicle_DoubleWishbones_ARB.json.  That wheeled vehicle 
model has an ARB defined for its 1st (front) axle.

I hope this helps.  Let me know how this goes.

Hi, Soowon,

My name is Colin Vanden Heuvel, I am the systems administrator at UW SBEL. I've seen the way that a lot of different hardware works with ProjectChrono, and I think I might be able to help you a little bit.

First off, let's talk about CPU. If you aren't doing work with granular media, you won't necessarily need the massive quantity of threads you would get using dual Intel Xeons or AMD Threadripper. While those processors perform very well with highly parallel workloads, you might see comparable or better results (and save some money) with a higher clock speed and a more modest number of threads. Intel CPUs tend to outperform AMD on single-threaded workloads at a given clock speed, so perhaps the Intel i7-7800X would be a better fit at a much lower price.

Since you aren't dealing with fluids, a GPU is more of a luxury than a necessity. You will want something nice for visualizations, but you needn't worry about purchasing the top of the line. This is just an example, so please don't consider it a serious recommendation, but the NVIDIA GTX 1050Ti is an effective but inexpensive card that would pair well with Chrono.

This is just an example, so please don't consider it a serious recommendation, but the NVIDIA GTX 1050Ti is an effective but inexpensive card that would pair well with Chrono.

The impact of one type of RAM over another is somewhat less noticeable than CPU or GPU. Higher overclocked frequencies can benefit a complex simulation, but configuring them can be a pain if you don't want to deal with it. For the most part, you just need to make sure that you have enough memory to run the simulation. I've found 32 GB to be a more than suitable amount, and depending on the amount of things you expect to do at once, 16 GB can still be plenty. Really, just try using chrono for a simulation on a machine you already have, see how much it uses, and buy an appropriate capacity using that information.

I hope this helps you. You certainly don't need to follow any of my suggestions, as I really can't make any guarantees without having perfect knowledge of your situation. If you have more questions, I'd be glad to help.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Building project with my own static library
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 22 Oct 2017 19:27:09 +0200

Hi Soowon,

Assuming I understood correctly what you want to do, I see two possible 
solutions here:

 1. Add a CMake target to create a library out of the functions in the
    myLib/ folder. Note that if you create a DLL you must make sure
    you have the proper __declspec for export and import (look at how we
    deal with that for the various Chrono DLLs).

    Then you can link in this library when you create the various
    executables for your projects.

 2. Include the (shared) sources from the myLib/ folder in the target
    for each project in CMake. Note that this doesn't mean that you
    actually duplicate (copy) these shared files in each project folder.

    To see something along these lines, look at the Chrono
    CMakeLists.txt in src/demos/vehicle/demo_ArticulatedVehicle.

Hope that this helps.
--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] Re: Reduction of CPU time with SIMD option
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 3 Aug 2022 13:08:58 +0000

Camille,

It is likely that the issues you are seeing are due to misaligned memory in your classes/structures if they happen to have members that are fixed-size Eigen types (such as ChMatrixNM, ChMatrix33, ChVectorN, etc).  You must include the macro EIGEN_MAKE_ALIGNED_OPERATOR_NEW in such classes (as we do everywhere relevant in Chrono; see for example ChFrame.h).

Currently, Chrono relies on SIMD acceleration only through Eigen.  So, it is a bit difficult to point exactly which solvers in Chrono benefit most from this.   But with heavy and judicious use of Eigen (as is done in some parts of Chrono, e.g., the new ANCF element implementations), you can and will see efficiency improvements.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] variable height terrain as road for chrono vehicle
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 09 Jul 2017 08:47:12 +0200

Hi Chaitanya,

Look at demo_VEH_HMMWV as an example of using a rigid terrain 
initialized from a mesh (from that test.obj Wavefront file) or a 
height-map (from test64.bmp).  To do that, you must change the terrain 
type at line 73 in demo_VEH_HMMWV.cpp to:
   RigidTerrain::Type terrain_model = RigidTerrain::MESH;
or
   RigidTerrain::Type terrain_model = RigidTerrain::HEIGHT_MAP;
respectively.

A rigid tire model (based on the ChRigidTire) template is exactly what 
the name implies: a rigid contact shape (default a cylinder, but you 
could also use a mesh) that is attached to the wheel body.  The "tire 
forces" in that case are just the frictional contact forces that are 
calculated by the underlying Chrono contact processing.  This of course 
does not capture the true tire dynamics (since real tire forces develop 
as consequence of tire deformation).   On the other hand, the Fiala tire 
model and its sibling, the Pacejka tire model, are empirical tire models 
that evaluate the tire forces (in the tangential contact plane) based on 
a set of heuristic parameters (6 for Fiala, more than 100 for Pacejka) 
which are usually obtained experimentally for a particular tire.   These 
models are widely used in vehicle dynamics, but have their own 
limitations: their range of applicability is relatively restricted to 
mostly flat (and rigid) terrain.  One alternative offered in Chrono is 
that of using a finite-element-based deformable tire, for example 
ChANCFTire (note that you must also enable the Chrono::FEA module to get
symbol: Re: [chrono] variable height terrain as road for chrono vehicle

text:
mostly flat (and rigid) terrain.  One alternative offered in Chrono is 
that of using a finite-element-based deformable tire, for example 
ChANCFTire (note that you must also enable the Chrono::FEA module to get 
that option).  Of course, there is no free lunch:  such an FEA-based 
tire is computationally expensive (as they require use of an implicit 
integrator, such as HHT, and of a smaller integration step-size).

Here are some references to some more information on these tire models:

  * For the Fiala tire model: http://sbel.wisc.edu/documents/TR-2015-13.pdf
  * For the Pacejka tire model:
    http://sbel.wisc.edu/documents/Justin_TR2014-16.pdf
  * For the ANCF deformable tire model:
    http://sbel.wisc.edu/documents/TR-2016-07.pdf

and the references therein.

--Radu

Hi Chaitanya,

Indeed, you should use a rigid terrain represented either through a mesh 
or through a height-map (the latter actually also constructs a 
triangular mesh under the hood).  You are correct in that I have not yet 
implemented the GetHeight() and GetNormal() for these types of 
terrain.   That is an issue only if you use certain types of tires 
(Fiala, Lugre, and Pacjeka) which do interrogate the terrain for that 
information.   If you use rigid tires or any of the FEA-based tires, 
height and normal information is not used (as the tire-terrain 
interaction is done through the underlying Chrono contact processing).

Having said that, I will look into completing the implementation of the 
rigid mesh-based terrain models .

Note that you can also create a non-flat terrain of SCM type, which is 
our implementation of the Soil Contact Model from DLR (Krenn & 
Hirzinger).  See chrono::vehicle::DeformableTerrain (I actually plan on 
changing the name of this class to something more informative, most 
likely SCMDeformableTerrain).   Like the rigid terrain, a terrain of 
this type can also be initialized from a triangular mesh or from a 
height-map.   Note that you can only use rigid tires or deformable (FEA) 
tires in conjunction with this type of terrain.

Best,
--Radu

Jose,

You can search online on how to see/set/modify environment variables in 
Windows.  For example:
https://superuser.com/questions/949560/how-do-i-set-system-environment-variables-in-windows-10

To use the Chrono::Python module, the path to the location of its *.pyd 
files must be appended to the PYTHONPATH environment variable which is 
used by python to find optional modules to be imported (such as the 
Chrono ones).  See:
https://docs.python.org/2/using/cmdline.html#envvar-PYTHONPATH

First, check if PYTHONPATH is defined.  If it exists, check that it 
contains the path to that 'ChronoPyEngine' folder and if it doesn't, 
append the path to the 'ChronoPyEngine' folder. If you do not see such 
an environment variable, create PYTHONPATH as a new environment variable 
and set it to the path to the 'ChronoPyEngine' folder.

Let us know if this fixes your problem,
--Radu

Hi Jose,

This is likely due to a missing PYTHONPATH environment variable.   
During CMake configuration, if the Chrono::Python module is enabled, we 
print a message with instructions on how to set/append to PYTHONPATH.  
That message is copied here:

To have access to the Chrono::Python wrapper modules, after building and 
(optionally) installing,
append one of the following to the PYTHONPATH environment variable:
      For the modules in the BUILD tree: 
C:/Users/Radu/Repositories/BUILD/chrono/bin/$(Configuration)

      For the modules in the INSTALL tree: 
C:/Users/Radu/Repositories/INSTALL/bin

Above, $(Configuration) represents the current build configuration 
(Release, Debug, RelWithDebInfo, etc)

Please let us know if this resolves the issue.

--Radu

Marcel is correct.  When running a Chrono-based program from a location other than where the distribution demos are, you must point to the correct path for the various data files.

Assuming you use the CMake Chrono project configuration script to link to the Chrono libraries either in a build directory or an install directory, you have access to a CMake variable (CHRONO_DATA_DIR) which contains the relevant information.   You must ensure this variable can be used from within your C++ code and then make a call such as
    SetChronoDataPath(CHRONO_DATA_DIR);
At the top of your main function.

See the example in the template_project<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/tree/develop/template_project> and look at how (1) the CMake variable is used in CMakeLists.txt to define a C++ macro and (2) how that is used in the call to SetChronoDataPath in my_example.cpp.

--Radu

Date: Thu, 30 Jun 2022 08:47:38 +0000

Marcel is correct.  When running a Chrono-based program from a location other than where the distribution demos are, you must point to the correct path for the various data files.

Assuming you use the CMake Chrono project configuration script to link to the Chrono libraries either in a build directory or an install directory, you have access to a CMake variable (CHRONO_DATA_DIR) which contains the relevant information.   You must ensure this variable can be used from within your C++ code and then make a call such as
    SetChronoDataPath(CHRONO_DATA_DIR);
At the top of your main function.

See the example in the template_project<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/tree/develop/template_project> and look at how (1) the CMake variable is used in CMakeLists.txt to define a C++ macro and (2) how that is used in the call to SetChronoDataPath in my_example.cpp.

--Radu

From: Marcel Offermans
Date: Thu, 30 Jun 2022 00:19:46 -0700 (PDT)

The obvious answer is that it is probably looking in the wrong place. That 
said, working out what the "current directory" is when running an 
executable can be a bit tricky depending on how you run it. So if you've 
built and executable for this demo, go to a command line and:

   1. Change directory to the folder where the executable lives.
   2. Make sure that from that folder, if you go one folder up, you see 
   your "data" directory (and it actually contains the files you need to run 
   this demo).
   3. Run the demo. It should now find the files.

Now if you're running inside the IDE (Visual Studio or whatever you are 
using) you can set this current directory to be whatever you want. What I 
have done to make my life a bit easier, is to add a few lines of code to 
the start of the main() of such demos that will print this directory:

// Output the current directory, just to make sure we understand where 
we're running.
#define PATH_MAX 1024
char buff[PATH_MAX];
_getcwd(buff, PATH_MAX);
std::string current_working_dir(buff);
GetLog() << "Working dir = " << current_working_dir << "\n\n";

Another thing that might help you is to explicitly set the data path. This 
was mentioned on the forum before, and you can do it somewhat like this 
(also do this at the start of main()):

// This can be used to point to different data paths (for core and vehicle 
modules):
chrono::SetChronoDataPath("../data/");
vehicle::SetDataPath("../data/vehicle/");

Hope this helps!

Sorry, there's currently no demo for using the FEA deformable terrain.  We mostly use granular terrain or the more expeditious SCM terrain for our deformable terrain simulations.

Hi Jaroslav,

no, it is not a ramp like in the picture, it is just a linear function 
y=C*x + D.

So, it is just an inclined line passing at height D for x=0, and with 
inclination C .

In the docs, D is called y0, and  C is called speed, hence also    y = 
y0 + x * speed

Note, if you want the zigzag ramp of your picture you need the 
ChFunction_sequence class, grouping a constant, a ramp, a constant. See 
demo_CH_functions.cpp

Alessandro Tasora

From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Wed, 26 Jul 2017 08:24:49 +0200

Hello Niels,

- there is no "automatic" tuning of the time step at the moment,  you
should provide a proper one at the beginning,

- you might compute a bound on dt using the CFL  condition,  as you said,
if using finite elements only (enable chrono FEA unit, and MKL or MUMPS
solvers - suggested) But adding constrained rigid bodies,  and contacts
maybe,  make things more complicate.

- the default timestepper with ChSystemNSC (ie with non smooth contact
formulation) is very stable and robust because it behaves like an implicit
solver: in my simulations I rarely had to go below dt=0.001s; for robotics
often 0.01s is good enough; but keep in mind that if you use FEA and you
want also contacts, at the moment you can't use ChSystemNSC and you must
use ChSystemSMC,  ie penalty for contacts, which requires shorter time
steps.  Something that requires hand tuning of dt.

Regards

Alessandro Tasora

In the scenario we are modeling (with minimal fidelity) screwing and 
unscrewing of threaded pipes.  The pipes are screwed together with high 
torque and are effectively locked together until a sufficient anti-torque 
is applied and the lock is broken and the pipes can be unscrewed.

I have a link engine for pipe A that is LinkLockLocked to pipe B which is 
effectively fixed.  We are accumulating torque on PipeA until the torque is 
sufficient to break the joint and the LinkLockLock is disabled.  At this 
point, pipe A has a response such that it is accelerated to 360 rad/s in 
the next time step.

In reality the response is damped by energy losses in breaking the joint 
and by reaction forces from the engine that quickly dissipate the 
reaction.  We tried applying an equivalent external torque opposite to the 
reaction torque, expecting that the sum of the two would result in a 
negligible response but we still observed a large angular acceleration in 
the first time step after the LLL was disabled.  

Next I am going to try reducing dt to a very small timestep to see if we 
can dissipate this reaction torque with opposing external torques in a few 
steps.  But basically, I know the response is damped and I am looking for 
the simplest way to nullify to response and zero the reaction torque.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Clear reaction force/torque on a link
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Sat, 12 Aug 2017 15:02:05 +0200

Dear Stewart,

can you explain more in detail the issue? I mean, why should you force 
reactions to be zero?

In general, reaction forces and torques in ChLink (and sub classes) are 
read-only, because they are computed during DoStepDynamics() or similar 
calls, where they are computed as lagrangian multipliers and 
automatically stored in each ChLink.

Alessandro

Dan

From: Rainer Gericke
Date: Thu, 15 Jun 2017 23:47:29 -0700 (PDT)

There are three steps to do:
1) configure a build directory with cmake
2) build all the programs and libraries
3) install the build to some place in the filesystem

If you never used cmake it is important to mention, that cmake can be used 
with a gui or as a 'normal' command line tool. For a beginner it is better 
to use the gui one. You can start it with the finder. Look at the 
installation guide of the chrono project. You can see cmake in actions, 
well it is the windows version but the Mac version looks more or less 
identical. I suggest to start just with the basic chrono modul and get this 
runnable. Later you can try to configure chrono with additional modules.

Good Luck

Rainer

Date: Mon, 02 Oct 2017 10:03:11 +0200

Michael,

Indeed, the simulations rendered in the animations you linked to used 
the SMC (i.e., smooth, penalty-based) contact method and the contact 
material was defined through those 4 coefficients.

Having said that, these codes use co-simulation, so both the SMC and NSC 
(non-smooth, complementarity-based) contact methods are supported on the 
terrain side. Moreover, when using SMC, the contact materials can 
optionally be defined through material properties (Young's modulus, 
Poisson ration, etc.). All these options are available through methods 
of the TerrainNode class.

Here's a link to a paper describing the full vehicle co-simulation 
framework: http://preview.tinyurl.com/yaglls87. It includes a discussion 
on using NSC for the terrain subsystem.

--Radu

text:
Subject: Chrono API changes
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 3 May 2017 12:09:40 +0200

Dear Chrono users,

The latest pushes to the main Chrono GitHub repository ('develop' 
branch) include several changes that affect the public API.  While every 
single program that uses Chrono will be affected, in most cases the 
required changes are pretty straightforward.

The main reason for these changes was to use more appropriate names and 
acronyms to refer to the two contact formulations available in Chrono 
and to provide a more consistent way of using them.  The new naming 
scheme uses the dichotomy:

  * non-smooth contact (NSC)
    aka "rigid contact", "complementarity-based"
    previously identified with "DVI" (from the typical mathematical
    model in this formulation)

  * smooth contact (SMC)
    aka "soft contact", "penalty-based"
    previously identified with "DEM" (a misnomer)

These new acronyms are used as postfixes for several Chrono classes 
(e.g., ChSystemNSC/ChSystemSMC, 
ChMaterialSurfaceNSC/ChMaterialSurfaceSMC, 
ChContactContainerNSC/ChContactContainerSMC, etc.), as well as in 
corresponding enums.

See below for a summary list of all changes.  Please post on the forum 
any issues or questions related to this.

Thanks,
Radu


-----------------------------------
Contact-method related name changes
-----------------------------------

- use NSC (non-smooth contact) and SMC (smooth contact) to differentiate 
between the two contact formulations in Chrono
- NSC replaces DVI and refers to "rigid contact" or 
"complementarity-based" formulation, typically resulting in a DVI problem
symbol: Chrono API changes

text:
between the two contact formulations in Chrono
- NSC replaces DVI and refers to "rigid contact" or 
"complementarity-based" formulation, typically resulting in a DVI problem
- SMC replaces DEM and refers to "soft contact" or "penalty-based" 
formulation, typically resulting in an ODE problem

(1) Main Chrono API changes
   - renamed base classes:
       ChMaterialSurfaceBase -> ChMaterialSurface
       ChContactContainerBase -> ChContactContainer
       ChProximityContainerBase -> ChProximityContainer
   - enums ChMaterialSurface::ContactMethod are now NSC (replaces DVI) 
and SMC (replaces DEM)
   - ChSystem is now an abstract base class which cannot be instantiated.
     Use either ChSystemNSC (replaces ChSystem) or ChSystemSMC (replaces 
ChSystemDEM).
   - the two corresponding types of contact containers are now 
ChContactContainerNSC (replaces ChContactContainerDVI)
     and ChContactContainerSMC (replaces ChContactContainerDEM)
   - the two types of contact material surfaces are ChMaterialSurfaceNSC 
(replaces ChMaterialSurface)
     and ChMaterialSurfaceSMC (replaces ChMaterialSurfaceDEM)
   - the two types for composite contact materials (i.e., material 
properties for a pair of contacting shapes)
     are now ChMaterialCompositeNSC (replaces ChMaterialCouple) and 
ChMaterialCompositeSMC (replaces ChCompositeMaterialDEM)

(2) Main ChronoParallel API changes:
   - in ChronoParallel, use either ChSystemParallelNSC (replaces 
ChSystemParallelDVI)
     or ChSystemParallelSMC (replaces ChSystemParallelDEM)
   - ChSystemParallelNSC and ChSystemParallelSMC do not have an optional
symbol: Chrono API changes

text:
ChSystemParallelDVI)
     or ChSystemParallelSMC (replaces ChSystemParallelDEM)
   - ChSystemParallelNSC and ChSystemParallelSMC do not have an optional 
argument anymore
   - the ChronoParallel enums SystemType are now SYSTEM_NSC and SYSTEM_SMC


-----------------------------------------------
Contact- and collision-related callback objects
-----------------------------------------------

(1) Refactor callback objects for consistency
   - all callback base classes are nested under an appropriate Chrono 
class (e.g., ChSystem, ChContactContainerBase, etc.)
   - callback classes do not have the 'Ch' prefix
   - a callback base class FooCallback has a pure virtual method with 
name 'OnFoo'
   - use methods named 'RegisterFooCallback' to specify a callback 
object of type FooCallback
   - ensure that all callback base classes define a virtual destructor

(2) Main API changes (list of callbacks)
   - ChSystem::CustomCollisionCallback (to allow adding additional 
collisions generated externally)
   - ChContactContainerBase::AddContactCallback (to allow modifying the 
composite material as contact pairs are added)
   - ChContactContainerBase::ReportContactCallback (to allow reporting 
or post-processing of contact information)
   - ChProximityContainerBase::AddProximityCallback (to allow processing 
proximity pairs as they are added)
   - ChProximityContainerBase::ReportProximityCallback (to allow 
reporting or post-processing of proximity pairs)
   - ChCollisionSystem::BroadphaseCallback (to allow processing of 'near 
enough' collision shapes as they are found in broadphase)
   - ChCollisionSystem::NarrowphaseCallback (to allow processing of
symbol: Chrono API changes

text:
- ChCollisionSystem::BroadphaseCallback (to allow processing of 'near 
enough' collision shapes as they are found in broadphase)
   - ChCollisionSystem::NarrowphaseCallback (to allow processing of 
geometric collision pairs as they are found in narrowphase)

(3) ChContactContainerBase::AddContactCallback was refactored to allow 
its use for both NSC and SMC contacts
   - an (optional) user-provided callback object of this type is now 
registered with the underlying contact container,
     and not with the Chrono system (as previously done)
   - its OnAddContact() method takes the composite material as a const 
pointer to a ChMaterialComposite object (base type)
   - the properties of the provided composite material can be changed
   - an override of OnAddContact() in a derived, concrete class must 
first downcast the provided pointer to the appropriate type:

Dear Ram,

sure, this is possible in Chrono.

First of all, you should NOT use the ChBodyEasy.... classes (like 
ChBodyEasyBox, ChBoedyEasySphere etc.) because they are limited to a 
single shape per body, as their names say. These are useful for quick 
creation of collision shapes + visualization shapes in a single shot, in 
fact this is the preferred way for examples showing collision, in the 
src/demos/ directory.

For your needs, you should use the ChBody class or the ChBodyAuxRef 
class (the latter if you want the reference to be in a different 
position respect to th COG). These classes define a body without any 
visualization and without any collision shape, so it is up to you to 
populate both the visualization shape(s) and the collision shape(s).

Note that there is no need to use an analogue to btCompoundShape as in 
Bullet, because a compound is automatically created in the guts of 
Chrono if you add more than a single collision shape to a singleChBody.

The steps are the folowing:

- you call mybody->GetCollisionModel()->ClearModel();

- you call N times the functions that populate the collision compound, 
as mybody->GetCollisionModel()->AddBox(...), 
mybody->GetCollisionModel()->AddSphere(...) etc. .. Look at the 
ChCollisionModel.h file for other functions.

- you complete the compound using mybody->GetCollisionModel()->BuildModel();

This is an example:

     fork = std::make_shared<*ChBody*>();
         app->GetSystem()->Add(fork);
         fork->SetPos(COG_fork);

Subject: Re: [chrono] General questions about Chrono
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 14 Feb 2018 12:46:37 +0100

Hi Davide,

Sorry for the late reply.

 1. Yes, you can have multiple Chrono instances in the same executable.
    An example of this are the co-simulation codes you can find in the
    Github chrono-projects repository
    (https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono-projects). Look for example
    in projects/cosimulation/test_HMMWV_cosimulation. That MPI program
    actually uses 6 instances of Chrono, one for simulating a vehicle,
    four using Chrono::FEA to independently simulate FEA-based tires,
    and one using Chrono::Parallel to simulate the granular terrain.

 2. Currently, there is only very limited support for check-pointing.
    All we implemented so far is in the functions
    chrono::utils::WriteCheckpoint and chrono::utils::ReadCheckpoint (in
    ChUtilsInputOutput.{h,cpp}). These functions can be used to store
    and restore the state of bodies in a system (intermediated through a
    text file) and were used mostly with granular dynamics problems.
    Depending on what you need to do, this may or may not be enough.
    Indeed, I made several simplifying assumptions in implementing those
    functions, including the assumption that collision shapes match
    visualization shapes. Moreover, only a subset of shape types are
    considered. Note also that only body states are stored so the
    system cannot include any other type of elements with internal state.

 3. Chrono::Parallel should be deterministic, except maybe for
    simulations that rely on particle generation utilities which use
symbol: Re: [chrono] General questions about Chrono

text:
3. Chrono::Parallel should be deterministic, except maybe for
    simulations that rely on particle generation utilities which use
    randomization.  There are two sets of such utilities, one under the
    chrono::particlefactory namespace (in src/chrono/particlefactory/),
    and the other under the chrono::utils namespace (in
    ChUtilsGenerators.{h,cpp} and ChUtilsSamplers.h).

I hope this answers your questions.
--Radu

This is the workflow:

- I use the SolidWorks 2014  CAD for generating the model, with parts 
and constraints

- I save the model into a .py file using Chrono::SolidWorks 
<http://api.chrono.projectchrono.org/introduction_chrono_solidworks.html>

- I load the .py file in a Python program using Chrono::PyEngine 
<http://api.chrono.projectchrono.org/introduction_chrono_pyengine.html>

- I add additional constraints, actuators and motion functions 
programmatically, using the Chrono API (from the Python side)

Note that I could obtain the same result by using C++ instead of Python; 
here I used Python for simplicity.

Look at this tutorial 
<http://api.chrono.projectchrono.org/tutorial_chrono_pyengine_demo_spider_robot.html> 
for the source code and for the CAD model.


NOTE: if you want to do this at home, you need the latest beta versions 
of the add-in and the Python wrapper, you can download the new 
installers here:

<http://www.projectchrono.org/assets/installers/ChronoEngine_SolidWorks_v2.07.exe>

Subject: Energy conservation and numerical dissipation
From: David Marten
Date: Wed, 4 Oct 2017 07:42:42 -0700 (PDT)

Hi all,

I have a question regarding the conservation of energy during time stepping 
simulations within CHRONO's FEA module. 

I set a structure to rotate using a 3D applied torque onto some nodes. 
After I remove the torque I observe that the rotation rate slows down. 
There is no physical damping within the model and no external 
forces/moments or gravity are applied.

The decay of the rotation rate seems to be changing with the time-step 
size, for smaller time steps there is less decay. I have also tried 
different time integrators but the rotation rate always decays.

How can I perform simulations for which the rotational momentum is 
conserved? I guess that some of it gets lost due to numerical dissipation, 
but is there a fix or workaround besides changing to uneconomically small 
time step sizes?

Thanks and regards,

David

From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Sun, 8 Oct 2017 10:44:54 +0200

Dear Rashnith

Chrono is unit-less. You can use whatever unit system you prefer 
(metric, imperial, etc.), although I suggest you to use the ISO SI 
international metric system, formerly known as MKS:

L (lenghts) :     meters [m]

M (masses):    kilograms [kg]

T (time):           seconds [s]

Other units are derived and follows naturally, ex. density is [kg/m^3], 
moment of inertia [kg m^2] etc

Anyway you can use other systems, just check that the values are 
coherent, ex. if you pick millimeters [mm] as lengths and grams [g] for 
masses (something that I'd suggest if you want to simulate very small 
objects like mechanical wrist watches, in order to have the CPU working 
on small numbers for better numerical precision) so the density must be 
input as [g/mm^3] values, etc.

have a nice day

Alessandro Tasora

Actually, I will try to explain how I calculated void ratio/density of settled specimen in here, so hopefully more people can benefit from it.In case it's unclear I am still willing to offer my help through skype or you can ask any question you have under this thread.Below, I explained how to calculated the void ratio and density of specimen with free surface poured into the container. In case the surface is not free (e. g. in your simulation you placed a plate on the sample of granular material) the way of calculating the density and the void ration is different.Anyway - for the specimen with free surface: First of all - I poured granular material to the container - so it's surface was not flat.Density of the specimen is equal to (mass of all the particles) / (volume of the settled sample)(volume of the settled sample) = (area of container's cross-section) * (height of highest particle)Void ratio = (volume of voids) / (volume of solids)(volume of voids) = (volume of the settled specimen) - (volume of solids)Since the surface was not flat - there are additional void spaces right at the surface of the settled specimen!!So, basically what I did was calculating void ratios and densities for specimen without taking into account a couple of top layers of the specimen (I noticed that void ratio/density started having constant values (they converged) when I didn't take into account two or three layers of the settled specimen).By first layer of particles I meant particles which are at the height between: [(height of the top particle),  (height of the top particle) - 1 * (particle diameter)]Second layer: [(height of the top particle) - 1 * (particle diameter),  (height of the top particle) - 2 * (particle diameter)]Third layer: [(height of the top particle) - 2 * (particle diameter),  (height of the top particle) - 3 * (particle diameter)]Note that when you don't take into account certain number of layer you should also decrease the values of (volume of the settled specimen), (volume of solids) and (volume of voids)I hope that the explanation above is clear.Regards,MKOd: mk_ma@interia.plDo: "Karl Tam" <karl.tam2013@gmail.com>; Wysłane: 23:19 Czwartek 2017-08-10Temat: Re: [chrono] Finding void ratio/density of packed particlesHi Karl,It's Michal at this end. text:
Hi Karl,
There is no tool to do this directly. It will require a small post-processing step, say in Python or something like this. Alternatively, you can have it in the Chrono model you set up, it’ll call
 for some data processing based on results at the end of the simulation.
That being said, you have access to the position of each body in the system.

Say you drop the bodies in a bucket. Then you approximate (based on the z-position of the bodies) the volume occupied by the bodies. Also, you know the number N of bodies in the bucket and their
 dimension. Thus, you’ll be able to compute the spatial volume occupied by the N bodies (call is N_S), and the sum of the volumes of the N bodies (call it N_B). I believe what you are interested in is N_B/N_S.
 
For an example of a test where we compute void ratios, see this tech report:
http://sbel.wisc.edu/documents/TR-2016-16.pdf

The files we used to do the cone penetration test are attached here (code generate by lab student Michal Kwarta). Perhaphs they’re helpful.
 
BTW, there are more tech reports that might be of interest here:
http://sbel.wisc.edu/Publications/

 
I hope this helps a bit. Good luck.
Cheers,
 
Dan
