Hi Karl,
There is no tool to do this directly. It will require a small post-processing step, say in Python or something like this. Alternatively, you can have it in the Chrono model you set up, it’ll call for some data processing based on results at the end of the simulation.
That being said, you have access to the position of each body in the system.
Say you drop the bodies in a bucket. Then you approximate (based on the z-position of the bodies) the volume occupied by the bodies. Also, you know the number N of bodies in the bucket and their dimension. Thus, you’ll be able to compute the spatial volume occupied by the N bodies (call is N_S), and the sum of the volumes of the N bodies (call it N_B). I believe what you are interested in is N_B/N_S.

For an example of a test where we compute void ratios, see this tech report:
http://sbel.wisc.edu/documents/TR-2016-16.pdf
The files we used to do the cone penetration test are attached here (code generate by lab student Michal Kwarta). Perhaphs they’re helpful.

BTW, there are more tech reports that might be of interest here:
http://sbel.wisc.edu/Publications/

I hope this helps a bit. Good luck.
Cheers,

Dan

Subject: Re: [chrono] Cascade module
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 3 Nov 2016 18:58:17 +0100

Hi Leonardo,

I know that following my advice from personal emails you finally fixed 
the problem, by explicitly appending the path to the includes of 
OpenCascade, for example on my laptop it is:

     INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES(${CHRONO_INCLUDE_DIRS})
INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES("D:\OpenCASCADE6.9.0\opencascade-6.9.0\inc")

But this was a quick fix, the blue line should not even be there. Now I 
examined the problem in detail, andI understood that there was a missing 
part in chrono/cmake/ChronoConfig.cmake.in , and the CHRONO_INCLUDE_DIRS 
never contained the path to the includes of OpenCascade.

Therefore *I made a change* to the ChronoConfig.cmake.in and I just 
submitted it to the GIThub.
Thanks to this modification, you should not need to use the additional  
INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES("...") trick above, because when you use

     INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES(${CHRONO_INCLUDE_DIRS})

in your CmakeLists.txt, now this is sufficient as the 
CHRONO_INCLUDE_DIRS should automatically get the path of OpenCascade 
directories, appended.
The same for CHRONO_LIBRARIES, that automatically contains Cascade 
libraries too, when you use

     TARGET_LINK_LIBRARIES(myexe ${CHRONO_LIBRARIES})

Give a try and tell me if this is ok (pull from GIThub and rebuild the 
Chrono solution, and to be safe, maybe you should delete the Cmake cache 
of your project)


Last note: remember that, unless you put the binaries (dlls) of 
OpenCascade in your PATH, you must at least copy those dlls in the same 
directory of your exe, otherwise it won't find them at runtime.

Subject: Re: Problem about SetRestitution and SetFriction
From: Dario Mangoni
Date: Thu, 16 Mar 2017 02:10:35 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Bowen,
the f in this case is a (floating-point) literal suffix. It's not a 
Chrono-related expression: it is a pure C/C++ expression! You can find a 
description of literals and their suffixes here: 
http://www.cplusplus.com/doc/tutorial/constants/
In short, the suffix just tells the compiler that the numbers that you are 
passing to SetRestitution() and SetFriction() are of float type. Otherwise 
the compiler would consider 0.1 and 0.4 - as well as any other decimal 
and/or exponential number literal - of double type (that's the C++ default).
IMHO, it's just a matter of good programming practice. The code *generally* 
works even without them. And in this specific case I'm sure it does.
However, for sake of completeness, please notice that there are some cases 
where their use can avoid unpleasant and unexpected/hard-to-track 
behaviours 
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/7662109/should-we-generally-use-float-literals-for-floats-instead-of-the-simpler-double

I'll let more expert users to comment on this, if I'm wrong!

Dario

Subject: Re: Pacejka Tire Model
From: Mike Taylor
Date: Thu, 15 Jun 2017 07:52:14 -0700 (PDT)

Rainer,

The Pacejka tire code was written by a previous lab member.  From what I 
could tell digging into it, the combined slip terms are always calculated 
and all of the Pacejka parameters are expected in the file in the correct 
order.  So that means you need values for all of the coefficients every 
time.

This means that if you do not have some of the coefficients, you can still 
use the code, but some extra preparation is required.  You will need to 
find the definition for the PAC2002 equations which will explain how each 
coefficient is used.  For the coefficients that you are missing, you'll 
need to determine how to ignore its effects.  For example, if it's a 
scaling factor, you might set it to 1 or if it was a curve shift the you 
could set it to 0.  The exact values to ignore those terms will have to be 
set uniquely for each coefficient.

Hopefully that helps,

Mike

same for the three axes, so I wonder why you have this result. But I 
have some ideas on the possible causes:

- 1000 rpm is a high value: it requires very small time steps. As a rule 
of thumb, you need at least 50 time steps per each revolution, to be on 
the safe side. Therefore I would not expect precise results with time 
steps larger than 1e-3 [s], regardless of other sources of error.

- you write that you use a ChLinkEngine: is it working in 'impose speed' 
mode? If so, for a _constant _angular velocity (and: for shaft centered 
in cube COG or in absence of gravity), this would need _zero_ torque 
during all the simulation. Given unavoidable numerical errors, it would 
not be exactly zero, I mean: almost zero, i.e. a noisy value of torque 
that oscillates about zero (and, for the very high value of Ixx Iyy Izz 
mentioned here, this fluctuating error could be high)

Note: the ChLinkEngine is obsolete. If you use the "develop" branch, 
instead of the "3.0.0" master branch, now the preferred way to create 
motors is the following: use the ChLinkMotor sub classes 
(ChLinkMotorRotationSpeed, ChLinkMotorRotationAngle, 
ChLinkMotorRotationTorque, etc.) See this link for more info:

http://api.projectchrono.org/development/motors.html

Finally: if you cannot figure out the source of problems, send me the

Subject: Re: [chrono] Chrono test_VEH_tireRig simulation
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 14 Feb 2018 11:46:17 +0100

A simple rig that would allow you to do that could be constructed using 
two additional bodies + the wheel and the following joints (assuming a 
reference frame with X forward and Z up):

  * prismatic joint between ground and bodyA with the translational DOF
    in the global X direction
  * prismatic joint between bodyA and bodyB with the translational DOF
    in the global Z direction
  * revolute joint between bodyB and the wheel body with the rotational
    DOF in the global Y direction

bodyB would act as the "quarter chassis" so set its mass to control 
vertical load on the tire.

In order to enforce different values of the longitudinal slip, you will 
need to use actuators to enforce a constant linear speed in X direction 
for bodyA and a corresponding constant angular velocity of the wheel 
with respect to bodyB. You could do this by replacing the first 
prismatic joint with a ChLinkMotorLinearSpeed between ground and bodyA 
(and set its "speed function" to a ChFunction_Const that returns the 
desired forward speed) and replace the revolute joint with a 
ChLinkMotorRotationSpeed (and set its "speed function" to a 
ChFunction_Const that returns the desired angular speed). In other 
words, use:

  * ChLinkMotorLinearSpeed between ground and bodyA
  * ChLinkLockPrismatic between bodyA and bodyB
  * ChLinkMotorRotationSpeed between bodyB and the wheel body

--Radu

Subject: API change to Chrono::Vehicle
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 20 Dec 2016 12:37:01 +0100

A quick note to the users of Chrono::Vehicle.

I just pushed to the develop branch a set of changes to allow specifying 
a full inertia tensor for the chassis rigid body (previously, only 
moments of inertia could be specified; in other words, it was implied 
that the chassis reference frame was aligned with the chassis principal 
axes).

Note that the (3x3 symmetric) inertia matrix must represent the inertia 
tensor with respect to a centroidal frame whose axes are aligned with 
the chassis body reference frame.  A new utility class 
(chrono::utils::CompositeInertia) can be used to calculate inertia 
properties of a composite body, by providing information on the 
centroidal frame, mass, and inertia of each sub-component (all relative 
to the body reference frame).  This utility class calculates the 
resulting COM location, total mass, and composite inertia tensor.

For a vehicle chassis specified through a JSON file, the format of the 
specification file has been changed to accept specifying one or more 
such sub-components (the current sample JSON files have been updated to 
reflect this change, although currently they all use a single component 
for the chassis composite).

Please let me know if you have any questions or comments about these 
changes.

Happy Holidays!
--Radu

Chris,

I just pushed a fix to this issue.  With this, the various install 
directories should be as follows:

*Windows*:
include headers:  ${prefix}/include
libraries: ${prefix}/lib64
runtime files: ${prefix}/bin    (this is for the Chrono DLLs)
data files: ${prefix}/data
demo executables: ${prefix}/bin

*Linux*:
include headers:  ${prefix}/include
libraries: ${prefix}/lib64
runtime files: ${prefix}/bin    (nothing should go there on Linux)
data files: ${prefix}/share/chrono/data
demo executables: ${prefix}/share/chrono/bin

Note that the Chrono demos are no longer installed under ${prefix}/bin/ 
on a Linux system (not an appropriate place for mere demos, especially 
if using the default installation target /usr/local/).

The project configuration scripts (ChronoConfig.cmake) were also fixed 
to properly reflect the new locations of the 'data' directory.

Please let me know if you see any other issues related to this.

Thanks,
Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Modelling cables with no bending stiffness
From: Antonio Martín Recuero
Date: Sat, 22 Apr 2017 13:13:03 -0400

Tristan,

The element ChElementBeamANCF does not seem appropriate for the modeling of
an element with no shear and little bending stiffness. With the
ChElementCableANCF
you may be able to set the cross section inertia to a small value such that
bending stiffness becomes very small. I think that the cross section of
this element is given by its diameter, which would not allow to separate
bending and axial behavior. However, you can go into this element's
implementation in ChElementCableANCF.h and reduce the area moment of
inertia I at will while leaving the axial behavior unchanged:

            ChMatrixNM<double, 12, 12> Kcurv;
            ChQuadrature::Integrate1D<ChMatrixNM<double, 12, 12> >(Kcurv,
 // result of integration will go there

 myformulaCurv,  // formula to integrate
                                                                   0,
       // start of x
                                                                   1,
       // end of x
                                                                   3
        // order of integration
                                                                   );
            Kcurv *= E * REDUCING_FACTOR* I * length;  // note Iyy should
be the same value (circular section assumption)

Best,
Antonio

text:
Subject: Modelling cables with no bending stiffness
From: Tristan de Lataillade
Date: Fri, 21 Apr 2017 03:27:37 -0700 (PDT)

Hi everyone,

I am trying to model cables with little or no bending stiffness in Chrono, 
allowing complete flexion of the cable while still having high axial 
stiffness.
Is there a way to model such behaviour with *ChElementCableANCF *and its 
*ChBeamSectionCable*?

It could be done with *ChElementBeamANCF* by setting the y and z components 
of the shear modulus to a very small value in *ChMaterialBeamANCF*, and 
ignoring the poisson effects with:
element->SetStrainFormulation(ChElementBeamANCF::StrainFormulation::
CMNoPoisson);

But the reason I would like to model it with the simpler element type 
ChElementCableANCF is that it seems to be more stable, particularly when 
collision detection is in play (where a simulation with a cable made with 
ChElementBeamANCF elements often breaks), and it can also be considerably 
faster to simulate. 

Cheers,

Tristan

In the field of multibody simulation, CHRONO 
<http://www.projectchrono.org> and MBDyn <https://www.mbdyn.org> 
represent two viable open-source solutions with a growing number of 
users. We aim at organizing a joint meeting where the users of both 
platforms could meet, exchange ideas, present their work, and learn from 
tutorials presented by expert lecturers.

It is not necessary to be proficient in Chrono or MBDyn to join this 
event: the meeting is informal and it is also open to new users that 
wish to learn from scratch one or both of these technologies; to this 
end there will be lessons and tutorials with hands-on sessions, lead by 
experienced teachers.

The meeting will also allocate some sessions for a mini-conference: 
participants are encouraged to prepare PowerPoint presentations, either 
to introduce themselves and to present their research activities in the 
field of computer simulation. This will be useful to present interesting 
applications of mechanical simulation (preferably using Chrono or MBDyn, 
but also other multibody software could be shown) and to stimulate 
exchange of ideas.

Go to the website for additional information on program and venue:
http://www.multibodymeeting.org

We wait you!

On behalf of the organizing committee

0.1m width and 0.1 m height. To ensure the stability of the simulation, I 
am using CFL condition.

For Young's modulus below 10^9 Pa, solver MINRES and integrator

displacement, although a numerical dissipation is observed.

For Young's modulus of 10^10 Pa, EULER_IMPLICIT_LINEARIZED overestimates

Dear Alan,

you are right about the documentation, we should add more pages to the 
manual in the web site. Currently one has to learn by looking at the 
demos/tutorials, or by reading the comments in the .h headers (or in 
Doxygen).

As you noticed, at least we strive to keep the .h comments as detailed 
as possible.

We will release a step-by-step tutorial for FEA in near future.

Speaking about cables:

1) you should look at demo_FEA_cables.cpp and demo_FEA_contacts.cpp  for 
two examples

2) if you are interested in 'twisting' you could use also the 
ChElementBeamEuler instead of ChElementBeamANCF (and the cpu speed is 
about the same)

3) collision between cables or cables & other shapes is posible, but for 
the moment only using penalty approaches, i.e. using the DEM contact 
model instead than the DVI contact (DVI would be faster and more 
stable). Also, both the ChElementBeamANCF and the ChElementBeamEuler  
would be approximated with sequences of spheres (not a big problem for 
cables, as they are circular in section) Have a look at  
demo_FEA_contacts.cpp.

4) When possible, for FEA, use the MKL module, so that you can use the 
MKL solver. This because with cables you might have large mass ratios in 
your systems, and the MINRES solver would converge too slowly. Btw. MKL 
is licensed, by Intel, but it is free for students etc.

Also:

- you asked about ChNonlinearSolver.. this is an obsolete part of the
symbol:

 suitability for structural analysis

text:
Also:

- you asked about ChNonlinearSolver.. this is an obsolete part of the 
code that might be removed or rewritten. Not used anyway

- you asked about ChSystem::DoStaticNonlinear : this performs a static 
nonlinear analysis by linearly increasing the applied loads in first N 
steps, then it continues in the last steps with the same load, up to 
when the Newton Raphson iteration converges or up to the max defined 
number of steps. These parameters can be set in function's arguments. 
Note, the initial 'ramp' of the applied loads helps when dealing with 
very large nonlinearities that could diverge. During the iteration it 
uses the tangent stiffess matrix as a jacobian in the Newton method, and 
the residual is the difference beteen internal FE forces and external 
applied loads. This must be used only with FEA problems, with properly 
defined constraints - although it could converge also in case of 
redundant constraints, but it would diverge if the system is 
underconstrained.

regards,

Alessandro

Windows. One way might be to download the source code for Python and build 
it using the same compiler that you will eventually use to compile your 
Chrono environment.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Assigning surface properties using DEM
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 21 Jun 2017 17:57:31 +0200

Hi Soowon,

The problem we are faced with here is that all these (coefficient of 
friction, coefficient of restitution, etc.) are really properties of the 
interaction between a pair of materials and not properties of a single 
material.    One possible solution would be to keep a database of all 
sorts of combinations (e.g., glass-steel, wood-concrete, etc).  But that 
is not a scalable and flexible enough alternative (we don't want to 
limit you to a fixed-size database of materials).  So we decided to keep 
these properties defined for a single material which works just fine as 
long as contacts involve bodies of similar materials.  But when dealing 
with contact between bodies of dissimilar materials we then need to 
provide a "combination law".  The ones you mention below are just simple 
defaults that we picked not as much from physical considerations, but 
rather for simplicity (as long as they are not completely unreasonable).

But we do know that there are better alternatives for calculating such 
composite properties.  This is precisely why I recently provided a 
callback mechanism through which the user can override these defaults to 
provide more theoretically sound combination formulas.  Look at the base 
class ChMaterialCompositionStrategy (defined in ChMaterialSurface.h) 
from which you can derive your own, overriding the combination law for 
any or all parameters; something like:

class CustomCompositionStrategy : public 
ChMaterialCompositionStrategy<float> {

Subject: Re: [chrono] Assigning surface properties using DEM
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 3 May 2017 12:57:07 +0200

Hi Soowon,

When using the smooth contact formulation (ie., a penalty approach), you 
have the option of selecting how the contact "spring" and "damping" 
coefficients are calculated internally. There are two options:

 1. Calculate these from physical material properties (Young's modulus,
    Poisson ratio, coefficient of restitution) using various
    constitutive laws
 2. Directly use the values specified in ChMaterialSurfaceSMC (note the
    name change, see my message from earlier today about API changes)

This selection is global (meaning that all contact pairs are treated one 
way or the other in a given simulation) and is typically made at the 
time the ChSystemSMC (previously named ChSystemDEM) is constructed:

  * in Chrono, the constructor of  ChSystemSMC takes an optional first
    argument named 'use_material_properties' (default 'true')
  * in Chrono::Parallel, you change this setting by directly accessing
    the global "data manager", something like:
    ChSystemParallelSMC sys;
    sys.GetSettings()->solver.use_material_properties = false;

Note that, in both cases, the default is to infer the contact 
coefficients from the material properties (i.e., option 1 above).

Note also that a ChMaterialSurfaceSMC carries data that allows it to 
work in either mode (see its member variables in 
ChMaterialSurfaceSMC.h).   However, if option 1 above is being used, 
then the member variables kn, kt, gn, gt are ignored; similarly, if 
option 2 is being used, young_modulus, poisson_ratio, and restitution
symbol: Re: [chrono] Assigning surface properties using DEM

text:
ChMaterialSurfaceSMC.h).   However, if option 1 above is being used, 
then the member variables kn, kt, gn, gt are ignored; similarly, if 
option 2 is being used, young_modulus, poisson_ratio, and restitution 
are not used.

If you are interested in the actual implementation, look at 
ChMaterialCompositeSMC (in ChMaterialSurfaceSMC.cpp) to see how 
properties of the contact material of two contacting shapes are combined 
into a "composite" contact material and at ChContactSMC::CalculateForce 
(in ChContactSMC.h) to see how the properties of the composite material 
are used to generate the contact forces.

Hope that this helps,
--Radu

Subject: Re: kn, kt, gn, and gt in contact model
From: Luning Fang
Date: Tue, 14 Jun 2022 12:05:36 -0700 (PDT)

In Chrono, there are different contact force models, and the computation is 
different when you use material-based property (Young's modulus, CoR and 
Poisson ratio) or user-input values.

Hertz contact force model refers to the elastic component of the normal 
force, because Hertz assumes that contact area is circular, bodies in 
contact are elastic, using elasticity theory, he derives that contact force 
is proportional to the 1.5 power of penetration (delta in the code). When 
the model is applied to SMC, researchers need a way to dissipate energy 
during the contact. Quite a few models are developed over the years to 
model the dissipation part (see Table 3.1 in this book 
<https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-3-319-30897-5.pdf>).

In your screenshot, the first method is originally proposed by Tsuji 
<https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/003259109288030L>, the 
second one is from Silbert 
<https://journals.aps.org/pre/pdf/10.1103/PhysRevE.64.051302>. Both are 
highly cited paper that Chrono used as reference. The first one use sqrt of 
mass times stiffness, to mimic a critical damping scenario (recall for a 
one DOF mass-spring-damper system, critical damping ensures mass returns to 
equilibrium in the shortest amount of time) This is desired in SMC 
simulation. For the second model, my understanding is that, since the model 
does not call for CoR, they use mass*velocity to model the change in 
momentum during the impact. If you are interested in the constitutive law
symbol: Re: kn, kt, gn, and gt in contact model

text:
simulation. For the second model, my understanding is that, since the model 
does not call for CoR, they use mass*velocity to model the change in 
momentum during the impact. If you are interested in the constitutive law 
of contact force models, these two papers have a thorough review on normal 
<https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0032591006004360> and 
tangential 
<https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0009250907008767> force 
models.

Now on the implementation side of things.... In Chrono, when you initialize 
ChSystemSMC, the default is that material-based parameters are used. If you 
don't assign any material properties, this is what's being set as default:

ChMaterialSurfaceSMC::ChMaterialSurfaceSMC()
: ChMaterialSurface(),
young_modulus(2e5),
poisson_ratio(0.3f),
constant_adhesion(0),
adhesionMultDMT(0),
adhesionSPerko(0),
kn(2e5),
kt(2e5),
gn(40),
gt(20) {}

Since contact is between a pair of bodies, if you have different materials, 
some strategies are used to "combine" the properties.

  
  virtual float CombineStiffnessCoefficient(float a1, float a2) const { return (a1 + a2) 
/ 2; }
  
  virtual float CombineDampingCoefficient(float a1, float a2) const { return (a1 + a2) 
/ 2; }

In ChContactSMC.h, mat.gn and mat.gt is the value after coefficients are 
being "combined", which enters force calculation. When you use GetGt(), as 
an API, what's being returned is the gt of one type of material you set up 
as a user. If you've never assigned gt to the material, the default is 20. 
Of course, you have the freedom to modify the "combine strategy" however

text:
an API, what's being returned is the gt of one type of material you set up 
as a user. If you've never assigned gt to the material, the default is 20. 
Of course, you have the freedom to modify the "combine strategy" however 
you want.

Thank you,
Luning

Subject: Re: [chrono] Chrono Vehicles Additional models
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 12 Dec 2016 11:16:17 +0100

Hi Chaitanya,

Assuming that the necessary subsystem templates for your new vehicle 
already exist in Chrono::Vehicle, it is not all that difficult to model 
a new vehicle.  The challenge there is mostly related to obtaining the 
proper data (dimensions, locations of attachment points, mass and 
inertia properties, etc).  In such a case, you can model a new vehicle 
either by providing a set of JSON files or else by implementing concrete 
classes for each of the vehicle's subsystems.

An example of the first route is the set of JSON files for a 5-ton MAN 
truck which are provided in the Chrono data directory 
(data/vehicle/MAN_5t).

If you want to go the other way, you can look at how that is done for 
the vehicles currently provided in the Chrono vehicle models library 
(see src/chrono_models/generic/ and src/chrono_models/hmmwv/ for wheeled 
vehicle models).  The concrete classes required to completely specify a 
vehicle in this manner are very thin classes.

However, if you want to model a vehicle that uses a subsystem for which 
Chrono::Vehicle does not currently provide a template (e.g., some 
suspension type other than those currently available), then you would 
have to first implement the (abstract) classes that specify a 
parameterized model for that new subsystem type, and then the 
corresponding concrete classes for the particular vehicle you want to 
model.  This is a more complex task.

As for a vehicle with a trailer, we currently do not have a formal
symbol: Re: [chrono] Chrono Vehicles Additional models

text:
model.  This is a more complex task.

As for a vehicle with a trailer, we currently do not have a formal 
template for a trailer subsystem.  However, we provide an example 
(demo_VEH_ArticulatedVehicle) in which we define a custom class for such 
a trailer (which is attached to the chassis of a wheeled vehicle).

Best,
--Radu

When you installed the preinstalled binaries, did you select the GLEW, 
GLFW, and GLM dependency packages? They should install automatically by 
default in a 'typical' install but can be disabled. GL_INVALID_ENUM sounds 
like a weird versioning problem, but the prepackaged versions should work 
out-of-box. 

The baseline requirements for Chrono are compute capability 2.0 or newer 
and an x86_64 or amd64 processor. If a newer processor is present that has 
AVX or SSE, Chrono will automatically detect its availability during the 
build process and include it as available. The installer doesn't check for 
these libraries, but the precompiled binaries shouldn't depend on them. In 
that case, an AVX unit test would fail, but GL wouldn't experience any 
problems. 

TL;DR: Chrono shouldn't have any problems with your hardware. I would try 
to run demo_CH_math from a command line, since I don't think it makes any 
GL output. It might appear to fail, when in fact it has run and finished. 
Some of the non-GL and -Irrlicht demos output to a command console which 
closes when execution ends.

Hi Bowen,

Well, the error messages are pretty clear:  even though the files are on 
your computer, your executable cannot find them.  As you can see from 
the messages printed to the console, by default a *relative *path is 
used to look for the required asset files (fonts, textures, etc.).

In other words, as they are written, all Chrono demos assume that the 
executables will end up in a folder that has a prescribed location 
relative to where the Chrono data/ folder exists.   More precisely, 
Chrono defines a global variable that holds the location of the data/ 
folder (by default this is *../data*). To use a Chrono data file, in 
your program you specify its location relative to where the data/ folder 
exists.  Then Chrono will prepend the value of that global variable.

Looking at the title of your console window in the 2nd picture, it 
appears that you are *not *actually trying to run demo_IRR_ballDEM, but 
rather a copy of that demo that you have *relocated*. In this case, you 
must indicate how/where the Chrono data files can be reached.   I don't 
know exactly how you set up this test of yours, but if you followed the 
'template_project' example provided with Chrono, please pay attention on 
how we set a preprocessor definition named CHRONO_DATA_DIR (in 
CMakeLists.txt at line 112) and how that is then used to invoke the 
function SetChronoDataPath (in my_example.cpp at line 38).   This 
function will simply change the value of the global variable mentioned

CMakeLists.txt at line 112) and how that is then used to invoke the 
function SetChronoDataPath (in my_example.cpp at line 38).   This

Subject: Re: [chrono] documentation on modeling cables
From: Antonio Martín Recuero
Date: Tue, 13 Sep 2016 09:53:57 -0500

Hi Chris,

You probably have two choices in Chrono for modeling steel cables: ANCF
beam elements and corotational Euler-Bernoulli beams. For the former
element, you can find a white paper here:
http://www.projectchrono.org/assets/white_papers/FEA/WP_ANCF.pdf; for the
latter, http://www.projectchrono.org/assets/white_papers/FEA/euler_beams.pdf
.

The demos demo_FEA_cables.cpp (ANCF) and demo_FEA_beams (corotational) can
come in handy as well. The ANCF demo attaches ANCF cable finite elements to
rigid bodies, which is a feature you might need for your problem. The rigid
bodies can be interconnected in any traditional way: Revolute, spherical,
prismatic, ... joints. Let us know if you have any other question.

Best regards,
Antonio

Subject: Re: [chrono] Removing_bodies_from_ChSystemParallel
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 12 Dec 2016 10:54:28 +0100

Hi Michael,

No, right now it is not possible to remove bodies from a 
ChSystemParallel.  Moreover, it is actually unsafe to call 
ChAssembly::RemoveBody() or ChAssembly::Remove() for a body in a 
parallel system.  This is something we need to fix properly and is on 
our to-do list.

Assuming you only want to take out of the simulation a couple of bodies, 
you can try to inactivate these bodies, by setting them as "fixed to 
ground" (body->SetBodyFixed(true)) and disabling collision for them 
(body->SetCollide(false)).

Also, if you are actually trying to remove a body and create a new one, 
you can just "re-purpose" the existing body, by overwriting its state 
(positions and velocities).

Hope that this helps,
--Radu

From: Shig_T
Date: Thu, 8 Dec 2016 20:59:20 -0800 (PST)

Hello,

These errors are caused because Swig fails to expand CH_FACTORY_TAG(), 
which is a preprocessor macro placed on nested header.
The macro was introduced on the commit 78d92b5, at 1st Dec., 2016. For now, 
you may use older version of chrono to avoid the trouble.

You can also solve these error with making some edits:
1. Open chrono_python/%err_file%.i, where %err_file% is the filename 
causing the error (in the above case, ChFunction_Base, ChCollisionModel and 
ChAsset).
2. Find a section that contains %includes and add the following line on a 
top of the section (see attached picture for example).
 %include "../chrono/core/ChClassFactory.h"

Then errors are fixed (I haven't tried to run python code after compile, 
though).

Reference: SWIG errors because of preprocessor directive - Stack Overflow 
<http://stackoverflow.com/questions/10760287/swig-errors-because-of-preprocessor-directive>
<http://stackoverflow.com/questions/10760287/swig-errors-because-of-preprocessor-directive>

Shig

Kishor, I pushed these changes.  There are now two new ChCollisionSystemBullet::RayHit functions which accept the collision filter group and mask as their last arguments.

--Radu

On 11/6/2018 3:05 AM, Kishor Bhalerao wrote:
Hi Radu,
I do not have any preference for the solution and am fine with casting the collision system to bullet if that is your preferred solution. I am anyway relying on the btIDebugDraw interface implementation which I provide as I cannot rely on irrlicht to display collision diagnostics. So that currently naturally locks me down to Bullet.

Kishor.

On Monday, November 5, 2018 at 3:07:20 AM UTC-8, Radu Serban wrote:

Hi Kishor,

Option 2 is indeed a bit more restrictive and implementing it as you described might affect some user code out there.   But something along these lines could be implemented in a safer, backward-compatible manner by adding an optional parameter to ChCollisionSystem::RayHit (something like 'force_all_collisions' with a default value of 'false').

For option 1, we cannot modify the signature of the (pure) virtual method ChCollisionSystem::RayHit with something that is Bullet-specific.  An alternative would be to provide an additional (non-virtual) function ChCollisionSystemBullet::RayHit which takes two additional arguments, filter_group and filter_mask.  The drawback for this approach is that you may need to cast the collision system to CgCollisionSystemBullet in order to call RayHit.

I favor this last approach.  Let me know if that would work for you and I can push a change for this.

On 11/1/2018 6:55 PM, Kishor Bhalerao wrote:
I was testing the ChCCollisionSystem::RayHit(ChVector<> from, ChVector<> to, ChRayhitResult& result) method.

Looking at the implementation in ChCollisionSystemBullet::RayHit(), I found the following two lines which perform the ray cast.


btCollisionWorld::ClosestRayResultCallback rayCallback(btfrom, btto);
this->bt_collision_world->rayTest(btfrom, btto, rayCallback);

The struct ClosestRayResultCallback derives from RayResultCallback which sets the m_CollisionFilterGroup to btBroadPhaseProxy::DefaultFilter which is 1.

Since the m_collisionFilterGroup is now set to 1, the method RayResultCallback::needsCollision() returns true only if the proxy filter mask has the first bit set to 1 which wasn't the case for me. So the ray hit always returns false.

There are two ways to fix this.

1. Either modify the RayHit method signature to take the filterGroup and filterMask as inputs from the user which can be added to the callback as


btCollisionWorld::ClosestRayResultCallback rayCallback(btfrom, btto);
symbol: Re: [chrono] Rayhit

text:
btCollisionWorld::ClosestRayResultCallback rayCallback(btfrom, btto);
rayCallback.m_collisionFilterGroup = filterGroup; //< User specified value
rayCallback.m_collisionFilterMask = filterMask; //< User specified value


rest of the code remaining the same. This would allow greater control over what collision models we are ray casting against.

2. The second approach is to just override the needsCollision() method to always return true. I have tested locally on my machine and both these approaches did give me the expected results.

Kishor.

create the granular system, load in a set of mesh-represented objects using 
*load_meshes*, then create the corresponding multi-body system (as 
*sys_ball* in the demo). In the simulation loop, the multi-body system is 
updated based on the force and torque data obtained from 
*collectGeneralizedForcesOnMeshSoup*. Note that in the demo *ball_force* 
stores the force and torque data, and if you instead have multiple (say *n*) 
objects (aka mesh families), then ball_force will have (6**n*) entries, 6 
entries per family. You need to then accumulate forces on them one by one.

This should work well if the objects of interest are of regular shapes so 
you can explicitly define inertia and such, like in the demo; I do not know 
whether or how you can do this with random shapes, I hope someone else can 
help.

Finally a side note, with the current implementation you need to call 
*meshSoup_applyRigidBodyMotion* like in the demo for at least once, so the 
meshSoup correctly initiates, even if your mesh does not move at all. But I 
think in your case this is not a problem.

Thank you,
Ruochun

Chaitanya,

"Generic_SimplePowertrain::m_max_speed = 5000;" is defined with units of 
rad/s, not RPM.  A value this high is helpful in testing out features, but 
it is not a realistic value for a typical car (5000*30/pi = 47746 RPM).

This engine model is not a good approximation of an internal combustion 
engine.  It is much closer to a simplified electric motor torque curve.  If 
you are running tests at a constant speed, then this model is likely good 
enough.  If you are trying to run a 0-60mph test, then you'll likely want a 
more detailed engine map based powertrain model or another higher fidelity 
model.

Regards,

Mike

repo, you need to keep in mind that that demo is running rigid tires that 
utilize Chrono's collision detection capabilities.  If you run the vehicle 
off of the terrain box that the tires are colliding with, there will be 
nothing to keep the vehicle from falling without end.  If you are trying to 
run long distances, you may want to consider using a different tire model. 
 Also, note that the max speed in the simple powertrain used in 
"demo_VEH_WheeledGeneric" is pretty high. 

The "demo_VEH_WheeledGeneric" demo is intended to be a test bed for testing 
out features, so you very well may need to modify it to fit your needs. 
 For example, the generic vehicle in "demo_VEH_WheeledGeneric" and "test_VEH_WheeledGeneric_Accel" 
use different tire models and different powertrains.

I just pushed a change to the generic vehicle suspension damping callback 
to correct the assertion error.  As far as I can tell, all the demos and 
tests in the repo with the generic vehicle work as defined. So if you are 
seeing something that is not working, please let us know

Chaitanya,

I would recommend using the generic vehicle that is defined through the 
concrete classes rather than the JSON files (Generic_Chassis.cpp and 
others).  You'll notice that the chassis mass is much higher in that file 
(1399.13kg).  If you want to use the JSON files, I would recommend 
adjusting them to match the parameters defined in the concrete class files.

The generic vehicle and the HMMWV are two different weight classes of 
vehicles.  The generic vehicle should be more representative of a passenger 
car.

As far as how to scale the inertia, that will depend on what you are trying 
to do.  If you want to assume that you are scaling the density of the 
vehicle when you can the mass, then you could scale the inertia by the same 
factor as the mass.  If you are assuming that you are scaling just the mass 
of the engine, then you'll need to come up with a different approach.  Your 
approach is going to depend on what question you are trying to answer with 
the simulations.

I hope that helps,

Mike

   please check the following:

- be sure you are in part editing mode, not assembly editing mode. You 
can turn on the "set body as collision shape" only one part at a time.

Note that there is a potential source of confusion in the nomenclature, 
because "solid bodies" in SolidWorks language looks like the "rigid 
body" term in Chrono language, but Chrono's rigid body is the SolidWorks 
part.

For more infos, look at

http://dynamics.eng.unipr.it/mediawiki/index.php/Demo_collision_shapes

(it is a tutorial on the old documentation site of Chrono, sorry we

text:
Subject: RE: [chrono] Is there a documentation for PyChrono?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 19 Aug 2022 14:46:26 +0000

Glad to hear you have it up and running!

Indeed, only the C++ API is documented, for a very simple reason: that’s the only one that can be parsed by doxygen; PyChrono is nothing but a set of wrappers automatically created by SWIG.

As such, the names of member variables and methods in PyChrono are *identical* to those in C++.  The only few differences are related to Python not having the concept of nested classes the way it is in C++.  So you will see references to some enum classes is done differently in Python code.

In your particular example, you conflate the radius that is a member variable of ChBodyEasySphere (named ‘radius’) and the radius that is a member of ChSphereShape (named ‘rad’).

Finally, ChCylinderShape does not have any member variable to set the cylinder height.  Instead, you provide the coordinates of the two end points (in the visual shape reference frame) which implicitly defines a cylinder height.  By the way, for consistency, I plan on changing this way of defining visualization cylinder shapes.

I hope this clarifies things,
--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] A Question about Chrono Validation Study
From: Dan Negrut
Date: Fri, 20 Apr 2018 14:30:45 +0000

Hi Qihan,
Thanks for your interest in Chrono.

The method called DVI doesn’t need a Young’s modulus since the way it models contact is via a rigid body assumption that leads to a DVI problem.
The value of the friction coefficient and the density of the material are within the physical range.
The PM simulation uses a value of K_N that is within the accepted range. See, for instance this paper that is cited more than 700 on google scholar:
https://journals.aps.org/pre/pdf/10.1103/PhysRevE.64.051302
Also, this paper (they all use values in the same range, usually three orders of magnitude than the actual value):
https://journals.aps.org/pre/pdf/10.1103/PhysRevE.74.021306

Finally, as shown in that plot, two different modeling and numerical solution methods; i.e., PM and DVI, give the same result, which is aligned with testing results.
A further discussion of Chrono and its validation is here:
https://journals.aps.org/pre/pdf/10.1103/PhysRevE.96.042905

I hope this helps but feel free to post follow up comments if you think we can assist.

Dan

Dear Jeroen,

the proper way to accomplish this is to use the ChLinkLockLock constraint
between your "moved" object and a generic fixed truss. As Radu already
suggested,  then you need to play with ChFunction objects in order to
impose the motion.

The  other way (using a fixed object and overwriting it's position and
speed) is not reccomended because if the moved object collides a free
object,  the free object will "feel" only the position of the fixed one,
but NOT the speed (like the fixed object is steady, even if you over wrote
it's speed by hand). So it could be good only for limited special cases.

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Kinematic bodies
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 22 Mar 2017 07:17:58 +0100

Hello,

That should work, as long as you do specify contact shapes associated 
with what you call 'kinematic bodies' and enable contact on those 
bodies.  After all, a body 'fixed' to ground (and such bodies are used 
in several of the Chrono demos) is just a special case of this -- where 
the position and orientation are fixed in time.

However, keep in mind that, if you "overwrite" the positions and 
rotations of bodies at each time step, this is a very rough 
approximation and will likely fail if such bodies are also connected 
through links.  It is your responsibility to understand what such an 
approximation means from a physical point of view. Even then, you must 
ensure that you do not 'move' these bodies in such a way that collisions 
are missed.

A more appropriate way to model something like this is to create a "weld 
link" (ChLinkLockLock) between such a body B and a "ground" body G 
(i.e., one for which you specified SetBodyFixed(true)).   Then use 
ChFunction objects to control the relative motion of B with respect to G.

Maybe you can provide some more details on what/how you tried to model 
this and on what you obtain.

--Radu

Jacob,

I'm confused: there's no ChTrailing/Trailing Arm code in Chrono, only

you added?

I have only added a template for a semi-trailing arm suspension 
(ChSemiTrailingArm) and the corresponding concrete class SemiTrailingArm 
which reads specification from a JSON file because, as far as I 
understand it, a trailing arm suspension is just a particular case of a 
semi-trailing arm (in that a trailing arm suspension has the arm pivots 
aligned with the transverse chassis direction, while in a semi-trailing 
arm suspension the arms are pivoted at inclined angles).  The template 
parameters that I implemented figures out the direction of those pivots 
(revolute joints) based on 2 hard-points (those identified by TA_O, for 
Trailing Arm Outer, and TA_I, for Trailing Arm Inner). So you should be 
able to model a trailing arm suspension by just making sure that the 
vectors corresponding to TA_O and TA_I differ in their y component only.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Trailing Arm Origin
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 23 Jan 2017 11:18:36 -0600

Hi Jacob,

I see you noticed that I added that template :-)

The assumptions for what the reference frame for the semi-trailing arm 
suspension (in fact, this is also true for any suspension) are:

  * the suspension reference frame must be aligned with the vehicle
    (i.e. the chassis) reference frame; that means an ISO reference
    frame with x towards the front of the vehicle, z up, and y to the left
  * the origin of the suspension reference frame must be in the
    longitudinal plane of symmetry (left/right); this is because we
    expect data to be specified only for the left side (and we mirror in
    y to obtain the corresponding locations for the right side)

Other than that, there is no other requirement in specifying a 
suspension reference frame.   For the concrete implementations that we 
provide as samples in Chrono::Vehicle, whether as concrete class 
implementations in the vehicle models library, or as JSON specification 
files, we do indeed fix the x and z coordinates of the suspension 
reference frame somewhere in that longitudinal symmetry plane.   As you 
mentioned, for the double wishbone suspension, we (arbitrarily) picked 
to specify all hard point locations with respect to a suspension frame 
whose origin is at the midpoint between the revolute joints connecting 
the lower control arms to the chassis.   Similarly, for the sample JSON 
specification file provided for a generic semi-trailing arm suspension, 
we (arbitrarily) picked the origin of the suspension reference frame to
symbol: Re: [chrono] Trailing Arm Origin

text:
the lower control arms to the chassis.   Similarly, for the sample JSON 
specification file provided for a generic semi-trailing arm suspension, 
we (arbitrarily) picked the origin of the suspension reference frame to 
be at the midpoint between the centers of the left/right spindles.

But you can specify a suspension (e.g. in a JSON file) using a reference 
frame that is different, as long as it still respects the two 
assumptions above.  This really means you can use a reference frame that 
is translated in x and/or z from the ones we happened to use.   Of 
course, once you do that, you will need to appropriately modify the 
vehicle specification to properly locate the suspension reference frame 
with respect to the vehicle reference frame.

I hope that this clarifies things.

Best,
--Radu

Dear Tam,

if you need run-time continuous generation of particles, one way is to 
put the generation code in the while() loop as you are doing, it looks 
ok - but at  first glance it seems to me that you forgot to update the 
Irrlicht asset system for the new particles; this can be done by adding 
these lines after your melipBody->AddAsset(mtextureelip);  line:

application->AssetBind(melipBody);
application->AssetUpdate(melipBody);

In fact application.AssetBindAll(); and application.AssetUpdateAll(); 
(that you wrote in your code just after the Irrlicht application is 
created) cannot bind&update the objects that are NOT YET created.. hence 
the need to call AssetBind and AssetUpdate for new stuff that you add 
later...


NOTE: in Chrono there is a more advanced system for continuous particle 
generation: look into src/chrono/*particlefactory*. This takes care of 
randomization, flow equalization, mass count, etc. , and you can see 
some demos in

demo_IRR_emitter.cpp

demo_IRR_emit_precessor.cpp

demo_IRR_emit_cluster.cpp

regards.

Alessandro Tasora

Subject: Re: [chrono] How to change the default physics units from meters to
 millimeters?
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 12 Jul 2018 13:12:44 +0200

hi Zachary

first of all, remember that the Chrono is unit-less, so we consider it 
based on the SI system [1lenght unit L=meter m][1mass unit M=kilogram 
kg][1 time unit T=second s] only for convenience, but it could be, say, 
[1lenght unit L=millimeter][1mass unit M=gram][1 time unit 
T=femtosecond] if you prefer.

The thing to remember, here, is that /also forces, torques, G 
accelerations, etc. should be introduced accordingly./ Ex. a force is 
dimensionally ML/T^2, ie in SI a force is kg m / s^2, so it is measured 
in N, Newton, but if you assume you are using millimeters, the number to 
enter for the same force must be scaled 1000 times as kg mm / s^2.  Same 
for other input data for your model.

This said, anyway:

yes, you could introduce very small objects, if you keep assuming the 
length measuring unit of Chrono is meters. This option is _not 
practical_, for many reasons.

1) collision detection tolerances.
You already noticed the boundingbox problem. Ok, you can fix the 
bounding box issue by reducing the collision envelope and the collision 
margin (see at the bottom of 
http://api.projectchrono.org/3.0.0/collision_shapes.html ). However 
there are some other hard-wired tolerances in the guts of the collision 
engine that might decrease precision of the contacts if you are using 
extremely small objects.

2) floating point algebra
Microprocessors compute products/sumts/etc. between real numbers using 
the floating point algebra (double precision floating points in the case

2) floating point algebra
Microprocessors compute products/sumts/etc. between real numbers using 
the floating point algebra (double precision floating points in the case 
of Chrono). It is a good approximation of real numbers, however floating 
point numbers can give some roundoff errors when they mix extremely big 
and extremely small values in computations (the machine epsilon known 
issue). Ok, for your objects, if they are millimiter sized, es 1e-3, it 
is not a big issue here, but if you start modeling objects with 1e-6 
dimension, say, this could start to be a problem. A rule of thumb is 
that it is better to have 'all your numbers' ranging in the [-2...+2] 
range, when possible, to exploit the max precision of the floating point 
algebra.


Ok, this is the best option I think.
Keep in mind what I said in the text above.

Note: probably you would need a shorter timestep /anyway, /even if using 
meters. It depends on the fact that in one large time step, say 0.01s, 
the displacement of a millimeter-sized tiny object within 0.01s would 
cause mm-sized displacements, hence causing tunneling artifacts.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Easymesh Body Attraction and Clamping
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 16 Mar 2017 15:36:20 +0100

Hi Mustafa,

I suspect the problem is with inverted normals.  You must set up your 
mesh so that the face normals point outwards.  For collision detection 
purposes, the normal of a triangular face is calculated using the 
right-hand rule and is dictated by the order in which you specify the 
indices of the vertices that make up that face.

In other words, if you have a triangle that connects vertices with 
indices i0, i1, and i2, specifying the order (i0, i1, i2) will result in 
a face normal that is opposite to the one you would obtain with the 
order (i0, i2, i1).

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Using Chrono in flexible gear contact
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 24 Mar 2017 11:07:02 +0100

Dear Refaat,

I assume you mean contact between flexible gears - otherwise, if you 
mean _rigid gears_, probably the only feature you need is the 
ChLinkGear, as demonstrated in *demo_IRR_gear.cpp*; it represents a 
'macroscopic' model of gear transmission (with bevel gears too, inner or 
outer, planetary or not, with proper bearing reactions, etc.)

An intermediate problem could be: _detailed contact(s) between gear 
teeth, but still considering rigid gears_. This could be done in 
classical Chrono DVI, just by creating two bodies with 3D meshes. Use 
the ChBodyEasyMesh to this end, ex in *demo_IRR_collision_trimesh.cpp*. 
(but if you are interested in just 2d rigid contacts, look at the 
*demo_IRR_collision_2d.cpp*, it is much faster and it can use 
circular-arc smoother approximations for profiles)

As for _deformable_ teeth: we haven't yet used Chrono in modeling 
contacts between flexible gear pairs. In principle, nothing prevents 
from using Chrono in this class of problems. Yet there are some 
potential issues, so here I write some guidelines, in random order:

- contacts in Chrono FEA must be computed using DEM contacts, i.e. using 
penalty. Nowadays is not yet possible to use DVI contacts, which are 
infinitely rigid, exact contacts - hopefully this will be possible in 
future releases. DEM contacts means that some stiffness must be assigned 
to contacts. Such stiffness must be very large if you do not want to see 
interpenetration between gear meshes (given the level of precision of
symbol: Re: [chrono] Using Chrono in flexible gear contact

text:
future releases. DEM contacts means that some stiffness must be assigned 
to contacts. Such stiffness must be very large if you do not want to see 
interpenetration between gear meshes (given the level of precision of 
modern gear involutes, probably you cannot accept more than 0.01mm of 
interpenetration, I guess), and high stiffness means very very short 
timestep.

- the 3D mesh should be quite dense, and uniformly triangulated on the 
surface. This for two reasons: if the involute profile is too 'edgy', 
with a rough approximation caused by too few triangles in the mesh, the 
slinding of the two involutes would result in a noisy force output. The 
seond reason is that in DEM you can impose stiffness on a "per contact" 
base, not on a "per unit of contact surface", so it would be wise to 
have an uniform number of contact points in a zone of contact so that 
the resulting total stiffness can be predicted/understood in some 
meaningful way.

- look at*demo_FEA_contacts.cpp*  for learning how the mesh-mesh 3d 
contact works.

- the FEA machinery of Chrono could use the MINRES solver, but for 
higher precision/performance we strongly suggest you to use the optional 
MKL unit or MUMPS unit (these depend on 3rd party libraries)

regards

Alessandro

This is a consequence of the current quadrature of the Timoshenko beam, which is potentially affected by shear locking if the length/width ratio is high. Hi Rainer,

You are correct, if not interested in the GPU-specific parts of Chrono, 
it is unfortunate to have to require a CUDA installation, just to be 
able to use thrust (with its OpenMP backend).

As you indicated, there is a stand-alone version of thrust and Chrono 
can actually be configured to work with that.  There is a CMake 
variable, THRUST_INCLUDE_DIR, which you can set.  Note that it must set 
it so that it points to the parent of the 'thrust' directory, because we 
use things like "#include <thrust/sort.h>".  Note also that this CMake 
variable is marked as "advanced" (I will look into changing it so that 
it is exposed if thrust is not automatically found).

Having said that, there is another issue with using the stand-alone 
version of thrust:  it appears that some thrust headers try to include 
cuda-specific headers without proper guards.  All Chrono libraries 
should still build fine.   But some Chrono unit tests and demos will 
fail to compile because those cuda headers are not available (if I 
recall correctly, these are programs which include 
ChSystemDescriptorParallel.h).

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Finding number of contacts on individual bodies
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 31 Aug 2017 10:34:01 +0200

Hi Karl,

Indeed, there is no Chrono function to directly obtain the number of 
contacts experienced by any given body in the system. The function 
ChSystem::GetNcontacts() should work, but it will report the total 
number of contacts at that particular time. This should be called from 
within the simulation loop.

To get what you want, one option is to use a callback of type 
ChContactContainer::ReportContactCallback and invoke, from within the 
simulation loop, the function ChContactContainer::ReportAllContacts() by 
passing it a pointer to your derived callback class. Your derived 
callback class should override the virtual method OnReportContact() 
which will be called once for each contact in the contact container. 
Since this method receives the two contactable objects as arguments, you 
can accumulate and keep track of contacts involving any (or all) the 
bodies in the system (maybe using a map or something like that).

Below is a sketch of how you can set this up. Of course, you would do 
something slightly different in your implementation of 
ContactManager::OnReportContact(). Note that I did not test this 
particular code.

Look also at the class ChTrackContactManager in the Chrono::Vehicle 
module for a more complex implementation of such a callback class.

class ContactManager : public ChContactContainer::ReportContactCallback {
  public:
  ContactManager(std::shared_ptr<ChBody> box) : m_box(box), 
m_ncontacts(0) {}
  void Reset() { m_ncontacts = 0; }

Subject: Re: [chrono] problem about cmake
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 7 Mar 2017 09:54:52 +0100

Bowen,

As you probably already know, in order to be able to build a project 
that uses Chrono, you must first configure and build the Chrono 
libraries.  Chrono is designed in a modular manner and has a central 
"core" (the main ChronoEngine library) augmented with several optional 
modules.  When you configure Chrono itself with CMake you have the 
option to enable the configuration and build of one or more of these 
optional modules.  Note that all these optional modules are *not 
enabled* by default.  If your external project makes use of 
functionality that is provided by such an optional Chrono module, then 
that module must be enabled during Chrono configuration.

Now, Chrono::Postprocess is such an optional module.  It is not build by 
default, unless you explicitly enable the CMake option 
ENABLE_MODULE_POSTPROCESS during the CMake Chrono configuration.

The error that you see when you try to configure your external project 
with CMake is pretty clear:

  * you request Chrono::Postprocess functionality as a *required *component
    This means that in your CMakeLists.txt script you probably have
    something like:
           find_package(Chrono COMPONENTS Postprocess CONFIG)

  * but you *did not enable* the building of Chrono::Postprocess during
    Chrono configuration
    This means that you left ENABLE_MODULE_POSTPROCESS unchecked

I hope that this helps.

--Radu

Hi all,

just a quick update. I was trying many things to get the modal analysis to 
work with no success. Finally I tried to set up the geometry in a different 
way.

As I explained before I constructed the shapes using single back element 
that I then connected via constraints. The resulting large number of 
constraints was actually causing most of the issues with the modal 
analysis. 

I finally set up the complex geometry in a different way, with beam 
elements that are connected via common nodes and obtained the shapes using 
the ChElementBeamEuler::*SetNodeBreferenceRot(...) *functionality.

After doing this most problems disappeared - I get consistent results for 
modal frequencies and mode shapes now. Rotational augmentation of the 
frequencies is also working pretty well and using realistic structural 
properties, the results appear to match measured literature data.

I'm quite happy with the results and am working on a publication at the 
moment.

Here is the screenshot of the CHRONO model of the vertical axis wind

Hi David,

Just a couple of comments in case you want to down the ANCF path. The
stiffness matrices calculated in Chrono for ANCF elements are exact, that
means that no term has been left behind. However, since ANCF uses inertial
coordinates, the geometric stiffness is not a term within a sum to obtain
the resulting stiffness matrix. If eigenvalue analysis is to be performed
to a rotating blade, it may be required to introduce a local frame, which
will define new local coordinates, and transform the equations of motion so
that you can have a linear system whose terms will be a function of the
angular velocity. In this sense, using ANCF for your goals may require
additional steps. Also, note that the current ANCF beam element available
in Chrono does not feature shear deformation; it also has some restrictions
as to what cross sections types can be used.

We expect to provide with more FEA options to the users soon: We are
starting to work on an alternative implementation for shear deformable
large deformation beams that can have arbitrary cross section. We plan on
having that implemented within a couple of months. In addition, we are
wrapping up the implementation of a higher-order ANCF shell element -solid
mechanics approach.

Regards,
Antonio

Hello David:

you are right about the geometric stiffness, it can make a difference in 
scenarios like yours. However in the ChElementBeamEuler (corotational 
beam) it is implemented using the formulation from Felippa et al. (to 
reuse elements for linear analysis) but not enabled because it caused

like   if(false) {...}

As for ChElementBeamANCF, they have the geometric stiffness implemented 
and working.

Same for the two shell elements: geometric stiffness implemented and 
working.

The geometric stiffness is not implemented in tetrahedrons solid 
elements because for the moment we had no scenarios that motivated this. 
It is more common for shells and beams, I mean, that geometric stiffness 
is needed.

To summarize:

  * ChElementBeamANCF (the 'cable' element) : K geometric implemented.
  * ChElementBeamEuler : K geometric implemented but NOT enabled
  * ChElementShellANCF: K geometric implemented
  * ChElementShellReissner: K geometric implemented
  * ChElementTetrahedron.. K geometric NOT implemented
  * ChElementHexahedron.. K geometric NOT implemented

Subject: Re: [chrono] Coefficient of Restitution
From: Alessandro Tasora

hi Jonathan,
   the SetEvalContactCn was meant for an advanced feature (variable 
coefficients depending on different zones on surfaces) that was 
supported in the past, it requires embedding chrono in a 3d modeler - 
and it is not your case.

What you rather need, is something like....

my_rigid_body->GetMaterialSurface()->SetRestitution(0.4f);

This sets the restitution coefficient of that body, that would be 0 by 
default.
Note, numbers in 0..1 range should be used.

The "f" after 0.4 is optional (it tells the compiler that the number is 
a "float" floating point single precision, avoiding a compiler warning 
for casting from double to float)

Another option is to share a single material among many objects and to 
set surface properties (friction, restitution etc) to that material 
only, and this is a bit more memory efficient. Something along the lines of

auto my_material = std::make_shared<ChMaterialSurface>();
material->SetRestitution(0.4f);
...
my_rigid_bodyA->SetMaterialSurface(my_material);
my_rigid_bodyB->SetMaterialSurface(my_material);
...

By the way: pay attention to the fact that restitution (as well as other 
surface properties as friction, etc.) should be 'per contact' basis... 
so what happens when two bodies with different properties come in 
contact? well, the default behavior in Chrono is that the smaller value 
is used among the two.

Finally, read the manual about those settings like 'min rebounce speed', 
etc. because collisions with nonzero restitution might introduce artifacts.

You can get the Windows Mumps DLLs from http://assets.projectchrono.org/downloads/Mumps-5.1.1.zip.
(note that this download link will also show up in the Chrono::Mumps installation instructions at http://api.projectchrono.org/development/module_mumps_installation.html when the documentation regenerates).

ChSolverMumps can help you check if there are redundant constraints:  if you do not explicitly enable "null pivot detection" (through a call to SetNullPivotDetection in Chrono 4.0.0, renamed EnableNullPivotDetection in the current code) you will get an error (Mumps return code -10) if there are redundant constraints and hence the system matrix is singular.  Mumps should still be able to solve the problem (by finding a solution in the null space) if you do enable "null pivot detection".

Regarding your other question, I do not see why having connected nodes and bodies at the same locations would lead to these problems.

Unless we can think of some other possible explanation, this may point to some bug in Chrono.  It would be useful if we had a simple example to reproduce the issue.

--Radu

From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 25 Aug 2016 22:35:32 +0200

hi David,

in fact I experienced a similar problem in the past, when using the 
MINRES solver. Looks like that the convergence of MINRES could be 
sub-optimal when using finite elements in some configurations, 
especially when adding some constraints too.
And this is even more critical when you use elements with large 
stiffness ratios, which is exactly the case of your beams (bending vs 
axial stiffness etc.)
So, when convergence is critical, MINRES might bailout when reaching the 
max number of iterations with an 'approximate' solution, and one side 
effect of a badly approximate solution is -among other things- also a 
'slowdown' of free object motions.

The solution would be to increase the iteration number of MINRES, in 
theory 20-30 could be ok also for big problems, but sometimes (because 
of numerical roundoffs, etc.) it stalls more than predicted by the 
theory, and increasing the max iteration limit too much (ex. 200-300 
iterations) would make the simulation exact, but very slow.

Preconditioning is a typical cure to the convergence problem of MINRES 
and other Krylov methods, but I managed to implement just a basic 
diagonal preconditioning, with diagonal constraint preconditioning. It 
cannot do magic, and in some cases (as in your test) it could even make 
things worse.

So, another solution would be to switch to another, more efficient solver.
Example. You can enable the MKL unit, in CMAKE, and compile it. You'll 
see some FEA demos that use the MKL solver: learn from them how to

Hi David,

It can very well be that large stiffness ratios plus constraints are
hindering convergence of the iterative solver. As you did, tinkering with
the parameters and options of the solver may resolve these issues. You can
also increase the number of iterations and/or monitor the equations
residue.

As an alternate and, probably, more robust solution, for complex FEA
problems, it may be advisable to use the direct solver Pardiso MKL, for
which Chrono provides wrapper methods. You can take a look at the FEA
demos/tests that use the MKL solver; e.g. demo_FEA_cablesMKL. Let us know
if you experience any other issues.

Regards,
Antonio

Subject: API changes related to ChVector and ChQuaternion
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 18 Feb 2017 11:29:14 +0100

Apologies for yet another set of changes to the Chrono public API :-)

To allow for some planned future developments in Chrono, we decided to 
change the internal representation of ChVector, ChVector2, and 
ChQuaternion to use arrays of fixed size (3, 2, and 4, respectively).  
The main benefit of this is that it allows an efficient implementation 
of indexing operator[].

With this, you cannot directly access members of such objects anymore.  
Instead you have to use methods such as x(), y(), z() for ChVector and 
e0(), e1(), e2(), e3() for ChQuaternion.  I obsoleted the inefficient 
ChVector::operator() for indexing. Instead, if needed, you can now use 
operator[] , provided for all 3 classes above.

Updating your codes to use this latest Chrono version should be 
straightforward.  Simple replace v.x with v.x(), q.e0 with q.e0(), and 
so on.   If you used the old indexing operator() for ChVector, simply 
change to operator[].

Best,
Radu

Subject: Install and first build troubleshooting
From: Dario Mangoni
Date: Mon, 24 Apr 2017 06:58:55 -0700 (PDT)

Dear Chrono users,
during our last Chrono tutorial in Parma (Italy) we collected some reports 
about some common install issues|oversights, especially with VS2017.
Before making the list, I would like to stress that many of them are OS, 
IDE or even COMMIT specific, so they could affect only some of you and only 
as far as the install procedure does not change.


Tips:
- [VS] during the Visual Studio setup please make sure to *install the C++ 
toolchain*; usually this is NOT the default.
  Symptoms: in the CMake log pane some errors about 
CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER-NOTFOUND or CMAKE_C_COMPILER-NOTFOUND are thrown.

- [VS2017 + *WIN8|WIN7|WIN<10*] during the Visual Studio 2017 setup please 
make sure to *install the Windows 8 SDK and the UCRT library*.
  Symptoms: Microsoft.CppCommon... throws an error like *MSB6006: “cmd.exe” 
exited with code 9009* or other missing libraries that are not found at 
run-time.

- [WIN+CMake] during the CMake setup you will be asked to *put the CMake 
executable in your PATH environmental variable*. Please do so, in fact 
VS2017 *could* complain if this is not done.
  Symptomps: some errors in the VS Output/Error List related to the fact 
that the CMake executable cannot be found.

- [WIN+CMake] never use the backslash "\" in paths; *use the slash* instead 
"/".

- [VS+CMake] the INSTALL target/project in Visual Studio is meant to copy 
relevant files (such as static and shared Chrono libraries and header 
files) in a separate "install" folder,
symbol: Install and first build troubleshooting

text:
- [VS+CMake] the INSTALL target/project in Visual Studio is meant to copy 
relevant files (such as static and shared Chrono libraries and header 
files) in a separate "install" folder,
  according to the CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX path that has been set in the last 
CMake run.
  If the CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX parent folder requires *administrative 
privileges* to be modified (like C:/Program Files), then VS must be run in 
admin mode before building INSTALL.
  BTW, please mind that you do not strictly need to run the INSTALL target 
in order to link against Chrono libraries.
  Symptomps: the INSTALL post-build event will not work; the error thrown 
is:

error MSB3073:
The command "setlocal
"C:\Program Files (x86)\CMake\bin\cmake.exe" -DBUILD_TYPE=Release -P 
cmake_install.cmake
if %errorlevel% neq 0 goto :cmEnd
:cmEnd
endlocal & call :cmErrorLevel %errorlevel% & goto :cmDone
:cmErrorLevel
exit /b %1
:cmDone
if %errorlevel% neq 0 goto :VCEnd
:VCEnd" exited with code 1.

- [VS+CMake] in the CMake gui you have different CMAKE_CONFIGURATION_TYPES 
such as Debug;Release;RelWithDebInfo;MinSizeRel.
  Please leave there ALL of them! Do not set "Release" or "Debug" manually 
from there, but use instead the drop-down menu in VS to do so.
  Symptomps: only Debug or Release build configuration is found in the 
Solution Configuration in VS.


Have a good setup!

From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 16 Dec 2018 17:00:39 +0000

Roberto,

Maybe you are confused by the 'auto' specifier which we tend to use in our demos for brevity? That simply specifies that the type of the variable ('ball' in your case) will be automatically deduced from its initializer (in this case, the type is std::shared_ptr<ChBody>).

So the function you want can take as argument either a copy of the shared pointer or a reference to it:

void foo(std::shared_ptr<ChBody> body) {...}
or
void bar(std::shared_ptr<ChBody>& body) {...}

In either case, inside the function you would access the body the same way. For example:
body->GetCollisionModel()->AddSphere(1);

And call the function as:
foo(ball);
or
bar(ball);

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Torsional Spring Joint
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 13 Sep 2020 09:51:59 +0200

The link forces are still there, but a while ago I changed the API for 
their usage. The functions SetForce_*** were removed; instead, you 
simply use GetFunction_*** which will create the underlying ChLinkForce 
object on its first invocation. For an example, see 
*utest_JOINT_rotspring 
*(https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/tests/unit_tests/joints/utest_JOINT_rotspring.cpp). 
Note that what you want to set is probably the Rz force, not the R force 
(since you work with a revolute joint with a single rotational degree of 
freedom about the joint's z axis).

Alternatively, you can use a *ChLinkRotSpringCB 
*(http://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_link_rot_spring_c_b.html) 
which allows you to include a general torque based on the relative 
orientation of two bodies. For an example, see *demo_IRR_rot_spring 
*(https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/irrlicht/demo_IRR_rot_spring.cpp).

--Radu

Shubhankar,

There is no “API” for that. You will need to implement your own template for a custom driveline that has the desired behavior.  You can look at the ones already available in Chrono.

I am not sure what you mean by “pinning the wheels on the same side”.  If you mean enforcing that they always have the same angular velocity, then you probably need to design a mechanism that enforces that.

But at the end of the day, you have to distribute the torque coming from the powertrain to all wheels.   A template such as ChShaftsDriveline4WD accomplishes that through a mechanism constructed with Chrono’s 1D shaft elements.  A template such as ChSimpleDriveline does that by splitting the torque and applying it directly to the 4 wheel axles (front-left, front-right, rear-left, rear-right).

I suggest you start with something similar to ChSimpleDriveline and simply change the logic for the torque splitting (so that you apply the same torque to both left wheels and to both right wheels, with a left/right split based upon the steering input).  You would do that in your override of the Synchronize method.

--Radu

Hi Shubhankar,

Chrono::Vehicle does not explicitly support skid steer vehicles (well, except tracked vehicles), but almost all pieces are available for you to model your own.

A related example is in demo_VEH_ArticulatedVehicle<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/tree/develop/src/demos/vehicle/articulated_vehicle> which models a vehicle with an articulated chassis.

But you are probably thinking of something like a Bobcat skid steer loader?  In that case, you can use a rigid axle<https://api.projectchrono.org/wheeled_suspension.html#wheeled_suspension_ChRigidSuspension> on the front and a rigid pinned axle<https://api.projectchrono.org/wheeled_suspension.html#wheeled_suspension_ChRigidPinnedAxle> on the rear. The only missing piece is then a driveline that mechanically links the wheels on the same side.  A simple custom model for such a driveline is easy to implement.

Maksim,

The contact frame (and hence the contact normal) is a geometric property 
of the interaction of two collision shapes, not of an individual 
shape. As illustrated in the attached image, the direction of the 
normal is "from shape A to shape B", which means that, relative to one 
of the bodies involved in the contact, it can be toward or away from the 
body, depending on whether that body is first or second for the purpose 
of that collision.

The "order" of shapes is given by the last two arguments to the function 
OnReportContact:

virtual bool OnReportContact(
  const ChVector<>& pA, ///< contact pA
  const ChVector<>& pB, ///< contact pB
  const ChMatrix33<>& plane_coord, ///< contact plane coordsystem (A 
column 'X' is contact normal)
  const double& distance, ///< contact distance
  const double& eff_radius, ///< effective radius of curvature 
at contact
  const ChVector<>& react_forces, ///< react.forces (if already 
computed). In coordsystem 'plane_coord'
  const ChVector<>& react_torques, ///< react.torques, if rolling 
friction (if already computed).
  ChContactable* contactobjA, ///< model A (note: some containers may 
not support it and could be nullptr)
  ChContactable* contactobjB ///< model B (note: some containers may 
not support it and could be nullptr)
) = 0;

So the X axis of the rotation matrix plane_coord (i.e. its first column, 
which you can obtain as plane_coord->Get_A_Xaxis()) will point from 
contactobjA toward contactobjB. In other words, if the shapes overlap

Maksim,

If I understand correctly what you want to do, then using the reporting 
capabilities of the Chrono contact container is indeed the solution. 
This is what Milad alluded to, but you should not have to create a new 
contact container; instead, you should use the one already associated 
with your Chrono system.

Look at the programs demo_IRR_callbackNSC and demo_IRR_callbackSMC for 
simple demonstrations of this capability. In a nutshell, what you want 
to do is write your own reporter class, derived from 
ChContactContainer::ReportContactCallback and implement the virtual 
function OnReportContact. When you ask the system (see below) to report 
contacts at any given time, your OnReportContact will be called once for 
each contact that exists at that time. The information you receive 
through its arguments will allow you to check if the current contact is 
one you care about (e.g., by checking if the "contactable" objects are 
those you want) and obtain information about the geometry of the 
collision, including the contact points on the two shapes (expressed in 
the global frame) and the 'contact frame' (also expressed in the global 
frame) whose X-axis is the contact normal direction.

Since MyReporter below is your own class, it can have any additional 
state (member variables) you might need to keep track of the particular 
contact you're interested in and/or perform any actions you want.

Once you have this user-defined class, you can invoke it at any time

Subject: Re: [chrono] Object with mass but no inertia
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 28 Apr 2017 14:53:29 +0200

hi Giovanni,

you _cannot _discard the rotational DOFs by using zero inertia, 
somewhere in Chrono guts this will end in division by zero.

Actually, if you want to discard rotational DOFs (ex particles that does 
not roll) the process should be opposite, setting very high (->infinite) 
inertia - although some solvers such as Barzilai-Borwein or APGD might 
have troubles also in such case.

Otherwise, avoid the ChBody object: in fact there is an object with no 
rotational DOFs: it is the ChFEANodeXYZ that is used also for 
tetrahedral meshes. It cannot have a collision or visualization shape 
assigned to it, though.

Alessandro
