Chances are that there is some CMake cruft that has gathered from the
initial `cmake src`. One way to clean this up is to run the following,
which will wipe out all changes in the repo and remove any untracked files,
restoring it to a pristine state:

    git clean -d -x -f -f ; git reset --hard # https://git.io/vaGgI

After running that, create a build directory (so it's easier to clean up
afterwards) and run CMake from inside there.

    $ git clone https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono.git
    $ mkdir chrono/build && cd chrono/build
    $ cmake .. # or `ccmake ..` if you want to configure some options
    $ make -j $(nproc)

It is a bit confusing that you have to use the top level dir instead of the
`src` dir as the CMake source dir. It also might be safe to finally
deprecate the `FindModernCXX` that CMake was complaining about - that file
is just a polyfill for people running ancient versions of CMake. I'll file
a PR this weekend if I have time. I'll also try to write some build
instructions for Arch/Debian/FreeBSD/Fedora/CentOS if I have time.

text:
Subject: Significant change in the Chrono 'develop' branch
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 12 Feb 2016 11:15:28 +0100

Dear Chrono users,

Just wanted to give you the heads up about a recent push to the 
'develop' branch of the Chrono GitHub repository which will definitely 
affect your own programs that use Chrono.  These changes relate to 
switching from our own implementation of smart pointers to the C++11 
std::shared_ptr.  The classes ChSharedPtr and ChSmartPtr were replaced 
throughout with std::shared_ptr.   The class ChShared was obsoleted.

Updating your programs to reflect these Chrono API changes should be 
relatively straightforward.  Please do not hesitate to contact us on 
this mailing list with any questions you might have.

I listed below a short set of conversion suggestions/hints (just the 
very basics, hopefully enough for most cases).

Best regards,
Radu


-----------------------------------

  * Types:
    OLD:
    ChSharedPtr<Foo>
    NEW:
    std::shared_ptr<Foo>

  * Constructors:
    OLD:
         ChSharedPtr<Foo> my_var(new Foo(arg1, arg2));
    NEW:
    auto my_var = std::make_shared<Foo>(arg1, arg2);
         or
    std::shared_ptr<Foo> my_var(new Foo(arg1, arg2));

  * Copy constructors
    OLD:
       ChSharedPtr<Foo>  var1;
          ChSharedPtr<Foo> var2(var1);
          ChSharedPtr<Foo> var3 = ChSharedPtr<Foo>(var1);
    NEW:
    std::shared_ptr<Foo> var1;
         std::shared_ptr<Foo> var2(var1);
         auto var3 = std::shared_ptr<Foo>(var1);

  * Casting
    OLD:
       ChSharedPtr<Foo>  var1;
         ChSharedPtr<Bar> var2 = var1.DynamicCastTo<Bar>();

Subject: Re: Loading files
From: Shig_T
Date: Tue, 9 Aug 2016 23:50:40 -0700 (PDT)

Hello Jonathan,

I cannot say for certain, but I suspect that there is possibility of a 
stack overflow.
Your four arrays(posx, posy, posz and radius) eat about 4 * 70322 * 8bytes 
= 2.25MB of memories in total, assuming that sizeof(double) == 8.
This can be large enough to exceed limit of stack size, depending on your 
environment (for example, the stack size defaults to 1MB in VisualStudio).

Anyway, I prefer to use some container such as std::vector instead of array 
for huge amount of data.
In this case, you might want to replace double posx[nspheres] with std::vector<double> 
posx(nspheres) etc. 
Then you don't have to worry about stack size since std::vector does not 
allocate data on stack but on free-store.

By the way, It seems that your particles are rigid spheres of uniform 
density.
If so, it may be worth to consider using ChBodyEasySphere rather than 
ChBody.

Sincerely,
Shig

every now and then, it may be good to wipe your build tree and 
reconfigure from scratch (so that you do not carry around in your cache 
obsolete variables).

Once the CMake build system is stable, it will be safe to simply use 
cmake like you do.

text:
Subject: Re: DEM-E, Crash during the simulation
From: Ruochun Zhang
Date: Wed, 31 Jul 2024 08:07:05 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Wenxuan,

1. Right now, the analytical boundaries in DEME are solids with infinite 
(directional) thickness. If you want a surface that has no thickness, you 
have to use a mesh. DEME comes with a 20 by 20 surface mesh in the file 
*plane_20by20.obj*. But be careful when using it, as it is still 
directional and you don't want particles to approach it from the back side. 
You can also scale *cube.obj* if you want a volume mesh.

2. Yes, the Rayleigh criterion is a good method to use. You may also have 
to empirically adjust it after selecting an initial value using the 
Rayleigh criterion. Based on your description, the cause might not be the 
step size. If the simulation does not immediately crash, then you can 
output the scenes with a high fps. The tens of frames before the crash 
should give you a good idea of what happened. I still bet it's the 
quality/correctness of the mesh.

Ruochun

Subject: Re: DEM-E, Crash during the simulation
From: Ruochun Zhang
Date: Tue, 30 Jul 2024 22:49:48 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Wenxuan,

Since you have 2 spheres but each sphere had more than 200 contacts, it 
could be one of the two causes...

1. Please check your overall box domain (*InstructBoxDomainDimension*) is 
larger than the geometry you have. If it is smaller, internally the contact 
detection may behave incorrectly.

2. The particles may be traveling at unusually large velocity so too many 
potential contacts with the mesh facets are detected, a.k.a. *"the 
simulation may have diverged and relaxing the physics may help"*. It might 
be related to the way how you are rendering the mesh, but to me, the mesh 
appears to have a suspicious texture. Can you show us if the inner wall of 
the mesh has a correct inward normal direction? This is important as the 
mesh--sphere contact in DEME is directional and if the normal is flipped, 
upon contact with the mesh, the spheres will be ejected with high velocity.

Thank you,
Ruochun

everything should be working fine.

One other note: just the heads up, we will eventually move all test*** 
programs out of the main Chrono repository, into the chrono-projects 
repository (also a public repository on GitHub).

Radu

Subject: Re: Changes to public API
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 7 Feb 2017 04:08:12 -0800 (PST)

A follow-up set of changes:  I switched to using strongly typed enum 
classes for the ChSolver and ChTimestepper types.  Here are the 
consequences of these changes:

   - Refer to a solver type like *ChSolver::Type::MINRES*
   - Refer to a timestepper type like *ChTimestepper::Type::HHT*

For users of Chrono::Python

   - Because of a bug in previous SWIG versions (as recent as 3.0.8), you 
   must use a newer release (*SWIG-3.0.12* was verified to work fine)
   - In Python code, refer to a solver type like 
   *chrono.ChSolver.Type_MINRES* (note how Python mangles in the name of 
   the strongly typed enum class)

--Radu


On Sunday, February 5, 2017 at 12:26:00 PM UTC+1, Radu Serban wrote:

text:
Subject: Changes to public API
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 5 Feb 2017 12:25:43 +0100

Dear Chrono users,

For consistency internally and across our public API, I pushed a set of 
changes that will very likely affect your own projects (if/when you pull 
the latest code from the 'develop' branch in GitHub).

Below is a summary of the changes and their impact on the public API.  
You can also look at how I updated the various demos, tests, and 
examples in the Chrono repository.

Please let me know if you encounter any issues related to this.

--Radu


*ChSystem*

  * Replaced raw pointers with shared_ptr for the member variables
    holding the solver, timestepper, system descriptor, and collision
    system objects.

  * The above affect the signature of related setter/getter methods

  * For consistency, renamed some ChSystem functions:
    ChangeSolverSpeed -> SetSolver
    ChangeSolverStab -> SetStabSolver
    GetSolverSpeed -> GetSolver
    GetSolverStab -> GetStabSolver
    ChangeCollisionSystem -> SetCollisionSystem
    SetIntegrationType -> SetTimestepperType
    GetIntegrationType -> GetTimestepperType
    ChangeContactContainer -> SetContactContainer

  * Move the enum definitions for solver types from ChSystem to ChSolver.
    These enum variables do not have the prefix "SOLVER_" anymore.
    To refer to a particular solver type (e.g., in calling the function
    ChSystem::SetSolverType), use for example ChSolver::MINRES (instead
    of the old ChSystem::SOLVER_MINRES).

  * Move enum definitions for timestepper types from ChSystem to
    ChTimestepper.
    These enum variables do not have the prefix "INT_" anymore.

*ChBody*

  * Replaced raw pointer with shared_ptr for the member variable holding
    the collision model.

  * The above affects the signature of SetCollisionModel and
    GetCollisionModel

  * For consistency, renamed ChBody function:
    ChangeCollisionModel -> SetCollisionModel

  * Note: lower-level functions (e.g., ChCollisionSystem::Add still use

*Chrono::Parallel*

    NARROWPHASETYPE -> NarrowPhaseType

Hello,

As for the second issue, the cause is that you are confusing member 
variables with local variables.
For example, see the code starting from line 97:

auto my_link_tlf = std::make_shared<ChLinkEngine>();
my_link_tlf->Initialize(trunk, leglf, ChCoordsys<>(ChVector<>(1.9, 0.6, 
1.1)));
my_link_tlf->Set_eng_mode(ChLinkEngine::ENG_MODE_SPEED);
app->GetSystem()->AddLink(my_link_tlf);

At this point, my_link_tlf doesn't point the member variable of MyBeetle; 
it is a local variable you declared here.
Hence member variables remain uninitialized and cause undefined behavior 
when you access them later.
Same things for other links (and bodies).

An easy solution here is to remove auto specifier.
In addition, there are also some general practices to avoid such confusion 
you made; use this-> notation when accessing members, append some prefix or 
suffix to member variable name, etc.

I'm not sure about the first issue, maybe some parameter tunings are 
required?
Changing the solver or increasing max solver iterations may help.

Sincerely,
Shig

Subject: Re: [chrono] About the ChLinkLockLock
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 18 Aug 2016 15:22:06 +0200

hi,

this kind of 'softness' of constraints might happen with the default 
SOLVER_SOR when there is a large mass ratio (or size ratio) between two 
connected parts, which might be your case.

To fix this problem you must

- either increase the number of iterations in the solver, ex:

application.GetSystem()->SetMaxItersSolverSpeed(120);

- and/or use a better solver. My suggestion is to use:

application.GetSystem()->SetSolverType(ChSystem::SOLVER_*BARZILAIBORWEIN*);
application.GetSystem()->SetMaxItersSolverSpeed(40);

Might be a bit slower, but more precise than the default.

Alessandro Tasora

Hi Sumaiya,

First, about the error you got for Part3, yes it's about running out of 
VRAM, thus a bad_alloc error. Again, I really suggest trying a 
smaller-sized simulation for a more reasonable runtime.

About reading CSV files into the solver, first let me say that it is not a 
part of the core functionalities of DEME, and what we are discussing here 
is really about a small auxiliary tool that somehow went wrong. The 
contact_pairs file here records the contacts existing at the end of the 
previous simulation. It's a piece of info many users need in their 
research, understandably; but here in Part2, we are just reading a 
checkpoint file to "restart" the simulation, and the contact pairs file is 
in fact not strictly necessarily, because even if you don't notify the 
solver the "old" existing contacts, the solver will figure them out once 
the simulation starts (still, it's not 100% the same, as in this case the 
solver thinks they are new contacts and loses all history info, such as 
contact persistent time, but this effect is minor). You could even comment 
out the *Contact_pairs_3e5*-related four lines, and it should still run.

Now, about geoA or A, geoB or B, they mean the contact entity ID in each 
contact (each line in that file records a contact). DEME uses generic data 
storage formats such as CSV, so as CSV header names, geoA or A does not 
matter and you can change them (to anything, in fact). It's just that the 
small utility, *ReadContactPairsFromCsv*, assumes the column names are geoA

The first is a comment. If you are indeed targeting hundreds of millions of 
particles, one full simulation can easily take days or months. So be 
cautious.

About reducing the number of particles generated in GRC_Part1 and 2: You 
could try modifying the *scales *vector. Just enlarge every number therein 
by a factor. This should generate proportionally larger particles, thus 
reducing the total number. An even better way is to simply generate 
particles (and optionally save them to a file to reuse later, like you see 
in *SlopeSlip* and *DP* tests) like how *WheelDPsimplified *did. This way, 
you don't generate the extremely small particles compared to the "full" GRC 
representations, which I believe sacrifices some expressiveness but 
dramatically reduces the computational cost.

Hi Sumaiya,

First I'd like to address the window-closes-immediately problem. You 
probably double-clicked the executable to run it, so when it crashes for 
some reason, the window closes, giving you no chance to see the error 
messages. You should try opening a command line prompt (PowerShell) first, 
then launch the executable there for the window to hold. It gives us a 
better chance of understanding what happened.

DEME is more tested on Linux, but I wouldn't say I strongly recommend Linux 
- I just recommend Linux. On Windows, it should still run correctly, I just 
don't know much about its efficiency. But if you do consider using Linux, 
maybe start with WSL2, it's quick to pick up for Windows users.

Back to the problem you had, based on the runtime you got for part1, 
perhaps you have a gaming card released some years back? Maybe a 2070? It 
could seriously have VRAM shortage for running part3, but perhaps fine for 
part2. Or the problem could just be that somehow it failed to load the 
GRC_XXX input file. We shall see when we have the error message. But since 
this is the hardware you have, if you are interested in DEM terramechanics, 
you could try *WheelDPSimplified*. The terrain representation there is much 
cheaper to run, and offers relatively comparable results to the more 
expensive terrain you just tried.

Part2 and 3 should generate separate output files.

Thank you,
Ruochun

Hello Zach,

Thank you for attaching your source code. It helps very well.

In short, modify line 216-217 as follows (in this way, 
*marker->Setname("link_ee")* is not necessary):

ChIrrTools::drawSegment(application.GetVideoDriver(), 
my_link_BC->GetMarker1()->GetAbsCoord().pos,
*my_marker_link1ee->GetAbsCoord().pos*, video::SColor(255, 255, 0, 0));

or:
if (*auto marker = my_body_C->SearchMarker("link_ee")*) {
ChIrrTools::drawSegment(application.GetVideoDriver(), 
my_link_BC->GetMarker1()->GetAbsCoord().pos,
*marker->GetAbsCoord().pos*, video::SColor(255, 255, 0, 0));
}
then both ways should work fine.

The reason why your code didn't work is, I say again, that *ChBody *doesn't 
have such a member.
In the following code, You're trying to find the marker named 
*my_marker_link1ee* from *inside* of *ChBody*:

my_body_c->my_marker_link1ee

The identifier *my_marker_link1ee* is declared *outside* of *ChBody*, *not 
inside**.*
Even you added the marker into the body, the identifier of the marker is no 
longer available inside of the body.
I hope it makes sense.

Sincerely,
Shig

These are the steps and changes I followed for installing chrono engine 
with modules FEA, FSI, PARALLEL, IRRLICHT and POSTPROCES. I post it becasue 
I think it may be useful for other people with a Mac machine. In my case I 
used a Mac with osx 10.10.2 (Yosemite) and Homebrew installed: 

1. Install openmp: 
$ brew install clang-omp 

2. Install boost 1.61.0 by typing from installation folder: 
$    ./bootstrap.sh 
$    ./b2 

3. Install blaze 2.2. Indicate right folders in file Configfile. In my 
case: 
BOOST_INCLUDE_PAT=/Users/munoz/code/Chronos/boost_1_61_0 
BOOST_LIBRARY_PATH=/Users/munoz/code/Chronos/boost_1_61_0/stage/lib 
BOOST_SYSTEM_LIBRARY=/Users/munoz/code/Chronos/boost_1_61_0/stage/lib 
BOOST_THREAD_LIBRARY=/Users/munoz/code/Chronos/boost_1_61_0/stage/lib 
MPI="yes" 
MPI_INCLUDE_PATH=/usr/local/opt/open-mpi/include 

Then just type make in installation folder and copy library in 
blaze-2.2/lib into /usr/local/lib 

4. Install Irrlicht 1.8.3 
Required XCode. In my case version 6.4 for MacOS 10.10.2. 
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/10335747/how-to-download-xcode-4-5-6-7-and-get-the-dmg-file 
http://www.irrlicht3d.org/wiki/index.php?n=Main.CompilingOnMacOSX 

Need to add in Makefile CXXFLAGS flag -ObjC++ (in order to recognise Mac 
Object-C++ and not only C++). See: 
https://github.com/openframeworks/openFrameworks/issues/2406 
and also force other variables to compile MacOSx. In total: 
CXXFLAGS += -ObjC++

Hi Alessandro,

thanks for the quick response.

*what do you mean for 'non reproductable'? I mean, do you compare the 
results of the constrained modal analysis vs some other software (es 
Abaqus) with same constraints? Or do you compare  constrained vs 
unconstrained, both with Chrono matrices **Because in the second case I am 
not surprised that adding even a simple constraint somewhere in the model 
will change all mode shapes. **Also: is there any redundancy in the 
constraints that you add? I mean, check the rank of Cq....  In case of 
redundancy, depending on the type of eigen solver, you may still get 
results but those will be unreliable.*

With non reproducable I mean that when I repeat the exact same simulation 
in CHRONO (that includes constraints) I get different results (modeshapes 
and frequencies). I just used three constrains without any redundancy.

I think that I found the main reason for the error that I experienced. 
During the simulation (at each timestep) I was modifying the constrained 
DOF via the SetConstrainedCoords() function. Then calles ChSystem->Update; 
ChSystem->Setup and exported the matrices from the ChSystem via the 
Get...Matrix functions. I modified the constraints to get a "fixed" rotor 
in the modal analysis from the "free" that rotates during the simulation to 
get the rotationally augmented frequencies (the fixed rotor is required to 
get certain modeshapes). Changing the constrained DOF at the rotor, then

in the modal analysis from the "free" that rotates during the simulation to 
get the rotationally augmented frequencies (the fixed rotor is required to 
get certain modeshapes). Changing the constrained DOF at the rotor, then 
updating the system and exporting the matrices, and then changing the 
constrained DOF back for the next timestep caused the issues that I was 
experiencing. I got the feeling that maybe not all matrices were updated in 
time as I sometimes also had crashes occur when calling the Get...Matrix 
functions directly after the calls to Update() and Setup().

*Yes, but those should not interfere. Each row in the jacobian is 'almost' 
normalized, in most constraints, so numbers usually range in the -1...+1 
interval. Probably, if the issues you get are due to numerical troubles 
with iterative solvers for eigenproblems (are you using Lanczos?) then it 
could be that the norm of the jacobian Cq is too large or too small respect 
to the values in M or K. In theory the norm of Cq should not change free 
eigenvalues, but in practice it happens that the numerical iterative 
eigensolver could crawl to the solution with more difficulty; therefore: 
try to pre-multiply or post-multiply the jacobian by some scaling and see 
what happens.*

Thanks for this suggestion. I tried pre-scaling the Cq matrix and could see 
an effect on the resulting mode shapes and frequencies. I'll see if I can 
get better results using the scaling!

Again, thanks a lot for your help and your suggestions!

Dear all,

I wrote in this forum a few months ago when I was successfully using CHRONO 
to develop a structural model for the wind turbine simulation code QBlade. 
I have not touched my code for a while but recently went back to work on 
the modal analysis functionality. 

To solve the Eigenvalue problem I use the GetMassMatrix, 
GetConstraintJacobianMatrix(&Cq), etc... functions from the CHSystem class 
to get the matrices. The the A and B matrices for the generalized 
eigenvalue problem are constructed and I use the LAPACK GEP function to 
solve.

Generally the resulting frequencies and modeshapes look reasonable - but 
the problem is that they are not reproducable, sometimes "new" modes emerge 
and frequencies are shifted when I use constraints in my model (using the 
exact same boundary conditions). As soon as I remove the constraints the 
resulting modelshapes and frequencies are fully reproducable again.I looked 
into the Cq matrix, that I got from the ChSystem and observed that many 
values are very small (up to 1E-37). 

Could a floating point error be the problem here? I guess that the modal 
analysis is very sensitive to small changes withing the input matrices.
Do you have any other Idea what the problem could be and how to possibly 
fix this? Or is there an inbuild alternative to constraints in CHRONO (that 
also allows to leave certain DOF "unconstrained")?

Thanks and kind regards,

David

Subject: RE: [chrono] Question wrt model definition rationale
From: Dan Negrut
Date: Thu, 01 Sep 2016 15:29:03 +0000

Hi Frank,
There is a long story behind it, but here’s how I see it.
We don’t have the bandwidth to do something like that.  We cannot be ADAMS ☺. And we are not trying to be ADAMS. Chrono is an open source code that people can use both for practical purposes (real-world problems) but also for research purposes.
Being open source, you can write a small driver and define  your model in C++ or Python and keep using it afterwards - compile the code once, and then use your own customized Chrono version over and over again.

Note that you can pre-generate  your model in SolidWorks and import in Chrono,  in case that something like this is useful.

One more point – you mentioned that you are interested in flex body dynamics. Just a FYI, there is support for ANCF and co-rotational formulations for beams, shells, and volumetric elements. This goes back to work that Hiroyuki Sugiyama at University of Iowa and Alessandro Tasora at University of Parma did over the last two years. In several days Antonio Recuero is going to publish a tech report that shows how an ANCF tire rolls over granular terrain. In other words, the these two nonlinear FEA formulations are working w/ friction and contact.

I hope this helps.

Thank you for your interest in Chrono,
Dan

Subject: Re: [chrono] Creation of complex terrains for multibody simulation
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 16 Mar 2016 13:42:23 +0100

Hi Steve,

Indeed, the RigidTerrain class allows creating an (obviously rigid) 
terrain surface with geometry specified in one of the following three ways:

  * a box with given x and y extents and the top (i.e. the driving
    surface) at a given height)
  * a triangular mesh read from a Wavefront OBJ file
  * a height map, specified through a BMP file -- in this case a
    tri-mesh is generated under the hood by interpreting the gray level
    in the provided BMP as heights

Look at demo_HMMWV on how to use any of the above three options (you can 
control which type of terrain is used by setting the variable 
terrain_model to one of RigidTerrain::FLAT, RigidTerrain::MESH, or 
RigidTerrain::HEIGHT_MAP).

Please let me know if you have problems or additional questions.
Thanks,
Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] instability
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Sun, 02 Mar 2014 11:20:40 +0100

dear Stephane,
    the simulation looks strange indeed, if the cylinder is passive 
(free cylinder sliding joint, ex. ChLinkLockCylindrical ) , it should 
not move.
Possible causes:

- Maybe you are using overconstrained systems (ie. iperstatic). In C::E 
there are no problems with iperstatic joints as long as they are 
aligned, but small misalignments might cause unwanted effects, depending 
on the type of solver.

- solver type: the default LCP solver in C::E is an iterative SOR / SSOR 
method that is good for real-time problems but it converges slowly when 
using odd mass ratios, ex. when simulating complex machinery. So an 
option is to switch to a slower but more convergent solver, ex. the 
projected Barzilai-Borwein, as in :
my_system.SetLcpSolverType(ChSystem::LCP_ITERATIVE_BARZILAIBORWEIN);
(Btw note that there is also an experimental 
ChSystem::LCP_ITERATIVE_PMINRES  new solver that converges even better 
than LCP_ITERATIVE_BARZILAIBORWEIN, although in special cases the 
convergence is not guaranteed - stay tuned for news)

- increasing max solver iteration count and enabling warm starting can 
help. For example:
     my_system.SetIterLCPwarmStarting(true);
     my_system.SetIterLCPmaxItersSpeed(200);

- timestep: of course too large timestep can cause problems.

- stepper type: currently there are two timestepping schemes, the 
default one is INT_ANITESCU, that solves a single LCP per timestep, and 
position errors (drifts) in joints are corrected by a stabilization 
term. You can try the alternative
symbol: Re: [chrono] instability

text:
default one is INT_ANITESCU, that solves a single LCP per timestep, and 
position errors (drifts) in joints are corrected by a stabilization 
term. You can try the alternative
    my_system.SetIntegrationType(ChSystem::INT_TASORA);
that solves 2 LCP per timestep, the first for unknown speeds and 
reactions, and the second for correcting position errors in joints. This 
is a bit slower but more precise in case of articulated systems.

- finally, another cause might be that in your case, the initial 
position&rotation of the cylinder/lever system is not perfectly 
satysfying some of the constraints, so a small impulse is created in the 
first step to 'assembly' everything and some parts get some momentum.

keep me updated,

Alessandro

Subject: Re: [chrono] Running Chrono without GUI
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 6 Oct 2016 16:46:00 +0200

Hi Jonathan,

Chrono does not have a GUI.  Rather, it consists of a collection of 
middle-ware libraries and the user is responsible for writing a driver 
program that calls into these libraries.

If you're asking about running a Chrono program without visualization, 
that is also possible.  You just do not construct the visualization 
object (whether Irrlicht or OpenGL).   Look at the demo_buildsystem 
example program distributed with Chrono. This program constructs and 
simulates a slider-crank mechanism without any visualization (it only 
prints out some state information to the terminal after each integration 
time step).

--Radu

hi Shig,

yes you are right - the ChLink class did not overload the Update() 
function of base class ChPhysicsItem, so you could not use your custom 
ChAsset for springs.

By the way, you had a good idea about drawing springs using assets - 
this is something I always postponed until I'd have had some spare time

serious stuff, as you correctly noticed. Tell me if your 'spring asset'

in red:


void ChLink::Update(double time, bool update_assets) {
     // 1 -
     UpdateTime(time);

*// This will update assets**
**    ChPhysicsItem::Update(time, update_assets);*
}


Does this fix the problem? If so, I'll submit this to the GIT.

Thanks for the feedback

Alessandro

Subject: Re: [chrono] Symmetrical .OBJ file
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Mon, 15 Aug 2016 19:30:18 +0200

Hi Soowon,

possible solutions:

- accept that Irrlicht 3D view is mirrored on X (note: only Irrlicht3D 
is left handed! all the internal coordinates of Chrono are right 
handed,so it is just a visualization issue).

- if you save the stream of .bmp screenshots from the Irrlicht view, 
later you can mirror them on X when you assembly them into an animation 
using for instance Adobe Premiere or VirtualDub (those tools can mirror 
the video easily).

- use the POVray rendering, from the POSTPROCESSING module, it has the 
correct right handed coordinate system - although this is not for 
real-time viewing.

In all cases I'd _avoid_ the trick of modifying the input .obj mesh so 
that it is mirrored and it 'looks ok' in Irrlicht. I did this in the 
past and it led to some headaches later (it might confuse you when 
adding constraints etc.).

If I had spare time I'd try to modify the Irrlicht module so that the 
camera has right handed perspective, but I'm sorry this is not on my top 
to-do list right now. If you look at 
http://irrlicht.sourceforge.net/forum/viewtopic.php?f=4&t=47734 someone 
already tried to fix this, but it causes non trivial issues with mesh 
backface culling, to be fixed as well.

best regards

Alessandro Tasora

Subject: Re: [chrono] Compression of particles (Collision model)
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 23 Aug 2017 11:05:13 +0200

Hi Rashnith,

The chrono-projects repository is set up as a collection of 
"third-party" applications that use Chrono functionality. They assume 
you already have Chrono built and installed. Different programs in 
'chrono-projects' expect different Chrono modules to have been enabled 
when Chrono was built. Some of them indeed expect that Chrono::Parallel 
functionality will be available. Others expect other modules. If you 
use CMake to configure the projects in the 'chrono-projects' repository, 
that should take care of checking what modules are available in your 
installation of Chrono and configure only a subset of the existing 
programs (and issue warnings about those that require functionality not 
present in your Chrono install).

Alternatively, you can of course just copy one of those programs from 
'chrono-projects' into your own Chrono source tree and build it together 
with the Chrono libraries and demos. But in this case also, if that 
particular program uses Chrono::Parallel functionality, then you must 
enable that module when you configure and build Chrono.

Radu

Rashnith,

When I suggested using a linear actuator, I failed to think of your 
desired application... This will not work for what you need because 
you effectively constrain the lid to move at a certain position, 
conflicting with the contact constraints. Compressing granular material 
with a lid constrained to move at a constant velocity is not a 
well-posed problem.

The simplest solution I can suggest is to remove that linear actuator 
(but not the translational joint) and make the lid heavy enough, so that 
it compresses the granular material under its own weight.

Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Compression of particles (Collision model)
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 19 Aug 2017 11:15:07 +0200

Rashnith,

You could connect the lid body to ground using a translational joint 
(ChLinkLockPrismatic), properly oriented, so that the lid has only a 
vertical translation degree of freedom.

In addition, to impose a constant velocity on the lid body, also include 
a linear actuator (ChLinkLinActuator) and set its distance function to a 
ramp function (ChFunction_Ramp) with slope equal to the desired velocity.

For an example of this combination, albeit for a different purpose, look 
in the 'chrono_projects' repository at the RigNode.cpp file 
(https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono-projects/blob/develop/projects/cosimulation/test_tireRig_cosimulation/RigNode.cpp), 
and see how m_prism_vel (the prismatic joint) and m_lin_actuator (the 
linear actuator) are created and set (lines 244-258 and 376-382).

By the way, the 'chrono_projects' public GitHub repository contains 
several more complex examples that may be useful as illustrations of 
Chrono use.

Hope that this helps,
--Radu

Subject: Changes to Chrono::Vehicle API
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 11 Sep 2016 23:19:56 +0200

Hello,

I wanted to let the users of Chrono::Vehicle know of some recent changes 
that affect the public API:

1.  Introduced a "chassis" subsystem.
Previously, data for chassis inertial properties and visualization 
information was maintained on the (derived) vehicle classes.  For 
consistency, this is now done through classes derived from ChChassis.

Any vehicle now has a chassis.  From an API point of view, this 
introduces an additional layer of indirection.  However, for 
convenience, several wrapper methods are provided at the ChVehicle level 
to access ChChassis members (e.g. ChVehicle::GetChassisBody())

2. Changed the mechanism for specifying visualization assets for vehicle 
subsystems.
For consistency, all vehicle subsystems are now derived from ChPart 
which provides the virtual methods for managing visualization assets. 
With the new mechanism it is now possible to change a subsystem's 
visualization on the fly (e.g., enable/disable visualization or change 
the visualization mode).

 From an API point of view, the main change is that the visualization 
mode (NONE, PRIMITIVES, MESH) must be specified only *after* 
initialization of the subsystem, using ChPart::SetVisualizationType().  
For convenience, derived vehicle classes (ChWheeledVehicle and 
ChTrackedVehicle) provide wrapper classes to control the visualization 
mode of their constituent parts.

3. Changed API for specifying contact material parameters for rigid 
tires and rigid terrain.
For consistency across Chrono::Vehicle, parameters for contact materials
symbol: Changes to Chrono::Vehicle API

text:
3. Changed API for specifying contact material parameters for rigid 
tires and rigid terrain.
For consistency across Chrono::Vehicle, parameters for contact materials 
are specified through the set of methods SetContactFrictionCoefficient, 
SetContactRestitutionCoefficient, SetContactMaterialProperties, and 
SetContactMaterialCoefficients (the latter two pertinent only for the 
penalty contact method).


See the various Chrono::Vehicle demos (in src/demos/vehicle/) for usage 
of the new API.  Please let me know of any issues with these changes.

--Radu

From: Tingnan Zhang
Date: Fri, 1 Aug 2014 16:36:10 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Prof. Negrut:

Those Matrix would better be class members to avoid dynamic allocation at 
every time step. 

Further more, I believe ChMatrixDynamic class could also benefit from 
similar design of stl containers.  The matrix could reserve() more spaces 
than its used column * row, by using book keeping variables: 
column_actual_size and row_actual_size.  And the reserved space can grow 
faster than linear (e.g. doubled) each time the function reserve is called. 

BTW, there is a well constructed, fast c++ matrix library, as many of you 
probably already know:

http://arma.sourceforge.net/speed.html 

I wonder if this is potentially beneficial for C::E.

Tingnan

text:
Subject: Chrono: allocating & deallocating large arrays
From: Dan Negrut
Date: Mon, 28 Jul 2014 15:34:49 -0500

I'm looking at the APGD solver (but I bet the other solvers are like this as
well) and see that each time we hit APGD we do this:

 
                ChMatrixDynamic<> mx(nc,1);

                ChMatrixDynamic<> ms(nc,1);

                ChMatrixDynamic<> my(nc,1);

                ChMatrixDynamic<> ml_candidate(nc,1);

                ChMatrixDynamic<> mg(nc,1);

                ChMatrixDynamic<> mg_tmp(nc,1);

                ChMatrixDynamic<> mg_tmp1(nc,1);

                ChMatrixDynamic<> mg_tmp2(nc,1);

                ChMatrixDynamic<> mb_tmp(nc,1);

 
Indeed, the number of contacts changes from step to step but I believe
allocating and deallocating large arrays comes at a pretty steep price.

What do you think of simply making these guys members of the APGD solver
class and potentially resizing them if the size is not too big?

We might waste a bit of space, yet I believe it'll save us a lot of time
since especially for large systems (3D printing example, more than 2 million
contacts) we take step-sizes of 1E-5. This might also explain why we need
one week to finish a 3D printing simulation.

 
Dan

connectivity

plotting of contact normals, and see where are contacts, if something 
goes wrong you can understand it here.

text:
Subject: Re: Fwd: Re: [chrono] Forced motion using a ChMarker
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Sat, 25 Oct 2014 17:12:28 +0200

Justin:  I suppose Kurt wants to impose a motion to a fixed body, and 
what you suggested (->Set_pos() , ->Set_pos_dt() etc.) would do the job 
UNLESS that body is connected to some other body - ex. a pendulum whose 
truss is moving according to Kurt's trajectories-.
If so, the constraint would not work 100% well, because it won't 'feel' 
speeds and acceleration of the fixed body.

So, the proper way to have a 'fixed' body 'B' following some motion, is 
to do this:
1) create a body A, and set it fixed.
2) create a body B, and do NOT set it fixed... it will fall to the 
ground normally, but now you do:
3) create a ChLinkLockLock between A and B. Now body B will stay in 
place as a fixed body, but you do also:
4) use  SetMotion_X() SetMotion_Y() SetMotion_ang() etc. in the 
ChLinkLockLock : this will impose the motion between B and A

Alessandro

From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 17 Oct 2014 13:22:08 +0200

Dear Kurt,


The axis of rotation of the ChLinkLockRevolute  is always the Z axis of 
the marker of the second object, that is also called the 'master' 
marker, as opposed to the 'slave' marker that is on the 1st object. If 
using the ChLinkLockRevolute::Initialize() function, you can pass a 
coordinate system expressed in the absolute frame: this will be used to 
impose the position of the two markers, perfectly overlapped at the 
beginning of the simulaiton. Assume the Z axis of that coordinate system 
is the axis of rotation of the revolute.

No, this was only for constraints that use the ChFunction stuff and 
SetMotion_X() SetMotion_Y() etc.  to impose rotation between two markers 
that do not have relative degreees of freedom. For instance: the 
ChLinkLockLock constraint is like a 'glue' that connects both xyz 
translations and xyz rotations, so one could have a marker rotating 
around the other by setting SetMotion_axis(Vector m_axis) and an 
increasing SetMotion_ang().
(This is one of the oldest parts of code in ChronoEngine so the comments 
in .h file are scarce)

Shortly: the axis of rotation cannot be changed in ChLinkLockRevolute , 
it is always the Z axis of the 2nd marker.

For the SetMotion_axis(Vector m_axis) it was in 2nd marker coordinate - 
although it is not what you need for the revolute joint, as I told you.

this is the coordinate whose Z axis is the revolute joint. Note that 
ChLinkLock::Initialize() can accept a ChCoordsys<> either in aboslute

ChLinkLock::Initialize() can accept a ChCoordsys<> either in aboslute 
coords (that is easier for you, I think) or as two body-relative 
ChCoordsys<>.

ok, those are in 2nd marker frame.

again, those are in 2nd marker frame.
btw The SetLimit_Rp is a limit on the angle of a cone that contains the 
axis of the 1st marker, ex as a shoulder.
Instead, SetLimit_D is a limit on the distance between the origins of

Again this is very old code in C::E with scarce comments in .h, but if

Subject: Re: Limits and axis of rotation for ChLinkLock
From: Justin Madsen
Date: Fri, 17 Oct 2014 03:56:38 -0700 (PDT)

To define an axis of rotation for ChLinkLockRevolute, use smart pointers 
and the methods provided by the ChLinkLock class.
When you call ->Initialize, the axis of rotation is about the global 
z-axis, which can be rotated according to the quaternion in the 
ChCoordSys<> object.
E.g. if you want to joint to rotate about the global y-axis in the intial 
configuration, you can create the proper quaternion by using a static 
function that rotates that global z-axis an angle of pi/2 about the x-axis.
There's also Q_from_NasaAngs() if you need a more complicated rotation.

namespace chrono{

my_rev_joint = ChSharedPtr<ChLinkLockRevolute>(new ChLinkLockRevolute);
ChQuaternion<> rot = Q_from_AngX(CH_C_PI_2);
rev_joint_c_sys = ChCoordSys<>( pos, rot);
my_rev_joint->Initialize( body1, body2, rev_joint_c_sys );


For those SetLimit() functions, I would think that the position or angular 
velocity upper/lower limits are measured w.r.t. the ChLinkMarkers, relM and 
relM_dt, which are the relative position and velocity from the joint marker 
on body 2 to body 1, e.g. r_2 - r_1 and v_2 - v_1.
Take a look at line 1130 in ChLinkLock.cpp: >>  m_force.x= 
limit_X->GetForce(relM.pos.x, relM_dt.pos.x);

I think ChLinkMarkers are expressed with respect to the coordinate system 
on body 2, but I would need Alessandro or someone else with a little more 
experience to verify it to be sure.

Take it easy,
Justin

symbol: Re: Leaf spring model in chrono

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Leaf spring model in chrono
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 2 Jun 2017 10:38:49 +0200

Hi Jacob,

this depends on the level of detail you need.

A - extreme detail: layered leaf springs with contacts between leaves

B - intermediate detail: leaf spring as a beam, maybe of variable 
thickness to account for multiple leaves layered in trapezoidal pattern,

C - low level of diteail: just a vertical stiffness

Assuming you do not need A, I'd go as follows:

for problem B, just use a small numer of beam elements in sequence like 
ChElementBeamEuler or the ChElementBeamANCF, the two at the ends being 
connected with a hinge and a small rocker, and for the intermediate 
elements use different material properties because they represent 
multilayered leaves, so do some back-the-envelope computation to 
understand the equivalent Jxx Jyy Jzz and area of a single setion. Note: 
this means you need the FEA unit, and the MINRES solver (or MKL or MUMPS 
if you want to install them), and this means you can't do non-smooth 
contacts.

for problem A, something I'd do is just using a vertical equivalent 
spring , ex ChSpringCB or such, where the K stiffness changes 
non-linearly according to a lookup table that you pre-compute on a leaf 
spring (experimentally, or numerically). For real-time scenarios, this 
is what I'd do.

have a nice day

Alessandro Tasora

Subject: Re: [chrono] Leaf spring model in chrono
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Mon, 29 Aug 2016 09:58:26 +0200

Hi Arun,

1)

my suggestion is that you use a vertical spring, whose stiffness is 
adjusted to match the leafspring vertical stiffness. Maybe you need 
non-linear stiffness here, as many leaf springs have a tangent stiffness 
which changes a bit with the deflection.

Then, if you need also the effect of the horizontal constraint (which 
should not be needed in many suspension architectures anyway, as it 
depends on auxiliary rods) then you can do this by using a 
ChLinkDistance constraint.

2)

if you need something more detailed, at the cost of higher computational 
times, you can model the leafspring using deformable elements. To this 
end you must compile the FEA module. Then you can use the 
ChElementBeamEuler to model the leaf springs, ex. with 6 elements could 
be enough (each with different size btw) whose Ixx moments of inertia 
are forced to be N*Ixx_i with N= number of leafs at that segment, Ixx_i 
the moment of inertia of a single leaf section (this to avoid modeling 
all leafs separately, that would require also complicate phenomena such 
as contact etc.)

Alessandro

Subject: Rotational Spring element?
From: Justin Madsen
Date: Fri, 2 Jan 2015 08:43:01 -0800 (PST)

Hi all,

I'm looking for something similar to ChLinkSpring,but that uses the angular 
displacement and velocity to determine the reaction spring torque, i.e., a 
rotational spring damper element. Has anyone implemented something similar 
to this?

I have three different options in mind:
1) Create a new class, ChLinkRotSpring, very similar in form to 
ChLinkSpring, but modified for angular rather than translational spring 
displacement. I've already created the class but haven't tested the 
functionality quite yet. 
https://github.com/jcmadsen/chrono/commit/08ad7961fc61171c9ebd986e76550b68c6235624 

2) Use powertrain components, by connecting ChShafts between the two bodies 
using ChShaftsBody and using a ChShaftsTorsionSpring between them. This is 
the most straightforward approach, but carrying around extra ChShaft and 
ChShaftsBody objects is a bit cumbersome and not elegant since the shafts 
don't rotate enough for their inertia to matter.

3) Use a slightly modified ChLinkSpringCB class, adding the functionality 
for a rotational spring to what's already there. This would be slightly 
less work than (1), but since a Rotational-Spring-Damper is a fairly basic 
component, it might not be a good idea to force the user to remember to 
create and pass a callback function to define the spring behavior.

Any ideas or feedback would be appreciated.

Take it easy,
Justin

From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 26 Sep 2014 07:19:34 -0700 (PDT)

Hi, you are right, the FEM elements are not affected by gravity, even if 
you have a non-zero gravity acceleration in ChSystem (that is -9.8 on y by 
default).

Currently, you have to provide a downward force for each FEM node, by 
yourself. I admit this is not very practical, but the FEM code is still in 
development, and I am thinking if it makes sense to wire the gravity to the 
ChSystem setting, or introduce more advanced 'force fields' objects that 
can be used for gravity and other effects too.

Also, about collisions: tetahedrons do not support collision detection yet 
- they simply compenetrate each other like ghosts. This is planned for a 
future release, though.

Alessandro

Subject: Re: [chrono] Building Chrono in Ubuntu
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 22 Dec 2016 11:18:02 +0100

Hi,

This is a problem with the Irrlicht Makefile which results in not being 
able to use the resulting static Irrlicht library for creating the 
shared ChronoIrrlicht library (on 64-bit systems; you wouldn't get this 
error on a 32-bit system).

The solution is suggested right in the error message: you must make sure 
that Irrlicht is compiled with the -fPIC flag.  For this, simply modify 
the Makefile in irrlicht-1.8.2/source/Irrlicht/ to add this flag to both 
CXXFLAGS and CFLAGS (note that this is already done if you build a 
shared Irrlicht library, but not for the default static library).

For more details on what's happening, you can search (for example) 
stackoverflow for "R_X86_64_32S".

Hope that this helps,
--Radu

pushed earlier today.

Side note: this bug was noticeable only with GCC (in debug mode). Visual

the case with the member variable 'container' -- to 0xcdcdcdcd.  This is

passed to the ChContactTuple constructor) and not on 'container' (the 
member variable).

Subject: Re: Series elastic motor (servo motor) and dc motor models
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 29 Oct 2015 14:20:17 +0100

Hi Tingnan,


Currently there is only the ChLinkEngine, that provides some operational 
modes:
ENG_MODE_ROTATION = 0,
ENG_MODE_SPEED,
ENG_MODE_TORQUE,
ENG_MODE_TO_POWERTRAIN_SHAFT,

These represent, in order:
- imposed torque (where torque can be a ChFunction of time)
- imposed position (where angle can be a ChFunction of time)
- imposed speed (where angular speed can be a ChFunction of time)
- connection to a 1D item of ChShaft type. Meanwhile that ChShaft can be 
connected to other ChShafts, ChShaftGear, ChShaftTorque, etc. etc. 
(those ChShaftXxxxxyyy  objects are 1D building blocks like those that 
you find in Amesim or Simulink). Btw.now I see that there is no demo on 
how to use this last mode. Also note that this mode has almost the same 
meaning of adding a ChShaftBody constraint between a rotating body and a 
ChShaft object, part of a driveline, as happens in Chrono Vehicle.

This is not available, currently.
What you could do in the short term is:
- use the ChLinkEngine in torque mode,
- control the torque using a PID that has the position error as input 
and torque as output,
- update the input/output of PID at each simulation step, maybe also 
clamping the torque value as you requested.

Note that there is a basic PID already available in C::E classes.

Of course if you want to reproduce a real electric motor with digital 
control (ex typical brushless servodrive on a fieldbus) you need to 
implement your own C++ 'advanced' controller that does something more
symbol: Re: Series elastic motor (servo motor) and dc motor models

text:
Of course if you want to reproduce a real electric motor with digital 
control (ex typical brushless servodrive on a fieldbus) you need to 
implement your own C++ 'advanced' controller that does something more 
sophisticated than a PID, i.e. do PIV, double PID, filtering, 
anti-windup, feedforward, etc. etc.


In fact, in ROTATION and SPEED mode the torque is a consequence of the 
constraint.
Note, in these cases you might consider switching to the BarzilaiBorwein 
LCP solver, as SOR might not converge to 100% satisfied constraints in 
max iter count.

Yes, Get_react_torque() is zero because it represent the torque given by 
geometric constraint (i..e something entering the system via lagrangian 
multipliers, so only for SPEED or ROTATION modes). The instant torque 
is, then, exactly the torque that you provide via your PID.

I do not understand what you mean for 'limiting the speed' here,... as 
you are using a PID, I suppose its setpoint is something that you 
provide, ex. the speed, and thus is something that you can limit from 
the beginning.

Let me know if you need help,

Alessandro

Subject: unit_IRRLICHT
From: Radu Serban
Date: Mon, 28 Jul 2014 17:46:30 -0500

FYI:  I have just pushed (to the 'develop' branch) a set of changes 
related to making the Irrlicht Chrono unit into a (shared) library 
(instead of having the entire interface implemented in header files).

The API changes are few and pretty straightforward:

  * if your program uses the Irrlicht interface, include headers as follows:
          #include "unit_IRRLICHT/ChIrrAppInterface.h"
  * for consistency, the class ChParticlesSceneNode was renamed to
    ChIrrParticlesSceneNode
  * you may need to explicitly include some other core Chrono headers
    which previously might have been included implicitly through the
    Irrlicht interface headers
  * if you were using the FindChronoEngine.cmake script provided with
    Chrono, you should use the updated one (available in src/cmake/)

The only file that still needs to be separated into header + 
implementations files is 'ChIrrEffects.h'.  I will do that at a later time.

I have also updated (as far as I can tell) all the Irrlicht demos that 
are provided with Chrono, including those from unit_FEM.

A note for Windows users: since we are now building a DLL for the 
Irrlicht interface, you will notice compilation warnings regarding "non 
dll-interface class ... used as base for dll-interface class ..." (VS 
warning C4275).  This is part of the "DLL hell"...   I'll be thinking of 
possible solutions to this issue;  any suggestions are certainly welcome.

Please let me know of any issues.

Thanks,
Radu

From: Harry Tobin
Date: Wed, 18 Mar 2015 04:54:41 -0700 (PDT)

OCC is currently in a constant state of flux, so you can expect this sort 
of problems every time a new version is released.  I addition, version 
7.0.0 will involve large refactoring/ redesign of the API including a 
probable refactoring of the OCAF/ XCAF systems, so the OCC unit will 
probably be broken at source level as well.

You have two options: 

1) Use the OCC version Chrono was developed with.  Not recommended since 
there are many bug and design fixes in later OCC versions.
2) Use the OCC unit as a guide to implement your own OCC functionality, 
this will help you gain some familiarity with OCC and adapt your code to 
future OCC changes.

As part of my PhD, I have made a simulation of a quadruped hybrid robot (with legs and wheels) using Chrono::Engine. Unfortunately, as soon as the robot turns (with the wheels theoretically well placed in order to allow a perfect turn without any drift), it begins to swing circularly until it overturns.

As part of my PhD, I have made a simulation of a quadruped hybrid robot (with legs and wheels) using Chrono::Engine. Unfortunately, as soon as the robot turns (with the wheels theoretically well placed in order to allow a perfect turn without any drift), it begins to swing circularly until it overturns.

So it now comes down to a simple four wheeled car. And even then the system swings when turning despite the constraints (cf. http://youtu.be/mixPm44sg4Y).

I think I have isolated well the problems when setting the coefficients of adhesion to zero and a non-zero initial speed : whatever the conditions are, if the robot travels in a straight line, no perturbation occurs, but as soon as there is a spin, the cylindrical constraints around the four wheels are broken, leading the chassis to circular swings... Of course, I have tried to play with the LCP types and parameters, but I haven't made any improvement... Maybe you'll have a more precise suggestion in my case...

I hope you'll have some idea of what actually happens...

Thank you for reading.

Arthur B.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Not normal 100% loading of CPU!!!
From: Radu Serban

Justin,

This is due to a certain setting in Chrono::Parallel which triggers a 
dynamic tuning of the number of threads (by default between 1 and the 
maximum available threads). That setting is enabled by default and the 
heuristics used in that algorithm are not always doing their job properly.

  * I you can update to the very latest version of Chrono (in the
    'develop' branch), I just pushed a commit that addresses this
    issue. In this latest code, I added a public method
    ChSystemParallel::SetNumThreads which you can use in one of two ways:
      o my_system.SetNumThreads(n_threads);
        In this case, the simulation will always use exactly the number
        of threads specified and the dynamic thread number tuning is
        disabled automatically.

      o my_system.SetNumThreads(n_threads, min_threads, max_threads);
        In this case, n_threads is ignored, the dynamic thread number
        algorithm is enabled and it will adjust the number of threads
        between the specified min_threads and max_threads values (these
        must satisfy 1 <= min_threads < max_threads <=
        omp_get_num_threads())

        In either case, you do not need to make any other additional
        calls (e.g., you do not need to call
        CHOMPfunctions::SetNumThreads(n_threads).

  * If you cannot update the Chrono code right now, you must manually
    turn off that dynamic thread tuning algorithm, using:
      CHOMPfunctions::SetNumThreads(n_threads);
symbol: Re: [chrono] Not normal 100% loading of CPU!!!

text:
* If you cannot update the Chrono code right now, you must manually
    turn off that dynamic thread tuning algorithm, using:
      CHOMPfunctions::SetNumThreads(n_threads);
      my_system.GetSettings()->perform_thread_tuning = false;

    Note that in the latest commit in which I introduced
    ChSystemParallel::SetNumThreads, I also removed public access to
    'perform_thread_tuning'.

Please let me know if this resolves your issue.

--Radu

From: Radu Serban

Hi Kurt,

Yes, we are aware of this issue and we will work on a fix soon.  In the 
meantime, you may want to reduce the number of OMP threads, just like 
you tried (you may want to even try using a single thread; depending on 
your problem size that may be the fastest).

In addition to calling ChSystem::SetParallelThreadNumber(), you also 
need to explicitly call omp_set_num_threads() -- for that you'll 
probably have to include omp.h.  There's also a static function 
SetNumThreads() defined in ChOpenMP.h which simply invokes 
omp_set_num_threads();  so both ways are really equivalent.

Alternatively, you could set the environment variable OMP_NUM_THREADS 
prior to executing your code.

Hope that this helps,
Radu

Hi Kishor,

I see...

Your solution will work because the decision for not considering contacts between two bodies that are fixed happens after the narrow phase collision processing (when the contacts is added to the contact container), so right after your callback gets called.   There are no immediate plans to change this behavior.  If/when that happens, we will hopefully be able to also provide a mechanism for identifying the particular collision shape within a collision model.

Having said that, I still think you need the modification (to NarrowphaseCallback::OnNarrowphase) I suggested so that you can explicitly discard a collision that involves one of your "sentinel" bodies.  This is because such a sentinel body (fixed) may also collide with some other body in the system that is not fixed -- in that case a contact will be generated and that would affect (undesirably) that other body.

There is another potential solution to this problem that does not require using these "dummy" bodies and allows using multiple shapes in the collision model, but that depends on the relationship between the actual contact shape and your "sentinel" collision shapes within the collision model.  Indeed, you could transform the coordinates of the collision point(s) reported in ChCollisionInfo into the local frame of the associated body and then use that information to infer which shape it corresponds to.  Of course, that is not a general solution and depends on the relative positions of the shapes in the model (and if you can unequivocally use the local point position to identify the shape).

Hi Kishor,

Your 2nd solution seems overly complicated and specific to the Bullet-based collision system.

I think the cleanest solution is to use the NarrowPhaseCallback, but not by relying on the user to modify the ChCollisionInfor structure (that may have unintended consequences and introduces a dependency on how contact is processed further down the line).   Instead, I would change the signature of the virtual function OnNarrowPhase to return a bool;  the user is then supposed to return 'true' if the collision is to be added to the collision system and 'false' if it should be ignored.   Then change lines  1325-1329 in ChCCollisionSystemBullet.cpp to something like:

bool add_contact = true;
if (this->narrow_callback)
     add_contact = this->narrow_callback->OnNarrowphase(icontact);
if (add_contact)
    mcontactcontainer->AddContact(icontact);

If you are going to test this approach, please let me know if it does what you need.  If so, I can implement it throughout Chrono and push this change.

--Radu

Hi Jacob,

To follow up on this: indeed, for Chrono::Vehicle I opted to implement 
an alternative way for POV-Ray rendering.  Unlike the approach in 
Chrono::Postprocess, where a POV-Ray script is generated for each 
desired frame, with the approach adopted in Chrono::Vehicle, you 
generate one data file for each desired frame.  These data files can 
then be processed (one at a time or in batch) by a single, common 
POV-Ray script.  This approach is more flexible and more scalable.

Note that we plan on eventually redesigning the POV-Ray support in 
Chrono::Postprocess.

Coming back to Chrono::Vehicle,  rendering with POV-Ray is a topic that 
is currently not properly documented anywhere, so let me try to fill in 
some of this gap here.

What you need to do is simply invoke the utility function 
WriteShapesPovray(), once for each desired render frame, passing it a 
file name that encodes the frame number.  Because the way the POV-Ray 
script is written (see below), I suggest you generate these file names 
such that the resulting data files are all placed in a sub-directory 
POVRAY of the output folder (just like it's done in our demos).   
Running the simulation will then generate one data file per render 
frame.  These are ASCII output files that are actually independent of 
POV-Ray (they simply contain system body states, joint information, and 
information of the visual assets at the particular simulation time for 
which they were generated).

With Chrono::Vehicle, in the directory src/demos/vehicle, we distribute
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: POV-Ray and Post Processing

text:
which they were generated).

With Chrono::Vehicle, in the directory src/demos/vehicle, we distribute 
a POV-Ray script (renderZ.pov) that can be used (maybe with some minor 
modifications) to render the scene using one of the above data files, or 
else a sequence of such data files.   To use it, copy it from the Chrono 
source directory to the output directory, at the same level as the 
POVRAY directory that contains the output data files.  Then make any 
required modifications to the script.  With one exception, most of these 
are at the top of the script (under the section "OPTIONS").  You can 
experiment with them, but the more important ones are:

  * fnum -- the frame number that you want rendered.
    You can either specify a single value, or else assume it is passed
    as an argument to the script (possibly as a range) and therefore
    available in the variable 'frame_number'.  The latter allows you to
    do batch rendering.
  * datafile -- modify this to reflect where the data files were
    generated and what pattern you used for their filename.
    As provided, the script assumes the data files are available in the
    directory POVRAY and that their name are of the form data_***.dat,
    where *** represents the frame number.   This is consistent with how
    these data files are generated in our demos.
  * camera settings -- 'cam_perspective' false uses orthographic
    projection (default is perspective); 'cam_loc' is the (fixed) camera
    location; 'cam_lookat' is the (fixed) point that gives the camera
    direction.
    NOTE: if you want the camera settings to change at each frame, based
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: POV-Ray and Post Processing

text:
location; 'cam_lookat' is the (fixed) point that gives the camera
    direction.
    NOTE: if you want the camera settings to change at each frame, based
    on the corresponding vehicle position (e.g. to have a camera
    following the vehicle, or pointing at the vehicle as it moves), you
    will have to overwrite the above settings further down in the script
    (look for the "CAMERA" section around line 588).  Modify the sample
    commented code snippets there.

Note that POV-Ray uses a left-handed frames with (default) Y up.  On the 
other hand, Chrono uses right-handed frames and, moreover, all 
Chrono::Vehicle models impose Z up (i.e. gravity in the -Z direction).  
The renderZ.pov script has code to perform all required conversions.  As 
such, when you specify camera settings, use a right-handed frame with Z 
up (i.e., work in the same reference frame as the one in which the 
vehicle itself was defined for Chrono::Vehicle).

Using meshes (provided through Wavefront OBJ files) as visualization 
assets adds a bit more complication.  If you want to use some of the 
meshes we already provide with Chrono, in addition to the above steps, 
you also need to copy the proper POV-Ray snippets (*.inc files) for the 
appropriate vehicle model (in the Chrono::Vehicle data directory) and 
place them next to the renderZ.pov script in the output directory.   For 
the HMMWV vehicle as an example, grab all the files in 
data/vehicle/hmmwv/POV-Ray.   Assuming MESH visualization was enabled in 
your program, the renderZ.pov script will look for the specific *.inc 
files and render the meshes.
symbol: Re: [chrono] Re: POV-Ray and Post Processing

text:
data/vehicle/hmmwv/POV-Ray.   Assuming MESH visualization was enabled in 
your program, the renderZ.pov script will look for the specific *.inc 
files and render the meshes.
However, if you want to use your own meshes, the process is quite a bit 
more complicated as you'd need to generate these POV-Ray *.inc files 
separately...

I realize this work flow is not that streamlined and requires a bit of 
tweaking and user intervention.  As I mentioned, when we get a chance we 
will work on improving this through Chrono::Postprocess.


Finally, as Mike mentioned, the time stepping of a vehicle system is 
performed through the wrapper Advance() functions, so there's no need 
(indeed, it's an error) to also explicitly call DoStepDynamics() on the 
underlying ChSystem of a vehicle object. That is done in 
ChVehicle::Advance().


I hope this helps and that you manage to generate the renderings you 
want.  Do not hesitate to ask for further clarifications.

Regards,
--Radu

Simon,

You can either:

  1.  Make sure the attachment points of the TSDA are such that they never flip. You can separate them by whatever amount you want, as long as you also modify appropriately the rest length (assuming you use the default linear spring-damper model), or
  2.  Specify a custom ChLinkTSDA::ForceFunctor and implement whatever you want/need. The evaluate() method which you would have to overwrite receives a reference to the TSDA element itself from which you can access whatever quantities you might need for that (e.g., the current locations of the attachment points).
--Radu

Hi Tingnan,

ok, interesting. (But how did you manage the .DynamicCastTo<...>() stuff?)

In fact, I'd avoid switching to the unique pointer as it would require a 
lot of rethinking in existing code.
Also, I decided for shared pointers as a design choice. This is the way 
that most 3D CAD software is implemented nowadays - most data is handled 
via shared pointers.

Right, I know that there are long inheritance trees in Chrono.
However this became necessary during the development, especially because 
of ChLink and similar constraints, and because of the desire to keep the 
FEA code very 'compatible' with the rigid body code. For instance, 
ChBody inherits from ChBodyFrame because in this way ChBodyFrame can be 
used also for the FEA nodes of Euler beams, and in this way one can 
apply ChLinkMate, for instance, either to rigid bodies and to beam nodes.

Of course I know that composition could help 'flattening' the 
hierarchies, but at the time I preferred inheritance.

Anyway -correct me if I am wrong- the performance penalty of virtual 
dispatches does not change if the inheritance tree is long or short; 
what can have a hit on the dispatch is the presence of _multiple_ 
inheritance, especially if made as "virtual inheritance" to cope with 
the (few, anyway) diamond problems.

This said, I always tried to avoid the virtual inheritance. If we get 
rid of the intrusive ChShared, the diamond problem would happen almost 
nowhere.
As per the normal multiple inheritance, I would like to avoid it, but in

When I experimented the std::shared_ptr I use the C++11 feature of type
alias:
http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/type_alias

Basically it allows you to write

template<class T> using ChSharedPtr = std::shared_ptr<T>

As for the shared_ptr vs unique_ptr part I think it is just a design choice
and how you manage the life time of objects across different modules.
Changing from shared_ptr to unique_ptr would require extensive
architectural redesign which may not be desirable at this stage.


As you have mentioned the vtable and inheritance, I would say that
inheritance is a rather larger problem exists in the C::E right now. For
the  inheritance diagram I attached here, there are just too many layers of
inheritance and some of them are just plain confusing.

[image: pasted1]

For example,  is there enough differentiation between the ChCoordSys,

Other comments that advocate for jumping on the C++11 shared_ptr soon:

- the current "intrusive" ChSharedPtr is based on inheriting from 
ChShared. There are some cases of 'diamond' inheritance of classes in 
chrono, so I had to use the 'virtual' inheritance from ChShared for 
those classes. I suspect this leads to a vtable dispatch when 
incrementing/decrementing the ChShared counter,hence penalizing the 
performance.

- the current ChShared counter is non atomic, so if multiple threads 
happen to increment/decrement the same pointer counter, this could cause 
problems. Rather than spending time in atomizing my ChShared 
increment&compare operation (that cannot be done lightly since it could 
spend some 100's clock ticks if not done properly), I'm waiting to go 
directly with the C++11 shared_ptr that has the atomic thread safe 
increment (as far as I read). And it should be fast and optimized, as 
state of the art.

- the ChSharedPtr cannot have a ChWeak equivalent as it is intrusive 
(already said above)

- the dynamic casting of ChSharedPtr requires a copy of the pointer 
object, and there are other places where ChSharedPtr are copied 
abundantly, and probably the c+ 'move semantics' could help to optimize 
the performance. I never used move semantics in ChSharedPtr, but I know 
it is used in std::shared_ptr, in sake of the best performance.

Tingnan,

Regarding the issue you mention with ChModelBullet::_injectShape(), it 
doesn't make sense to put stack objects in a shared pointer (after all, 
the purpose of a shared pointer is to tie a heap object to the stack).

A function with a signature like that of _injectShape() should never be 
part of the *public* API.  Instead, it should always take as argument a 
shared pointer, thus putting the burden of properly constructing the 
shared pointer on the user.  Of course, they could still wrap a stack 
object and pass that -- but that's really the user's problem at that point.

However, for a *private* function like ChModelBullet::_injectShape(), we 
can hopefully assume that the Chrono developers will know that it should 
always be called with a heap-allocated object :-)

--Radu

P.S.  On a different note, I don't know if using ChSmartPtr here is 
quite appropriate in the first place, because of the interfacing to 
Bullet which is done through raw pointers anyway. I think ChModelBullet 
should just assume ownership of the btCollisionShapes objects (Bullet 
does not claim ownership of them) and just keep the raw pointers in a 
std::vector. Alessandro, what are your thoughts here?

Subject: Re: [chrono] Direction of Gravity
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 20 Aug 2017 09:32:01 +0200

John,

All you need to do is use the function ChSystem::Set_G_acc, something like:
mysys.Set_G_acc(ChVector<>(0, 0, -9.8));

Note that there is no implied reference frame in Chrono. The only 
reason why the default has gravity in the negative Y direction is 
because of the Irrlicht run-time visualization system which has Y up.

--Radu

Zach,

I didn't try to compile your code, but rather took only a quick look at 
it.  The problem seems to be that you didn't add the link to the 
system;  just like you did with the bodies, you must include a call such as:

my_system.AddLink(my_link);

As for adding visualization geometry, you can indeed use Irrlicht 
primitives (lines, segments, etc.) or else you can add some 
"visualization assets" to each body that you want visualized -- look in 
some of the demos for how that's done.

Hope that this helps,
Radu

From: Alessandro Tasora

hi Stephane,


There is no 'direct' method, so what you could do is to access the two 
collision models of the two ChBody objects, get their Bullet collision 
models wrapped in them, then get the btCollisionWorld that is wrapped 
inside the ChCollisionSystemBullet (get the ChCollisionSystemBullet from 
your ChSystem), finally do btCollisionWorld::contactPairTest().
This is not 100% straightforward because you must play with low-level 
Bullet stuff.

We will consider this for a future feature in ChCollisionSystemBullet 
and other ChCollisionSystem-inherited classes.

best regards.

A.Tasora

16.04 LTS. If you think I could change something than give me a hint.

*1. Check/Install a C++ compiler*

   - Check if GNU C++ compiler is installed on your system by searching for 
   G++ in your package manager

*2. Install CMake*
You have 2 options to install the following packages: 

   - Open your package manager and install the following packages: cmake; 
      cmake-data; cmake-qt-gui; extra-cmake-modules
   
*OR*

   - Open your Terminal and type:
      sudo apt-get install cmake cmake-data cmake-qt-gui extra-cmake-module
      
      
*3. Install a GIT client*
You have 2 options to install the following packages: 

   - Open your package manager and install the following packages: git; 
      git-gui
   
*OR*

   - Open your Terminal and type:
      sudo apt-get install git git-gui
      
      
*4. Download the project by cloning the Git repository*

   - Open your Terminal and type: 
   sudo git gui
   
   - Click on *Clone Existing Repository*
   - Enter at *Source Location* the following:

text:
- Click on *Clone Existing Repository*
   - Enter at *Source Location* the following: 
   https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono.git

   choice. I recommend to do it at: 
   /opt/chrono/source
   To create this directory, change to the Terminal and enter: 
   sudo mkdir /opt/chrono && sudo mkdir /opt/chrono/source
   
   - Enable *Recursively clone submodules too*
   - Click on *Clone*

   <http://downloads.sourceforge.net/irrlicht/irrlicht-1.8.2.zip>

The problem is that you have to adapt the С++ natively (i.e. not managed) in 
the environment of C++ / CLI application (managed).
Therefore, it is necessary to make changes to the sourse code. Rather, 
changes in the organization of the compilation.
You can use #pragma managed(push, off) and #pragma managed(pop)  to combine 
native and managed code in the same compilation unit.
I'm not having much experience in C++/CLI. You need to know more about adapting 
the С++ natively in C++ / CLI and experiment with it.

For me, it is better not to use C++/CLI :) Why do you use it? 
If you need a comfortable and well-wrapper, using Qt C++ ;)

Roman

Subject: Re: [chrono] Default Units? Or User Responsible?
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 8 Oct 2015 08:43:34 +0200

Hi Bradley.
Chrono is dimensionless.
Just pick three units for (length time mass) dimensions,  and be coherent
for all derived units.

For instance: I often assume SI units of [m kg s] , therefore when I enter
a force, it is in Newtons [N],  i.e. [kg m /ss]

Just keep in mind that for huge or microscopical mechanisms it is better to
scale everything so that Chrono will work with numbers approximately in the
-1..+1 range,  especially for lengths,  because collision detection has
some special tolerances and it works better in those sizes.

For instance one of my students is simulating a clock escapement, so he
uses millimeters as lengths.

Alessandro

Hello Sebastian,

Though I'm not exactly sure what you want, but porting C::E into C# doesn't 
seem to be easy.
You might, theoretically, be able to call C::E from C# by writing wrappers 
or something, 
but it's almost making C# version of module_python. I don't think it is 
easier way.

Alternatively, how about using interprocess communications, e.g. sockets or 
pipes?
For instance, create a C# app and C++ app separately, send some data from 
C# to C++, calculate them on C++ (you can use C::E here), and send back the 
result.
In this way, you don't need efforts of code porting—just write C# and C++ 
code.
(Some trouble might occur if you must work with a lot of data, though.)

Sincerely,
Shig.

Hi Martin,
short answer: it's fine to stick with LP64.

long answer:
The ILP64 flag enables for 64-bit integer: this would allow to handle 
bigger matrices (as the number of non-zeros and/or the number of 
rows/column increases, the matrix storage asks for bigger indexes), at the 
cost of higher storage occupation.
As the Intel documentation says: "Choose the ILP64 interface if your 
application uses Intel MKL for calculations with large data arrays..." and 
it says that the LP64 is still the choice for compatibility reasons.
In Chrono we are currently using *int* as index variable type - we are not 
using *size_t* (that would be unsigned) or *long long int* either - and its 
*sizeof(int)* value may change depending on compiler|OS|architecture.
Usually is 32bit (4bytes) on both 32 and 64bit systems (so the LP64 
default), however for some GCC compilers is actually 64.

The ChronoMklEngine is an interface between the MKL library and Chrono, so 
we have to satisfy both. Because of this we chose to stick with the 32bit 
version.
However there are two points to underline:
- we did not use MKL in scenarios in which a so big matrix was needed, so 
we didn't invest time in using 64bit integers;
- we are testing Chrono (and MKL) in different OS and with different 
compilers: we never had problems regarding the varying size of the *int *type: 
the MKL library *MKL_INT *always matched the *int* variable
- however, I do not exclude that it may happen that the MKL library has to

the MKL library *MKL_INT *always matched the *int* variable
- however, I do not exclude that it may happen that the MKL library has to 
be linked with -DMKL_ILP64 in the case the *int *size changes to 64bit; or 
with the flag -DMKL_INT=size_t or -DMKL_INT=int

BTW, you can find a relevant article here

About the rock breakage test we gave in the paper, it should be exactly 
that demo: Fracture_Box. Run it and it should give you what we had in the 
paper.

To answer your other questions...
1. This is not strictly a DEME question, nor an easy one necessarily. DEME 
only cares about the position and radius of the initial spheres, and how 
you generate them is in itself a research problem that you have to solve 
yourself. It's even more complex considering it's not just about filling a 
volume represented by a mesh, but you need the interior spheres' 
overlapping pattern to become an appropriate apparatus for representing the 
initial internal force. I might have read about some other people's elegant 
solutions but they are not off the top of my head. If I were to do it, I'd 
probably write a script that uses planes to intersect the mesh of the rock, 
then fill the intersection with spheres until the volume is completely 
filled layer by layer.

2. The rest are CMake questions. For now, if you just wish to easily 
compile your own script and without worrying about the potential 
co-simulations, then adding a demo is fine. Put the script in the demo 
folder, add its name to the CMakeList.txt in the demo folder, and then 
recompile (make or ninja) the project.

3. Same as above. Note that modifying and supplying a custom force model 
does not necessarily require you to rebuild the project, if the custom 
model is loaded from a file. When the executable is run, the content of
symbol: Re: DEM-Egnine-installation

3. Same as above. Note that modifying and supplying a custom force model 
does not necessarily require you to rebuild the project, if the custom 
model is loaded from a file. When the executable is run, the content of 
that file will be read and executed, so simply modifying that file and then 
run the executable is fine. This however, applies to a force model file 
located in a location that you know and control (you may want to supply the 
full path to that file in your script), not the force model files in the 
source code! The ones in the source code are not read when a demo is run, 
as the solver reads the files in the build folder by default, or whatever 
location you tell it to read. If you supply your force model with a string 
in the demo itself like I did in an example, then obviously you have to 
recompile the project every time you modify that demo script.

since the discussion has moved well beyond what the title suggests already.
