Hi Dr. Shen,

1. I haven't added direct vtk output for sphere/clump information. They are 
now written in csv format. But you can use your own tool to convert csv to 
vtk. The information you need is all there. You can specify what goes into 
the output file by calling the method *SetOutputContent* like the following
*DEMSim.SetOutputContent({"VEL", "ACC"});*

2. Again, this is something you can derive from the simulation status, but 
DEME does not have a one-liner to compute that. You can compute the kinetic 
energy through the linear and angular velocities of each particle, and 
compute the potential through the positions of each particle at different 
points in time. The information can all be queried through trackers. For 
the kinetic energy though, there is a convenient call to compute that which 
is through inspectors
*auto KE_finder = DEMSim.CreateInspector("clump_kinetic_energy");*
You can find this example in the demo SingleSphereCollide.

However, if you also need to know respectively the contribution of friction 
and damping, this is more complex, and you need to write a custom force 
model that records this information. This is an advanced usage and a bit 
more challenging. I also find this not that meaningful in many real-world 
DEM applications because the damping and friction coefficients can be very 
heuristic anyway.

*WriteContactFile*. An example can be found in the demo GRCPrep_Part1 or 2 
or 3. You should also specify what goes into those contact files by calling

Subject: Re: [chrono] Can a ChBody collision model have a list of families
 that it doesn't collide with?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 30 Jan 2015 19:01:31 -0600

Justin,

Indeed the maximum number of collision families is 16 (this could be 
relaxed, but it seems sufficient for now).  This is not per body 
(technically collision model), but rather this is the total number of 
collision families that can be defined in a system.  A given body can be 
set as member of any one of these families.  A family ID must be an 
integer between 0 and 15, inclusively.   By default, a body belongs to 
family 0.

Each collision model maintains a mask (this is a short, hence the limit 
of 16 families in the entire system) whose bits indicate whether or not 
the body collides with a given family.  In other words, if the 5th bit 
is set, then the body collides with all bodies in family 5.   If the 5th 
bit is unset, the body does not interact with any other body declared to 
be in family 5.   By default, all bits in this mask are initialized to 
1, indicating that the body interacts with bodies in all families.  Note 
that there seems to be a bug in Chrono where only the first 8 bits of 
the mask are actually set (i.e. the mask is initialized to 0xFF) -- I'll 
look into this.

What this all means is that you can indeed call 
SetFamilyMaskNoCollisionWithFamily() as many times as you want for a 
given collision model (body), of course up to 16 times.  In your example 
below, assuming wheel_family = 2 and terrain_family = 7, the mask for 
the collision model associated with roller_body would end up being 0xFF7B.

Dan

First of all, thank you very much for your advice!
I have tried HHT integrator and set its parameter alpha to 0.0, 
unfortunately, the result still appears unphysical.
However, I have just implemented a different way to simulate this problem. 
The general idea is to set two ChLinkMotorRotationSpeed. (1). When 
Initialize the revolution of egg, define a virtual rigid body as Master 
Frame, COG of cup as Slave Frame, and the speed as egg revolution speed. 
(2). For the rotation of egg, we define COG of cup as Master Frame, COG of 
egg as Slave Frame, and the speed as the egg rotation speed. In this way, 
the egg inherits the rotation of the cup and thus has the effect of 
revolution. It is worth noting that the COGs of virtual rigid body and cup 
are in the same projection point in the direction of rotation axis.

Best wishes

Chao

From: Dan Negrut

Chao – it might be that the numerical integration formulas that we’re using in Chrono are not the best fit for you. If you look at celestial mechanics, I imagine you’d need symplectic integrators, perhaps high order. We don’t have that.
I would give the HHT integrator a shot. I would set alpha to zero to get a trapezoidal integration formula, which in principle doesn’t dissipate energy and is second order. Not clear if that would work, but give it a shot and let us know if it made any difference.
Good luck.
Dan

There is some inconsistency in the geometry definitions, partly caused by 
me I'm sure. 

For example:

A ChBox has the following data members:
    ChMatrix33<> Rot;  /// Rotation of box
    ChVector<> Pos;    /// Position of center
    ChVector<> Size;   /// Hemi size (extension of box from center to 
corner)

A ChCylinder has:
    ChVector<> p1;
    ChVector<> p2;
    double rad;

and ChEllipsoid has:
    Vector center;
    Vector rad;

The ChVisualization asset takes care of the rotation and position 
information so the geometry should not hold this data. Here is what I 
suggest:

ChBox, ChCylinder and ChEllipsoid only store the size vector
     ChVector<> Size; 

This would break the Povray exporter however, so the code would need to be 
changed from something like:
       ChQuaternion<> boxrot = 
myobjshapeasset->GetBoxGeometry().Rot.Get_A_quaternion();
To:
       ChQuaternion<> boxrot = myobjshapeasset->Rot.Get_A_quaternion();
because the rotation is already stored at the shape level

ChBox would also need to be modified so that the GetP*() function accept 
the position/rotation of the box and then return the corner point. 

Do people have any thoughts about this?
If there are no issues I will go ahead and make the necessary changes

Thanks,
Hammad

Hi Max,

Look at ChLoadBodyBodyBushingSpherical (and look also at demo_IRR_link_bushing).  I believe this is what you want?

As for the coordinate system orientation, note that Chrono itself does not impose any particular frame.  You are free to set up your model however you want (make sure to set ChSystem::Set_G_acc, the default is indeed gravity acting in negative Y).  The main reason many of our demos use Y up is because this is the default in our current run-time visualization which is based on Irrlicht.  Unfortunately, support for Z up in Chrono::Irrlicht needs some work (the camera requires some fixes).
Having said that, our vehicle modeling module (Chrono::Vehicle) imposes an ISO reference frame which does have Z up.  You can look in there what I did to get the Irrlicht visualization working properly.
One last word of caution about Irrlicht:  while Chrono uses right handed frames, Irrlicht uses left handed frames. As such, the renderings will actually be mirrored left/right.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Problem with ChShaftsClutch model.
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Thu, 25 Jun 2020 23:09:06 +0200

Dear David

sorry I missed your message on the forum , I am replying just now.

The fact is that ChShaftsClutch is a constraint that uses a non-smooth 
dynamics formulation (set valued force law, for sharp transition between 
sticking/non-sticking) and, as such, it cannot be used together with 
finite elements - which is your case if I remember correctly.

Probably in future I will provide a new solver that will be able to 
solve DVI nonsmooth dynamics AND finite elements, but it is not 
available right now. So a short term trick would be to create your own 
"clutch" viaa smooth force law, ex. a regularization (mollification) of 
the stepwise "torque vs slipping velocity" curve, and this could fit 
inside your FEA problems and your HHT solver. To this end, one option 
could be to inherit from the *ChLoadBodyBody *class.

best regards

Alessandro

From: Justin Madsen
Date: Wed, 16 Jul 2014 15:20:17 -0500

Tiangnan,

The SOR solver is meant to solve unilateral constraints (contacts and
impulses) quickly and efficiently. Bilateral constraints tend to wiggle
around a bit if you use this solver, but increasing the number of velocity
iterations, or the stability clamp will help. MINRES is more accurate, but
can be much slower. Also, last time I checked the SOR solver had some
issues with large mass ratios between bodies (in your case, small soil
particles contacting a wheel with presumably much larger masses).

Alessandro or Hammad will know better how to exactly tune these parameters,
and I'll leave it to Alessandro to tell you which of his journal papers
would be a good read for you!

Take it easy,
Justin

Subject: Re: [chrono] Tension in elements / nodes
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 23 Jun 2017 10:16:31 +0200

Dear Tristan,

you are right, the EvaluateSectionForceTorque() function for the 
ChElementCableANCF is not yet implemented.

I am not the author of that class so I can just give you a hint for a 
quick fix: just use the

EvaluateSectionStrain(const double eta, const ChMatrix<>& displ, 
ChVector<>& StrainV)

function, that is implemented. In the StrainV.x  value you get the axial 
strain (in the comments in the .h file it's written that StrainV 
contains "x=torsion, y=bending" but I suspect 'torsion' is a typo 
because, looking at the function, it is computing axial strain, and 
there is no torsion in ANCF beams, after all).

After you have the axial strain, you can compute the axial tension F by 
multiplying by section material properties of area and young modulus, as 
F=A*E*StrainV.x

Let me know if this workaround is working.


Another option is to use ChElementBeamBernoulli elements, they use 
corotational Euler-Bernoulli elements that are as fast as the ANCF cable 
elements, the difference with ANCF is that they also compute torsion.

regards,

Alessandro Tasora

Subject: Re: [chrono] Cannot set right-handed coordinate system for ChBody
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Tue, 8 Oct 2019 11:16:14 +0200

Dear Tobias,

the Chrono coodinate system is right-handed, indeed. The issue is that 
the default visualization system (Chrono IRRLICHT module) just uses a 
left-handed system, and all pictures look mirrored. But internally the 
data is correct. So please do NOT change the ChMatrix33 data of ChBody 
because it is already right handed. It is only a visualization problem 
of the Irrlicht module.

For instance: if you take a screen snapshot image and flip it 
horizontally, you'll see that the coordinate systems are correct.

This said, as a patch one would simply flip the camera projection matrix 
of Irrlicht. Unfortunaltely, there is no easy way to flip the projection 
matrix in Irrlicht without affecting the Irrlicht optimization 
algorithms (especially, triangle backface culling), and in fact we are 
considering moving to a more powerful visualization library for future 
relases of Chrono.

regards,

Alessandro Tasora

Subject: Re: Large deformation on Shell Elements ?
From: Mike Taylor
Date: Thu, 12 Dec 2024 14:51:13 -0800 (PST)

Solenne,

I'm most familiar with the ANCF elements.  The ANCF formulation supports 
both geometric and material non-linearities.  Currently most of the ANCF 
elements in Chrono are formulated with only a linear viscoelastic material, 
but they do inherently support moderately large deformations (i.e. large 
angle bending, but not plastic like flows.)

Here are a few thoughts on things to try:

If you've only tried to run a static analysis, you might want to 
try running a dynamic analysis with a slowly applied load with a relatively 
large amount of damping to dynamically settle to the "static" solution?  

If you are running a static analysis, are you running the linear static or 
nonlinear static analysis version?  If you are using the nonlinear static 
analysis, what argument are you giving that function?

If you haven't already examined refining your mesh (using more elements), 
you might want to give that a try as well.

Finally, the ANCF Shell 3423 element has a relatively low order (linear) 
interpolation function.  You could also try an element with a richer/higher 
order interpolation function like the "ChElementShellANCF_3833"element.

Best Regards,

Mike Taylor

Hi Jiang,

You are correct, ChLineArc (and similar classes) are 2D objects.

As for creating an OBJ file, this must be done outside Chrono. This is a 
standard format (Wavefront obj) and practically any 3D authoring tool is 
able to export a mesh in this format.   In fact, this is a pretty 
straightforward (text) format, so for very simple models you can even 
generate the OBJ file by hand.  See for example 
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavefront_.obj_file

Radu

Option 1: You could model the belt as a bunch of discrete rigid bodies connected by revolute joints or bushings interacting with the CVT cones via friction and contact.
Option 2: You could you the FEA module to create a nonlinear FEA mesh of the belt interacting with the CVT cones via friction and contact.
Option 3: You could look for a simpler model that might meet your needs.  I'm not sure what that would look like.

Options 1 and 2 will be computationally expensive, with option 2 being potentially very computationally expensive.  You might want to take a look at some of the tracked vehicle models to get an idea for runtimes to determine if they will be too computationally expensive to use for controls tuning.  The tracks on those vehicles interact with the road wheels via 3D contact, which would be similar to what you would need for the CVT model.

I hope that helps,

Mike

Thanks to the implementation of the tangent stiffness matrix of constraints

pendulum + cart problem are complete if

state-space representation of the system by yourself. The generalized form 
of the state-space representation is preferred because of the present of 
the constraint Jacobian matrix (Cq).

Good luck!

Chao PENG

Hi Thomas,

I know this thread is ancient (by today's standard), but I just want to 
give an explanation of the scoop.obj issue you've been having. 

That is because the original scoop.obj has no facet normal information in 
it. Chrono::Granular relies on this information to do contact detection 
properly. In future releases of Chrono::Granular we will add more tangible 
error message if this information is not given in the obj mesh file.

The fix is, as you pointed out, as simple as loading it into a CAD (or 
perhaps rendering) tool and then exported it. This is because these tools 
typically output files complying with the formatting conventions. If you 
compare your original and "new" obj files, you will see the new one has 
many lines started with "vn", those are the facet normal lines missing in 
the original one, Blender added them for you.

Now you might ask how Blender knows the correct facet normal. There are 
several possibilities. For a closed 3D object people usually set the normal 
direction of its surface to be outward, perhaps Blender is able to figure 
it out based on that. Or more likely, because the ordering of triangle 
points in each facet infers a facet normal direction (based on the 
right-hand rule), Blender simply derived the normal using it. Note although 
you are lucky that scoop.obj is (according to my inspection) oriented 
correctly so the facet normal is pointing outwards, that may not always be 
the case, depending on how you generate meshes. Chrono::Granular requires

check that before simulations.

Subject: Re: Linear actuator
From: Ivan Metrikin
Date: Tue, 22 Jul 2014 15:47:52 -0700 (PDT)

Hi Justin, 

I’ve had the exact same problem some time ago, and my solution at that time 
was to use the Lpointer->ConstraintsBiLoad_C call in the LCPprepare_load 
method of ChSystem. Specifying recovery_clamp equal to the desired velocity 
divided by the timestep and setting do_clamp to true allows using SetMotion 
method of ChLinkLock with the desired end location of the actuator as 
argument (using ChFunction_Const). It is just a workaround, but worked 
sufficiently good for my problem and was very fast to implement.

However, in the future I think it would be really useful to have a ‘native’ 
linear velocity-based actuator in C::E, implemented along the lines of what 
you wrote, in order to avoid such hacks.

Ivan

Hi all,

Recently I've been building a test rig that requires the use of a linear 
actuator. I know that it is possible to just apply the desired 
position/velocity directly to the body, since the test rig is attached to 
the ground and the prismatic joint the actuator is part of does not move 
relative to the ground. This won't be feasible if the body on which the 
prismatic joint and actuator are applied to moves relative to the absolute 
coordinates.

I've made some additions to the linear actuator class, ChLinkLinActuator, 
to mimic the functionality you see in ChLinkEngine, namely being able to 
set the actuation type between: displacement, velocity, or force based. I 
have a preliminary implementation that works most of the time, but there is 
some funny stuff going on. sometimes the direction of the applied velocity 
switches seemingly arbitrarily when using the velocity actuation type.

I'm just wondering if anyone has been working on this class, or has an 
implementation of a linear actuator they are using before I jump into 
working out the bugs in mine.

Thanks,
Justin

text:
Subject: RE: [chrono] Beginner Question (Vehicle): How do I create a simulation
 for a new car?
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 23 Mar 2021 18:01:12 +0000

Chrono is a collection of middleware libraries.  As such, it is indeed the responsibility of the user (i.e. you) to write the main driver that calls Chrono functions.  The demos distributed with Chrono are examples of such programs that you would have to write.

Regarding vehicle models, the Chrono::Vehicle module provides two different ways of creating a new model using the available templates:  (1) by implementing a set of concrete subsystems (with parameters corresponding to the actual vehicle you are modeling); or (2) by providing a set of JSON files with the concrete parameters for the vehicle you try to model.

Chrono::Vehicle is accompanied by a separate library (ChronoModels_vehicle) which provides several pre-built vehicle models (HMMWV, Sedan, Gator, etc.).  These can be used as they are, or else used as examples for building your own model.   Similarly, the Chrono distribution includes (in its data/ directory) complete sets of JSON files specifying various vehicles (HMMWV, Sedan, etc).   Again, these can be used as examples on how to provide your own JSON files for whatever vehicle you want to model.

The Chrono distribution provides demos using both models from the models library (and not only for the HMMWV; see for example demo_VEH_Sedan, demo_VEH_CityBus, etc, etc) as well as using models defined through JSON specification files (see for example demo_VEH_WheeledJSON;  as given, this demo will use the set of JSON files modeling the “Sedan” passenger car, but a one-line code change can make it use other models (see lines 174-178 in the demo’s source).

Hello all,

I took one more try and finally solved my issue. To anyone who has a 
similar problem, note that Bodies in Chrono have a default Collision 
Envelope. If the envelope is too large for the scale of your simulation, 
this can cause things to collide much sooner than expected and result in 
strange behavior.

Best,
Jessica

Hi Daye,

I assume you use a ChSystemNSC (and not the SMC contact method, not a 
Chrono::Parallel system)?

One thing to check is that body masses and inertias are set properly and 
consistently and that you do not have huge discrepancies (some much, 
much lighter than others).

A second, more likely, reason for the behavior you see has to do with 
robustness and accuracy of the underlying Bullet collision detection 
algorithm for shapes that are "flat" (very different aspect ratio in one 
direction) like yours seem to be. To verify this, try to modify your 
code to use shapes with less variation in aspect ratio (like those in 
the demo I mention below).

I cannot locate the code for that vehicle ditch crossing (that is a 
relatively old simulation). But you may want to look at 
demo_IRR_emit_cluster which is quite similar to your problem and uses 
convex hull collision shapes. That demo uses the particle factory 
classes in Chrono, but you can navigate through the code down to where 
the ChBodyEasyConvexHull bodies are created.

--Radu

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Simulation falling apart
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 15 Feb 2019 09:49:42 +0000

I agree with Alessandro that the issue is likely due to a badly conditioned system stemming from large discrepancies in masses.  Increasing the number of iterations should help with that, maybe also changing the solver (e.g. to Barzilai-Borwein like you have it commented out or to APGD).

Skimming through your code, a couple more comments:

  *   It's pretty clear you have bodies with vastly different masses (e.g. b5 versus b6).  I'm not sure what the mass ratio turns out to be exactly, but likely pretty large.
  *   While Chrono is unit-independent, you want to keep everything consistent.  The default gravitational acceleration is [0, -9.8, 0], thus assuming SI units.  All your bodies have a density of 1 (which would now mean 1 kg/m3, so about air density).  You may want to reconcile these.
  *   I'm not sure what you are trying to model, but you could get rid of what appear to be bodies meant only to model pins of a revolute joint (those attached to their 'parent' body with a MateFix joint, that is bodies b3 and b5). You could just remove those from the system and connect the revolute joints directly to the 'parent' body (e.g., connect b4 directly to b2 at the appropriate joint location).  For visualization purposes, you can always add an additional visualization cylinder to one of the joined bodies.  Eliminating these small bodies should alleviate your convergence issues (while also making the problem smaller).  Kinematics will be unchanged and, if you really want to, you could also distribute the eliminated mass to the bodies connected by the revolute joints.

Subject: RE: [chrono] Question on extracting suspension hardpoint forces in
 Chrono (HMMWV model)
From: Radu Serban
Date: Thu, 21 May 2026 06:08:57 +0000

I forgot to mention the most straightforward approach: replacing the kinematic joints with bushings.
Now, while some of the Chrono::Vehicle templates (including ChDoubleWishbone) support using a bushing in place of the ideal revolute joint to connect a control arm to the chassis, they are still set up to use only one such element. However, using compliant bushings makes it possible to use 2 of them to connect a control arm to the chassis and allow extracting meaningful reactions at these 2 connection points.
The easiest way to do this in Chrono::Vehicle, that does not require writing a new suspension template, is to use the ChGenericWheeledSuspension<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1vehicle_1_1_ch_generic_wheeled_suspension.html> template which allows you to define an arbitrary suspension mechanism specified via a JSON file. You can simply modify the sample HMMWV_DoubleWishboneFront_replica.json<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/main/data/vehicle/hmmwv/suspension/HMMWV_DoubleWishboneFront_replica.json> specification file provided as an example in the Chrono distribution.

--Radu


From: 'Radu Serban' via ProjectChrono <projectchrono@googlegroups.com>
Sent: Wednesday, May 20, 2026 10:19 PM
To: ProjectChrono <projectchrono@googlegroups.com>
Subject: RE: [chrono] Question on extracting suspension hardpoint forces in Chrono (HMMWV model)

Yang Kang,

With the default vehicle model in Chrono where all bodies are rigid, the kinematic connection between the chassis and a suspension control arm is fully defined with a single revolute joint. The two hardpoints are provided so that we can define the direction of the axis of rotation of that revolute joint (and for purposes of visualizing the control arm).  Using two (co-axial) revolute joints would result in a system with redundant constraints. While some of the Chrono solvers can deal with such systems, that would still not help you in extracting meaningful reaction forces, as these are non-unique in a system with redundant constraints.

Yang Kang,

With the default vehicle model in Chrono where all bodies are rigid, the kinematic connection between the chassis and a suspension control arm is fully defined with a single revolute joint. The two hardpoints are provided so that we can define the direction of the axis of rotation of that revolute joint (and for purposes of visualizing the control arm).  Using two (co-axial) revolute joints would result in a system with redundant constraints. While some of the Chrono solvers can deal with such systems, that would still not help you in extracting meaningful reaction forces, as these are non-unique in a system with redundant constraints.

Bottom line is that you cannot get meaningful reaction torques in such cases unless you model at least one of the connected bodies as deformable. You can do that with the Chrono::FEA capabilities, but this is not exposed in the Chrono::Vehicle templates.

--Radu

I’m a graduate student currently using Project Chrono, through PyChrono, for vehicle simulation and fatigue analysis.

The objective of my work is to obtain force and torque data from an HMMWV_Full simulation, performed on SCM terrain, and use these forces and torque as input for FEA analysis of the vehicle’s suspension components.

In my investigation of the double wishbone suspension model, I noticed that the Upper and Lower Control Arms (UCA/LCA) are defined with two hardpoints on the chassis side (front and rear locations). However, in the Chrono model, this is represented with a single revolute joint.

tire_step_size = step_size

hmmwv.SetContactMethod(contact_method)
hmmwv.SetChassisCollisionType(chassis_collision_type)

Subject: Changes in the shared pointer API.
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Sat, 21 Jun 2014 16:47:28 -0700 (PDT)

*IMPORTANT. *
The last commit 
<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/commit/57e3c127639830bef2bcb2cdf45dd2bcf5406543> 
into the GIT 'develop' branch of Chrono::Engine introduced a change that 
might give compilation errors in projects based on the old API. It is a 
simple improvement that will require just few changes in the code, if any; 
for the rest, previous code will work as before.

The change is that if you used to cast between shared pointers of 
*ChSharedPtr* type, now you will need to add  "mypointer.
*DynamicCastTo<...>()*".

Background

Previously, casting between ChSharedPtr shared pointers was too 'liberal', 
in the sense that it also allowed casting bwtween unrelated pointer types.
Not only this was inconsistent with the way that C++handles normal 
pointers, but also this left room to programmer mistakes.

Solution

In the new ChSharedPtr it happens that:
- casting between shared pointers is automatic if upcasting from a 
specialized class to a parent class, or between same classes, as in c++ 
pointers; in this case your code does not need any changes.
- casting between shared pointers in downcasting from a base class to a 
specialized class now explicitly *requires a dynamic casting*, otherwise 
you get a compiler error.
- casting between unrelated pointers will generate a compiler error at 
compile time.

The dynamic casting can be obtained by using the new   DynamicCastTo<>()  
function, or by using the new    dynamic_casting_chshared<>(...)   method
symbol: Changes in the shared pointer API.

text:
The dynamic casting can be obtained by using the new   DynamicCastTo<>()  
function, or by using the new    dynamic_casting_chshared<>(...)   method 
that is very similar to c++ dynamic_casting.
This means that in this commit we had to change many parts of the code 
where a base shared pointer was previously cast to specialized classes by 
doing simply

   ChSharedPtr<MySpecialClass>myspecialized = mybase;

into the new:
   ChSharedPtr<MySpecialClass>myspecialized = 
mybase.DynamicCastTo<MySpecialClass>();

Note that this requires more typing, but it is less prone to 
misunderstandings than the previous approach.

Please look at the improved demo_sharedptr.cpp.
Few examples: suppose that we have three classes, and two of them are 
inherited as ccTestB is child of ccTestA:

  ccTestA
     ccTestB

  ccTestC

This said: look at the example code:

....

        ChSmartPtr<ccTestA> pA(new ccTestA);

From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Fri, 12 Feb 2021 15:44:24 +0100

Dear Mingwu,

some hints here: I would split the problem in two parts: 1) computing 
FEA internal forces , 2) assigning a prescribed displacement

*1) computing FEA internal forces*

There are various options.
The most immediate is calling 
ChSystem::LoadResidual_F(ChVectorDynamic<>& R, const double c) with c=1, as

mysystem->LoadResidual_F(R, 1.0);

Keep in mind, your R vector must be sized as the n. of variables, ex. 
use mysystem->GetNcoords_v() to get this number in advance.
The issue with this method is that it stores _all_ forces in R, both 
external and internal. If you have no gravity, no loads, etc. etc., then 
it could be fine anyway.

Otherwise, you could call ChMesh::IntLoadResidual_F(const unsigned int 
off, ChVectorDynamic<>& R, const double c) with c=1, and with the proper 
offset, where offset is 0 if the mesh is the only thing you added to the 
system, otherwise -for example- if you added two bodies and a mesh to 
the system, offset is 6+6=12, etc.

This IntLoadResidual_F is a low level function, that stores in R only 
the internal loads of the finite elements added to mesh, at current 
state, so external loads are not stored in R.

Also note: set R to zero before calling LoadResidual_F because these 
"Load..." functions do a += operation, they are incremental.

*2) assigning a prescribed displacement*

This is not so obvious: in Chrono there are corotational FE and other 
types of FE, so "displacement" can have different meanings (local,
symbol:
Re: [chrono] evaluation of internal force with known displacement
 field (FEA)

text:
This is not so obvious: in Chrono there are corotational FE and other 
types of FE, so "displacement" can have different meanings (local, 
total, etc.), but I am sure you can do whatever you need by using the 
two following functions, that allows you to /set /the system in a 
configuration state, or to /get /the current state (you can get the 
state, increment the DOF you want, store it again, call 
IntLoadResidual_F(), etc.)

ChSystem::StateGather(ChState& x, ChStateDelta& v, double& T) here 
only the x part is relevant to you - positions and rotations, v contains 
speeds, T is time

ChSystem::StateScatter(const ChState& x, const ChStateDelta& v, const 
double T, bool full_update)

Note, if you need to increment a state x by some dv, instead of doing 
xnew=x+dv, rather use

ChSystem::StateIncrementX(....)

because it is the most general way that accounts also for the cases 
where the size of x is different from size of dv because  x contains 
rotations in SO3 as quaternions (4 scalars) whereas dv contains rotation 
vectors or other so(3) Lie algebra stuff (3 scalars).

regards

Alessandro Tasora

Hi Liam,

We see your simulation crashed at the first step, which shows problems with 
the initial setup. 

In your script, you didn't scale the clump info in the 3_clump.csv file, 
and left a note saying there's no need. Did you modify the file or is it 
still the same file bundled with DEM-Engine? If it's the same, then the 
clump has a size ≈ 2, as large as your simulation domain. This can explain 
the error you had, since if 70000 such particles overlap together, no 
matter how you divide the domain, a bin will intersect with most of them.

In the picture you did not render the particles, but why? You need to 
visualize them to understand the problem.

About the utility that prevents particles from spawning in the mesh, I 
think it's a nice-to-have and won't be too difficult to implement, but it 
is currently not our priority to make it a part of the package. You could 
easily write it yourself using C++ or Python though. DEM-Engine has support 
for smartly disabling these particles before the simulation starts, but 
it's an advanced usage. For now I suggest sampling the particles at safe 
locations and then letting them settle.

Thank you,
Ruochun

Hi Bradley,

As far as I can tell the beam element implemented in Chrono in the header
file ChElementBeamEuler.h uses displacements and linearized angles as
coordinates. This allows the finite element to describe longitudinal
(axial) strain [sect_ek(0)], shear strains about the two axes of the cross
section [sect_ek(1)] and [sect_ek(2)], torsional deformation [sect_ek(3)],
and bending strain (curvature) about the two axes of the cross section [
sect_ek(4) ] and [sect_ek(5) ]. Those axial, torsional, bending, and shear
strains are used below, in the same file, to define the forces acting on
the beam cross section (as Force.x, Force.y, Force.z., MTorque.x,
MTorque.y, and MTorque.z). Note that this element uses a local frame
attached to each element to describe large rotations, so you may need to
use what is described below in the same file as " // Generic computation,
by rotating and translating the constitutive // matrix of the beam:".

Thanks,

Antonio

Hi Bradley,

The formulation of Euler-Bernoulli beams is derived in terms of axial and 
bending strains/stresses, so usually there are no full stress tensors 
involved -which is more related to the geometry of three-dimensional 
solids. To plot or evaluate axial and bending strains you can use the 
method EvaluateSectionStrain of the ANCF beams, for example. If you are 
interested in stresses, you only have multiply the axial strain by the 
modulus of elasticity (E) and the bending strain, calculated in StrainV.y, 
by E*I, where I is the second moment of area. This must define the state of 
stress of the Euler-Bernoulli finite elements as implemented in Chrono. 

Regards,

Antonio

(1) LONGER ANSWER: no matter what OS you are on, the executable must be 
able to find the libraries (easy truth).
Here there is a little difference between Linux|MacOS and Windows.
In Windows you must:
- tell the linker where to find the static library that contains the 
symbols that you will LATER find in the relative shared library. These 
static libraries shouldn't have to be in the envvars, but they have to be 
provided at the linking line.
- tell the executable where the shared libraries. These are not provided at 
linking line, but they have to be set in the envvars.
In MacOS you do not have such difference: the libraries that you link to at 
compile-time are the same libraries that you use at run-time.
So, what you provide at linking line, at what you have to set in the 
envvars, is the same stuff!

*LONGER EXPLANATION*: MKL offers different ways to link their library 
<https://software.intel.com/en-us/articles/a-new-linking-model-single-dynamic-library-mkl_rt-since-intel-mkl-103>. 
In any case you should specify: the Interface Layer (so LP64, ILP64, IA32, 
ecc...), the Threading Layer (sequential, intel, PGI, tbb, etc...) and the 
Computational Layer (_core_, etc...).
The fastest and optimized way is to link always to the same libraries 
(namely *mkl_rt* and* libiomp5md*) and then to choose the Interface and 
Threading layer through Environmental Variables (point 3), so that you do 
not have to link specifically to mkl_intel_lp64, etc...
The Intel installer leaves you all the freedom and flexibility to do 
whatever you would like, so it doesn't set any of these variables, leaving 
this undesirable task to the user.
Actually you will find, in the MKL help, a lot of suggestions to use the MKL 
Link Line Advisor 
<https://software.intel.com/en-us/articles/intel-mkl-link-line-advisor>, 
that should assist you through the process. It just says the same things 
that I summarized above, but if you need to customize the options here is 
the best place to look at.

simulation crashes due to the subsequent large velocity. If your 
simulations did crash exactly after frame 10 and frame 60, then since they 
should be the frames right after a new batch of particles are added into 
the simulation, this appears to be more likely.

There are a few things you can do:
1. Increase the initial separation in the sampler. In line 103, you can 
change the separation to be something like 2.5*scales.at(0). This reduces 
the risk of initial penetration. Although I would indeed be a bit surprised 
that this consistently happens in your simulations twice.
2. Relax the physics as suggested. You can change the CoR of all the 
materials to something like 0.1. It increases the damping and should not 
change the final settling result, just makes the contact easier to 
calculate. Again, I feel doubt since it never happens to me.
3. The hanging problem could also be related to large velocities, or not 
enough memory. If everything in the simulation is moving large velocity 
(meaning the simulation probably already diverges), then a lot of false 
positive contacts could be detected and the long contact array could eat 
all the memory. This is by far the most common cause of hanging. I don't

Hi Declan,

I am not perfectly clear on what you mean by being “able to call on the point vA”, but you cannot have OnReportContact return it.  That method is called internally by ReportAllContacts and must return ‘true’ or ‘false’, informing the caller (ReportAllContacts) to continue processing the next contact or stop processing, respectively.

If you want to extract all vA points in a list, you can do something like:

class MyReportContactCallback(chrono.ReportContactCallback):
    def __init__(self):
        chrono.ReportContactCallback.__init__(self)
        self.points = []
    def OnReportContact(self,vA,vB,cA,dist,rad,force,torque,modA,modB):
        self.points.append(vA)
        return True        # return False to stop reporting contacts
    def ResetList(self):
        self.points = []
    def GetList(self):
        return self.points

my_rep = MyReportContactCallback()

while (my_system.GetChTime() < 1.2) :
    my_system.DoStepDynamics(0.01)

    my_rep.ResetList()
    my_system.GetContactContainer().ReportAllContacts(my_rep)
    crt_list = my_rep.GetList()
    print('time=', my_system.GetChTime(), ' num. contacts=', my_system.GetContactContainer().GetNcontacts())
    print(*crt_list, sep='\n')

Is this what you need?
--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Narrowphase Contact History
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 3 May 2017 12:31:50 +0200

In Chrono::Parallel, while using Bullet is an experimental option, the 
main algorithm for narrow-phase collision of convex shapes is MPR 
(Minkovski Portal Refinement), see XenoCollide 
(http://xenocollide.snethen.com/).

Like GJK, this generic algorithm also provides a single collision point 
for a pair of shapes and we do not have any feature in place to try to 
approximate the contact set like Bullet does.   As such, stacking and 
similar problems are indeed problematic.

Having said that, for certain pairs of simple contact shapes, the 
Chrono::Parallel narrow-phase collision system also implements 
analytical methods which do provide an appropriate number of contact 
points (potentially more than one).  In fact, the default narrow-phase 
mode in Chrono::Parallel (NARROWPHASE_HYBRID_MPR) always first looks for 
an analytical method for each given pair of shapes and, if none is 
available, falls back onto MPR.

Unfortunately, we do not have yet a box-box analytical collision 
function.  Implementing that has been on my TODO list for a while now.  
When available, that method will generate up to 8 contact points between 
two colliding boxes (depending on the current configuration).

On final note: for granular dynamics, Chrono::Parallel uses multi-core 
(through OpenMP) and not GPU.

Best,
--Radu

to this later. That is when you have further questions.

3. It's possible. To answer your question, *ChGranularChronoTriMeshAPI *
inherits *ChGranularSMC_API* , so it basically does everything 
*ChGranularSMC_API*  does and a bit more. For the initialization, *ChGranularChronoTriMeshAPI

*meshSoup* as well. For *setElemsPositions*, I'm also a bit surprised it is

*ChGranularSMC_API::setElemsPositions*, then you should be able to set 
velocity when using *ChGranularChronoTriMeshAPI*. After all, it's just a 
wrapper and it calls *setParticlePositions*, and *setParticlePositions* can 
take velocity info and defaults velocity to 0 if not given.

text:
Subject: RE: [chrono] Creating hollow closed box in Multicore
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 13 Jul 2024 05:52:53 +0000

Gianni,

If you are interested in collisions of your internal components with the inside of the box, then utils::CreateBoxContainer<https://api.projectchrono.org/group__chrono__utils.html#ga5a4915221a0bb565bf7bf06239545c57> allows creating a closed box (i.e. with 6 walls); see its last argument (optional, default: false).  No need to create a separate body for the “lid” and connect it through a weld joint (which would only add additional states and constraints).

Otherwise, the easiest way is to simply create one solid box and ignore collisions with any of the internal components by using collision families (set the box in one collision family and all internal components in a different one, then disable any collisions between the two families). See ChCollisionModel::SetFamily<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_collision_model.html#ab591335fd235fb5590e7204f4b7ad5bf> and ChCollisionModel::DisallowCollisionWith<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_collision_model.html#a93ece48505bc18dce4fb53645f61b2bb>.

Of course, all of this assumes your internal components carry collision geometry. Otherwise, you do not need to do anything special.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Maybe some bug in SCM deformable terrain
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 17 Apr 2019 13:35:03 +0000

Hi Jiaxi Liu,

Early on when I started Chrono::Vehicle, we decided that vehicle systems will follow a particular frame convention. The one we selected is the ISO vehicle frame (Z up, X forward, Y to the left).  This is unlike the rest of Chrono which does not have any particular frame convention (except that it's easier to work with Y up when using the Irrlicht run-time visualization).
Unfortunately, the SCM terrain was implemented with Y up by default (changing this default to be Z up, consistent with everything else in Chrono::Vehicle, is on my todo list).  This is why, in all Chrono::Vehicle demos that use the SCM terrain type (e.g., demo_VEH_DefSoil) you will see a call like
   terrainD->SetPlane(ChCoordsys<>(VNULL, Q_from_AngX(CH_C_PI_2)));
When I added the moving-patch feature, knowing that I will eventually switch the default in SCM to be Z up, I already made that assumption (and that is currently hard-coded).

Having said that, when I make the switch to Z up in SCM terrain, I will look into making the moving patch feature more flexible so that it will take into account the user-selected orientation of the "SCM reference plane".   Until then, it shouldn't be too difficult for you to locally modify the code to change to moving patch feature to work with Y up.  By the way, is there a particular reason why you cannot use the Chrono::Vehicle frame convention? Are you usin the SCM terrain outside Chrono::Vehicle?

Finally, you are correct: the call to SetupAuxData is missing in that particular overload of Initialize.  I will push a fix shortly.

Hi Michael,

No, that is the mass and inertia of the solid volume bounded by the mesh

ChTriangleMeshConnected::ComputeMassProperties(), is a direct 
implementation of David Eberly's approach, described at 
https://www.geometrictools.com/Documentation/PolyhedralMassProperties.pdf. 
It is assumed that the triangle mesh is closed and has no holes.

Den torsdag den 28. maj 2015 kl. 19.25.47 UTC+2 skrev Alessandro Tasora:
Dear Morten, for simulations with rigid contacts I suggest you to use

mphysicalSystem.SetLcpSolverType(ChSystem::LCP_ITERATIVE_BARZILAIBORWEIN);

or the ChSystem::LCP_ITERATIVE_APGD  solver (they have similar convergence properties).
Raise their iteration count using

mphysicalSystem.SetIterLCPmaxItersSpeed(100);

or higher.

Also, for the integrator, leave the Anitescu timestepper for the moment. All others (in the 'develop' branch of the GIT) are under testing and will be available in future (they do not work yet with hard contacts for the moment).

Note, lower timestep as usual means more precise results (the nice news is that the LCP solver converges usually faster when the integrator uses small timesteps)

best regards

Alessandro

All others (in the 'develop' branch of the GIT) are under testing and 
will be available in future (they do not work yet with hard contacts for 
the moment).

Note, lower timestep as usual means more precise results (the nice news 
is that the LCP solver converges usually faster when the integrator uses 
small timesteps)

Deniz,

First of all, you are correct, you must create and attach a collision shape to the FEA mesh.  A surface mesh is likely the appropriate choice (the other option is a node cloud, but that will let objects smaller than the mesh size fall through).  I should maybe modify the FEADeformableTerrain to create this automatically, but as I mentioned in previous messages, you are the only one who is even considering using this type of deformable terrain model.

You are not doing anything wrong.  You can certainly share the same contact material between the vehicle wheels and the terrain mesh.  But you can also create a different contact material for each.  Just keep in mind that, at any given identified collision pair, the contact forces are resolved using a so-called “composite material” whose properties are obtained using the current composition rules.  These all have defaults (specific to each material property); for example, by default the coefficient of friction of a composite material is set as the minimum of the coefficients of friction of the two interacting materials.  See the default implementation of ChMaterialCompositionStrategy<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/0da8189dd2df13c7c8e6af9c16536fc851816e12/src/chrono/physics/ChMaterialSurface.h#L95>.  One or more of these rules can be overridden by the user by providing your own derived class; see ChSystem:: SetMaterialCompositionStrategy<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_system.html#a57543bef675c62f6fd7164bf7379fb8b>.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Using different absolute reference coordinate system in
 extension software
From: Radu Serban
Date: Fri, 02 Jun 2017 10:29:57 +0200

Hi Francois,

This is actually a non-issue.   Chrono *does not* have any implied 
reference frame!

It is true that the default for the gravity vector is to have it acting 
along the negative Y direction, but the reason for that is just that 
most demos use the Irrlicht run-time visualization system which itself 
uses a coordinate system with Y up.   (As a separate note, note that 
Irrlicht uses left-handed frames, while Chrono uses right-handed 
frames;  as such, in all Irrlicht-based demos, things are mirrored 
left/right).

In any case, the *only* thing you have to do is to set the gravity 
vector along whatever direction you want, using ChSystem::Set_G_acc().  
For example:
my_system.Set_G_acc(ChVector<>(0, 0, -9.81));

By the way, if you look at the implementation of the Chrono::Vehicle 
module (in src/chrono_vehicle), you will notice that the assumption 
there is that all vehicle systems follow the ISO convention (meaning a 
reference frame with Z up and X forward, implying Y to the left).   To 
deal with the Irrlicht reference frame, we have a customized class for 
Irrlicht visualization of vehicle systems which forces the Irrlicht 
camera to use Z up (of course, there's still nothing we can do about the 
left-handedness of the Irrlicht frames).

Hope that this clarifies things.

Best,
--Radu

decide how the step size should change if you change the properties. For

required step size. That's how I typically do it.

Hi Yves,

This is expected. The step sizes 1e-4, 5e-5, and 3e-5 you used gave 
unphysical responses since they were not fine enough to capture the 
collision. Past those, it becomes better. I'd like to note that the test 
scenario is challenging to begin with, since the ball impacts with a high 
velocity and the wall stiffness is very high (2.5e11 Pa), making the 
contact difficult to resolve. I am not surprised at all that it requires a 
step size as small as 1e-5s. You should try smaller step sizes too, and 
they should converge to a specific bouncing pattern, and this is perhaps 
the way to find an appropriate step size to use (the largest one that gives 
this "converged" bouncing).

In reality, the vast majority of DEM simulations use artificially reduced 
stiffness to relax the physics, with empirically decided step sizes. The 
rule is trying to ensure that the contact events are resolved with no less 
than 4 time steps (but more is even better), but it's not always necessary 
to do separate tests to find that out. Reasonable bulk metrics like total 
energy or max velocity are sometimes enough of an indicator of good 
simulations, plus many simulations have main physics driven by prolonged 
contacts like grinding rather than "hard" collisions, making resolving 
"worst" contacts like the collisions that happen only in parts of the 
simulation not a big concern.

for on-fly step size change, should the physics change significantly at

Subject: Re: [chrono] Problem about cohesion settings
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 3 May 2017 13:49:45 +0200

Hi Scott,

(Note that I am using new names that were changed just earlier today -- 
see my post to the mailing list for a couple of hours ago.)

The short answer is yes, you can change the contact material properties 
for any body in your system at any time during the simulation (that is 
within your simulation loop, between successive integration steps).  For 
that, you could use something like:

  * body->GetMaterialSurfaceNSC()->SetCohesion  for an NSC system
    (non-smooth contact, previously named as "DVI")
  * body->GetMaterialSurfaceSMC()->SetAdhesion for an SMC system (smooth
    or penalty-based contact, previously named as "DEM")

There's unfortunately a discrepancy in the names of the methods used to 
deal with this material property that I plan on fixing soon.

So you could loop over all bodies in the system and set their 
adhesion(cohesion) to 0.   But this means that there would be no such 
cohesive force between any two shapes in your system from that point on 
(note that the cohesion property of a "composite" material corresponding 
to a pair of contacting shapes is obtained as the minimum of the 
cohesion values from each shape).

Now, I am not sure what exactly you want to do, but I suspect you want 
to be able to actually control adhesion between two "classes" of 
bodies.  This is simpler or a bit trickier, depending on how you set up 
your simulation.   Here are some thoughts:

 1. In sequential Chrono, you could provide a callback of type
    callbackChContactContainer::AddContactCallback which would allow you
symbol: Re: [chrono] Problem about cohesion settings

text:
1. In sequential Chrono, you could provide a callback of type
    callbackChContactContainer::AddContactCallback which would allow you
    to change "composite" material properties.  If provided, this
    callback is invoked every time a new contact is created. You would
    have to use information available in the first argument (of type
    collision::ChCollisionInfo) of the virtual method OnAddContact which
    you would have to implement.   See the two new demos I added
    recently: demo_IRR_callbackNSC and demo_IRR_callbackSMC as a start. 
    You'll also need to figure out a mechanism (based on simulation time
    or some other flag) to figure out when to actually modify the
    composite material properties.

 2. The callback above is ignored in Chrono::Parallel.  A potential
    solution in that case (which, by the way, would work with a
    sequential Chrono system as well) is to tag somehow the bodies so
    that you can differentiate them.   You can use the optional
    "identifier" which you can set on any body (using
    ChObj::SetIDentifier) and make sure you give them your unique
    values.  Then, in a loop over all bodies, you selectively change the
    cohesion properties (use ChObj::GetIDentifier).  For this, keep in
    mind that the cohesion value for a "composite" material is obtained
    as the minimum of the values from the two contacting shapes.

 3. Finally, if you are using the chrono::utils::Generator class to
    create your granular material, you are a little bit more limited in
    what you can do, but a solution similar to the one in #2 above can
symbol: Re: [chrono] Problem about cohesion settings

text:
3. Finally, if you are using the chrono::utils::Generator class to
    create your granular material, you are a little bit more limited in
    what you can do, but a solution similar to the one in #2 above can
    make use of the function Generator::setBodyIdentifier.   This
    function allows you to specify the identifier of the first body
    created by that generator (all other bodies it creates will have
    successively increasing identifiers).  With this, you can create
    each block of bodies with a known range of identifiers.  As such,
    whenever you need to, you can again loop over all bodies and figure
    out those for which you want to adjust contact material properties.

I hope that this helps.  Note however, that I didn't test any of the 
above.  So please let me know if/how this works.

Best,
Radu

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] Problem about cohesion settings
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sat, 22 Apr 2017 11:10:39 +0200

Hi Scott,

I assume your question is about the gray and orange balls still clinging 
to each other at the end.

Currently, what you try to do is not possible.  The reason for this is 
that cohesion and adhesion are treated identically in Chrono.  More 
precisely, the adhesion/cohesion coefficient for the "composite" 
material used for the interaction of a pair of contact shapes is 
obtained by taking the minimum of the corresponding coefficients 
specified for each shape.

In the case of the Chrono demo you mention, the desired effect is 
obtained by using a non-zero coefficient for the particles in the 
aggregate balls, but a zero coefficient for the fixed box obstacle.  As 
such, we can have cohesion within the aggregate balls, but no adhesion 
between the aggregates and the box.

In your case however, you need non-zero cohesion values for the 
materials used for both types of balls (gray and orange).  As such, you 
end up also having adhesion between the two different materials (see 
also my comment at the end).

I am actually planning on adding a feature in Chrono to allow users to 
overwrite the default combination laws for calculating properties of 
these "composite" materials.  Once available, this new feature should

Bent – sorry for the (very) late reply. I can confirm that there is an issue with collision detection of non-convex trimeshes.  Looking at the results, I suspect a bug in edge-edge collision. But I did not write this part of the code and have never looked at it very closely.  The reason things appear to work fine for the original track-shoe meshes in demo_MBS_collision_trimesh<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/main/src/demos/mbs/demo_MBS_collision_trimesh.cpp> is that these are relatively fine meshes and so collision pairs get generated between many features of these meshes.  When switching to box meshes, any issue in a particular type of pairwise feature interaction will result in obvious errors. By the way, I pushed a modification of that demo that allows switching between the two types of meshes and control other setting s to help identify such problems.  If I get some time, I will chase down this bug; or hopefully someone else gets to it before me.

Antoine – having said all that, for your particular problem with gears, I would still try to leverage collision between convex shapes as that is a much more robust algorithm.  Instead of providing the entire gear mesh as one collision shape for a gear body, it would be much better (for robustness, but also computational efficiency) to create a model for the collision shape of a single tooth (that is a convex mesh) and then replicate that as many times as necessary in the collision model associated with the gear body.  Look at the function CreateLuggedGeometry() in demo_VEH_SCMTerrain_WheeledVehicle<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/main/src/demos/vehicle/terrain/demo_VEH_SCMTerrain_WheeledVehicle.cpp> for an example of generating a (non-convex) collision model by assembling multiple instances of the same (convex) mesh and using convex hull collision shapes for each of these parts.

We're looking at a few thousand sand grains.  The particle shapes, however, are complex in that they are derived from microCT scans of natural grains. The shapes are defined using triangular surface meshes.  We also have convex hulls for them that we've made using HACD.

The reason why we are looking for a solution involving periodic boundaries is that the depositional pack that we would create with Chrono would serve as input for other models of mechanical deformation, "pressure solution", and crystal growth that work best with periodic boundaries.

Additionally, for problems like this we should be able to get a more realistic packing geometry using many fewer grains if we use periodic lateral boundaries compared to the case where we use a container with rigid lateral bounds.  That should speed things up quite a bit for simple grain drop simulations while also providing a better basis simulating depositional fabrics for cases where the grains are moving laterally from wind or water currents.

--Rob

Subject: Re: [chrono] Issue adding tiled RigidTerrain
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 30 Jan 2019 07:45:46 +0000

Huck,

This is not correct C++ syntax (which doesn't support named parameters).  Instead you should use something like:

auto patch = terrain.AddPatch(ChCoordsys<>(ChVector<>(terrainPosition[1], terrainPosition[2], terrainPosition[3]), QUNIT),
                              ChVector<>(terrainLength, terrainWidth, 10),
                              true, 1, true);

(search online for more information on "C++ optional arguments)

In case you want larger tiles (which you probably do if your terrain patch dimensions are large, else you'd get unnecessarily many contact shapes), you would do something like:

auto patch = terrain.AddPatch(ChCoordsys<>(ChVector<>(terrainPosition[1], terrainPosition[2], terrainPosition[3]), QUNIT),
                              ChVector<>(terrainLength, terrainWidth, 10),
                              true, 20, true);
or
auto patch = terrain.AddPatch(ChCoordsys<>(ChVector<>(terrainPosition[1], terrainPosition[2], terrainPosition[3]), QUNIT),
                             ChVector<>(terrainLength, terrainWidth, 10),
                             true, 20);

Note above that you do not have to explicitly specify optional arguments at the end of the list if you are fine with their default values (in this case, the last argument 'visualization' has a default value of true).  This is also why your code without tiling worked fine as you coded it;  the last 3 (optional) arguments take their default values: false for 'tiled', 1 for 'max_tile_size' (ignored anyway because no tiling), and true for 'visualization'.

Andrea,
The current SPH solver in Chrono::FSI is only for incompressible fluids. There’s no plan to add support for compressible fluids. For that, your best bet is to co-simulate with some other specialized solver (this is routinely done by people in the wind energy industry, several of whom use Chrono for modeling wind turbines).
--Radu

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] About adding constraints
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 24 Jun 2020 09:56:20 +0200

Juntao He,

For what you need, you should only use a prismatic joint 
(ChLinkLockPrismatic). That allows a single degree of freedom, a 
translation along the Z axis of the joint reference frame (which you can 
orient however you need to match the direction you're interested in). 
This also means that a prismatic joint already "locks" the (relative) 
orientation of the connected bodies, so you do not need to add any 
additional constraints (such as a ChLinkLockAlign).

If you also want to control the displacement along the direction of the 
translational DOF, instead of using a ChLinkLockPrismatic, you may want 
to consider using a ChLinkMotorLinear*** with a "PRISMATIC" guide 
constraint. There are different flavors of those motors which allow you 
to specify a time function for displacement, velocity, or force along 
that direction. (Note that there is an inconsistency in Chrono, which 
we should probably fix at some point, in that the translation direction 
for a ChLinkMotorLinear is along the X axis of the joint frame).

--Radu

From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 3 Apr 2018 23:40:37 +0200

Martin,

A couple of weeks ago I pushed a change that should help with this issue 
(commit ab851e11c on March 3). If you could update to the latest 
version in the 'develop' branch, what you will want to do is mark all 
ChTriangleMeshShape visualization assets as 'static' (i.e. as rigid, 
non-deformable trimeshes) by calling the method SetStatic(true). This 
will skip an expensive update at every single step. The reason I didn't 
make this the default was for backward compatibility with existing user 
code.

The reason why disabling rendering in the simulation loop did not have 
any effect is that this visualization asset update occurs anyway, as 
part of the underlying system update.

Please let me know if this helps.
--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] Re: URDF support
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 21 Feb 2023 13:16:15 +0000

As Luning mentioned, there is currently no support for reading a model specified through a URDF file. Not because Chrono uses an absolute coordinate formulation, as that is irrelevant here. Having said that, I intend to add this capability in the near future.

As for your question regarding flexible body dynamics, FFRF is not one of the formulations implemented in Chrono. We support ANCF and co-rotational.

--Radu

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: local acceleration
From: Radu Serban
Date: Sun, 26 May 2019 16:12:25 +0000

Hi Zamir,

The functions you are attempting to use deal with the case where the point on body also has relative motion to the body frame; i.e. it is not fixed in the body frame.
In particular, when you do something like:
  auto acc = body->PointAccelerationParentToLocal(body->GetPos(), body->GetPos_dt(), body->GetPos_dtdt());
you should indeed get (0,0,0) indicating that the point you specified (in this case the body center of mass) has 0 acceleration *with respect to the body frame*.

By the way, I realize that these functions have somewhat confusing names and are not all that well documented -- we will have to work on fixing that.

If I understand correctly what you are after, all you need to do is take the body acceleration expressed in the global frame (as reported by ChBody::GetPos_dtdt) and express it in the body local frame.  You can do this using, for example:
  auto acc_local = body->TransformDirectionParentToLocal(my_body->GetPos_dtdt());
This will give you the acceleration of the body origin (its center of mass) expressed in the (centroidal) body frame.

If you want to find the acceleration of some point *fixed* in the body frame, you could use something like:
  auto acc_global = body->PointAccelerationLocalToParent(local_point);
  auto acc_local = body->TransformDirectionParentToLocal(acc_global);
The first line will give you the acceleration of the body-fixed point, expressed in the global frame; the second one will express that acceleration in the (centroidal) body frame.

--Radu

  1.  Indicate what *version* of Chrono you are using? There have been recent changes to the project configuration script.  Tell us the commit you are at.  Ideally, pull the very latest code in the main branch, so that we’re all looking at the same code.

Hi Alvaro,


  1.  That is by design.  It is the user’s responsibility to ensure that dependency DLLs are found (either by adding their location to the path environment variable or else by manually copying them next to their executables).  We decided that a Chrono installation should not bundle all dependency DLLs, first because some dependency libraries (unlike Irrlicht) come with very many DLLs and second because this can lead to issues with existing local installations of those libraries.

  2.  I cannot reproduce this issue. Executables of the demos install fine in all my tests.  You may want to double check that building demos is enabled when you configure Chrono or for any other changes you may have made locally.

Subject: Re: [chrono] Re: Mesh import into Parallel
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 1 Feb 2017 09:04:04 +0100

Jack,

First of all, you should reconsider your model.  Do you really need to 
use a contact mesh with 11574 triangles for an object that is about 7cm 
x 5cm x 9cm?  What kind of interactions do you hope to capture?  We 
always recommended to use simplified contact representations, either 
composed of primitive shapes (depending on what exactly you want to 
capture, your mesh can be easily covered fairly closely with a couple 
dozen boxes) or else using a coarser mesh.  Moreover, in the latter 
case, it is much more efficient to use a convex decomposition of the 
contact mesh (i.e., split the mesh into the union of convex hulls);  for 
a contact trimesh, each triangle represents a contact shape, while each 
convex hull is treated as a single contact shape.

Having said that, I found and fixed an issue in the Chrono::Parallel 
broad-phase collision detection which resulted in the crash you 
reported.  I pushed the fix to the 'develop' branch of the Chrono

Hi David,

This issue is a weakness in the default assumption we made that a sphere 
can have at most 12 contacts. This assumption is made to save GPU memory 
and to help identify some large-penetration problems in simulation which is 
typical with insufficient time step size. This assumption is fine with 
near-rigid spherical contacts, but problematic when meshes are involved 
(each mesh facet in contact with a sphere eats up one slot as well). 
Imagine a sphere sitting on the tip of a needle made of mesh, it could have 
contacts with tens of mesh facets, and we haven't counted the sphere 
neighbors it can potentially have.

The fix is easy, please go to the file *ChGpuDefines.h* (in 
chrono\src\chrono_gpu), and replace
*#define MAX_SPHERES_TOUCHED_BY_SPHERE 12*
by
*#define MAX_SPHERES_TOUCHED_BY_SPHERE 20*
or some even larger number if you need it. Rebuild it and your script 
should run fine. Note the error messages are hard-coded to say 12 is not 
enough if  *MAX_SPHERES_TOUCHED_BY_SPHERE* is exceeded, so if 20 is not 
enough and you need even more, just change it and do not let the error 
messages confuse you.

Another thing is that it is better to use meshes with relatively uniform 
triangle sizes. I attached a rebuilt mesh based on your original one. It's 
optional and does not seem to affect this simulation, but it's a good 
practice.

To answer your other questions: Unfortunately C::GPU does not currently 
have an *efficient* way of streaming particles into the system. The method

text:
To answer your other questions: Unfortunately C::GPU does not currently 
have an *efficient* way of streaming particles into the system. The method 
you are using (re-initialization) is probably what I would do too if I have 
to. With a problem size similar to yours, it should be fine. And C::GPU 
does not have an official API that enforces manual particle position 
changes. However this should be fairly straightforward to implement. The 
naive approach is of course, do it on the host side with a for loop. If you 
care about efficiency, then we should instead add one custom GPU kernel 
call at the end of each iteration, that scans the z coordinates of all 
particles, and add an offset to them if they are below a certain value. It 
would be nice if you can tailor it to your needs, but if you need help 
implementing this custom kernel you can let us know (it may be good to add 
it as a permanent feature).

Lastly, I don't know if you are interested or not but in the new generation 
of DEM simulator that we are currently developing, apart from supporting 
non-trivial particle geometries, there will be *efficient* ways to do both 
things (sleeper and active entities; periodic boundary with no extra cost). 
It is not out yet, however.

Thank you,
Ruochun

If Simplex works you probably have a solver convergence problem.  You 
should set the iteration to values higher than the default ones as you need 
more iterations for the assembly and LCP solvers to converge.  Also try 
reducing your time step and set the number of parallel threads to one.

 See the functions ChSystem::DoStaticNonlinear(...)  and DoStaticRelaxing

they don't converge, there is something wrong with the way you setup the 
system.

text:
Subject: Re: Forced motion of a ChBody and a failing link
From: Harry Tobin
Date: Tue, 10 Feb 2015 13:25:36 -0800 (PST)

It looks like you are creating an assembly of constrained bodies.  Try 
increasing the 
number of outer iterations to satisfy the constraints using the ChSystem::
SetMaxiter(int m_maxiter);
function (default is 6) Also see ChSystem::SetIterLCPmaxItersStab and other 
settings in the ChSystem class for adjusting the number of iterations and 
tolerances for the constraint solver.  

Also, consider creating the link explicitly using ChMarkers:
ChSharedPtr<ChMarker> marker1=ChSharedPtr<ChMarker>(new ChMarker);
body1->AddMarker(marker1);
marker1->Impose_Abs_Coord(c_sys1);/// a coordinate system 
similarly for body2 add marker2.

and create the link explicitly using ChLinkMarkers::ReferenceMarkers(...).  
Then use my_link->ReferenceMarkers(marker1.get_ptr(),marker2.get_ptr()); 
to add them to the link.

Remember that you must create a new marker for the body each time you add 
it to a link. 
I have found the Initialize(...) function to be unreliable for creating 
multiple constrains on bodies, although internally, it is pretty similar to 
the code above.


I hope this helps.

Subject: RE: [chrono] pychrono and multicore support
From: Radu Serban
Date: Wed, 26 Mar 2025 19:14:33 +0000

Hi Sean,

Performance of code based on PyChrono is only marginally (if at all) worse that that of code directly using the Chrono C++ libraries. PyChrono is just a set of SWIG-generated wrappers around the C++ Chrono code.

However, if you think that your code would benefit from using the Chrono::Multicore module (note that this is not a guarantee, as 300 particles is not all that many – you may want to provide some details on what geometry you use for these bodies), you will have to port your code to C++ because the Chrono::Multicore module is currently *not* SWIG-wrapped and as such not available through PyChrono.

Best,
Radu

Hi Mathias,

The most complete SMC model is implemented in the Chrono::Multicore module.  I never got around to bring up the corresponding SMC model in the core Chrono module to the same level (although that is on one of the many TODO lists I keep).
Compared to the Chrono core implementation (see the implementation in ChContactSMC.h<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/ca60083b2de78732f398adb895f1540ccfadd8b2/src/chrono/physics/ChContactSMC.h#L45>), the SMC contact model in Chrono::Multicore (see ChIterativeSolverMulticoreSMC.cpp<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/ca60083b2de78732f398adb895f1540ccfadd8b2/src/chrono_multicore/solver/ChIterativeSolverMulticoreSMC.cpp#L56>) has the following two main additional features:

  *   A multi-step tangential displacement model (see this paper<https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281538010_On_the_Importance_of_Displacement_History_in_Soft-Body_Contact_Models> for details on why that is important in SMC); and
  *   Rolling and spinning friction

With the above, the kind of simulations you are interested in will give the expect results. In fact, such behaviors are implemented and tested in a series of tests that are included in the Chrono distribution: see the unit tests for multicore SMC contact<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/tree/main/src/tests/unit_tests/smc_contact/multicore>.

Having said all of that, please note that the Chrono::Multicore module is currently *not* SWIG wrapped and as such not available through PyChrono.

Mathias – unfortunately, I do not have the time/expertise to take a deep dive in your post. But I’ll offer some quick suggestions, perhaps you’ll find them useful.

There are many ways to handle friction and contact in Chrono. Which one you should choose depends on what you want to simulate.

If things don’t pan out in PyChorno, you might want to look into the C++ solver, which is an overset of what you find in PyChrono. For all purposes, PyChrono makes library calls into Chrono.

Also, a recent frictional contact implementation that you can use is in Chrono DEM: https://github.com/projectchrono/DEM-Engine.
This is what you want to use if you are interested in large numbers of bodies mutually interacting. It has good penalty support for handling friction and contact.

Dan

Subject: Re: Simulating Superellipsoids in DEM Engine
From: Ruochun Zhang
Date: Sat, 8 Mar 2025 03:24:25 -0800 (PST)

There are quite a few demos that feature ellipsoidal shapes in DEM-Engine 
(Centrifuge, Plow, RotatingDrum...), which can be used as starting points. 
I'd suggest you try those out and see how ellipsoidal particles are defined 
in them via "clumping" together spheres of different sizes. Then you can 
tweak the sphere composition to make them look more like superellipsoids, 
like adding some outer-ring small spheres to account for the sharp edges.

This is probably the easiest. I do understand that sphere clump does not 
naturally extend to super-ellipsoidal shapes due to the fine features; this 
is not even fair for the sphere-clump approach as the tools that use 
functional shape representations favor superellipsoids exactly because they 
happen to be a clean mathematical. If you indeed need more accurate 
super-ellipsoidal shapes in DEM-E and you won't need a huge number of 
particles, then there are methods to systematically create clumps that 
represent a volumetric mesh, or even sphere-decompose methods that use a 
large number of spheres to represent a fine surface mesh, both of which can 
be used in conjunction with DEM-E. But we can discuss these advanced 
approaches if you are sure you need them.

Thank you,
Ruochun

Michael,

To clarify what Alessandro said, in order to have different colors for 
different visualization shapes attached to a given body, you need to use 
multiple "asset levels" and add a shape asset and a color asset to each 
one of them.
Look at demo_IRR_assets 
(https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/develop/src/demos/irrlicht/demo_IRR_assets.cpp) 
for an example of using asset levels (because this question was asked 
before, I just pushed an update to that demo to use different colors for 
shapes attached to the same body).

By the way, we will soon be working on a refactoring of the 
visualization asset system in Chrono and will also address this issue at 
that time.

--Radu

On 9/7/2020 8:13 AM, Alessandro Tasora wrote:

text:
Subject: Re: [chrono] About the color variable in ChVisualization class
From: Alessandro Tasora
Date: Mon, 7 Sep 2020 08:13:08 +0200

You are right.
The original method for setting colors is the ChColorAsset, and it is used
by Irrlicht. This has two benefits: it does not waste bytes of memory when
the color is not used (ex.in simulations of millions of objects) and it
spreads the information down the hierarchies of assets when using
ChAssetLevel groups. Anyway it taxes more coding so someone introduced the
more immediate SetColor method in the ChVisualization classes, and this led
to the unfortunate situation where we have two different ways for setting
colors.
Thanks
Alessandro Tasora

From: Radu Serban

Hi Alan,

Chrono data files are assumed to be specified relative to the location of the data directory in the build tree.  By default, it is assumed that the data directory is one level up from wherever the executables are created.

Chrono::Vehicle data files are assumed to be specified relative to the location of the data/vehicle directory in the build tree.  By default, it is assumed that the data directory is one level up from wherever the executables are created, so Chrono::Vehicle looks for its files in ../data/vehicle.

In Visual Studio, you will therefore need to set the properties of your project you are currently debugging (e.g., demo_VEH_HMMWV) so that the "Working Directory" is ${OutDir) and not $(ProjectDir).   You can find this setting under Properties->Debugging->Working Directory.

By the way, you can change the location of the data directory (default ../data/) for Chrono using the function SetChronoDataPath.
Similarly, you can change the location of the vehicle data directory (default ../data/vehicle/) for Chrono::Vehicle using the function vehicle::SetDataPath.

On a different note, I suggest you look into using the newer ChPac02 and ChPac89 tire models.  These models can be specified through JSON specification files (a couple of sample data files are provided under data/vehicle/...)

--Radu

Subject: RE: [chrono] Add ODE in project:chrono
From: Radu Serban
Date: Tue, 3 Sep 2024 16:21:17 +0000

Hi Stefan,

Look at ChExternalDynamics<https://api.projectchrono.org/classchrono_1_1_ch_external_dynamics.html>. I implemented that class precisely for this type of use. See demo_MBS_external_dynamics.cpp<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/blob/main/src/demos/mbs/demo_MBS_external_dynamics.cpp> for an example of using this mechanism to integrate the van der Pol ODE system.
Currently, ChExternalDynamics only supports 1st order ODEs which you would specify by providing a class derived from ChExternalDynamics and implementing the necessary virtual methods (to provide the RHS, initial conditions, and optionally the Jacobian).
In the near future, I intend to extend it to also support DAEs (index-3 to begin with).

The recent FMI module in Chrono also relies on this mechanism to importing a model exchange FMU (note that the FMI standard only supports model exchange FMUs with dynamics described by ODEs). See the fmi_modex<https://github.com/projectchrono/chrono/tree/main/src/demos/fmi/fmi_modex> demo for an illustration of building a model exchange FMU (also for the van der Pol problem) and integrating it within a Chrono system.

Best,
Radu
